122168.q: At which university did the plant ecologist Christian Körner teach as a professor for many years?
122168.e: Christian Körner headed plant ecology at the Botanical Institute of the University of Basel for decades.
122168.m: Christian Körner did research as a professor in Basel.

122169.q: Which standard work on the ecology of high mountain plants was written by Christian Körner?
122169.e: “Alpine Plant Life” sums up how plants function in high mountains and is a textbook used worldwide.
122169.m: Körner’s textbook is called “Alpine Plant Life”.

122170.q: According to Christian Körner, which factor mainly determines the position of the natural tree line worldwide?
a: The temperature during the growing season
122170.e: Körner showed that the tree line worldwide lies at similarly low temperatures during the growing season. Trees can then no longer build enough new tissue.
122170.m: The tree line is determined mainly by temperature.

122171.q: What was the crane in the forest at Hofstetten near Basel, where Körner's group did research, used for?
a: For adding CO2 to tree crowns
122171.e: With the Swiss Canopy Crane, extra CO2 was released into the crowns of tall trees. This made it possible to test whether a mature forest grows faster with more CO2.
122171.m: The Basel crane was used to study the effect of more CO2 on old trees.

122172.q: How does Christian Körner define the alpine zone in the same way everywhere in the world?
a: As the area above the natural tree line
As the area above 2000 m above sea level
As the area with snow in July
As the area above the snow line
122172.e: Because fixed altitudes do not fit at every latitude, Körner uses the climatic tree line as the lower limit of the alpine zone.
122172.m: The alpine zone begins above the natural tree line.

122173.q: According to Körner, which environmental factor changes with altitude in the same regular way everywhere on Earth, unlike rainfall, for example?
122173.e: Körner distinguished factors that depend directly on altitude, such as air pressure and temperature, from factors linked to altitude only in some regions, such as rainfall or wind.
122173.m: Air pressure falls evenly with altitude everywhere.

122174.q: According to Körner's theory, which process limits plant growth first in the cold?
122174.e: At low temperatures a plant can still make sugar but can hardly turn it into new tissue. Tissue formation, the so-called sink, is the bottleneck.
122174.m: In the cold, plants do not lack sugar but cell growth.

122175.q: Which country does the plant ecologist Christian Körner originally come from?
122175.e: Christian Körner was born in Austria and studied in Innsbruck before moving to Basel.
122175.m: Christian Körner was born in Austria.

122176.q: What does the international programme GLORIA study on mountain summits?
a: How plant life is changing due to climate change
How fast the glaciers are melting
How many climbers visit the summits
How rock is weathered by frost
122176.e: GLORIA is a worldwide network that observes the plant life of mountain summits over the long term to detect the effects of climate change.
122176.m: GLORIA observes the plants on mountain summits around the world.

122177.q: Why are mountain summits especially good places to observe the effects of climate change on plants?
a: Cold-adapted species there react sensitively to warming
Most of Europe's plant species grow there
No rain or snow ever falls on summits
Summit plants grow exactly the same every year
122177.e: On summits, species live at their cold limit. Even small changes in temperature shift which species can grow there. The GLORIA network is coordinated from Vienna.
122177.m: Summit plants show early how climate change is working.

122178.q: Why does GLORIA record the plants on the same plots again and again?
a: To detect changes over the years
Because the plants would otherwise die
To measure the height of the summits again
122178.e: In each region, several summits at different altitudes are studied. The surveys are repeated on the same plots every few years, so changes become visible.

122179.q: On what principle are the summits of a GLORIA region chosen?
a: In steps from the tree line up to the nival zone
All summits at exactly the same altitude
Only the highest summits in each country
Only summits with a cable car
122179.e: The summits range from around the tree line up into the nival zone. In this way a whole altitude gradient is covered.
122179.m: GLORIA summits form a staircase from the tree line to the permanent snow.

122180.q: What are permanently marked plots called, on which researchers record the plants again and again over many years?
122180.e: Permanent monitoring plots are marked precisely and surveyed regularly. In GLORIA they are squares with sides of one metre just below the summits.
122180.m: On permanent plots, the same spot is recorded again and again.

122181.q: What have researchers been observing in the plant life on many Alpine summits for decades?
a: Warmth-loving species from lower altitudes are increasing
Forests are now growing on the summits
122181.e: Warmth-loving species from lower altitudes are increasing, while cold-loving ones are becoming rarer. As a result, the plant community is becoming more warmth-loving.
122181.m: Because of warming, summit communities are becoming more warmth-loving.

122182.q: What did a study of around 300 European summits, published in “Nature” in 2018, show?
a: The number of species is increasing faster and faster
The number of species is falling sharply
The number of species stays the same
122182.e: New species from lower altitudes arrived on the summits studied, and this increase accelerated in step with warming.
122182.m: The number of plant species on Europe's summits is growing faster and faster.

122183.q: According to a GLORIA study from 2012, in which mountains did the number of species on summits decrease?
122183.e: In northern and temperate mountains the number of species increased. In the Mediterranean region it decreased, probably because of growing drought.
122183.m: In the Mediterranean region, summits are losing plant species because of drought.

122184.q: What is meant by frost drought?
a: Drying out when the ground is frozen
Freezing because of ice in the cells
Dying from the weight of snow
122184.e: When the ground is frozen, the roots cannot take up water. If the plant still loses water through its leaves, it dries out.
122184.m: Frost drought means dying of thirst in winter.

122185.q: When does frost drought occur most often at the tree line?
a: In late winter on sunny days
On spring nights when it rains
122185.e: In late winter the sun is already strong, but the ground is still frozen. The water balance then becomes strongly negative.
122185.m: Sunny days in late winter are the most dangerous for frost drought.

122186.q: Why do needles lose a lot of water on sunny winter days?
122186.e: Sunlight can warm needles well above the air temperature. As a result water evaporates, which cannot be replaced from the frozen ground.
122186.m: In winter, the sun's warmth drives the evaporation from needles.

122187.q: Why are young needles at the tree line particularly vulnerable to frost drought?
a: Their wax layer has not fully developed
122187.e: Because of the short summer, the protective cuticle does not develop fully. More water is lost through it in winter.
122187.m: An immature cuticle lets water escape from needles in winter.

122188.q: Why do no trees grow above the tree line, even though dwarf shrubs thrive there?
a: Trees stick out of the protective snow cover and suffer from cold and drying out
The soil there contains no water
There is too much oxygen there
Trees need more sun than there is there
122188.e: Dwarf shrubs stay protected under the snow in winter. Trees stick out and are exposed to cold, wind and frost drought, and the short growing season is no longer enough.
122188.m: At the tree line, trees lack the protection of the snow cover.

122189.q: Which parts of a tree at the tree line are best protected from frost drought?
122189.e: Under the snow it is dark, damp and evenly cool. There the needles hardly lose any water.
122189.m: Under the snow, branches are protected from drying out.

122190.q: How can you recognise damage from frost drought in spring?
a: By white spots on the bark
122190.e: Dried-out needles turn reddish-brown and later fall off. Often only the parts above the snow cover are affected.
122190.m: Frost drought shows up as brown needles.

122191.q: What protects evergreen garden plants such as cherry laurel from frost drought?
122191.e: Evergreen plants lose water through evaporation even in winter. Watering on frost-free days and providing shade make up for the loss.
122191.m: Evergreen plants need water in winter too.

122192.q: What triggers the frost hardening of mountain plants in autumn?
122192.e: The plants react to the shortening days and the first cold. They then gradually build up protective substances and become more frost-hardy.
122192.m: Short days and cold make plants frost-hardy in autumn.

122193.q: In many frost-tolerant plants, where does ice form so that the cells survive?
122193.e: If ice forms between the cells, water is drawn out of the cells without ice crystals destroying them. Ice inside a cell would be deadly.
122193.m: Frost-hardy plants only let ice form between their cells.

122194.q: Why do plants store sugar in their cells in winter?
122194.e: Dissolved sugar lowers the freezing point of the cell sap and stabilises membranes. This lets the cells survive lower temperatures.
122194.m: In plant cells, sugar works like antifreeze.

122195.q: What is it called when water cools below 0 °C without forming ice, which some plant tissues make use of?
122195.e: Pure water in small spaces can stay liquid below 0 °C as long as there are no ice nuclei. Some tissues survive light frost in this way.
122195.m: Supercooled water stays liquid below zero degrees.

122196.q: Which Alpine plant often pushes its flowers through the melting snow cover in spring?
122196.e: The snowbell (Soldanella) starts growing while still under the snow. Its violet bells often appear in small holes in the old snow.
122196.m: The snowbell flowers right through the snow.

122197.q: What advantage do cushion plants such as moss campion have in high mountains?
a: It is warmer and calm inside the cushion
They store salt against the frost
122197.e: The dense, dome-shaped form slows the wind and stores heat. Inside it is much warmer than in the surrounding air.
122197.m: A cushion is a small greenhouse for the plant.

122198.q: What are red pigments such as anthocyanins in the leaves of many high mountain plants for?
122198.e: Anthocyanins work like a sunscreen. They filter high-energy light and so protect the leaf tissue.
122198.m: Red pigments protect mountain plants from strong radiation.

122199.q: Which evergreen dwarf shrub grows on windswept ridges in the Alps that are often free of snow in winter?
122199.e: The trailing azalea, also called alpine azalea, survives extreme cold and wind without protective snow. It is typical of wind-exposed edges.
122199.m: The trailing azalea survives on snow-free windy ridges.

122200.q: On average, by how much does the air temperature in the Alps fall for every 100 m of altitude?
122200.e: Rising air expands and cools. On average the temperature falls by about 0.6 °C for every 100 m.
122200.m: For every 100 metres of altitude it gets about 0.6 degrees colder on average.

122201.q: At an altitude of 400 m the temperature is 14 °C. With a drop of 0.6 °C per 100 m, what temperature would you expect at 2500 m?
122201.e: The difference in altitude is 2100 m, so 21 times 0.6 °C equals 12.6 °C. 14 °C minus 12.6 °C equals 1.4 °C.
122201.m: Multiply the number of hundreds of metres by the drop per 100 m.

122202.q: How does the length of the growing season change with increasing altitude?
122202.e: Higher up, the snow lies longer and autumn starts earlier. So the plants have less time to grow and flower.
122202.m: The higher up, the shorter the plants' growing season.

122203.q: Which vegetation is typical of the subalpine zone of the Swiss Alps?
a: Coniferous forest up to the tree line
122203.e: The subalpine zone is dominated by spruce, larch and Swiss stone pine and reaches up to the tree line.
122203.m: The subalpine zone is the zone of coniferous forest.

122204.q: At an altitude of 5500 m, by roughly how much is air pressure lower than at sea level?
122204.e: Air pressure roughly halves every 5500 m. At this altitude it is only about 500 hPa.
122204.m: At 5500 m, air pressure is about half as high as at sea level.

122205.q: How does UV radiation change with increasing altitude?
122205.e: With altitude, the layer of air above becomes thinner and filters out less UV radiation. Reflection from snow adds to this.
122205.m: The higher you climb, the stronger the UV radiation.

122206.q: Why are altitude gradients in the mountains good natural experiments for climate research?
a: The climate changes a lot over a short distance
The soils are the same everywhere
122206.e: A few hundred metres of altitude correspond to large temperature differences, for which you would have to travel hundreds of kilometres on flat land. This makes it possible to compare climate effects in a small area.
122206.m: A mountainside shows many climate zones over a short distance.

122207.q: Why is it often colder on the valley floor than on the slope above in Alpine valleys in winter?
a: Because of a pool of cold air during an inversion
Because of stronger sunshine down below
Because of warm glacier air above
Because of higher air pressure on the slope
122207.e: Cold, heavy air flows into the valleys at night and collects there. Above it lies warmer air, so for once the temperature rises with altitude.
122207.m: During an inversion, the cold air lies at the bottom of the valley.

122208.q: How does the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the air change with increasing altitude?
122208.e: The proportion of CO2 in the air stays almost the same, but because the total pressure falls, the partial pressure of CO2 falls too. This makes photosynthesis slightly harder.
122208.m: At altitude, plants have less CO2 pressure available.

122209.q: Which flowering plant was found on the Dom in Valais at about 4500 m and is considered the highest-growing flowering plant in the Alps?
122209.e: Purple saxifrage forms small cushions with violet flowers. It has been recorded on the Dom at about 4500 m.
122209.m: Purple saxifrage flowers higher than any other plant in the Alps.

122210.q: Which plant with white to pink flowers grows in the Alps at over 4000 m, for example on the Finsteraarhorn?
122210.e: Glacier crowfoot is one of the highest-growing flowering plants in Europe and grows on silicate scree.
122210.m: Glacier crowfoot grows at over 4000 m.

122211.q: How was it first proved that summit plants are moving upwards because of warming?
a: By comparison with old species lists
By measuring the thickness of glaciers
122211.e: Researchers visited summits whose plants had already been recorded in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Many of them now had considerably more species.
122211.m: Old species lists show that plants are moving towards the summits.

122212.q: Why are plant species of the summit region considered particularly endangered by global warming?
a: They need a lot of fertiliser
122212.e: As it gets warmer, strongly competitive species move up from below. But above the summit there is no more habitat for the cold-lovers to escape to.
122212.m: Above the summit there is no room to escape.

122213.q: Which living things grow on rocks in the Alps right up to the highest summits?
122213.e: Lichens are partnerships between a fungus and an alga. They tolerate drying out and cold and still grow where no flowering plant can survive.
122213.m: Lichens grow even on the highest rocks.

122214.q: On which side of an Alpine summit do you usually find the most plant species?
a: The same number on all sides
122214.e: South-facing slopes get more sun, lose their snow earlier and are warmer. So more species usually grow there than on the shady north side.
122214.m: The sunny south sides of summits are richer in species.

122215.q: Which growth forms are most common among flowering plants on high summits?
122215.e: Close to the ground it is warmer and less windy. That is why summit plants usually grow flat as cushions or leaf rosettes.
122215.m: Summit plants usually grow as flat cushions or rosettes.

122216.q: What are plants called that grow above the climatic snow line?
122216.e: Above the snow line lies the nival zone. Plants there grow in small snow-free spots and rock crevices.
122216.m: Nival plants live above the snow line.

122217.q: Roughly how much of fresh powder snow is air?
122217.e: Fresh powder snow consists mostly of trapped air. Air is a poor conductor of heat, which is why snow insulates so well.
122217.m: Snow insulates because it is almost entirely air.

122218.q: What is the temperature usually like at ground level under a thick layer of snow?
122218.e: The snow cover holds in the warmth of the ground and shields it from the cold air. So the ground underneath usually stays just around freezing point.
122218.m: Under a lot of snow, the ground stays around zero degrees.

122219.q: What are hollows in the mountains called where snow lies for a particularly long time?
122219.e: In snowbeds the snow-free period is often only a few weeks long. A special plant community adapted to short summers grows there.
122219.m: In snowbeds the snow lies until well into the summer.

122220.q: Which tiny woody plant is typical of snowbeds?
122220.e: The dwarf willow grows only a few centimetres tall, and its trunk grows underground. It is considered one of the smallest trees in the world.
122220.m: The dwarf willow is a dwarf among trees.

122221.q: How does the rock ptarmigan protect itself on very cold winter nights?
a: It digs itself into the snow
It flies down to the Swiss Plateau
It looks for shelter in barns
122221.e: In a snow hole it is much warmer than on the surface. This way the ptarmigan saves energy.
122221.m: The ptarmigan uses the snow as a warm blanket.

122222.q: What is the habitat between the ground and the snow cover called, where mice, for example, stay active in winter?
122222.e: Under the snow it is dark, but evenly cool and calm. Small mammals dig tunnels there and find food.
122222.m: Under the snow there is a winter habitat of its own.

122223.q: What danger do alpine plants face if the snow melts earlier in spring?
a: The seeds no longer germinate at all
The plants get too little light
122223.e: Without a protective snow cover, young shoots and buds are directly exposed to frosty nights in spring. This can damage them badly.
122223.m: Early snowmelt can bring plants frost damage.

122224.q: What happens to the ground in cold winters with little snow?
122224.e: Without an insulating snow cover, frost penetrates deep into the ground. This can damage roots and soil organisms.
122224.m: Without snow, the ground freezes deeply.

a: A species that has survived in isolation since the Ice Age
A boulder carried along by a glacier
A tool from the Ice Age
An animal that lives in glacier ice
122225.e: Glacial relicts are species that remained in cold special sites after the Ice Age, while their main range moved north or uphill.
122225.m: Glacial relicts are remnants of Ice Age life.

122226.q: Which woody plant occurs as a glacial relict in some raised bogs of the Jura?
122226.e: The dwarf birch is widespread in the Arctic. In Central Europe it survives only in a few cool, wet places.
122226.m: The dwarf birch is an Ice Age relict in raised bogs.

122227.q: Why do some plant species occur in the Arctic and in the Alps, but not in the area in between?
a: After the Ice Age they retreated north and uphill
Migrating birds carry their seeds back and forth every year
People planted them in both places
They evolved again independently in both places
122227.e: During the Ice Age such species lived in the ice-free area between northern Europe and the Alps. Afterwards they retreated north and uphill. This is called an arctic-alpine distribution.
122227.m: Arctic-alpine species were split into two areas by the Ice Age.

122228.q: Which plant is the cold phase known as the “Younger Dryas” at the end of the last Ice Age named after?
122228.e: Dryas is the scientific genus name of mountain avens. Its remains are common in deposits from this cold phase.
122228.m: The Younger Dryas is named after mountain avens.

122229.q: Which Alpine mammal has an arctic-alpine range that dates back to the Ice Age?
122229.e: The mountain hare lives in the far north and in the Alps. The two areas were separated after the Ice Age.
122229.m: The mountain hare lives in the Arctic and in the Alps.

122230.q: Why do glacial relicts often survive in raised bogs?
a: They are cool, wet and poor in nutrients
They are warm and very dry
122230.e: On the cool, nutrient-poor bog soils, strongly competitive species hardly stand a chance. This allowed Ice Age species to survive there.
122230.m: Raised bogs are islands for Ice Age plants.

122231.q: Where can glacial relicts survive even at low altitudes?
a: In boulder fields with cold air
122231.e: In some boulder fields, cold air flows out of the gaps in summer. The cool microclimate allows mountain species to survive far below.
122231.m: Cold boulder fields are refuges for Ice Age species.

122232.q: What did the landscape of the Swiss Plateau look like shortly after the glaciers retreated?
122232.e: After the ice retreated, the Swiss Plateau was at first treeless and like tundra. Only as it got warmer did birches, pines and later broadleaf trees move in.
122232.m: After the Ice Age, the Swiss Plateau was first a tundra.

a: A place of retreat during the Ice Age
A mountain hut by a glacier
A glacial lake in the mountains
A moraine ridge in the foothills
122233.e: In glacial refugia, plants and animals survived the cold periods. From there they recolonised the areas that became free after the Ice Age.
122233.m: Species survived the Ice Age in refugia.

122234.q: In which regions did many of Central Europe's broadleaf trees survive the last Ice Age?
a: The Iberian Peninsula, Italy and the Balkans
Poland, the Baltic States and Finland
122234.e: On the southern European peninsulas the climate was mild enough for forests. Beech, oak and other trees returned from there.
122234.m: Europe's southern peninsulas were refugia for trees.

122235.q: What are ice-free summits called that stuck out of an ice sheet and are thought to be possible refugia?
122235.e: Nunataks are rock islands in the ice. Some Alpine plants may have survived the Ice Age on them.
122235.m: A nunatak is a mountain peak that sticks out of the ice.

122236.q: Why are the Southern Alps, such as the Bergamo Alps, particularly rich in endemic plants?
a: They were ice-free refugia on the edge
122236.e: On the edge of the Alps, some areas stayed free of ice. Species survived there, some of which did not spread far and therefore occur only there.
122236.m: Ice-free edges of the Alps are rich in endemic species.

122237.q: When did the last glaciation of the Alps reach its maximum?
122237.e: At the last glacial maximum, the glaciers reached far out into the Swiss Plateau. After that they melted back quickly.
122237.m: About 20,000 years ago the ice was at its greatest extent.

122238.q: In the classic division, what is the last cold period in the Alpine region called?
122238.e: The classic division names the cold periods after rivers in the Alpine foothills. The most recent one is the Würm glaciation.
122238.m: The last Ice Age in the Alps is called the Würm glaciation.

122239.q: How can former refugia be recognised today using genetic methods?
a: By identical genetic material in all individuals
122239.e: Populations lived in refugia for a very long time. They built up more genetic variants than the areas colonised later.
122239.m: Old refugia show up as great genetic diversity.

122240.q: Which source is used to reconstruct how trees returned after the Ice Age?
122240.e: Pollen is preserved layer by layer in lake sediments and peat. This shows when each tree species returned to an area.
122240.m: Pollen in bogs and lakes tells the history of the forest.

122241.q: Where is the Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF based?
122241.e: The SLF is in Davos in the canton of the Grisons. Among other things, Switzerland's avalanche bulletin is produced there.
122241.m: The SLF does its research in Davos.

122242.q: What is examined in a snowpack test with a ram penetrometer?
a: The strength of the snow layers
The salt content of the snow
The colour of the snow crystals
122242.e: The ram penetrometer is driven into the snow with a falling weight. The resistance shows hard and soft layers, which is important for assessing avalanches.
122242.m: The ram penetrometer shows hard and soft layers in the snow.

122243.q: What is typical of a slab avalanche, the most common type of avalanche in accidents?
a: A slab of snow breaks away over a wide area
It starts at a single point
It consists only of chunks of ice
122243.e: In a slab avalanche, a connected layer of snow slides off on a weak layer. It is often triggered by winter sports enthusiasts themselves.
122243.m: A slab avalanche breaks away as a large plate.

122244.q: When does the SLF regularly publish the avalanche bulletin in winter?
a: Only when there is fresh snow
122244.e: In winter the bulletin appears every day at 5 pm. If necessary it is updated in the morning at 8 am.
122244.m: In winter, the avalanche bulletin comes out every evening at 5 pm.

122245.q: How many levels does the European avalanche danger scale used by the SLF have?
122245.e: The scale goes from low through moderate, considerable and high to very high.
122245.m: Avalanche danger is given in five levels.

122246.q: At which danger level do most fatal avalanche accidents involving snow sports enthusiasts happen?
122246.e: At level 3 many people are out and about, and the danger is often underestimated. At levels 4 and 5 most people do not go on tours.
122246.m: Level 3 is especially treacherous for snow sports enthusiasts.

122247.q: Where does much of the measurement data that the SLF uses for the avalanche bulletin come from?
a: From automatic stations in the high mountains
From weather balloons over the sea
From seismographs on the Swiss Plateau
122247.e: Automatic stations in the mountains continuously measure snow depth, wind and temperature. In addition there are reports from observers on site.
122247.m: Automatic mountain stations provide data for the avalanche bulletin.

a: Ground that stays frozen all year round
Frost that only occurs at night
122248.e: Permafrost is ground that stays below zero degrees continuously for at least two years. In the Alps it occurs mainly in high, shady places. If it thaws, slopes can become unstable.

122249.q: On which mountain above Davos is the SLF's long-established test site?
122249.e: The snow cover has been measured on the Weissfluhjoch for decades. It is one of the oldest snow measurement sites in the high mountains.
122249.m: The SLF has been measuring snow on the Weissfluhjoch for decades.

122250.q: Which alpine rose indicates a soil containing lime?
122250.e: The hairy alpine rose grows on limestone, the rusty-leaved one on acidic silicate soils. Bilberry and common heather also avoid lime.
122250.m: The hairy alpine rose grows on limestone.

122251.q: Koch's gentian and Clusius's gentian look very similar. What is the main difference between where they grow?
a: The altitude, below or above 4000 metres
How close they are to a lake
122251.e: Koch's gentian grows on acidic silicate, Clusius's gentian on limestone. Closely related species like these, which replace each other on different rock, are called vicariant species.
122251.m: Koch's gentian grows on silicate, Clusius's gentian on limestone.

122252.q: How do soils on silicate rock such as granite and gneiss usually differ from limestone soils?
122252.e: Granite and gneiss weather into acidic soils low in lime. Lime, on the other hand, buffers acids and keeps the pH high. That is why different plants often grow on the two types of rock.
122252.m: Silicate soils are usually acidic, limestone soils alkaline.

122253.q: What are plants called that only grow on soil rich in lime?
122253.e: Strictly calcicole plants are tied to soil with a lot of lime and a high pH. Calcifuge species avoid such soils.
122253.m: Strictly calcicole plants grow only on limestone.

122254.q: Which yellow-flowered primrose typically grows on limestone cliffs in the Alps?
122254.e: The auricula is a yellow-flowered rock plant of limestone mountains. The pink-flowered hairy primrose, by contrast, grows on silicate rock.
122254.m: The yellow auricula loves limestone cliffs.

122255.q: Which rocks dominate large parts of the Central Alps and so shape the silicate flora?
122255.e: The Central Alps consist largely of crystalline rock such as granite and gneiss. On them acidic soils form with typical silicate flora, such as the rusty-leaved alpine rose.
122255.m: Granite and gneiss carry a typical silicate flora.

122256.q: Why do many silicate plants avoid soils rich in lime?
a: Iron is hard to obtain there
Lime is as poisonous to them as salt
Limestone soils are always too wet
122256.e: At a high pH they find it hard to absorb iron and other nutrients. The leaves then turn yellow; this is called lime chlorosis.
122256.m: On limestone, some plants suffer from iron deficiency.

122257.q: Where in Switzerland is limestone flora mainly found?
a: In the Jura and the northern Limestone Alps
On the molasse of the Swiss Plateau
122257.e: The Jura and the limestone ranges on the northern edge of the Alps consist mostly of limestone. The Central Alps, by contrast, are often made of gneiss and granite.
122257.m: The Jura and the northern Limestone Alps are areas of limestone flora.

122258.q: On which rock does edelweiss prefer to grow in the Alps?
122258.e: Edelweiss grows mainly on stony grassland and rock ledges containing lime. It is rare on acidic silicate.

122359.q: Which part of the brain does the hypothalamus belong to?
122359.e: The hypothalamus lies below the thalamus and is part of the diencephalon (interbrain).
122359.m: The hypothalamus is part of the diencephalon.

122360.q: Which hormone from fat tissue tells the hypothalamus how big the fat reserves are?
122360.e: The more fat is stored, the more leptin fat cells release. In the hypothalamus, leptin damps down the feeling of hunger.
122360.m: Leptin from fat tissue damps down hunger in the hypothalamus.

122361.q: Where is the pituitary gland, which is controlled by the hypothalamus?
a: Directly below the hypothalamus at the base of the brain
In the neck in front of the larynx
In the chest behind the breastbone
122361.e: The pituitary gland hangs on a short stalk below the hypothalamus and sits in a bony hollow at the base of the skull.
122361.m: The pituitary gland hangs directly below the hypothalamus.

122362.q: Which body quantity is mainly regulated by the hypothalamus to a set point of around 37 °C?
122362.e: The centre for temperature control lies in the hypothalamus. It compares the measured temperature with the set point and triggers sweating or shivering.
122362.m: The hypothalamus is the body's thermostat.

122363.q: Which sensory cells in the hypothalamus register whether the blood is too concentrated and trigger thirst?
122363.e: Osmoreceptors measure the osmolarity of the blood. If it rises, thirst develops and more ADH is released.
122363.m: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus report blood that is too salty.

122364.q: Which stimulus resets the internal clock in the hypothalamus every day?
122364.e: The retina tells the hypothalamus whether it is light or dark. In this way the day-night rhythm is adjusted to the surroundings every day.

122365.q: What is the hormonal stress axis called that starts from the hypothalamus and ends with the release of cortisol?
122365.e: Under stress, the hypothalamus stimulates the adrenal cortex to make cortisol through several hormone stages. This chain is also called the HPA axis.
122365.m: The HPA axis links the hypothalamus, the pituitary gland and the adrenal cortex.

122366.q: Which two hormones are made in the hypothalamus and stored and released in the posterior pituitary?
122366.e: ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin are made in nerve cells of the hypothalamus. They travel along the cells' extensions to the posterior pituitary and are released into the blood there.
122366.m: ADH and oxytocin come from the hypothalamus and are released in the posterior pituitary.

122367.q: Why is the hypothalamus called the link between the nervous system and the hormone system?
a: Its nerve cells make hormones themselves
It consists only of gland cells
It makes all the body's hormones
122367.e: The hypothalamus has neurosecretory cells: nerve cells that make hormones and release them into the blood. In this way it turns nerve signals into hormone signals.
122367.m: Neurosecretory cells make the hypothalamus the link between nerves and hormones.

122368.q: Which pituitary hormone is released by TRH from the hypothalamus?
122368.e: TRH (thyrotropin-releasing hormone) stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH. TSH then stimulates the thyroid.
122368.m: TRH releases TSH, and TSH drives the thyroid.

122369.q: Which pituitary hormone is released by CRH?
122369.e: CRH (corticotropin-releasing hormone) stimulates the production of ACTH in the pituitary gland. ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to make cortisol.
122369.m: CRH leads to the release of cortisol via ACTH.

122370.q: Which releasing hormone promotes the release of growth hormone?
122370.e: GHRH (growth hormone-releasing hormone) from the hypothalamus stimulates the release of somatotropin in the anterior pituitary.
122370.m: GHRH gives the signal for growth hormone.

122371.q: Which hormone of the hypothalamus inhibits the release of growth hormone?
122371.e: Somatostatin is an inhibiting hormone: in the pituitary gland it slows down the release of somatotropin and also of TSH.
122371.m: Somatostatin is the brake for growth hormone.

122372.q: Which messenger substance from the hypothalamus inhibits the release of prolactin from the pituitary gland?
122372.e: The release of prolactin is mainly held back by the hypothalamus. The inhibiting factor is dopamine, which is therefore also called prolactin-inhibiting hormone.
122372.m: Dopamine from the hypothalamus slows down the release of prolactin.

122373.q: By which route do the releasing hormones travel from the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary?
a: Through small blood vessels in the pituitary stalk
Through the cerebrospinal fluid in the spinal cord
122373.e: The hypothalamus and the pituitary gland are linked by their own small system of blood vessels in the pituitary stalk. In this way the releasing hormones reach their target quickly and in high concentration.
122373.m: Releasing hormones reach the pituitary gland through blood vessels in the pituitary stalk.

122374.q: To which class of substances do most releasing hormones of the hypothalamus belong?
122374.e: Releasing hormones such as TRH, CRH and GHRH are short chains of amino acids, in other words peptide hormones. They act through receptors on the cell membrane.
122374.m: Releasing hormones are mostly peptide hormones.

122375.q: What prevents the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland from releasing too much CRH and ACTH?
122375.e: When the cortisol level rises, cortisol inhibits the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland. As a result, CRH and ACTH fall, and the control loop stays in balance.
122375.m: Cortisol slows down its own release through negative feedback.

122376.q: What does a low TSH together with a raised thyroxine in the blood indicate?
122376.e: If the thyroid itself makes too much hormone, the large amount of thyroxine inhibits the pituitary gland through feedback. That is why TSH is low even though thyroxine is high.
122376.m: With an overactive thyroid, TSH is low and thyroxine is high.

122377.q: How does a high thyroxine level affect the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland?
a: It inhibits the release of TRH and TSH
It increases the release of TRH and TSH
It only increases the release of ACTH
122377.e: Through negative feedback, thyroxine reports that there is enough thyroid hormone. TRH and TSH then fall, and the thyroid is stimulated less.
122377.m: A lot of thyroxine slows down TRH and TSH.

122378.q: Why must long-term cortisone treatment be reduced slowly rather than stopped suddenly?
a: The body's own cortisol production is suppressed by feedback
The liver needs time to detoxify
122378.e: Cortisone taken as a medicine inhibits CRH and ACTH through negative feedback, so the adrenal cortex then makes little cortisol. If the medicine is stopped suddenly, cortisol is missing, which can be dangerous.
122378.m: After long cortisone treatment, the adrenal gland has to start up again slowly.

122379.q: In a control loop, what is an outside influence called that moves the actual value away from the set point?
122379.e: A disturbance variable changes the controlled value from outside, for example cold changing body temperature. The control loop then evens out this deviation.
122379.m: A disturbance variable pushes the actual value away from the set point.

122380.q: Which process in the body is an example of positive rather than negative feedback?
122380.e: In blood clotting, clotting factors that have formed activate further factors, so the process reinforces itself. That is positive feedback.
122380.m: Positive feedback reinforces a process instead of slowing it down.

122381.q: How does the pituitary gland's release of ACTH react when the adrenal cortex is destroyed and hardly makes any cortisol?
122381.e: Without cortisol, the inhibiting feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland is missing, and ACTH rises sharply. Because ACTH also stimulates the pigment cells, the skin of those affected often becomes darker.
122381.m: If the end hormone is missing, the controlling pituitary hormone rises.

122382.q: What happens in the pancreas when blood sugar rises, and how does this feed back?
a: More insulin lowers blood sugar, and then insulin release falls
More glucagon lowers blood sugar permanently
Less insulin makes blood sugar rise further
Cortisol is released and lowers the sugar
122382.e: High blood sugar stimulates the release of insulin. Insulin lowers blood sugar, and the falling sugar in turn reduces insulin release: a negative feedback.
122382.m: Blood sugar regulates its own lowering through insulin.

122383.q: Which part of a control loop measures the current actual value?
122383.e: The sensor measures the actual value and reports it to the controller. In the hormone system, these are for example receptors for hormones or glucose.
122383.m: The sensor measures, the controller compares, the actuator acts.

122384.q: How many iodine atoms does a thyroxine molecule (T4) contain?
122384.e: The number in the abbreviation T4 stands for the four iodine atoms in the molecule. Triiodothyronine (T3) has three iodine atoms.
122384.m: T4 has four iodine atoms and T3 has three.

122385.q: Which thyroid hormone is the biologically more active form in the target cells?
122385.e: In the tissues, thyroxine is mostly converted into T3 by removing one iodine atom. T3 binds much more strongly to the nuclear receptor.
122385.m: T3 is the active form of thyroid hormone.

122386.q: What effect does thyroxine have on the body's basal metabolic rate?
a: It has no effect on it
122386.e: Thyroid hormones increase energy use and heat production in almost all tissues. With an overactive thyroid, the basal metabolic rate rises clearly.

122387.q: In which protein is thyroxine stored in the follicles of the thyroid?
122387.e: The thyroid hormones are formed on a large protein, thyroglobulin, and stored in the colloid of the follicles. When needed, they are split off.
122387.m: Thyroxine is stored on thyroglobulin in the follicle.

122388.q: Which autoimmune disease leads to an overactive thyroid through antibodies against the TSH receptor?
122388.e: In Graves' disease, antibodies activate the TSH receptor permanently, and the thyroid makes too much hormone. Typical signs are a racing heart, weight loss and sometimes bulging eyes.
122388.m: In Graves' disease, antibodies stimulate the thyroid.

122389.q: Which substance is usually taken as hormone replacement for an underactive thyroid?
122389.e: Levothyroxine is artificially made T4. It is taken daily as a tablet and partly converted into T3 in the body.
122389.m: With an underactive thyroid, levothyroxine replaces the missing thyroid hormone.

122390.q: Since which year has iodised table salt been used in Switzerland against goitre and iodine deficiency?
122390.e: In 1922 Switzerland was one of the first countries to introduce iodised salt. Goitre and cretinism then declined sharply.
122390.m: Switzerland has been fighting iodine deficiency with iodised salt since 1922.

122391.q: What is the consequence of an untreated congenital lack of thyroid hormone?
122391.e: Thyroid hormones are essential for the brain to mature. Without treatment, intellectual disability and short stature result, which is why newborn babies are tested for it.
122391.m: Newborns are tested for a lack of thyroid hormone because the brain needs thyroxine.

122392.q: Why does iodine deficiency cause a goitre?
a: Raised TSH makes the thyroid grow
Iodine builds up in the neck
Thyroxine piles up in the tissue
122392.e: Without iodine, too little thyroxine is made, the inhibition of the pituitary gland disappears and TSH rises. TSH stimulates the thyroid to grow.
122392.m: Iodine deficiency leads to a goitre through a lot of TSH.

122393.q: What is the most important natural glucocorticoid in humans?
122393.e: Cortisol (hydrocortisone) is the most important glucocorticoid in humans. It is made in the adrenal cortex.
122393.m: Cortisol is the most important glucocorticoid.

122394.q: In which hormone gland is cortisol made?
122394.e: Cortisol is made in the cortex of the adrenal glands, which sit on the kidneys. Its release is controlled through the pituitary gland.
122394.m: Cortisol comes from the adrenal cortex.

122395.q: How does cortisol affect the blood sugar level?
a: It only lowers it at night
122395.e: Cortisol promotes the making of new glucose in the liver (gluconeogenesis) and reduces glucose uptake in some tissues. As a result, blood sugar rises.

122396.q: What are synthetic glucocorticoids such as prednisone mainly used for in medicine?
a: To build muscle in healthy people
122396.e: Glucocorticoids suppress inflammatory and immune reactions. They help, for example, with asthma, rheumatism or allergic reactions.
122396.m: Glucocorticoids have a strong anti-inflammatory effect.

122397.q: What is a typical side effect of taking cortisone in high doses for a long time?
122397.e: Too much cortisone changes the metabolism: fat builds up on the trunk and face, the skin becomes thin, and blood sugar and bone loss increase.
122397.m: High-dose cortisone over a long time has clear side effects.

122398.q: From which starting substance are glucocorticoids made in the body?
122398.e: Glucocorticoids are steroid hormones. All steroid hormones are built from cholesterol.
122398.m: Steroid hormones such as cortisol are made from cholesterol.

122399.q: At what time of day is the cortisol level normally highest in a healthy person?
122399.e: Cortisol follows a daily rhythm: it rises in the second half of the night and peaks in the morning. In the evening the levels are lowest.
122399.m: Cortisol is highest in the morning and lowest in the evening.

122400.q: Where is the receptor that cortisol binds to in the target cell?
122400.e: Cortisol is fat-soluble and passes through the cell membrane. It binds to a receptor in the cytoplasm, which then changes gene expression in the nucleus.
122400.m: Steroid hormones act through receptors inside the cell.

122401.q: What is the most important mineralocorticoid in humans?
122401.e: Aldosterone is the most important mineralocorticoid. It regulates the balance of sodium and potassium.
122401.m: Aldosterone is the most important mineralocorticoid.

122402.q: Where in the body is the hormone aldosterone made?
122402.e: Aldosterone is made in the outer layer of the adrenal gland, the cortex. The adrenal medulla, by contrast, makes adrenaline.
122402.m: Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex.

122403.q: What effect does aldosterone have in the kidney?
a: Sodium is taken back and potassium is excreted
Sodium and potassium are both excreted
Calcium is taken back and phosphate is excreted
122403.e: In the distal tubule and the collecting duct, aldosterone promotes the reabsorption of sodium. In exchange, potassium is excreted, and water is kept back along with the sodium.
122403.m: Aldosterone keeps sodium and gets rid of potassium.

122404.q: Which enzyme from the kidney starts the chain that leads to the release of aldosterone?
122404.e: When blood pressure in the kidney falls, renin is released. It starts the production of angiotensin II, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone.
122404.m: Renin from the kidney starts the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

122405.q: How does aldosterone affect blood pressure?
a: It raises it, because more salt and water stay in the body
It lowers it, because more water is excreted
It has no influence on it
It lowers it, because the heart beats more slowly
122405.e: Aldosterone makes the kidney take back sodium, and water stays in the body along with the sodium. The blood volume rises and with it the blood pressure.
122405.m: Aldosterone raises blood pressure through salt and water.

122406.q: Why are hormones such as aldosterone called “mineralocorticoids”?
a: They regulate the salt balance and come from the adrenal cortex
They are taken in from mineral water
122406.e: “Mineral” stands for salts such as sodium and potassium, “corticoid” for their origin in the cortex of the adrenal gland.

122407.q: What happens if the adrenal cortex makes too little aldosterone?
a: The body loses salt and blood pressure falls
122407.e: Without aldosterone, the kidney excretes too much sodium and water. Those affected have low blood pressure and often crave salt, as in Addison's disease.
122407.m: Without aldosterone, the body loses salt and blood pressure.

122408.q: What does a medicine that blocks the effect of aldosterone do?
a: The kidney excretes more sodium and water
The kidney keeps back more sodium
122408.e: If aldosterone cannot work, the kidney takes back less sodium. Water is lost along with the sodium, while potassium tends to stay in the body.
122408.m: If aldosterone is blocked, the kidney excretes more salt and water.

122409.e: Somatotropin is made by the somatotropic cells of the anterior pituitary and released into the blood.
122409.m: Growth hormone comes from the anterior pituitary.

122410.q: Which organ does somatotropin stimulate to make growth factors for bones and tissues?
122410.e: Growth hormone works largely indirectly: it makes the liver release growth factors into the blood, which then promote growth.
122410.m: Many effects of growth hormone work through the liver.

122411.q: What results from too much somatotropin in childhood, while the growth plates are still open?
122411.e: As long as the growth plates are open, too much growth hormone leads to excessive growth in height. This is called pituitary gigantism.
122411.m: Too much growth hormone in childhood makes you very tall.

122412.q: What is the condition called when too much somatotropin is made after the growth plates have closed?
122412.e: In adults, the long bones no longer grow in length; instead the hands, feet, chin and nose get bigger. The most common cause is a benign tumour of the pituitary gland.
122412.m: In adults, acromegaly enlarges the hands, feet and facial features.

122413.q: During which phase is somatotropin released especially strongly?
122413.e: The biggest release of growth hormone happens shortly after falling asleep, in the deep sleep phases. Enough sleep is therefore important for growth.
122413.m: Growth hormone is released mainly during deep sleep.

122414.q: How does somatotropin affect the blood sugar level?
a: It has no effect at all
122414.e: Somatotropin acts as an opponent of insulin: it promotes the production of glucose and reduces glucose uptake. That is why it counts as one of the hormones that raise blood sugar.
122414.m: Somatotropin works against insulin and raises blood sugar.

122415.q: Where does the somatotropin used today to treat short stature come from?
a: From the pituitary glands of deceased people
122415.e: Growth hormone used to be obtained from the pituitary glands of deceased people, which transmitted cases of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Today it is produced by genetic engineering in bacteria or cell cultures.
122415.m: Growth hormone is now produced safely by genetic engineering.

122416.q: Why does growth hormone have to be injected rather than swallowed as a tablet?
a: As a protein, it would be broken down in the digestive tract
The tablets would be too large
It only works directly in the muscle
122416.e: Somatotropin is a large peptide hormone made of amino acids. In the stomach and intestines it would be digested like protein from food and would not reach the blood in an effective form.
122416.m: Protein hormones such as somatotropin must be injected.

122417.q: Where do the cells of the islets of Langerhans release their hormones?
a: Into the lymph of the intestine
122417.e: The islet cells are endocrine: they release insulin and glucagon directly into the blood vessels. The rest of the pancreas releases digestive juice into the intestine.
122417.m: The islets of Langerhans release their hormones directly into the blood.

122418.q: Which cells of the islets of Langerhans produce insulin?
122418.e: Beta cells make up most of the islet cells and produce insulin.

122419.q: Which hormone do the alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans produce?
122419.e: Alpha cells produce glucagon, the opponent of insulin. Glucagon raises blood sugar.

122420.q: Which hormone is produced by the delta cells of the islets of Langerhans?
122420.e: Delta cells produce somatostatin, which inhibits the release of insulin and glucagon in the surrounding area.
122420.m: Delta cells produce the inhibiting hormone somatostatin.

122421.q: Roughly what share of the mass of the pancreas do the islets of Langerhans make up?
122421.e: By far the largest part of the pancreas produces digestive enzymes. The islets make up only around 1 to 2 per cent of the organ's mass.
122421.m: The islets of Langerhans are only a small part of the pancreas.

122422.q: Why are the islets of Langerhans called “islets”?
a: They lie scattered as small clusters of cells in the rest of the gland tissue
They float freely in the abdomen
122422.e: The hormone-producing clusters of cells lie like islands in the tissue that produces digestive juice. Paul Langerhans described them in 1869 as a student without knowing their function.
122422.m: The islets of Langerhans lie scattered throughout the pancreas.

122423.q: What happens to the beta cells in type 1 diabetes mellitus?
a: They are destroyed by the body's own immune system
122423.e: In type 1 diabetes, immune cells attack the beta cells. Once a large proportion has been destroyed, the missing hormone has to be supplied from outside for life.
122423.m: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune destruction of the beta cells.

122424.q: How does glucagon act in the liver?
a: It promotes the breakdown of glycogen
It promotes the build-up of glycogen
It inhibits the release of glucose
It promotes the production of bile
122424.e: In the liver, glucagon stimulates the breakdown of glycogen and the production of new glucose. The glucose is released into the blood and blood sugar rises.
122424.m: Glucagon releases sugar from the liver's stores.

122425.q: Which researchers succeeded in isolating insulin in Toronto in 1921?
122425.e: In 1921 Banting and Best obtained insulin from the pancreases of dogs. As early as 1922 a patient was treated with it for the first time.
122425.m: Insulin was isolated by Banting and Best in 1921.

122426.q: What is the central disorder at the start of type 2 diabetes mellitus?
a: Too much glucagon because of a tumour
122426.e: In type 2 diabetes, muscle, fat and liver cells respond less well to insulin. At first the pancreas even produces more insulin; later it becomes exhausted.
122426.m: Type 2 diabetes usually begins with insulin resistance.

122427.q: Which medicine in tablet form is usually considered the first choice for type 2 diabetes?
122427.e: Metformin mainly inhibits the production of new glucose in the liver and improves sensitivity to insulin. On its own it hardly ever causes low blood sugar.
122427.m: Metformin is the standard medicine for type 2 diabetes.

122428.q: Roughly what share of all cases of diabetes is type 2?
122428.e: With around 90 per cent of all cases, type 2 diabetes is by far the most common form of diabetes.
122428.m: Most people with diabetes have type 2.

122429.q: What is measured in a fasting blood sugar test?
a: The sugar level in the blood after several hours without food
The sugar in the urine after breakfast
The amount of sugar in food
The store of insulin in the pancreas
122429.e: For the test you must not eat anything for at least eight hours. If the blood sugar is then clearly raised on repeated occasions, this points to diabetes.
122429.m: Fasting blood sugar is measured without eating beforehand.

122430.q: What does a glucose tolerance test check?
a: How well the body processes a large amount of sugar
How much sugar someone eats each day
Whether someone can taste sugar well
How much sugar the muscles store
122430.e: You drink a sugar solution and the blood sugar is measured afterwards. If it is still too high after two hours, the body is processing sugar poorly.
122430.m: The glucose tolerance test shows how well the body processes sugar.

122431.q: Which eye disease is a typical long-term consequence of poorly controlled diabetes?
122431.e: Permanently high blood sugar damages the small blood vessels of the retina. This diabetic retinopathy can even lead to blindness.
122431.m: Diabetes can damage the blood vessels of the retina.

122432.q: What does the word “mellitus” in diabetes mellitus mean?
122432.e: “Mellitus” comes from Latin and means sweet as honey. In the past, diabetes was recognised by the sweet taste of the urine.
122432.m: Diabetes mellitus literally means a flow as sweet as honey.

122433.q: Which measure has been shown to improve insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes without medicine?
122433.e: Working muscles take up glucose even independently of insulin and become more sensitive to insulin. Exercise and weight loss are cornerstones of treatment.
122433.m: Exercise makes the muscles more sensitive to insulin again.

122434.q: What does the HbA1c value measure?
a: The proportion of haemoglobin with glucose attached
The number of red blood cells
The amount of insulin in the blood
The current blood sugar in real time
122434.e: HbA1c is glycated haemoglobin. The value shows what percentage of the haemoglobin is bound to glucose.
122434.m: HbA1c shows how much haemoglobin has sugar attached.

122435.q: Over what period does the HbA1c value reflect the average blood sugar?
122435.e: Red blood cells live for around 120 days. That is why HbA1c shows the average blood sugar of the last two to three months.
122435.m: HbA1c is the blood sugar memory of the last two to three months.

122436.q: For which disease is the HbA1c value checked regularly?
122436.e: HbA1c shows the average blood sugar of the past few months. That is why it is the most important control value in diabetes.
122436.m: HbA1c is the most important long-term value in diabetes.

122437.q: In which blood cells is the haemoglobin found that sugar binds to in HbA1c?
122437.e: Haemoglobin is the red pigment in the red blood cells. Part of it combines with glucose from the blood.
122437.m: HbA1c forms in the red blood cells.

122438.q: What happens to the HbA1c value if blood sugar is too high for weeks?
122438.e: The more glucose there is in the blood, the more of it binds to haemoglobin. Permanently high blood sugar therefore makes the HbA1c rise.
122438.m: High blood sugar over weeks raises the HbA1c.

122439.q: Why does HbA1c show the blood sugar of the last two to three months?
a: Because red blood cells live for around 120 days
Because the liver stores sugar for three months
Because insulin works for three months
Because the kidneys only filter every three months
122439.e: Haemoglobin collects glucose throughout the whole lifespan of a red blood cell. This is around 120 days.
122439.m: The lifespan of the red blood cells determines the memory of HbA1c.

122440.q: Why do you not need to fast before an HbA1c measurement?
a: The value hardly depends on short-term fluctuations
Because eating always lowers the value
Because the measurement is done in urine
Because the glucose is filtered out
122440.e: HbA1c reflects an average over weeks. A single meal hardly changes it at all.
122440.m: HbA1c does not require a fasting blood sample.

122441.q: What advantage does HbA1c have for monitoring diabetes over time?
a: It shows long-term blood sugar control
It shows acute low blood sugar immediately
122441.e: Because HbA1c reflects the average of the past few months, it is well suited for assessing treatment. However, it does not detect short episodes of low blood sugar.
122441.m: HbA1c is used to assess treatment over months.

122442.q: What is the steady release of insulin by an insulin pump throughout the day called?
122442.e: The basal rate covers the basic need for insulin around the clock. It can be programmed differently for each hour.
122442.m: The basal rate covers the basic need for insulin.

122443.q: What is the extra amount of insulin released by the pump for a meal called?
122443.e: For the carbohydrates in a meal or to correct high values, you release a bolus at the press of a button.
122443.m: For meals, the pump releases a bolus.

122444.q: Which type of insulin is normally used in an insulin pump?
122444.e: The pump continuously releases small amounts of fast-acting insulin. Because it acts quickly, the dose can be finely adjusted hour by hour.
122444.m: An insulin pump works with fast-acting insulin.

122445.q: Into which tissue does an insulin pump release the insulin?
a: Into the fatty tissue under the skin
122445.e: The insulin flows through a fine cannula into the fatty tissue under the skin (subcutaneously). The cannula is changed every few days.
122445.m: The pump releases insulin under the skin.

122446.q: Why does ketoacidosis quickly threaten if the insulin supply from the pump is interrupted?
a: There is no depot of long-acting insulin
The pump then releases too much insulin
The insulin becomes toxic in the pump
The body immediately produces too much glucagon and insulin
122446.e: With a pump, there is only a little fast-acting insulin in the body. If the supply fails, insulin runs out after a few hours and the body breaks down fat into ketone bodies.
122446.m: If the pump fails, insulin runs out quickly.

122447.q: What are systems called in which a glucose sensor and an insulin pump adjust the dose automatically?
122447.e: In automated insulin delivery, an algorithm continuously calculates the amount of insulin from the sensor values. Meals usually still have to be entered by the user (hybrid closed loop).
122447.m: A closed-loop system connects sensor and pump automatically.

122448.q: What does a continuous glucose monitoring system (CGM), often combined with an insulin pump, measure?
a: The sugar in the tissue fluid under the skin
The insulin level in the blood
The blood pressure on the upper arm
122448.e: A small sensor under the skin continuously measures the glucose level of the tissue fluid. The values appear on the mobile phone or the pump.
122448.m: A CGM sensor measures sugar continuously under the skin.

122449.q: What is an insulin pump called that sticks directly onto the skin without a tube?
122449.e: Patch pumps contain the insulin reservoir and cannula in a small housing that is stuck directly onto the skin and controlled by a device.
122449.m: A patch pump sticks onto the skin without a tube.

122450.q: Which molecule is the best-known second messenger?
122450.e: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) carries the signal from hormones such as adrenaline or glucagon into the inside of many cells.
122450.m: cAMP is the classic second messenger.

122451.q: Which enzyme makes cAMP from ATP?
122451.e: After being activated by a G protein, adenylate cyclase converts ATP into cAMP.
122451.m: Adenylate cyclase turns ATP into cAMP.

122452.q: How is a hormone signal passed on after cAMP has been formed in the cell?
a: cAMP activates enzymes that pass on the signal
cAMP leaves the cell again as a hormone
cAMP is immediately built into the DNA
cAMP destroys the receptor on the membrane
122452.e: cAMP switches on enzymes in the cell. These change other proteins and so trigger the actual response of the cell.
122452.m: cAMP switches on enzymes in the cell.

122453.q: Why do peptide hormones such as glucagon need a second messenger?
a: They cannot cross the cell membrane
They only act in the cell nucleus
They are destroyed in the blood immediately
122453.e: Peptide hormones are water-soluble and cannot pass through the lipid bilayer. They bind to a receptor on the outside, and a second messenger carries the signal inside.
122453.m: Water-soluble hormones need a second messenger.

122454.q: Which molecule links a hormone receptor to adenylate cyclase?
122454.e: When a hormone binds to a G protein-coupled receptor, a G protein is activated. This switches on adenylate cyclase.
122454.m: A G protein connects the receptor and adenylate cyclase.

122455.q: Which ion also serves as a second messenger in many cells, for example in muscle contraction?
122455.e: When the calcium concentration inside the cell rises, this triggers reactions, for example the contraction of muscle fibres or the release of messenger substances.
122455.m: Calcium is an important messenger inside the cell.

122456.q: Why is a molecule such as cAMP called a “second messenger”?
a: The hormone is the first messenger, the molecule in the cell the second
It is always formed only at the second contact with a hormone
It only works for one second
It was the second hormone ever discovered
122456.e: The hormone brings the message as far as the cell membrane. Inside the cell, a second messenger such as cAMP carries the message on.
122456.m: The second messenger carries the hormone's signal into the cell.

122457.q: Why must a second messenger signal be broken down again quickly in the cell?
a: So that the cell can respond to new signals
Because otherwise the hormone flows back into the blood
So that the cell produces more hormones
122457.e: If cAMP were not broken down, the cell would stay switched on permanently. Enzymes break down the messenger so that the signal ends and the cell is ready to receive again.
122457.m: A signal must also be switched off again.

122458.q: What is the advantage of a signalling cascade with a second messenger?
a: The hormone reaches the cell nucleus
122458.e: A single hormone molecule activates many enzyme molecules, each of which forms many cAMP molecules. In this way a small stimulus produces a large response.
122458.m: A signalling cascade strongly amplifies a weak hormone signal.

122459.q: Which scientist introduced the terms “positive” and “negative” charge in the 18th century?
122459.e: Around 1747 Benjamin Franklin interpreted electricity as an excess or lack of an electric fluid and called the two states positive and negative. The terms are still used today.
122459.m: The terms positive and negative charge go back to Benjamin Franklin.

122460.q: How can the unit 1 coulomb be expressed in SI base units?
122460.e: Charge is current times time (Q = I · t). One coulomb is the charge that flows through a cross-section of a conductor in 1 s at 1 A.

122461.q: How much charge flows through a cable if a current of 2 A flows for 30 seconds?

122462.q: What does the law of conservation of charge say?
a: In a closed system the total charge stays constant
Every object is always electrically neutral
Charge can only flow in metals
Positive charge turns into negative charge over time
122462.e: Charges can be separated or moved, but neither created nor destroyed. The sum of all charges in a closed system does not change.
122462.m: The total charge of a closed system is conserved.

122463.q: Why can a metal rod held in your bare hand hardly be charged by rubbing?
a: The charge flows away through the rod and the body
122463.e: Metal is a good conductor, and the human body also conducts. The charge separated by rubbing flows away through the hand straight away.
122463.m: Conductors lose charge immediately through conducting connections.

122464.q: A glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth and is then positively charged. What has happened?
a: The rod has given electrons to the cloth
The rod has taken protons from the cloth
New charge was created in the rod
122464.e: During rubbing, electrons pass from the glass to the silk. The glass then lacks electrons and is positive, while the cloth is equally strongly negative.
122464.m: In frictional electricity only electrons move.

122465.q: What is the name of the series in which materials are ordered by the charge they take on when rubbed together?
122465.e: In the triboelectric series, materials that tend to give up electrons when rubbed are on one side and materials that tend to take up electrons are on the other. The further apart two materials are, the more strongly they become charged.
122465.m: The triboelectric series predicts how materials become charged when rubbed.

122466.q: What happens to a charged metal object if you connect it to the earth with a conductor?
122466.e: The Earth is a huge reservoir of charge. Electrons flow away or in through the connection until the object is neutral.

122467.q: What has been true of the elementary charge since the revision of the SI system in 2019?
a: Its numerical value is fixed exactly
It is measured again every year
It is twice as large as before
It now only applies to electrons
122467.e: Since 2019 several natural constants, including the elementary charge, have been set to fixed values. Since then the ampere has been defined through this constant.
122467.m: Since 2019 the elementary charge has been an exactly fixed natural constant.

122469.q: Why are no free particles with one-third charges observed in experiments?
a: Quarks only occur bound inside composite particles
One-third charges immediately decay into light
The measuring instruments are too imprecise
122469.e: Quarks do carry one-third charges, but the strong interaction always locks them inside particles such as protons or neutrons (confinement). Their total charge is always a whole-number multiple of e.
122469.m: Because of confinement, quarks never appear on their own.

122470.q: What is the charge of an up quark?
122470.e: Quarks carry fractions of a third: up quarks +2/3 e, down quarks -1/3 e. A proton (uud) therefore has 2/3 + 2/3 − 1/3 = +1 e.
122470.m: Quarks carry fractions of the elementary charge.

122471.q: What charge does a muon, the heavy relative of the electron, carry?
122471.e: The muon is a lepton like the electron, but about 207 times heavier. It carries the same charge as the electron, so one negative elementary charge.
122471.m: Like the electron, the muon carries the charge -e.

122472.q: Roughly how large is the charge of one mole of electrons (the Faraday constant)?
122472.e: The Faraday constant is the product of the Avogadro constant and the elementary charge: 6.022 · 10^23 /mol · 1.602 · 10^-19 C ≈ 96,485 C/mol.
122472.m: One mole of elementary charges gives about 96,500 coulombs.

122473.q: What charge does a positron, the antiparticle of the electron, carry?
122473.e: Antiparticles have the same mass as their particle but the opposite charge. The positron therefore carries one positive elementary charge.
122473.m: The positron is a positively charged anti-electron.

122474.q: What is the charge of a calcium ion Ca²⁺?
122474.e: The ion has given up two electrons, so its charge is 2e = 2 · 1.602 · 10^-19 C ≈ 3.2 · 10^-19 C.
122474.m: A doubly charged ion carries two elementary charges.

122475.q: In which direction does the Coulomb force between two point charges act?
a: At right angles to the line joining them
In a circle around the charges
122475.e: The Coulomb force acts along the straight line through both charges: away from each other for like charges, towards each other for unlike charges.
122475.m: The Coulomb force acts along the line joining the charges.

122476.q: How does the Coulomb force change if you double the distance between two charges?
122476.e: Because F ~ 1/r², the force becomes 2² = 4 times smaller at twice the distance.
122476.m: Twice the distance gives a quarter of the force.

122477.q: How does the Coulomb force change if you double both charges and keep the distance the same?
122477.e: The force is proportional to the product Q1 · Q2. If you double both, the product becomes 2 · 2 = 4 times larger.
122477.m: The Coulomb force grows with the product of the two charges.

122478.q: Roughly how large is the Coulomb constant k?
122478.e: The Coulomb constant is k = 1/(4πε0) ≈ 8.99 · 10^9 N·m²/C². It is very large, which is why electric forces are strong.
122478.m: The Coulomb constant is almost nine billion in SI units.

122479.q: What force acts between two charges of 1 µC each, 1 m apart (in a vacuum)?
122479.m: Even small charges produce measurable forces.

122480.q: With which instrument did Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measure the force between charges in 1785?
122480.e: Coulomb used a torsion balance, in which the twisting of a thin thread measures the very small forces.
122480.m: Coulomb measured electric forces with a torsion balance.

122481.q: Why does gravity between the proton and the electron play practically no role in the atom?
a: It is unimaginably weaker than the electric force
It is shielded by the nucleus
122481.e: Both forces decrease with 1/r². But the electric attraction is about 10^39 times stronger than gravity, so it determines the structure of atoms.
122481.m: In the atom the electric force is unimaginably stronger than gravity.

122482.q: Which other law of nature has the same mathematical form as Coulomb's law?
122482.e: Both laws have the form constant times the product of two quantities divided by r². But gravity is always attractive, while the Coulomb force can also repel.
122482.m: Coulomb's law and the law of gravitation are built the same way.

122483.q: How does the force between two ions change if they are in water (εr ≈ 80) instead of a vacuum?
122483.e: In a medium the Coulomb force is divided by the relative permittivity εr. That is why salts dissolve easily in water: the ions hold together much more weakly.
122483.m: Water greatly weakens the force between ions.

122484.q: Where do electric field lines begin and end?
a: They begin at positive and end at negative charges
They begin at negative and end at positive charges
They begin and end at infinity
122484.e: Electrostatic field lines have sources and sinks: they run from positive to negative charge. Their direction shows the force on a positive test charge.
122484.m: Field lines run from plus to minus.

122485.q: Why can two electric field lines never cross?
a: At each point the field has only one direction
Because they only exist in metals
122485.e: A field line shows the direction of the force at a place. If two lines crossed, the force there would have two directions, which is impossible.

122486.q: What shape is the field line pattern of a single point charge?
a: Radial, like a star in all directions
122486.e: For a point charge the field lines run in straight lines radially outwards (positive) or inwards (negative).
122486.m: The field of a point charge is radial.

122487.q: At what angle do electric field lines meet a metal surface in electrostatic equilibrium?
122487.e: If the field had a component along the surface, the free electrons would move. In equilibrium the field is therefore perpendicular to the conductor.
122487.m: Field lines are perpendicular to conductor surfaces.

122488.q: In a field line diagram, what does a high density of field lines show?
122488.e: The closer together the field lines are, the greater the field strength at that point.
122488.m: Dense field lines mean a strong field.

122489.q: Which scientist introduced the vivid concept of field lines into physics?
122489.e: In the 19th century Michael Faraday described electric and magnetic forces with lines of force in space. James Clerk Maxwell later put this into mathematical form.

122490.q: In which direction is an electron accelerated in an electric field?
a: Against the direction of the field
In the direction of the field
At right angles to the field
122490.e: The field direction is defined as the direction of the force on positive charges. On the negatively charged electron the force therefore acts the opposite way.
122490.m: Electrons move against the field lines.

122491.q: Which particle is not deflected when it flies through an electric field?
122491.e: An electric field only exerts a force on charged particles. The neutron is electrically neutral and carries straight on.
122491.m: Neutral particles do not feel an electric field.

122492.q: Why should the test charge used to measure an electric field strength be as small as possible?
a: So that it hardly changes the field being measured
So that it is accelerated faster
Because large charges do not exist
So that it has no mass
122492.e: Every charge creates its own field and can move the charges that produce the field. A very small test charge hardly disturbs the original field.
122492.m: A small test charge does not disturb the field being measured.

122493.q: Which unit is equivalent to newtons per coulomb (N/C)?
122493.e: 1 N/C = 1 J/(C·m) = 1 V/m. Both units are used for electric field strength.
122493.m: Field strength is measured in volts per metre.

122494.q: A force of 6 mN acts on a test charge of 2 µC. What is the field strength?
122494.m: Field strength is force divided by charge.

122495.q: How does the field strength of a point charge change if you triple the distance?
122495.e: For a point charge, E = k · Q / r². At three times the distance, E becomes 3² = 9 times smaller.
122495.m: The field of a point charge decreases with 1/r².

122496.q: Roughly above what field strength do sparks jump in dry air under normal conditions?
122496.e: The dielectric strength of dry air is roughly 3 kV per millimetre. Above this, the air becomes conductive and a spark forms.
122496.m: Air can withstand about three kilovolts per millimetre.

122497.q: What force acts on an electron in a field with a strength of 1000 V/m?
122497.m: The force on a charge is charge times field strength.

122498.q: What acceleration does an electron (m ≈ 9.11 · 10^-31 kg) experience in a field of 1000 V/m?
122498.e: a = e · E / m = 1.602 · 10^-16 N / 9.11 · 10^-31 kg ≈ 1.76 · 10^14 m/s². Because of the tiny mass, the acceleration is huge.
122498.m: Electrons are accelerated enormously even in weak fields.

122499.q: How large is the electric field strength inside a closed metal cage that is charged on the outside?
a: It rises sharply towards the centre
122499.e: The charges spread out on the outside of the metal so that their fields cancel out inside. That is why a Faraday cage, such as a car, protects against lightning.
122499.m: Inside a Faraday cage the electric field is zero.

122500.q: Why is electric field strength a vector quantity?
a: It has a magnitude and a direction
122500.e: Field strength tells you how strongly and in which direction a force acts on a positive charge. That is why it is given as a vector.
122500.m: Field strength is a vector with magnitude and direction.

122501.q: How is electric voltage related to potential?
a: It is the difference between two potentials
It is the product of two potentials
It is the reciprocal of the potential
It has nothing to do with potential
122501.e: The voltage between two points A and B is U = φA − φB, so it is a potential difference.

122502.q: How does the electric potential behave inside a charged metal object in equilibrium?
a: It rises sharply towards the centre
It is infinitely large at the centre
122502.e: Inside a conductor in equilibrium the electric field is zero. Without a field the potential does not change, so the whole conductor is at a single potential, which need not be zero.
122502.m: A conductor in equilibrium has the same potential everywhere.

122503.q: How are equipotential surfaces positioned relative to the electric field lines?
122503.e: The potential does not change along an equipotential surface. That is why the field is everywhere perpendicular to these surfaces.
122503.m: Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to the field lines.

122504.q: How much work must be done to move a charge along an equipotential surface?
122504.e: Work in a field is W = q · U. On an equipotential surface the potential difference is zero, so the work is too.
122504.m: Moving along an equipotential surface takes no work.

122505.q: How much work does the field do on a charge of 2 µC that passes through a potential difference of 50 V?
122505.m: The work in a field is charge times potential difference.

122506.q: Roughly how fast is an electron after it has passed through a voltage of 100 V from rest?
122506.e: From e · U = ½ · m · v² it follows that v = square root of (2eU/m) = square root of (2 · 1.602 · 10^-17 J / 9.11 · 10^-31 kg) ≈ 5.9 · 10^6 m/s.
122506.m: Even small voltages make electrons very fast.

122507.q: How does the potential of a point charge depend on the distance r?
a: It does not depend on r
122507.e: For a point charge, φ = k · Q / r if the potential at infinity is set to zero. So it falls off more slowly than the field strength.
122507.m: The potential of a point charge falls off with 1/r.

122508.q: Which reference point is often chosen as a potential of 0 V in electrical engineering?
a: The positive terminal of the battery
The live conductor of the socket
The output of the power supply
122508.e: Potential is only defined up to a constant. In circuits the earth or ground is usually set as 0 V, in theory often a point infinitely far away.
122508.m: The zero point of potential can be chosen freely, usually the earth.

122509.q: What is the basic structure of a capacitor?
a: Two conductors separated by an insulator
A wire wound into a coil
Two semiconductors with a p-n junction
A metal rod in an acid
122509.e: A capacitor consists of two conducting electrodes with an insulator (dielectric) between them. Energy is stored there in the electric field.
122509.m: A capacitor consists of two insulated conductors.

122510.q: What is the time constant when a 100 µF capacitor is charged through a 10 kΩ resistor?
