122510.m: The time constant is resistance times capacitance.

122511.q: To what percentage of the final voltage is a capacitor charged after one time constant τ?
122511.e: During charging, U(t) = U0 · (1 − e^(-t/τ)). For t = τ this gives 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.63.
122511.m: After one time constant a capacitor is about two thirds charged.

122512.q: What must you pay special attention to when fitting an electrolytic capacitor?
122512.e: Electrolytic capacitors are polarised. Connected the wrong way round, they can heat up and even burst.
122512.m: Electrolytic capacitors must be connected with the correct polarity.

122513.q: How does a charged capacitor behave in a direct current circuit?
a: It lets the direct current through unhindered
It turns it into alternating current
122513.e: Once the capacitor is fully charged, no more current flows because the insulator does not let charges through. Alternating current, however, can pass it through constant recharging.
122513.m: A charged capacitor blocks direct current.

122514.q: What is the total capacitance of two 10 µF capacitors connected in series?
122514.m: In series the total capacitance is smaller than each single one.

122515.q: What total capacitance do 10 µF and 22 µF give when connected in parallel?
122515.e: In a parallel connection the capacitances add up: 10 µF + 22 µF = 32 µF.
122515.m: Capacitances connected in parallel add up.

122516.q: What is the name of the first capacitor, invented around 1745, a glass jar lined with metal foil?
122516.e: The Leyden jar was discovered independently around 1745 by Ewald Georg von Kleist and Pieter van Musschenbroek. The metal linings inside and outside form the two electrodes.
122516.m: The Leyden jar was the first capacitor.

122517.q: How is the capacitance of a capacitor defined?
122517.e: Capacitance tells you how much charge a capacitor stores per volt: C = Q/U.

122518.q: What is the capacitance of a capacitor that stores a charge of 1 mC at 5 V?
122518.m: Capacitance is charge divided by voltage.

122519.q: How does a capacitive touchscreen detect the touch of a finger?
a: The finger changes the capacitance at that point
The finger presses two films together
The finger interrupts a beam of light
122519.e: Under the glass lies a grid of electrodes. The conductive finger changes the capacitance locally, and the electronics work out the position from this.
122519.m: A touchscreen measures changes in capacitance caused by the finger.

122520.q: How much charge does a 47 µF capacitor store at 12 V?

122521.q: What is the capacitance of the Earth, seen as a conducting sphere with a radius of 6,371 km?
122521.m: Even the whole Earth has a capacitance of less than one millifarad.

122522.q: In what ranges do the capacitances of ordinary capacitors in electronic circuits lie?
122522.e: One farad is a very large unit. Ordinary capacitors have values from a few pF through nF and µF up to the mF range.
122522.m: Ordinary capacitances are tiny fractions of a farad.

122523.q: Which type of capacitor reaches capacitances of several thousand farads?
122523.e: Double-layer capacitors store charge on a very large, porous electrode surface at a tiny distance from the electrolyte. This gives them very high capacitances at a low voltage.

122524.q: How does the capacitance of a capacitor change if you double the voltage applied?
122524.e: Capacitance only depends on design and material. At twice the voltage the charge doubles, and the ratio Q/U stays the same.
122524.m: Capacitance does not depend on voltage.

122525.q: Which formula is used to calculate the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor?
122525.e: The capacitance grows with the plate area A and the relative permittivity εr and decreases with the plate separation d.
122525.m: Large plates close together give a large capacitance.

122526.q: How does the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor change if you halve the plate separation?
122526.e: Because C ~ 1/d, half the separation leads to twice the capacitance.
122526.m: Half the separation gives twice the capacitance.

122527.q: A parallel-plate capacitor is filled with a dielectric with a relative permittivity εr = 5. How does the capacitance change?
122527.e: Capacitance is proportional to εr. The dielectric is polarised and weakens the field, so that more charge fits at the same voltage.
122527.m: A dielectric increases the capacitance by the factor εr.

122528.q: What is the electric field like between the plates of an ideal parallel-plate capacitor?
122528.e: Between the plates the field lines run parallel and equally dense. Field strength and direction are the same everywhere, so the field is uniform.
122528.m: There is a uniform field in a parallel-plate capacitor.

122529.q: What is the field strength in a parallel-plate capacitor with a voltage of 200 V and a plate separation of 4 mm?
122529.m: In a parallel-plate capacitor the field strength is voltage divided by separation.

122530.q: What is the capacitance of an air-filled parallel-plate capacitor with a plate area of 100 cm² and a separation of 1 mm (ε0 = 8.85 · 10^-12 F/m)?
122530.m: Air-filled parallel-plate capacitors only have small capacitances.

122531.q: A charged parallel-plate capacitor is disconnected from the voltage source and the plates are pulled apart. What happens to the voltage?
122531.e: Without a source the charge Q stays constant. The capacitance falls as the separation grows, and because U = Q/C the voltage rises.
122531.m: At constant charge the voltage rises when the capacitance falls.

122532.q: A parallel-plate capacitor stays connected to the voltage source while the plates are pulled apart. What happens to the charge on the plates?
122532.e: The source keeps U constant. Because C falls as the separation grows, Q = C · U decreases and charge flows back to the source.
122532.m: At constant voltage the charge falls with the capacitance.

122533.q: Why is the field at the edge of a real parallel-plate capacitor no longer uniform?
a: The field lines bulge outwards at the edge
There is no charge at the edge
The plates are thicker at the edge
The voltage is zero at the edge
122533.e: At the edge of the plates the field lines curve out of the gap (edge effect). Only well inside is the field truly uniform, especially when the separation is small compared with the size of the plates.
122533.m: At the edge of a parallel-plate capacitor the field is curved.

122534.q: How large is the electric field strength inside a closed Faraday cage when there is a static field outside?
122534.e: The free charges in the metal shell move so that their field exactly cancels the outside field inside.
122534.m: Inside a Faraday cage the electric field is zero.

122535.q: Against which kind of field does an ordinary Faraday cage made of thin metal not protect?
122535.e: A Faraday cage cancels electric fields by moving charges. A constant magnetic field, such as the Earth's magnetic field, passes through it, which is why a compass works inside.
122535.m: A Faraday cage shields electric fields, but not static magnetic fields.

122536.q: Why does a convertible with a fabric roof offer hardly any protection in a thunderstorm?
a: It lacks a closed metal shell
122536.e: Protection needs a conducting shell around the passengers. A fabric roof does not conduct and does not form a Faraday cage.
122536.m: Only a conducting shell protects against lightning.

122537.q: Why do the microwaves not get through the perforated mesh in the door of a microwave oven?
a: The holes are much smaller than the wavelength
122537.e: The wavelength in a microwave oven is about 12 cm, while the holes are only a few millimetres across. The mesh therefore acts like a closed metal wall.
122537.m: A mesh shields waves whose wavelength is much larger than its holes.

122538.q: Where does the excess charge of a charged, hollow metal object sit in equilibrium?
122538.e: Like charges repel each other and spread out as far apart as possible. In equilibrium they sit on the outer surface.
122538.m: Charge sits on the outside of a conductor.

122539.q: What did Michael Faraday show in 1836 with a room he had lined all round with metal foil?
a: The inside stays free of any field despite strong charging from outside
Metal attracts lightning from the surroundings
Electric charge collects inside the room
Metal foil creates a magnetic field itself
122539.e: Faraday strongly charged the metal-lined room from outside. His instruments inside still showed no charge, because the charges spread only over the outer shell.
122539.m: A conducting shell keeps electric fields out of the inside.

122540.q: Which part of a coaxial cable acts as a Faraday cage for the signal?
a: The outer shield of wire mesh
122540.e: The conducting outer conductor completely surrounds the inner conductor. It keeps out interference from outside and stops the signal radiating outwards.
122540.m: The shield of a coaxial cable protects the signal.

122541.q: Why does a mobile phone often have poor reception in a closed metal lift?
a: The lift car shields the radio waves
The lift produces too much heat
The phone is discharged in the lift
The air in the lift is too dry
122541.e: A conducting lift car acts as a Faraday cage for electromagnetic waves. The radio signals are strongly weakened.
122541.m: Metal shells weaken mobile phone signals.

122542.q: What is meant by electrostatic induction?
a: The shifting of charge in a conductor caused by an outside electric field
The transfer of charge by touching
The production of current by light
122542.e: If you bring a conductor into an electric field, its free electrons move. Opposite charges appear on opposite sides.
122542.m: Electrostatic induction is the separation of charge in a conductor by an outside field.

122543.q: What is the corresponding process in an insulator called, in which only the charges within the molecules are shifted?
122543.e: Insulators have no free electrons. An outside field only shifts the centres of charge in atoms and molecules or lines up dipoles.
122543.m: In insulators you speak of polarisation rather than electrostatic induction.

122544.q: A negatively charged rod is brought near an uncharged metal sphere. What charge appears on the side facing the rod?
122544.e: The sphere's electrons are repelled by the negative rod and move to the far side. The near side becomes positive.
122544.m: Electrostatic induction produces the opposite charge on the near side.

122545.q: A negatively charged rod is brought near a metal sphere, the sphere is briefly earthed, the earth connection is removed and then the rod is taken away. What charge does the sphere have?
122545.e: Through the earthing, the repelled electrons flow away. After disconnecting and removing the rod, the sphere lacks electrons and is positively charged.
122545.m: Charging by induction gives the opposite charge to the rod.

122546.q: Why is an uncharged metal sphere attracted by a charged rod?
a: The induced opposite charge is closer to the rod
The sphere always has some leftover charge
122546.e: The opposite charge is closer to the rod than the like charge. Because the force decreases with distance, the attraction wins.
122546.m: Electrostatic induction leads to attraction even of uncharged conductors.

122547.q: Why are you protected from lightning in a car with a metal body during a thunderstorm?
a: The car body acts as a Faraday cage
The rubber tyres insulate the car
The windows keep out the lightning
The car battery conducts the lightning away
122547.e: The charges move on the outside of the metal shell, and inside the electric field stays practically zero. The lightning current flows over the outside of the body to the ground.
122547.m: A closed metal shell shields electric fields.

122548.q: What is the total charge of an isolated, uncharged conductor in which charges have been separated by electrostatic induction?
122548.e: In electrostatic induction charges are only shifted, not added. The positive and negative parts are equally large, so the sum stays zero.
122548.m: Electrostatic induction shifts charges without changing the total charge.

122549.q: What does an uncharged electroscope show if you only bring a charged rod near it without touching it?
122549.e: Through electrostatic induction, charges are pushed to the lower end and the pointer is deflected. If you take the rod away, the deflection goes back again.
122549.m: An electroscope is deflected by induction as soon as a charged rod comes near.

122550.q: Around which year did Robert Millikan determine the elementary charge precisely with his oil drop experiment?
122550.e: Millikan achieved his precise result in 1910 and published it in 1911. An improved analysis followed in 1913.

122551.q: Why can the buoyancy of the oil drops in air often be ignored in simple analyses of Millikan's experiment?
a: Air has a much lower density than oil
There is no buoyancy in air
The electric field cancels the buoyancy
122551.e: Buoyancy depends on the density of air, about 1.2 kg/m³. Oil has a density of about 900 kg/m³, so buoyancy is only just over one thousandth of the weight.
122551.m: Because air density is low, the buoyancy of the drops is tiny.

122552.q: Why did Millikan use oil instead of water for the drops?
a: Oil hardly evaporates, so the mass stays constant
122552.e: Water drops would evaporate and change their mass. Oil drops stay almost unchanged over the time of the measurement.
122552.m: Oil hardly evaporates, so the mass of the drop stays the same.

122553.q: Which condition applies to an oil drop that is hovering in the air in Millikan's experiment?
a: The electric force and the weight are equally large
The weight is twice as large
122553.e: When hovering, the upward electric force q · E exactly balances the weight m · g. From this the charge q can be calculated.
122553.m: When hovering, the electric force and the weight balance each other.

122554.q: An oil drop of 4.9 · 10^-15 kg hovers in the capacitor (d = 5 mm) at U = 1500 V. What charge does it carry (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
122554.m: The charge of the drop follows from the hovering condition.

122555.q: What important result about electric charges did Millikan's experiment deliver?
a: Charges are always whole-number multiples of a smallest charge
Charges can be as small as you like
122555.e: All the measured drop charges were multiples of the same basic value. This showed that electric charge is quantised.
122555.m: Electric charge only comes in whole portions.

122556.q: Which law did Millikan use to work out the radius of the drops from their sinking speed?
122556.e: When sinking at a steady speed, the weight equals the Stokes drag force 6π · η · r · v. From this follows the radius and therefore the mass of the drop.
122556.m: Stokes' drag reveals the radius of the oil drops.

122557.q: What did Robert Millikan win the Nobel Prize in Physics for?
a: For measuring the elementary charge and work on the photoelectric effect
For discovering the electron and the proton
122557.e: Millikan won the Nobel Prize in 1923. He determined the elementary charge with oil drops and confirmed Einstein's equation for the photoelectric effect.
122557.m: Millikan was honoured for the elementary charge and the photoelectric effect.

122558.q: Which cut-off year is used in Europe, after which introduced species count as neobiota?
122558.e: Neobiota are species that reached a new area through humans after the discovery of America in 1492. With the beginning of world trade, the spread of species increased greatly.
122558.m: Neobiota are species introduced by humans after 1492.

122559.q: How do neobiota usually reach a new area?
a: Through humans, for example with trade and transport
Through migrating birds on their journeys
122559.e: Neobiota are spread by humans, either on purpose, for example as ornamental plants, or by accident, for example with goods and vehicles.
122559.m: Neobiota are brought to new areas by humans.

122560.q: What are non-native fungus species called that have been introduced by humans?
122560.e: Neomycetes are introduced fungi, for example the cause of ash dieback. The part “myces” comes from the Greek word for fungus.
122560.m: Introduced fungus species are called neomycetes.

122561.q: What are plants called that reached Central Europe through humans in prehistoric times, for example with early farming?
122561.e: Archaeophytes are “old immigrants” that came with humans in prehistoric or ancient times, for example many arable weeds such as the cornflower. Neophytes only came in modern times.
122561.m: Archaeophytes are plants that came to Europe with humans very early on.

122562.q: Which organisation keeps Switzerland's “Black List” of invasive non-native plants?
122562.e: Info Flora is the national data and information centre for the Swiss flora. It keeps a Black List and a Watch List of invasive neophytes.
122562.m: Info Flora keeps the Black List of invasive neophytes in Switzerland.

122563.q: How is the invasive yellow nutsedge usually spread from field to field in Switzerland?
a: By the wind over long distances
122563.e: Yellow nutsedge spreads mainly through small underground tubers. These stick in soil on tractors, harvesters and planting material and so reach new fields.
122563.m: Yellow nutsedge is spread with soil on farm machinery.

122564.q: Why is Japanese knotweed so difficult to control?
a: It sprouts again from small pieces of rhizome
122564.e: Japanese knotweed forms a deep, widely branching rhizome system. Even small fragments can sprout again, which is why soil containing rhizomes must not be moved.
122564.m: Japanese knotweed sprouts again even from small pieces of rhizome.

122565.q: Why is the sap of giant hogweed dangerous for people?
a: It makes the skin sensitive to light
122565.e: The sap contains furocoumarins, which make the skin phototoxic. Combined with sunlight, blisters similar to burns develop.
122565.m: With sunlight, giant hogweed sap causes burns on the skin.

122566.q: Which continent does Canadian goldenrod, which is invasive in Switzerland, originally come from?
122566.e: Canadian goldenrod comes from North America and was brought to Europe as an ornamental plant and a plant for bees. Today it forms dense stands that crowd out native plants.
122566.m: Canadian goldenrod comes from North America.

122567.q: In ecology, when do we speak of a biological invasion?
a: When a non-native species becomes established and spreads widely
When a native species dies out
When migrating birds leave in autumn
When a new species arises through mutation
122567.e: A biological invasion occurs when a species spread by humans multiplies and spreads on its own in the new area. This often has negative effects on nature, the economy or health.
122567.m: In a biological invasion, a non-native species spreads widely.

122568.q: Why can introduced species often multiply especially strongly in a new area?
a: They lack natural enemies and diseases there
All animals avoid them there because they are unfamiliar
They lose their ability to reproduce in the new area
The climate there is always warmer than at home
122568.e: In its homeland, a species is kept in check by predators, parasites and diseases. If these opponents are missing in the new area, the species can spread unchecked.
122568.m: Without natural enemies, introduced species spread easily.

122569.q: Which amphibian, introduced to Australia in 1935 to control pests, itself became a devastating invasive species?
122569.e: The cane toad was supposed to eat beetles in sugar cane fields. However, it spread rapidly and poisons many native predators with its skin toxin.
122569.m: In Australia, the cane toad itself became a plague.

122570.q: What was the result of introducing the Nile perch into Lake Victoria?
a: Many endemic cichlid species died out
122570.e: The predatory Nile perch ate large numbers of cichlids, many of which lived only in Lake Victoria. As a result, hundreds of species declined sharply or died out.
122570.m: The Nile perch caused a mass extinction of cichlids in Lake Victoria.

122571.q: Which introduced animal species wiped out most of the native forest birds on the Pacific island of Guam?
122571.e: The brown tree snake probably reached Guam with military transports after the Second World War. Without natural enemies it multiplied strongly and ate the island's forest birds.
122571.m: On Guam, the brown tree snake wiped out almost all the forest birds.

122572.q: Which disease do introduced North American crayfish such as the signal crayfish pass on to the native noble crayfish?
122572.e: North American crayfish usually carry the crayfish plague pathogen without falling ill. For the noble crayfish and other European species, however, the disease is almost always fatal.
122572.m: Signal crayfish pass the deadly crayfish plague on to native crayfish.

122573.q: What is the often decades-long period called, during which an introduced species hardly spreads before suddenly becoming invasive?
122573.e: During the lag phase a new species stays inconspicuous, for example because it first has to adapt genetically or suitable conditions are missing. An explosive burst of spreading can follow.
122573.m: Before spreading widely, a new species often goes through a lag phase.

122574.q: Which animal did the settler Thomas Austin release in Australia in 1859, starting one of the best-known biological invasions?
122574.e: In 1859 Thomas Austin released wild rabbits for hunting. Without enough enemies they multiplied explosively and still cause great damage to vegetation and farming today.
122574.m: The wild rabbits released in 1859 became a plague in Australia.

122575.q: What did the global biodiversity council IPBES conclude in 2023 about the role of invasive species?
a: They were involved in about 60 per cent of documented extinctions
122575.e: The 2023 IPBES report found that invasive species played an important role in about 60 per cent of recorded extinctions worldwide. They are among the five most important direct drivers of biodiversity loss.
122575.m: Invasive species are among the most important causes of species extinction.

122576.q: What does the tens rule of invasion biology describe?
a: Only about one species in ten makes the next step towards invasion
One species in ten dies out every year
Invasive species spread ten times faster
You need ten animals to establish a species
122576.e: Of the species introduced, about one in ten escapes into the wild, of these about one in ten becomes established, and of these about one in ten becomes harmful.
122576.m: According to the tens rule, about one species in ten makes the next step.

122577.q: According to the tens rule, how many out of 1000 introduced species become invasive pests?
122577.e: Over three stages with a success rate of about 10 per cent each, about 1 pest remains out of 1000 introduced species. So 1000 times 0.1 times 0.1 times 0.1 equals 1.
122577.m: According to the tens rule, only about one in a thousand introduced species becomes invasive.

122578.q: According to the tens rule, how many out of 1000 introduced species become permanently established in the wild?
122578.e: About 10 per cent of the introduced species turn up in the wild, which is 100. Of these, about 10 per cent become established, so 10 species.
122578.m: According to the tens rule, about ten out of a thousand introduced species become established.

122579.q: Why is the tens rule only described as an average?
a: The actual rates vary greatly from group to group
Because exactly ten species were studied
Because it only applies to plants
Because it is laid down by law
122579.e: The number ten is a rough average. Depending on the group of species and the region, the success rates are much lower or higher.
122579.m: The tens rule is only a rough average.

122580.q: According to the tens rule, how many out of 1000 introduced species turn up in the wild?
122580.e: About 10 per cent of introduced species escape into the wild, so about 100 out of 1000. Of these, about 10 become established.
122580.m: According to the tens rule, about one in ten introduced species escapes into the wild.

122581.q: Which plant is a well-known example of an invasive species in Switzerland?
122581.e: Japanese knotweed was introduced as an ornamental plant. It grows very fast, crowds out native plants and can damage riverbanks and buildings.
122581.m: Japanese knotweed is an invasive plant.

122582.q: In the tens rule, which stage follows a species occasionally escaping into the wild?
122582.e: The stages are: introduced, occasionally escaped, established and finally harmful or invasive. Only an established species reproduces permanently without human help.
122582.m: In the tens rule, escaping into the wild is followed by establishment.

122583.q: From a scientific point of view, what kind of statement is the tens rule?
122583.e: The tens rule describes rough averages from many observations. For individual species or groups, the rate can differ greatly.
122583.m: The tens rule is a statistical rule of thumb, not a law of nature.

122584.q: What does the enemy release hypothesis say to explain invasive species?
a: They benefit from the absence of their natural enemies
They have a higher mutation rate
122584.e: In the new area there are often no predators, parasites and pathogens that keep the species in check at home. As a result it can multiply more than native competitors.
122584.m: According to the enemy release hypothesis, invasive species are free of their enemies in the new area.

122585.q: According to the enemy release hypothesis, which enemies does an introduced plant mainly lack in the new area?
122585.e: Specialists depend on one particular host species and are therefore rarely introduced along with it. Generalists in the new area, however, may well attack the plant.
122585.m: Introduced species mainly lack specialised enemies in the new area.

122586.q: Why can an introduced plant grow especially strongly without its enemies?
a: It needs less energy for defence
It can suddenly fix nitrogen from the air
122586.e: Making defensive substances costs a plant a lot of energy. If the enemies are missing, it can put this energy into growth and spreading instead.
122586.m: Without enemies, energy goes from defence into growth.

122587.q: Which control method is based directly on the enemy release hypothesis?
122587.e: In classical biological control, specialised opponents from the area of origin are deliberately introduced. This restores the lost pressure from enemies.
122587.m: Classical biological control deliberately introduces the missing enemies.

122588.q: With which insect were invasive prickly pear cacti successfully pushed back in Australia from the 1920s onwards?
122588.e: The caterpillars of the South American cactus moth (Cactoblastis cactorum) eat prickly pears from the inside. They cleared huge areas in Queensland and New South Wales of the cacti.
122588.m: In Australia, the cactus moth pushed back the invasive prickly pears.

122589.q: Why must an insect released to control an invasive plant be tested for a long time beforehand?
a: It must not attack native plants
It must be able to fly as fast as possible
122589.e: An introduced opponent should only harm the target plant. Otherwise it could itself become an invasive species and endanger native plants.
122589.m: Biological control agents must be specialised on their target species.

122590.q: How can the enemy release hypothesis be tested empirically?
a: By comparing attack by enemies in the home range and the new range
122590.e: Researchers compare how many parasites, pathogens and predators a species has in its homeland and in the new area. Much less attack in the new area supports the hypothesis.
122590.m: The hypothesis is tested by comparing attack by enemies in the home range and the new range.

122591.q: Which limitation of the enemy release hypothesis often appears over time?
a: Native enemies adapt to the new species
122591.e: The longer a species lives in the new area, the more native herbivores and pathogens use it. The advantage of being free of enemies therefore often decreases.
122591.m: The advantage of being free of enemies often fades over time.

a: Affecting other plants through chemicals released
122592.e: In allelopathy, plants release substances through their roots, leaves or leaf litter. These inhibit or promote the germination and growth of other plants.
122592.m: Allelopathy is the chemical influence on other plants.

122593.q: Which Greek words make up the term allelopathy?
122593.e: Allelopathy comes from the Greek “allelon” (mutual) and “pathos” (suffering). The term was coined in 1937 by the Austrian botanist Hans Molisch.

122594.q: Which allelopathic substance does the walnut tree produce, which inhibits the growth of many plants beneath it?
122594.e: Juglone forms from precursors in the leaves, roots and fruit husks of the walnut tree. It inhibits germination and growth in many plants.
122594.m: The walnut tree inhibits other plants with juglone.

122595.q: Why are some invasive plants with chemical defences especially successful in the new area?
a: The native plants are not adapted to these substances
It rains more and more in the new area
The substances fertilise the soil only for them
Native animals spread the substances further
122595.e: Plants in the invaders' homeland have had time to adapt to their defensive substances. Native species in the new area, by contrast, are defenceless against them. This is known as the novel weapons hypothesis.
122595.m: New chemical weapons help invasive plants against unprepared neighbours.

122596.q: Which tree, invasive in Ticino, releases the allelopathic substance ailanthone?
122596.e: The tree of heaven (Ailanthus altissima), which comes from China, produces ailanthone, which inhibits the growth of other plants. It is spreading strongly, especially on the southern side of the Alps.
122596.m: The tree of heaven inhibits other plants with the substance ailanthone.

122597.q: Which organisms does garlic mustard, invasive in North America, harm through substances released by its roots?
a: The root nodule bacteria of peas
122597.e: Garlic mustard releases breakdown products of glucosinolates that inhibit mycorrhizal fungi. Native trees that depend on these fungi therefore grow less well.
122597.m: In North America, garlic mustard harms mycorrhizal fungi.

122598.q: How can sorghum suppress neighbouring weeds with its roots?
a: It releases inhibiting substances into the soil
It takes light away from the weeds through its roots
It lures pollinators away from the weeds
It lowers the soil temperature sharply
122598.e: The root hairs of sorghum release the substance sorgoleone. It inhibits photosynthesis in neighbouring weeds, a typical example of allelopathy.
122598.m: Sorghum inhibits weeds with substances from its roots.

122599.q: How is allelopathy used deliberately in farming?
a: Cover crops and mulch suppress weeds
Fruit ripens more slowly in storage
122599.e: Certain cover crops such as rye release inhibiting substances as they break down. As a result fewer weeds germinate and fewer herbicides are needed.
122599.m: Thanks to allelopathy, cover crops can suppress weeds.

122600.q: Which class of antibodies is responsible for the immediate reaction in a pollen allergy?
122600.e: In people with allergies, the immune system makes IgE antibodies against harmless pollen proteins. These bind to mast cells and trigger the allergic reaction on renewed contact.
122600.m: IgE antibodies play the main role in pollen allergy.

122601.q: Which messenger substance is released from mast cells in a pollen allergy and causes sneezing and itchy eyes?
122601.e: When pollen allergens bind to the IgE on mast cells, these release histamine. Histamine widens blood vessels and irritates nerves, which is why antihistamines help.
122601.m: Histamine causes the typical symptoms of hay fever.

122602.q: Which medical term describes an allergy triggered by pollen, with a runny nose and irritated eyes?
122602.e: Pollinosis is the medical name for hay fever. It mainly affects the mucous membranes of the nose and eyes.
122602.m: In medicine, hay fever is called pollinosis.

122603.q: With an untreated pollen allergy, what is meant by the allergy “moving down a floor”?
a: The symptoms spread to the bronchi and asthma develops
The allergy switches from birch to grass
The allergy spreads to the skin
122603.e: When this happens, the inflammation moves from the upper airways to the lower ones. Allergic asthma develops, which is why early treatment is recommended.
122603.m: When an allergy moves down a floor, hay fever turns into allergic asthma.

122604.q: Which federal office runs Switzerland's national pollen monitoring network?
122604.e: MeteoSwiss measures the concentration of pollen in the air at many stations. The data are used in pollen forecasts for people with allergies.
122604.m: MeteoSwiss runs the Swiss pollen monitoring network.

122605.q: Which food often causes an itchy mouth as a cross-allergy in people allergic to birch pollen?
122605.e: A birch allergen resembles a protein in apples. The immune system confuses them, which leads to oral allergy syndrome. Cooking usually destroys the protein.
122605.m: People allergic to birch pollen often react to raw apples too.

122606.q: What is the treatment called in which the body is accustomed to increasing doses of an allergen over several years?
122606.e: In hyposensitisation (specific immunotherapy), allergens are given regularly as injections or tablets. This makes the immune system more tolerant; treatment usually lasts three to five years.
122606.m: Hyposensitisation gets the body used to the allergen.

122607.q: Roughly how common is hay fever in Switzerland?
a: About one person in five is affected
About one person in a hundred is affected
Only children under ten are affected
122607.e: According to aha! Swiss Allergy Centre, about a fifth of the population suffers from a pollen allergy. This makes it one of the most common chronic illnesses.
122607.m: In Switzerland, about one person in five has hay fever.

122608.q: Which region does the Asian long-horned beetle originally come from?
122608.e: The beetle (Anoplophora glabripennis) is native to China and Korea. From there it was introduced to North America and Europe.
122608.m: The Asian long-horned beetle comes from China and Korea.

122609.q: How was the Asian long-horned beetle mainly introduced to Europe?
a: With packaging wood such as pallets
122609.e: The larvae live in wood and survive transport in untreated wooden pallets and crates. In this way they reached Europe with deliveries of goods, for example stone.
122609.m: The long-horned beetle travels as a larva in packaging wood.

122610.q: Which part of a tree is damaged by the larvae of the Asian long-horned beetle?
a: The wood of the trunk and branches
122610.e: The larvae first feed under the bark and then bore deep tunnels into the wood. This weakens even healthy broadleaf trees, which can die or break.
122610.m: The larvae of the long-horned beetle eat away the wood of healthy broadleaf trees.

122611.q: Which genus of tree does the Asian long-horned beetle attack particularly often in Europe?
122611.e: The beetle attacks many broadleaf tree species but prefers maples. Poplars, willows, birches and horse chestnuts are also at risk, but conifers are not.
122611.m: The Asian long-horned beetle prefers maple trees.

122612.q: How can you recognise an adult Asian long-horned beetle?
a: Shiny black with white spots and very long antennae
Red with black dots and short antennae
Brown and hairy with a sting
122612.e: The beetle is about 2.5 to 3.5 cm long, shiny black and has irregular white spots. Its black and white ringed antennae are longer than its body.
122612.m: The long-horned beetle is black with white spots and long antennae.

122613.q: Which signs on the trunk reveal an infestation with the Asian long-horned beetle?
a: Perfectly round exit holes about 1 cm across
122613.e: The adult beetles bore their way out of the wood through round holes about as thick as a finger. In addition there are chewed fibres and wood shavings at the foot of the trunk.
122613.m: Round exit holes about one centimetre wide give away the long-horned beetle.

122614.q: How is an infestation with the Asian long-horned beetle dealt with in Switzerland?
a: Infested trees are felled and destroyed
The beetles are lured with food and released
The infestation is left to disappear by itself
122614.e: The beetle is a particularly dangerous quarantine organism and must be reported. Infested trees are felled, shredded or burned, and the surrounding area is monitored for years, also with sniffer dogs.
122614.m: Infested trees are felled and destroyed to wipe out the beetle.

122615.q: Under the international standard ISPM 15, how is packaging wood usually treated to kill wood pests?
a: It is washed with salt water
122615.e: ISPM 15 usually requires heat treatment in which the core of the wood reaches at least 56 degrees Celsius for at least 30 minutes. Treated wood carries a mark.
122615.m: Under ISPM 15, packaging wood is heat-treated.

122616.e: The cause is the sac fungus Cryphonectria parasitica. It enters the bark through wounds and destroys the cambium.
122616.m: Chestnut blight is caused by a fungus.

122617.q: From which region was the cause of chestnut blight introduced?
122617.e: Cryphonectria parasitica comes from East Asia, where the local chestnut species are largely resistant. It reached North America and Europe with plant material.
122617.m: The cause of chestnut blight comes from East Asia.

122618.q: What was the result of chestnut blight in North America in the 20th century?
a: The American chestnut was almost completely wiped out
122618.e: From 1904 the fungus spread from New York and killed billions of American chestnuts. The once common forest tree now mostly survives only as shoots from old stumps.
122618.m: Chestnut blight wiped out almost all American chestnuts.

122619.q: Which tree species is affected by chestnut blight in Ticino?
122619.e: The sweet chestnut (Castanea sativa) shapes the chestnut groves of southern Switzerland. The fungus only attacks true chestnuts, not the horse chestnut, which is not related botanically.
122619.m: Chestnut blight attacks the sweet chestnut, not the horse chestnut.

122620.q: How can a virus help sweet chestnuts against chestnut blight?
a: It infects the fungus and weakens it
It kills the spores in the air
It attracts birds that eat the fungus
122620.e: A virus can infect the pathogen and make it less aggressive. This is called hypovirulence: the bark wounds heal over and the tree survives.
122620.m: A virus can weaken the chestnut blight fungus.

122621.q: Why was chestnut blight milder in Europe than in North America in the long run?
a: Hypovirulent strains of the fungus spread naturally
There are no chestnuts in Europe
The fungus cannot survive the winter in Europe
122621.e: In Europe, hypovirulent strains spread spontaneously and damped the epidemic. In North America, among other things, the greater genetic diversity of the fungal strains hindered the spread of the virus.
122621.m: In Europe, hypovirulent fungal strains slowed chestnut blight.

122622.q: How does the cause of chestnut blight get into the tree?
122622.e: Spores of the fungus are spread by wind, rain and animals. They infect the tree through bark injuries, for example after hail, frost or pruning.
122622.m: Chestnut blight enters the tree through wounds in the bark.

122623.q: Which symptom is typical of chestnut blight?
a: Orange-red fruiting bodies and dead shoots above the bark wound
White pustules on the leaves in spring
122623.e: The fungus forms orange fruiting bodies in the infected bark. Because it girdles the branch, the parts above it wilt, and their brown leaves often stay hanging.
122623.m: Chestnut blight shows up as orange-red fruiting bodies and wilting branches.

122624.e: Fire blight is caused by the bacterium Erwinia amylovora. It enters the plant mainly through flowers and wounds.
122624.m: Fire blight is caused by the bacterium Erwinia amylovora.

122625.q: Which group of plants is mainly affected by fire blight?
a: Pome fruit such as apple, pear and quince
Cereals such as wheat and barley
Conifers such as spruce and fir
122625.e: Fire blight attacks members of the rose family related to pome fruit. Besides apple, pear and quince, ornamental plants such as cotoneaster, firethorn and hawthorn are also hosts.
122625.m: Fire blight mainly attacks pome fruit such as apple, pear and quince.

122626.q: Which continent does fire blight originally come from?
122626.e: Fire blight was first described in North America in the 18th century. It reached Europe in the 20th century, first England.
122626.m: Fire blight originally comes from North America.

122627.q: How did fire blight get its name?
a: Infected plant parts look as if they have been burnt
It only occurs after forest fires
122627.e: Leaves, flowers and shoots turn brown to black and stay hanging on the tree. As a result they look as if they have been scorched by fire.
122627.m: Plants infected with fire blight look as if they have been burnt.

122628.q: Which typical symptom of fire blight appears on young shoots?
a: The shoot tips bend into a hook
The shoots grow twice as fast
122628.e: Infected shoot tips wilt and bend like a shepherd's crook. In damp weather, bacterial ooze can also seep out.
122628.m: Shoot tips bent into a hook are a typical symptom of fire blight.

122629.q: Which animals carry the fire blight pathogen from flower to flower during blossom time?
122629.e: The bacterial ooze is sticky and is picked up by pollinators. Bees and other insects then spread the pathogen to other flowers.
122629.m: Bees can carry the fire blight pathogen from flower to flower.

122630.q: In what weather during blossom time is the risk of fire blight infection greatest?
122630.e: The bacteria multiply especially fast on the stigmas of the flowers at warm temperatures and high humidity. That is why forecasting models give warnings in such conditions.
122630.m: Warm, damp weather during blossom time encourages fire blight.

122631.q: Which tool do fruit growers use to decide the right time for protective measures against fire blight?
a: An infection forecasting model based on weather data
122631.e: Forecasting models such as Maryblyt calculate the risk of infection from temperature, humidity and stage of flowering. Agroscope and cantonal advisory offices publish warnings during blossom time.
122631.m: Fruit growers use forecasting models to estimate the risk of fire blight.

122632.q: Why do cargo ships take on ballast water?
a: For stability and draught when there is little cargo
As drinking water for the crew
122632.e: Without cargo, a ship sits too high in the water and becomes unstable. Ballast water in tanks balances the weight and is released again at the destination port.
122632.m: Ballast water keeps empty ships stable.

122633.q: Why is ballast water an important pathway for biological invasions?
a: It carries organisms and larvae to foreign ports
It heats the sea a lot
It contains plant seeds from forests
122633.e: Plankton, larvae, algae and bacteria are taken in with the water. When it is released at the destination port, these organisms can settle in a new area.
122633.m: Ballast water carries sea creatures across the oceans.

122634.q: Which international convention on ballast water came into force on 8 September 2017?
a: The IMO Ballast Water Management Convention
The Washington Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species
122634.e: The International Maritime Organization's ballast water convention was adopted in 2004. It requires ships to treat or exchange their ballast water.
122634.m: The IMO ballast water convention has applied since 2017.

122635.q: Why should ballast water be exchanged as far out on the open sea as possible?
a: Coastal organisms usually survive poorly in the open ocean
There are no ocean currents there
122635.e: The convention requires the exchange to take place, where possible, at least 200 nautical miles from the coast. Coastal organisms taken on are released in the open ocean, and the new water contains hardly any coastal species.
122635.m: Ballast water is exchanged far out at sea.

122636.q: Which method is often used on board to treat ballast water?
122636.e: Many systems filter out larger organisms and kill smaller ones with UV light or chlorine produced by electrolysis. This way ships meet the D-2 performance standard.
122636.m: Ballast water is often filtered and treated with UV light.

122637.q: Which species, introduced with ballast water, caused the anchovy fishery in the Black Sea to collapse in the 1980s?
122637.e: The comb jelly from the western Atlantic ate zooplankton as well as fish eggs and larvae. Its mass increase contributed to the collapse of the anchovy stocks.
122637.m: An introduced comb jelly damaged fishing in the Black Sea.

122638.q: Which Asian crab probably reached Europe with ballast water and now burrows into riverbanks?
122638.e: The Chinese mitten crab was discovered in Germany at the beginning of the 20th century. It travels far upstream, digs burrows in banks and clogs fishing nets.
122638.m: The Chinese mitten crab came to Europe with ships.

122639.q: Which United Nations organisation is responsible for the ballast water convention?
122639.e: The IMO, based in London, regulates safety and environmental protection in shipping. It drew up the convention and monitors how it is put into practice.
122639.m: The IMO is responsible for the rules on ballast water.

122640.q: Which mussel species was discovered in North America's Great Lakes in 1988, having arrived there with ballast water from Europe?
122640.e: The zebra mussel was discovered in 1988 in Lake St. Clair between Lake Huron and Lake Erie. It spread quickly and causes high costs there at water intakes.
122640.m: The zebra mussel reached North America's Great Lakes with ballast water.

122641.q: Where does the quagga mussel originally come from?
a: From the Black Sea and Caspian region
122641.e: The quagga mussel (Dreissena rostriformis bugensis) comes from the catchment area of the Dnieper and the Southern Bug. From there it spread via waterways and ships.
122641.m: The quagga mussel comes from the Black Sea region.

122642.q: What is the quagga mussel named after?
a: An extinct zebra of the steppes
The noise it makes when opening
122642.e: The quagga was an extinct form of zebra with a coat that was only partly striped. The mussel has similar stripes on its shell.
122642.m: The quagga mussel is named after an extinct zebra.

122643.q: How does the quagga mussel differ ecologically from the related zebra mussel?
a: It also colonises soft beds and great depths
It lives only in flowing water
122643.e: The quagga mussel tolerates colder temperatures and can also settle on muddy beds more than 100 metres deep. As a result it is replacing the zebra mussel in many lakes.
122643.m: Unlike the zebra mussel, the quagga mussel also colonises deep lake beds.

122644.q: How does the quagga mussel feed?
a: It filters plankton out of the water
122644.e: As a filter feeder it draws in water and sieves out suspended particles and plankton. Large populations make the water clearer but take plankton away from the food chain.
122644.m: The quagga mussel feeds by filtering plankton from the water.

122645.q: Which technical problem does the quagga mussel cause in Swiss lakes?
a: It clogs the pipes of drinking water intakes
It eats through steel ships' hulls
It makes the lakes freeze over
122645.e: The mussels attach themselves in dense colonies to pipes and filters with byssus threads. Water suppliers therefore have to carry out costly cleaning or rebuild their facilities.
122645.m: Quagga mussels clog water pipes and intakes.

122646.q: How does the quagga mussel most often get from one lake to the next?
a: With boats and the leftover water in them
With migrating birds over the Alps
122646.e: Its free-swimming larvae survive in leftover water in boats, and young mussels stick to the hull. That is why boats should be cleaned and dried before moving to another body of water.
122646.m: Boats carry the quagga mussel from lake to lake.

122647.q: Why does the quagga mussel spread so quickly in a lake?
a: It produces huge numbers of tiny, free-swimming larvae
It can crawl over land from lake to lake
122647.e: A female releases hundreds of thousands of eggs. The larvae drift in the water for a few weeks before settling, and so are spread over a wide area.
122647.m: The quagga mussel spreads through countless free-swimming larvae.

122648.q: In which large Swiss border lake was the quagga mussel first recorded in 2016?
122648.e: The quagga mussel was discovered in Lake Constance in 2016 and has since spread massively. It now also colonises great depths there.
122648.m: Since 2016 the quagga mussel has been spreading in Lake Constance.

122649.q: How can you recognise the Asian tiger mosquito?
a: Black with white stripes and a white stripe down its back
Brown with no markings and very large
122649.e: The tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus) is small with a black and white pattern. A single white stripe running lengthwise on its thorax is typical.
122649.m: The tiger mosquito is black and white with a white stripe on its back.

122650.q: When does the Asian tiger mosquito mainly bite?
a: Not at all, it only drinks nectar
122650.e: Unlike many native mosquitoes, the tiger mosquito is active during the day. It bites especially in the morning and late afternoon.
122650.m: The Asian tiger mosquito bites mainly during the day.

122651.q: In which canton was the Asian tiger mosquito first recorded in Switzerland in 2003?
122651.e: In 2003 the tiger mosquito reached Ticino from Italy via road traffic. Today it is widespread there and also occurs north of the Alps.
122651.m: The tiger mosquito was first discovered in Ticino in 2003.

122652.q: Which pathogens can the Asian tiger mosquito transmit in principle?
122652.e: The tiger mosquito can transmit certain tropical viruses if it has previously bitten an infected person. In southern Europe this has already led to local outbreaks of dengue and chikungunya.
122652.m: The tiger mosquito can transmit dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses.

122653.q: Where does the Asian tiger mosquito prefer to lay its eggs?
a: In small amounts of water such as plant saucers and watering cans
122653.e: The females lay their eggs just above the waterline in small containers. That is why emptying standing water around the house is the most important prevention.
122653.m: Standing water in small containers is the tiger mosquito's nursery.

122654.q: Which property of its eggs makes it easier for the Asian tiger mosquito to be spread around the world?
a: They only hatch in the tropics
122654.e: The eggs can survive long dry periods and, in temperate areas, the winter too. In this way they crossed continents, for example in used car tyres.
122654.m: The tiger mosquito's drought-resistant eggs travel the world easily.

122655.q: Which biological agent is used against tiger mosquito larvae?
122655.e: Bti is a bacterium whose protein crystals specifically damage the gut of mosquito larvae. It is harmless to most other animals.
122655.m: The bacterium Bti is used against tiger mosquito larvae.

122656.q: Which method using males made infertile was tested in Ticino to control tiger mosquitoes?
122656.e: In the sterile insect technique, sterilised males bred in the laboratory are released. Females that mate with them lay eggs that cannot develop.
122656.m: Sterile males can be used to reduce the number of tiger mosquitoes.

122657.q: Why has the Asian tiger mosquito been spreading strongly in Europe for several decades?
a: Through worldwide trade in goods and milder winters
Because migrating birds spread its eggs
Because it was released for pollination
Because it only breeds in salt water
122657.e: The eggs travel in used car tyres and plants, for example, and adults in cars and lorries. Milder winters make survival easier. It was first recorded in Europe in Albania in 1979.
122657.m: Trade and global warming help the tiger mosquito in Europe.

122757.q: Which organelle is found in plant cells but is missing in animal cells?
122757.e: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis; animal cells have no chloroplasts.
122757.m: Only plant cells and algae have chloroplasts.

122758.q: Which small organelle breaks down long-chain fatty acids and splits toxic hydrogen peroxide with the enzyme catalase?
122758.e: Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes; the hydrogen peroxide produced is broken down by catalase into water and oxygen.
122758.m: Peroxisomes detoxify hydrogen peroxide with catalase.

122759.q: Which structure separates the contents of the nucleus from the cytoplasm?
122759.e: The nuclear envelope consists of two membranes and is pierced by nuclear pores through which substances are exchanged.
122759.m: The nuclear envelope with its nuclear pores surrounds the genetic material.

122760.q: What is the membrane called that surrounds the large central vacuole of a plant cell?
122760.e: The tonoplast separates the cell sap of the vacuole from the cytoplasm and regulates the exchange of substances.
122760.m: The vacuole of the plant cell is surrounded by the tonoplast.

122762.q: Why is part of the endoplasmic reticulum called the “rough ER”?
a: It is surrounded by a cell wall
122762.e: Under the electron microscope the rough ER looks grainy because many ribosomes are attached to the outside of its membranes.
122762.m: The rough ER is studded with ribosomes.

122763.q: What is the main task of the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
a: Making membrane proteins and proteins for secretion
122763.e: Proteins are made at the rough ER that are built into membranes or exported from the cell; in the process they enter the inside of the ER.
122763.m: Proteins for membranes and for export are made at the rough ER.

122764.q: Which substances are mainly made at the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
a: Lipids such as phospholipids and steroids
122764.e: The smooth ER has no ribosomes; it synthesises lipids, including membrane phospholipids and steroid hormones.
122764.m: The smooth ER is the lipid factory of the cell.

122765.q: Which structure is the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum directly connected to?
122765.e: The ER emerges directly from the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope; its interior is connected to the space between the two nuclear membranes.
122765.m: The ER and the nuclear envelope form one continuous membrane system.

122766.q: What task does the especially extensive smooth ER perform in liver cells?
122766.e: In liver cells, the smooth ER contains enzymes that chemically convert medicines and toxins so that they can be excreted.
122766.m: The smooth ER of the liver helps with detoxification.

122767.q: How do newly made proteins get from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus?
a: In membrane vesicles that bud off
122767.e: Transport vesicles bud off from the ER, fuse with the membranes of the Golgi apparatus and release their cargo.
122767.m: Vesicles transport proteins from the ER to the Golgi apparatus.

122768.q: What causes a ribosome to bind to the ER during protein synthesis?
a: A signal peptide on the new protein
A start codon on the mRNA
A poly-A tail on the mRNA
122768.e: A signal sequence at the start of the growing chain is bound by a recognition particle (SRP), which guides the ribosome to the ER membrane.
122768.m: A signal peptide sends proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum.

122769.q: What is a single stack of flattened membrane cisternae of the Golgi apparatus called?
122769.e: The Golgi apparatus of a cell consists of one or more dictyosomes, that is, stacks of flat membrane sacs.
122769.m: A Golgi stack is called a dictyosome.

122770.q: In which cells did Camillo Golgi discover the organelle named after him in 1898?
122770.e: Camillo Golgi stained nerve cells with silver salts and discovered a fine network inside the cell. In 1906 he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.
122770.m: Golgi discovered his organelle in nerve cells.

122771.q: Which side of the Golgi apparatus receives the vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum?
122771.e: The cis side faces the ER and serves as the receiving side; vesicles are sent off from the opposite trans side.
122771.m: The Golgi apparatus receives on the cis side and dispatches on the trans side.

122772.q: What is the main task of the Golgi apparatus?
a: Storing and reading the genetic material
122772.e: In the Golgi apparatus, proteins from the ER are processed further, given address labels and packed into vesicles for their destination.
122772.m: The Golgi apparatus is the post office and packing station of the cell.

122773.q: Which chemical change do many proteins undergo in the Golgi apparatus?
a: They are split into amino acids
They are reduced to fatty acids
122773.e: In the Golgi apparatus, the sugar chains attached in the ER (glycosylation) are modified and extended; this produces glycoproteins.
122773.m: In the Golgi apparatus, many proteins receive their final sugar chains.

122774.q: How are secretory proteins packed by the Golgi apparatus released from the cell?
122774.e: Secretory vesicles move to the cell membrane, fuse with it and empty their contents outside.
122774.m: In exocytosis, vesicles fuse with the cell membrane.

122775.q: Which organelle is formed when vesicles bud off from the Golgi apparatus?
122775.e: Vesicles containing digestive enzymes bud off from the trans side of the Golgi apparatus and become lysosomes.
122775.m: Lysosomes come from the Golgi apparatus.

122776.q: What task do Golgi vesicles perform in plant cells after nuclear division?
122776.e: The vesicles supply material for the new cell wall and fuse in the middle of the cell to form the cell plate, which separates the daughter cells.
122776.m: Plant cells form a cell plate between the daughter cells.

122777.q: In which cells is the Golgi apparatus particularly well developed?
a: In gland cells with a lot of secretion
122777.e: Cells that release many substances, such as goblet cells or cells of the pancreas, need a lot of packing and dispatch capacity.
122777.m: Cells that secrete a lot have a large Golgi apparatus.

122778.e: Ribosomes are complexes of ribosomal RNA and numerous proteins, made up of a large and a small subunit.
122778.m: Ribosomes consist of RNA and proteins.

122779.q: What sedimentation coefficient do the ribosomes in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells have?
122779.e: Eukaryotic ribosomes in the cytoplasm sediment at 80 Svedberg; their subunits are 60S and 40S.
122779.m: 80S ribosomes work in the cytoplasm of eukaryotes.

122780.q: Which step of protein biosynthesis do ribosomes carry out?
122780.e: At the ribosome, the base sequence of the mRNA is translated into a chain of amino acids.
122780.m: Ribosomes translate the mRNA into proteins.

122781.q: What is a group of ribosomes called that read the same mRNA at the same time?
122781.e: Several ribosomes can work one after another on one mRNA; in this way many copies of a protein are made at once.
122781.m: A polysome consists of several ribosomes on one mRNA.

122782.q: Which RNA brings the amino acids to the ribosome?
122782.e: Transfer RNA carries an amino acid and uses its anticodon to recognise the matching codon of the mRNA.
122782.m: The tRNA delivers the amino acids to the ribosome.

122783.q: Why can antibiotics such as tetracycline harm bacteria without seriously disturbing protein synthesis in the human cytoplasm?
122783.e: The ribosomes of bacteria differ in size and structure from the cytoplasmic ribosomes of humans, so some drugs bind specifically only to the bacterial ones.
122783.m: Many antibiotics specifically attack the ribosomes of bacteria.

122784.q: What distinguishes ribosomes from organelles such as lysosomes or mitochondria?
a: They are larger than the nucleus
122784.e: Ribosomes are molecular complexes without a surrounding membrane and are found in all cells, including bacteria.
122784.m: Ribosomes are not surrounded by a membrane.

122785.q: Roughly what pH is found inside a lysosome?
122785.e: Lysosomes are acidic; their digestive enzymes work best at a pH of around 4.5 to 5.
122785.m: The inside of a lysosome is acidic.

122786.q: What kind of enzymes do lysosomes contain?
122786.e: Lysosomes contain dozens of hydrolytic enzymes that split proteins, nucleic acids, fats and carbohydrates.
122786.m: Lysosomes digest substances with acid hydrolases.

122787.q: Why are lysosomes sometimes called the “stomach” of the cell?
a: They produce stomach acid for the body
They take up food from the intestine
122787.e: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes and break down cell components and particles taken in. They were discovered by the Belgian researcher Christian de Duve.
122787.m: Lysosomes are the digestive vesicles of the cell.

122788.q: What is the process called in which a cell breaks down its own damaged components in lysosomes?
122788.e: In autophagy, cell components are enclosed by a membrane and digested with lysosomes; Yoshinori Ohsumi received the Nobel Prize for this in 2016.
122788.m: In autophagy, the cell recycles its own components.

122789.q: What is the cause of lysosomal storage diseases such as Tay-Sachs disease?
a: A fault in the nuclear envelope
122789.e: If a particular breakdown enzyme is missing, undigested substances build up in the lysosomes; in Tay-Sachs these are gangliosides in nerve cells.
122789.m: In storage diseases, the lysosomes lack a breakdown enzyme.

122790.q: How is the acidic environment in the lysosome maintained?
a: By proton pumps in the membrane
122790.e: An ATP-dependent proton pump (V-ATPase) continuously transports hydrogen ions into the lysosome.
122790.m: Proton pumps keep the lysosome acidic.

122791.q: Why do lysosomal enzymes that get into the cytoplasm usually cause only little damage?
a: They are hardly active at neutral pH
They are immediately converted into ATP
122791.e: The hydrolases need an acidic environment; in the almost neutral cytoplasm (pH about 7.2) they work only weakly.
122791.m: Lysosomal enzymes only work properly in acidic conditions.

122792.q: What is the vesicle called that forms when a phagosome fuses with a lysosome?
122792.e: Phagocytes take bacteria into a phagosome; after fusion with a lysosome, the bacteria are digested in the phagolysosome.
122792.m: Phagocytes digest their prey in the phagolysosome.

122793.q: Which three types of filament make up the cytoskeleton of animal cells?
a: Microtubules, actin filaments and intermediate filaments
Microtubules, collagen fibres and elastin fibres
122793.e: The cytoskeleton consists of microtubules, actin filaments (microfilaments) and intermediate filaments.
122793.m: The cytoskeleton consists of three kinds of filament.

122794.q: Which protein are microtubules made of?
122794.e: Microtubules are hollow tubes made of dimers of alpha and beta tubulin.

122795.q: What tasks does the cytoskeleton perform?
a: It gives the cell its shape and makes movement possible
122795.e: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibres. It supports the cell, transports substances and makes movements such as cell division possible.
122795.m: The cytoskeleton is the scaffold and transport network of the cell.

122796.q: Which structure made of microtubules pulls the chromosomes apart during cell division?
122796.e: During mitosis, microtubules form the spindle apparatus. Its fibres attach to the chromosomes and pull the halves to the poles of the cell.
122796.m: The spindle apparatus distributes the chromosomes during cell division.

122797.q: Which protein forms the intermediate filaments in the epithelial cells of the skin?
122797.e: Keratins are typical intermediate filaments of epithelial cells and make skin, hair and nails tough.

122798.q: From which structure do most microtubules originate in animal cells?
122798.e: The centrosome with its two centrioles is the most important organising centre for microtubules in animal cells.

122799.q: Which arrangement of microtubules does a cross-section through a cilium or flagellum of eukaryotes show?
122799.e: Nine doublet microtubules surround two single central microtubules; the motor protein dynein makes the doublets slide against each other.
122799.m: Cilia have nine doublet microtubules around two central ones.

122800.q: Which protein of the cytoskeleton works together with myosin in the muscle cell?
122800.e: During muscle contraction, myosin heads pull on the actin filaments. As a result the filaments slide into each other and the muscle shortens.
122800.m: Actin and myosin make the muscle contract.

122801.q: In which order do the classic phases of mitosis take place?
122801.e: Mitosis begins with prophase, followed by metaphase, anaphase and finally telophase.
122801.m: The phases of mitosis are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.

122802.q: In which phase of mitosis are the sister chromatids pulled to the poles of the cell?
122802.e: In anaphase, the sister chromatids are separated from each other and pulled by the spindle fibres to opposite poles.
122802.m: In anaphase, the chromatids move apart.

122803.q: To which protein structure of the chromosomes do the spindle fibres attach?
122803.e: The kinetochore is a protein complex at the constriction of the chromosome to which the microtubules of the spindle bind.
122803.m: Spindle fibres attach at the kinetochore.

122804.q: What is the division of the cytoplasm after nuclear division called?
122804.e: Nuclear division (karyokinesis) is followed by cytokinesis, in which the cell body splits into two daughter cells.
122804.m: After nuclear division, cytokinesis divides the cell body.

122805.q: In which phase of mitosis do the chromosomes condense enough to become visible under a light microscope?
122805.e: At the beginning of mitosis the chromatin condenses strongly; the chromosomes become recognisable as threads.
122805.m: In prophase, the chromosomes become visible.

122806.q: In which phase of mitosis do new nuclear envelopes form around the two sets of chromosomes?
122806.e: In telophase the chromosomes uncoil again and new nuclear envelopes and nucleoli form.
122806.m: In telophase, two new nuclei are formed.

122807.q: How is the cytoplasm divided in animal cells at the end of mitosis?
a: By the breakdown of the nucleus
122807.e: A ring of actin and myosin contracts beneath the membrane and pinches the cell in two along a cleavage furrow.
122807.m: Animal cells pinch in two when they divide.

122808.q: In which phase of the cell cycle is the DNA copied?
122808.e: In the synthesis phase (S phase) of interphase, all the DNA is replicated.
122808.m: The DNA is copied in the S phase.

122809.q: What is the state called into which many specialised cells, such as nerve cells, leave the cell cycle?
122809.e: Cells in the G0 phase no longer divide but remain metabolically active; some can re-enter the cycle.
122809.m: Resting cells are in the G0 phase.

122810.q: Which proteins rise and fall periodically in the cell cycle and activate certain kinases that control the process?
122810.e: Cyclins bind to kinases (CDKs) and so allow the transition to the next phase of the cycle; afterwards they are broken down.
122810.m: Cyclins set the rhythm of the cell cycle.

122811.q: Which protein is called the “guardian of the genome” because it stops the cell cycle when DNA is damaged?
122811.e: When DNA is damaged, p53 stops the cycle until the damage is repaired, or triggers programmed cell death; its gene is mutated in many tumours.
122811.m: The protein p53 protects the cell from dividing with damaged DNA.

122812.q: Which stage makes up most of the cell cycle in most dividing cells?
122812.e: Interphase, with the G1, S and G2 phases, usually lasts many hours, while the actual nuclear division takes only about an hour.
122812.m: The cell spends most of its time in interphase.

122813.q: What are genes called that normally slow down cell division and whose failure can contribute to cancer?
122813.e: Tumour suppressor genes inhibit division or promote repair; if both copies fail, this brake is missing.
122813.m: Tumour suppressor genes act as a brake on cell division.

122814.q: What is the limited number of divisions that normal human body cells can go through in cell culture called?
122814.e: In 1961 Leonard Hayflick showed that normal fibroblasts divide only about 40 to 60 times and then stop.
122814.m: Normal body cells cannot divide endlessly.

122815.q: Which ends of the chromosomes become shorter with every cell division in many body cells?
122815.e: DNA polymerase cannot fully copy the end of a strand; that is why, without the enzyme telomerase, the telomeres shorten with each division.
122815.m: Telomeres protect the ends of chromosomes and become shorter with age.

a: The random thermal motion of the particles
122816.e: Particles move randomly because of their thermal energy (Brownian motion); this results in a net flow from the place of higher to the place of lower concentration.
122816.m: Diffusion is based on the random movement of particles.

122817.q: What does Fick's first law state?
a: The flow of particles is proportional to the concentration gradient
The flow of particles is independent of concentration
The pressure is proportional to the temperature
122817.e: According to Adolf Fick, the steeper the concentration gradient, the more substance flows per unit of time.
122817.m: A steeper concentration gradient speeds up diffusion.

122818.q: How does a rise in temperature affect the speed of diffusion?
122818.e: At higher temperatures the particles move faster, and the diffusion coefficient increases.

122819.q: How does glucose passively enter many body cells via GLUT transport proteins?
122819.e: GLUT transporters let glucose pass through the membrane along its concentration gradient without using ATP.
122819.m: Facilitated diffusion uses transport proteins but no energy.

122820.q: Which substance can diffuse most easily straight through the lipid bilayer of a membrane?
122820.e: Small non-polar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂ dissolve in the fatty interior of the membrane; ions and large polar molecules need transport proteins.
122820.m: Small non-polar molecules pass through membranes easily.

122821.q: Why is the huge surface area of the alveoli so important for gas exchange?
a: The amount of diffusion increases with the exchange surface
A large surface raises body temperature
Active transport takes place on large surfaces
122821.e: The flow of diffusing gas is proportional to the area; many small alveoli create a surface of roughly 100 square metres.
122821.m: Large surfaces make fast gas exchange possible.

122822.q: How does the time particles need to diffuse across a distance change if the distance is doubled?
122822.e: The average diffusion time grows with the square of the distance; twice the distance means about four times the time. That is why diffusion is only efficient over short distances.
122822.m: Diffusion is only fast over short distances.

122823.q: What happens once the concentrations have evened out in diffusion?
a: Particles keep moving, but there is no net flow
122823.e: At equilibrium, the same number of particles move in both directions; the concentration therefore stays the same everywhere.
122823.m: Diffusion equilibrium is a dynamic equilibrium.

122824.q: What happens to red blood cells that are placed in distilled water?
a: They shrink into a spiky shape
122824.e: The inside of the cell is more concentrated than pure water; water flows in until the membrane tears (haemolysis).
122824.m: Red blood cells burst in pure water.

122825.q: What is it called when the protoplast pulls away from the cell wall after a plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution?
122825.e: In the hypertonic solution the vacuole loses water, the protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the rigid cell wall.
122825.m: Plant cells undergo plasmolysis in a concentrated solution.

122826.q: What is the internal pressure of a plant cell against its cell wall, which keeps herbaceous plants upright, called?
122826.e: Through osmotic uptake of water, the vacuole presses the cell contents against the cell wall; if water is lacking, the plant wilts.
122826.m: Turgor makes plant parts firm and plump.

122827.q: Which membrane proteins allow water to pass through especially quickly?
122827.e: Aquaporins are water channels; Peter Agre received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2003 for discovering them.
122827.m: Aquaporins are the water channels of the cell membrane.

122828.q: What concentration does a physiological saline solution have, which is roughly isotonic with blood?
122828.e: A solution with 0.9 g of sodium chloride per 100 ml has roughly the same osmotic value as blood plasma.
122828.m: Physiological saline contains 0.9 per cent salt.

122829.q: How does the osmotic pressure of a solution change if the concentration of dissolved particles is doubled?
122829.e: Osmotic pressure is proportional to the number of dissolved particles. Twice as many particles produce about twice the pressure.
122829.m: More dissolved particles mean more osmotic pressure.

122830.q: Why do strawberries release juice when you sprinkle them with sugar?
a: Water moves out by osmosis towards the sugar solution
The sugar dissolves the cell walls
The sugar is actively pumped into the cells
122830.e: The sugar forms a very concentrated solution on the outside; water flows out of the fruit cells.
122830.m: Sugar draws water out of fruit by osmosis.

a: It uses an ion gradient that was built up beforehand
It splits ATP directly at the transporter
It only takes place in plant cells
It works without a transport protein
122831.e: A secondary active transporter couples the movement of a substance to the backflow of ions whose gradient was built up by an ATP-driven pump.
122831.m: Secondary active transport uses the energy from ATP indirectly.

122832.q: What is transport called in which two substances are carried in the same direction at the same time?
122832.e: In symport, two substances move together in the same direction through the same transport protein.
122832.m: In symport, two substances travel together in the same direction.

122833.q: What fundamentally distinguishes active transport from diffusion?
a: It works against a concentration gradient
122833.e: Active transport can move substances from a place of lower to a place of higher concentration and needs energy for this, usually from ATP.
122833.m: Active transport needs energy and can work against the gradient.

122834.q: What is the uptake of droplets of fluid by infolding of the cell membrane called?
122834.e: In pinocytosis (“cell drinking”), the membrane pinches off small vesicles of fluid towards the inside; this vesicle transport needs energy.
122834.m: In pinocytosis, the cell drinks small amounts of fluid.

122835.q: Which medicines inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase of the parietal cells and so reduce stomach acid?
122835.e: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole block the pump that transports hydrogen ions into the stomach.
122835.m: Proton pump inhibitors slow down acid production in the stomach.

122836.q: Which German physicist built the first electron microscope with Max Knoll from 1931 and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1986?
122836.e: Ernst Ruska developed the electron microscope with Max Knoll at the Technical University of Berlin and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.
122836.m: Ernst Ruska is regarded as the inventor of the electron microscope.

122837.q: Which Swiss biophysicist from the University of Lausanne received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for contributions to cryo-electron microscopy?
122837.e: Jacques Dubochet developed a method of freezing samples in a flash in glass-like ice; he shared the prize with Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson.
122837.m: Jacques Dubochet made biomolecules in ice visible for the electron microscope.

122838.q: Why does an electron microscope achieve a much higher resolution than a light microscope?
a: Electrons have a much shorter wavelength
122838.e: Resolving power depends on the wavelength; fast electrons have a wavelength of only a few picometres.

122839.q: Why must there be a high vacuum in the electron microscope?
a: Air molecules would scatter the electrons
Electrons only form from light in a vacuum
122839.e: Electrons are deflected by even a few gas molecules; without a vacuum the beam would become blurred and weakened.
122839.m: Electron microscopes work in a vacuum.

122840.q: Which type of microscope produces three-dimensional-looking images of surfaces, such as the head of a fly?
a: Stereo magnifier with a light source
122840.e: The SEM scans the surface with a fine beam of electrons and analyses the electrons knocked out; this produces images that look three-dimensional.
122840.m: The scanning electron microscope shows surfaces in three dimensions.

122841.q: What is used to focus the electron beam in an electron microscope?
122841.e: Electrons are deflected by magnetic fields; coils carrying a current therefore act as electromagnetic lenses.

122842.q: Why do images from the electron microscope originally appear only in shades of grey?
a: Electrons have no colour as visible light does
The electrons are sent through colour filters
122842.e: Colours arise from different wavelengths of visible light. Electron images only show how strongly electrons are scattered; coloured images have been coloured in afterwards.
122842.m: Coloured electron microscope images are coloured in afterwards.

122843.q: Which cell structure can be clearly seen in the electron microscope but not in the light microscope?
122843.e: Ribosomes measure only around 20 to 30 nm and are therefore far below the resolution limit of the light microscope of about 200 nm.
122843.m: Ribosomes can only be seen in the electron microscope.

122844.q: Which plastids store large amounts of starch in potato tubers?
122844.e: Amyloplasts are colourless plastids that build glucose into starch grains and store them.
122844.m: Amyloplasts are the starch stores of the plant cell.

122845.q: Which plastids give ripe tomatoes and carrots their red to orange colour?
122845.e: Chromoplasts contain carotenoids such as lycopene or beta-carotene and colour fruits, roots and flowers.

122846.q: What are the reaction spaces of a eukaryotic cell that are separated by membranes called?
122846.e: Membranes divide the cell into compartments so that opposing metabolic processes such as building up and breaking down can take place at the same time.
122846.m: Membranes divide the cell into separate reaction spaces.

122847.q: What are the fine channels called that connect neighbouring plant cells through the cell wall?
122847.e: Plasmodesmata are channels lined with membrane through which the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells is connected.
122847.m: Plasmodesmata connect plant cells to each other.

122848.q: Which proteins inside the rough ER help newly made chains to find their correct shape?
122848.e: Chaperones such as BiP bind to unfolded protein chains in the ER and support their correct folding; misfolded proteins are sorted out.
122848.m: Chaperones help proteins to fold correctly.
