122849.q: At which constricted point are the two sister chromatids of a chromosome joined?
122849.e: The centromere is the constriction of the chromosome; there the chromatids remain joined until they are separated.
122849.m: Sister chromatids are joined at the centromere.

122850.q: What is the result of mitosis?
a: Four cells with half a set of chromosomes
Two cells with different genetic material
One cell with a double nucleus
122850.e: In mitosis, each chromosome is distributed evenly between two nuclei. The daughter cells have the same genetic material as the parent cell. Four cells with half a set are produced in meiosis.
122850.m: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells.

122851.q: What is transport called in which two substances are carried in opposite directions at the same time?
122851.e: An antiporter exchanges substances, for example the sodium-calcium exchanger, which carries calcium out of the cell while sodium flows in.
122851.m: In antiport, two substances are exchanged for each other.

122852.q: Why do drinking solutions for diarrhoea contain a little sugar as well as salt?
a: Sugar helps the intestine take up sodium and therefore water
Sugar stops the movement of the intestine
Sugar makes the solution keep longer
122852.e: In the small intestine, glucose and sodium are taken up together by a transporter. Water follows, so the body loses less fluid.
122852.m: Sugar and salt together help the intestine to take up water.

122853.q: Which pump uses ATP to transport sodium out of the cell and potassium into the cell?
122853.e: The sodium-potassium pump carries three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. It maintains the resting potential of the cells.
122853.m: The sodium-potassium pump works with energy from ATP.

122854.q: What disadvantage does electron microscopy have compared with light microscopy for biological samples?
a: No preparation at all is needed
122854.e: There is a vacuum in the electron microscope, and samples are fixed, sliced or frozen. Living cells in motion cannot be viewed in this way.
122854.m: You cannot see living cells in the electron microscope.

122855.q: A voltage of 230 V is applied to a resistor of 46 Ω. What is the current?
122855.e: According to Ohm's law, I = U/R, so 230 V / 46 Ω, which gives 5 A.
122855.m: Current is voltage divided by resistance.

122856.q: A current of 0.25 A flows through a resistor of 480 Ω. What voltage is across it?
122856.e: U = R·I, so 480 Ω · 0.25 A, which gives 120 V.
122856.m: Voltage is the product of resistance and current.

122858.q: An ohmic resistor draws a current of 0.5 A at 12 V. What current flows at 30 V?
122858.e: The resistance is 12 V / 0.5 A, so 24 Ω. At 30 V, 30 V / 24 Ω flows, so 1.25 A.
122858.m: With constant resistance, the current grows in the same ratio as the voltage.

122859.q: What is the unit ohm in SI base units?
122859.e: One volt is kg·m²/(s³·A); divided by one ampere, this gives kg·m²/(s³·A²) for the ohm.
122859.m: One ohm is one volt per ampere.

122860.q: What is the electrical conductance of a resistor of 40 Ω?
122860.e: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, so 1/40 Ω, which gives 0.025 S or 25 millisiemens.
122860.m: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance.

122861.q: What is the resistance of a copper wire 20 m long with a cross-section of 0.75 mm² (ρ = 0.0178 Ω·mm²/m)?
122861.e: R = ρ·l/A gives 0.0178 · 20 / 0.75, so about 0.47 Ω.
122861.m: The resistance of a wire grows with its length and falls with its cross-section.

122862.q: Which metal has the lowest resistivity at room temperature?
122862.e: At about 0.016 Ω·mm²/m, silver has the lowest value of all metals, just ahead of copper; because of the price, copper is mostly used.
122862.m: Silver conducts best of all metals.

122863.q: What is the SI unit of resistivity?
122863.e: From ρ = R·A/l the unit is Ω·m²/m, so Ω·m; in engineering Ω·mm²/m is also common.

122864.q: A wire is replaced by a wire of the same kind with twice the length and twice the diameter. How does the resistance change?
122864.e: Twice the diameter means four times the cross-section. With twice the length this gives 2/4, so half the resistance.
122864.m: The cross-section grows with the square of the diameter.

122865.q: How long must a constantan wire with a cross-section of 0.2 mm² (ρ = 0.50 Ω·mm²/m) be for it to have 10 Ω?
122865.e: From R = ρ·l/A it follows that l = R·A/ρ, so 10 · 0.2 / 0.50, which gives 4 m.
122865.m: The length of wire needed follows from resistance, cross-section and material.

122866.q: Why is the alloy constantan used for precision resistors?
a: Its resistance hardly depends on temperature
122866.e: Constantan (copper and nickel) has an almost vanishing temperature coefficient; its resistance stays nearly constant when it heats up.
122866.m: Constantan hardly changes its resistance when heated.

122867.q: A Pt100 sensor has exactly 100 Ω at 0 °C and a temperature coefficient of 0.00385 1/K. Roughly what is its resistance at 50 °C?
122867.e: With R = R₀·(1 + α·ΔT) you get 100 Ω · (1 + 0.00385 · 50), so about 119.3 Ω.
122867.m: In metals, resistance rises with temperature.

122868.q: Currents of 3 A and 1.5 A flow into a junction, and one branch carries 2 A out. What current flows out in the fourth branch?
122868.e: According to the junction rule, the sum of the currents flowing in equals the sum of the currents flowing out: 4.5 A minus 2 A gives 2.5 A.
122868.m: As much current flows out of a junction as flows in.

122869.q: Two resistors are connected in series to 12 V. There is a voltage drop of 7.5 V across the first. What voltage is across the second?
122869.e: According to the loop rule, the sum of the partial voltages equals the source voltage: 12 V minus 7.5 V gives 4.5 V.
122869.m: In a loop the partial voltages add up to the source voltage.

122870.q: Which physical principle is the junction rule based on?
a: Constancy of the speed of light
122870.e: No charge can pile up or disappear at a junction, so the same amount of charge per unit time must flow in as flows out.
122870.m: The junction rule follows from the fact that charge is not lost.

122871.q: Which conservation law is the loop rule based on?
122871.e: A charge that travels once round a closed loop arrives back at the same potential. The energy gained and given off must balance, so the sum of the voltages is zero.
122871.m: The loop rule follows from the conservation of energy.

122872.q: Two batteries of 9 V and 3 V are connected against each other in a loop, and the total resistance is 20 Ω. What current flows?
122872.e: Sources connected against each other are subtracted: 9 V minus 3 V gives 6 V, and 6 V / 20 Ω gives 0.3 A.
122872.m: Voltage sources connected against each other weaken each other.

122873.q: A 40 Ω resistor is connected in parallel with a 10 Ω resistor, and the total current is 1 A. What current flows through the 10 Ω resistor?
122873.e: The currents divide in inverse proportion to the resistances: I₁ = 1 A · 40/(10 + 40), so 0.8 A.
122873.m: The larger share of the current flows through the smaller resistor.

122874.q: Which quantity is the same in all branches of a parallel circuit?
122874.e: Each parallel branch forms a loop without a source with the others; that is why the same voltage is across all branches.
122874.m: Components connected in parallel have the same voltage.

122875.q: What is the equivalent resistance of 47 Ω, 33 Ω and 20 Ω in series?
122875.e: In a series circuit the resistances add up: 47 + 33 + 20 gives 100 Ω.
122875.m: In series the resistances add up.

122876.q: What is the equivalent resistance of 60 Ω and 30 Ω in parallel?
122876.e: For two resistors in parallel, R = R₁·R₂/(R₁ + R₂), so 1800/90, which gives 20 Ω.
122876.m: Resistors in parallel give a smaller total resistance.

122877.q: Three resistors of 12 Ω each are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
122877.e: For n equal resistors in parallel, the result is R/n, so 12 Ω / 3, which gives 4 Ω.
122877.m: Equal resistors in parallel divide their value by their number.

122878.q: A 10 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel combination of 30 Ω and 60 Ω. What is the equivalent resistance?
122878.e: The parallel combination gives 30·60/90, so 20 Ω; adding 10 Ω in series gives 30 Ω in total.
122878.m: Mixed circuits are worked out step by step from the inside outwards.

122879.q: What is always true of the equivalent resistance of a parallel circuit?
a: It is smaller than the smallest single resistance
It is larger than the largest single resistance
122879.e: Each extra branch opens another path for the current; the total conductance is the sum of the individual conductances.
122879.m: More parallel paths lower the total resistance.

122880.q: A series combination of 25 Ω and 35 Ω is in parallel with 40 Ω. What is the equivalent resistance?
122880.e: The series branch has 60 Ω; in parallel with 40 Ω this gives 60·40/100, so 24 Ω.
122880.m: First combine the series branches, then the parallel circuit.

122881.q: Which resistor must be connected in parallel with 120 Ω so that the equivalent resistance is 40 Ω?
122881.e: From 1/R = 1/40 minus 1/120 it follows that 1/R = 2/120, so R = 60 Ω.
122881.m: In parallel circuits the reciprocals of the resistances add up.

122882.q: What is the equivalent resistance of a series of 2 Ω, a parallel combination of 6 Ω and 3 Ω, and 4 Ω?
122882.e: 6 Ω in parallel with 3 Ω gives 18/9, so 2 Ω. In series with 2 Ω and 4 Ω this gives 8 Ω.
122882.m: Parts of a circuit are combined step by step into one equivalent resistance.

122883.q: Two equal resistors give 40 Ω in series. What is their equivalent resistance when connected in parallel?
122883.e: Each resistor has 20 Ω; in parallel, two equal resistors give half of a single one, so 10 Ω.
122883.m: Two equal resistors in parallel have half the single value.

122884.q: An unloaded voltage divider made of R₁ = 1 kΩ and R₂ = 2 kΩ is connected to 12 V. What voltage is across R₂?
122884.e: U₂ = U · R₂/(R₁ + R₂), so 12 V · 2/3, which gives 8 V.
122884.m: The larger voltage drop is across the larger resistor.

122885.q: An unloaded divider connected to 9 V has R₁ = 10 kΩ. How large must R₂ be so that exactly 3 V is across R₂?
122885.e: There is a drop of 6 V across R₁ and 3 V across R₂. The voltages are in the same ratio as the resistances, so R₂ = 10 kΩ · 3/6, which gives 5 kΩ.
122885.m: The partial voltages are in the same ratio as the partial resistances.

122886.q: What happens to the output voltage of a voltage divider if you connect a load in parallel with R₂?
122886.e: The load forms a parallel combination with R₂ that has a smaller resistance; as a result, less voltage drops across this part.
122886.m: A load lowers the output voltage of a voltage divider.

122887.q: A divider with R₁ = R₂ = 10 kΩ is connected to 12 V. A load of 10 kΩ is connected in parallel with R₂. What is the output voltage?
122887.e: R₂ in parallel with the load gives 5 kΩ. The output voltage is 12 V · 5/(10 + 5), so 4 V.
122887.m: A loaded voltage divider delivers less voltage than when unloaded.

122888.q: Which component is an adjustable voltage divider with a sliding contact?
122888.e: In a potentiometer, a movable wiper divides a resistance track into two parts; this allows the voltage picked off to be adjusted smoothly.
122888.m: A potentiometer is an adjustable voltage divider.

122889.q: In an unloaded divider connected to 20 V, R₁ is three times as large as R₂. What voltage is across R₂?
122889.e: R₂ has a quarter of the total resistance, so a quarter of the voltage is across it: 20 V / 4 gives 5 V.
122889.m: Each partial resistor gets its share of the total voltage.

122890.q: In a twilight switch, a light-dependent resistor (LDR) forms the lower part of a voltage divider. What happens to its voltage when it gets dark?
122890.e: In the dark the resistance of the LDR rises sharply; this gives it a larger share of the total voltage.
122890.m: A light-dependent resistor has a high resistance in the dark.

122891.q: An unloaded divider made of 1.5 kΩ and 4.5 kΩ is connected to 24 V. What voltage drops across the 1.5 kΩ resistor?
122891.e: The current is 24 V / 6 kΩ, so 4 mA. Across the 1.5 kΩ resistor there is a drop of 4 mA · 1.5 kΩ, so 6 V.
122891.m: The shared current determines the partial voltages.

122892.q: A battery with an open-circuit voltage of 1.5 V and an internal resistance of 0.5 Ω delivers 0.4 A. What is the terminal voltage?
122892.e: Across the internal resistance there is a drop of 0.4 A · 0.5 Ω, so 0.2 V. The terminal voltage is 1.5 V minus 0.2 V, so 1.3 V.
122892.m: Under load the terminal voltage of a source falls.

122893.q: A car battery has an open-circuit voltage of 12 V and an internal resistance of 0.02 Ω. What is the short-circuit current?
122893.e: In a short circuit only the internal resistance limits the current: 12 V / 0.02 Ω gives 600 A.
122893.m: The internal resistance limits the short-circuit current.

122894.q: A source shows 9.0 V with no load and still 8.0 V with a load of 0.5 A. What is its internal resistance?
122894.e: The voltage loss of 1.0 V occurs across the internal resistance: Rᵢ = 1.0 V / 0.5 A, so 2 Ω.
122894.m: The drop in voltage under load tells you the internal resistance.

122895.q: At what load resistance does a voltage source deliver the greatest possible power to the load?
a: When it equals the internal resistance
When it is twice the internal resistance
122895.e: With impedance matching, that is when the load resistance equals the internal resistance, the power in the load is at its maximum; the efficiency is then only 50 per cent.
122895.m: Power matching means equal load and internal resistance.

122896.q: A source with an open-circuit voltage of 6 V has an internal resistance of 3 Ω. What is the maximum power it can deliver to a load?
122896.e: With power matching, P = U₀²/(4·Rᵢ), so 36/12, which gives 3 W.
122896.m: The maximum load power depends on the open-circuit voltage and the internal resistance.

122897.q: Why do the headlights often dim briefly when a car is started?
a: The high starter current causes a voltage drop across the internal resistance
The alternator switches off the lamps
122897.e: The starter motor draws several hundred amperes; even a small internal resistance makes the terminal voltage drop noticeably.
122897.m: Large currents lower the terminal voltage of a battery.

122898.q: A source with an open-circuit voltage of 4.5 V and an internal resistance of 1 Ω supplies a load resistance of 8 Ω. What current flows?
122898.e: The internal and load resistances are in series: I = 4.5 V / (1 Ω + 8 Ω), so 0.5 A.
122898.m: The internal resistance is in series with the load.

122899.q: A 12 V car lamp draws 5 A. What is its power?
122899.e: P = U·I gives 12 V · 5 A, so 60 W.
122899.m: Electric power is voltage times current.

122900.q: What current flows through a 2000 W kettle connected to 230 V?
122900.e: I = P/U gives 2000 W / 230 V, so about 8.7 A.

122901.q: What power does a heating resistor of 52.9 Ω take at 230 V?
122901.e: P = U²/R gives 52,900 V² / 52.9 Ω, so 1000 W.
122901.m: At a fixed voltage the power grows when the resistance gets smaller.

122902.q: A current of 3 A flows through a 20 Ω resistor. How much power is converted?
122902.e: P = I²·R gives 9 A² · 20 Ω, so 180 W.
122902.m: Power rises with the square of the current.

122903.q: A lamp rated 60 W at 230 V is run at 115 V. What is its power if the resistance stays constant?
122903.e: Because P = U²/R, half the voltage gives a quarter of the power: 60 W / 4 gives 15 W.
122903.m: Half the voltage means a quarter of the power at the same resistance.

122904.q: Two 230 V filament bulbs, one of 100 W and one of 25 W, are connected in series to 230 V. Which one shines more brightly?
122904.e: The 25 W bulb has four times the resistance. In series the same current flows, so according to P = I²·R it converts more power.
122904.m: In a series circuit the larger resistance gets more power.

122905.q: An electric motor takes 1.5 kW of electrical power and gives out 1.2 kW of mechanical power. What is its efficiency?
122905.e: Efficiency is useful power divided by power supplied: 1.2 kW / 1.5 kW gives 0.8, so 80 per cent.
122905.m: Efficiency compares the useful power with the power taken in.

122906.q: A 230 V socket is protected by a 10 A fuse. What is the maximum total power that may be connected?
122906.e: P = U·I gives 230 V · 10 A, so 2300 W; more power would trip the fuse.
122906.m: The fuse limits the power that can be connected.

122907.q: A 2 kW fan heater runs for 3 hours. How much electrical energy does it use?
122907.e: W = P·t gives 2 kW · 3 h, so 6 kWh.
122907.m: Electrical energy is power times time.

122908.q: A 1.5 kW hairdryer runs for 10 minutes a day. What does that cost over 30 days, assuming 30 centimes per kWh?
122908.e: Per day that is 1.5 kW · 1/6 h, so 0.25 kWh, and in 30 days 7.5 kWh. That costs 7.5 · 0.30 francs, so 2.25 francs.
122908.m: Electricity costs are energy times the tariff.

122909.q: An appliance constantly uses 5 W on standby. How much energy is that in a year of 365 days?
122909.e: 5 W · 24 h · 365 gives 43,800 Wh, so 43.8 kWh.
122909.m: Even small continuous users add up over the year.

122910.q: A smartphone battery has a nominal voltage of 3.7 V and a capacity of 4000 mAh. Roughly how much energy does it store?
122910.e: Energy is voltage times charge: 3.7 V · 4.0 Ah gives 14.8 Wh.
122910.m: Battery energy is nominal voltage times capacity.

122911.q: An appliance works for 30 minutes at 12 V and 2 A. How much electrical work is done?
122911.e: W = U·I·t gives 12 V · 2 A · 1800 s, so 43,200 J or 43.2 kJ.
122911.m: Electrical work is voltage times current times time.

122912.q: How long does a 2 kW kettle with no losses take to heat 1 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C (c = 4190 J/(kg·K))?
122912.e: You need 4190 · 1 · 80, so about 335 kJ. Divided by 2000 W this gives about 168 s.
122912.m: Heating time is the heat needed divided by the power.

122913.q: How much energy does a 2.2 kW oven use in 45 minutes of continuous operation?
122913.e: 45 minutes is 0.75 h; 2.2 kW · 0.75 h gives 1.65 kWh.
122913.m: For kilowatt hours, minutes must be converted into hours.

122914.q: What is the microscopic cause of Joule heating in a metal wire?
a: Collisions of the electrons with the particles of the lattice
Friction of the protons in the nucleus
122914.e: The conduction electrons give up energy when they collide with the vibrating metal ions; the lattice vibrates more strongly and the wire heats up.
122914.m: Electrical heating comes from electrons colliding in the metal lattice.

122915.q: A current of 2 A flows through a 5 Ω resistor for one minute. How much heat is produced?
122915.e: Q = I²·R·t gives 4 A² · 5 Ω · 60 s, so 1200 J.
122915.m: Electrical heating grows with the square of the current.

122916.q: How does the heating power in a resistor change if the current is doubled?
122916.e: Since P = I²·R, twice the current produces four times the heating power.
122916.m: Twice the current means four times the heat.

122917.q: An immersion heater with a resistance of 46 Ω is connected to 230 V for 5 minutes. How much heat does it give off?
122917.e: The power is 230² / 46, so 1150 W. In 300 s this produces 1150 W · 300 s, so 345,000 J or 345 kJ.
122917.m: The heat given off is power times operating time.

122918.q: In which appliance is Joule heating the actual purpose?
122918.e: In a toaster, heating wires glow to toast bread; in motors or chargers, on the other hand, electrical heating is a loss.
122918.m: Heating appliances use electrical heating on purpose.

122919.q: A heating wire connected to a fixed voltage is shortened. How does its heating power change?
122919.e: A shorter wire has a smaller resistance. At a fixed voltage, P = U²/R, so the power rises.
122919.m: At a fixed voltage a smaller resistance heats more strongly.

122920.q: Why is electrical energy transmitted over long distances at high voltage?
a: For the same power the current is smaller, and so are the losses
More heat is produced at high voltage
122920.e: For the same power P = U·I, the current falls as the voltage rises; the line losses I²·R drop sharply.

122921.q: A line with 0.5 Ω transmits 100 kW at 10 kV. How large is the line loss?
122921.e: The current is 100 kW / 10 kV, so 10 A. The loss is 10² A² · 0.5 Ω, so 50 W.
122921.m: Line losses are calculated with the square of the current.

122922.q: By what factor do the line losses fall if the same power is transmitted at ten times the voltage?
122922.e: Ten times the voltage means a tenth of the current; since the loss grows with I², it falls to a hundredth.
122922.m: Losses fall with the square of the increase in voltage.

122923.q: At which voltages does Swissgrid operate the Swiss transmission grid?
122923.e: Switzerland's extra-high-voltage grid works at 380 kV and 220 kV and is run by the national grid company Swissgrid.
122923.m: The Swiss transmission grid works at 220 and 380 kilovolts.

122924.q: An extension cable has a total resistance of 0.6 Ω and carries 10 A. How much power is lost in the cable?
122924.e: P = I²·R gives 100 A² · 0.6 Ω, so 60 W, which heats the cable.
122924.m: Long, thin cables heat up at high current.

122925.q: A supply line has a resistance of 0.4 Ω and carries 16 A. How large is the voltage drop along the line?
122925.e: The voltage drop is I·R, so 16 A · 0.4 Ω, which gives 6.4 V.
122925.m: Part of the voltage is lost along cables.

122926.q: Which advantage speaks in favour of high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission over very long distances?
a: There are no reactive currents caused by capacitances
Direct current is easier to transform
It needs no insulation at all
122926.e: With alternating current, long cables and lines constantly recharge, which causes reactive currents; with direct current this does not happen, especially in undersea cables.
122926.m: Direct current suits very long distances and undersea cables.

122927.q: With the same current, how do the line losses change if you double the cross-section of the conductor?
122927.e: Twice the cross-section halves the line resistance; with the same current, I²·R is therefore halved too.

122928.q: What is the name of the effect in which a superconductor pushes an outside magnetic field out of its interior?
122928.e: In 1933 Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld showed that superconductors expel magnetic fields; that is why a magnet can float above them.
122928.m: Superconductors push magnetic fields out of their interior.

122929.q: Which two researchers discovered high-temperature superconductivity at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon in 1986?
122929.e: Johannes Georg Bednorz and Karl Alexander Müller found superconducting copper oxide ceramics and won the Nobel Prize in Physics as early as 1987.
122929.m: High-temperature superconductivity was discovered in Rüschlikon.

122930.q: Why was the discovery of superconductors with critical temperatures above 77 K so important technically?
a: They can be cooled with liquid nitrogen
They then work at room temperature
They then need no cooling at all
122930.e: 77 K is the boiling point of liquid nitrogen, which is much cheaper and easier to handle than liquid helium.
122930.m: Liquid nitrogen makes high-temperature superconductors practical.

122931.q: What are the superconducting magnets of the LHC at CERN near Geneva cooled with?
122931.e: The magnet coils are cooled to about 1.9 K with superfluid helium. Liquid nitrogen at 77 K would be too warm for these superconductors.
122931.m: The LHC's magnets are colder than outer space.

122932.q: What is the temperature below which a material becomes superconducting called?
122932.e: Below the critical temperature the electrical resistance suddenly drops to zero.
122932.m: Below the critical temperature a superconductor conducts without losses.

122933.q: According to BCS theory, which particles are responsible for classic superconductivity?
122933.e: According to Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer (1957), electrons form pairs through lattice vibrations, and these pairs move through the metal without scattering.
122933.m: Cooper pairs move through the lattice without resistance.

122934.q: What do you observe when a current is started in a superconducting ring?
a: It keeps flowing without any measurable weakening
122934.e: Because the resistance is zero, no energy is lost; persistent currents in superconducting rings keep flowing for years.
122934.m: In superconductors current flows round a loop without losses.

122935.q: In a balanced bridge, R₁/R₂ = R₃/Rₓ with R₁ = 100 Ω, R₂ = 200 Ω and R₃ = 150 Ω. What is Rₓ?
122935.e: From R₁/R₂ = R₃/Rₓ it follows that Rₓ = R₃·R₂/R₁, so 150 · 200 / 100, which gives 300 Ω.
122935.m: When balanced, the resistances of both branches are in the same ratio.

122936.q: How can you tell that a Wheatstone bridge is balanced?
a: No current flows in the bridge branch
The total current is at its maximum
122936.e: When balanced, both midpoints have the same potential; the meter in the bridge diagonal shows zero.
122936.m: A balanced bridge has no current in the diagonal.

122937.q: What is a Wheatstone bridge mainly used for?
a: For precisely measuring an unknown resistance
For measuring the speed of light
122937.e: You compare the unknown resistance with known resistances until the bridge is balanced. It was invented by Samuel Hunter Christie and made famous by Charles Wheatstone.
122937.m: A Wheatstone bridge measures resistances precisely.

122938.q: What advantage comes from the null balance of a bridge circuit?
a: The result does not depend on the supply voltage
122938.e: When balanced, only the ratios of the resistances count; fluctuations in the battery voltage do not affect the result.
122938.m: With null balance the supply voltage does not matter.

122939.q: On a 1 m slide-wire bridge with a comparison resistor of 30 Ω, the balance point is at l₁ = 40 cm. Rₓ/30 Ω = l₁/l₂. What is Rₓ?
122939.e: With l₂ = 60 cm it follows that Rₓ = 30 Ω · 40/60, so 20 Ω.
122939.m: In a slide-wire bridge, lengths of wire replace the resistance ratio.

122940.q: What are Wheatstone bridges often used for in measurement technology?
122940.e: Strain gauges change their resistance only very slightly; in a bridge these small changes become measurable as a diagonal voltage.
122940.m: Bridge circuits make the tiniest changes in resistance measurable.

122941.q: A bridge connected to 10 V has three resistors of 1000 Ω each and a sensor of 1100 Ω. Roughly what voltage does the bridge diagonal show?
122941.e: One midpoint is at 5.00 V, the other at 10 V · 1100/2100, so about 5.24 V. The difference is about 0.24 V.
122941.m: An unbalanced bridge gives a diagonal voltage.

122942.q: A bridge is balanced with R₁ = 470 Ω, R₂ = 1000 Ω and R₃ = 2350 Ω. What is Rₓ if R₁/R₂ = R₃/Rₓ?
122942.m: From three known resistances you can calculate the fourth.

122943.q: A component carries a current of 10 mA at 2 V, 20 mA at 4 V and 30 mA at 6 V. What is its resistance?
122943.e: The ratio U/I is constant: 2 V / 0.010 A gives 200 Ω. The component behaves ohmically.
122943.m: If U divided by I is constant, a component behaves ohmically.

122944.q: How does the current change if you triple the resistance at the same voltage?
122944.e: Because I = U/R, the current at a fixed voltage is inversely proportional to the resistance.
122944.m: At a fixed voltage the current falls when the resistance rises.

122945.q: A heating wire draws 4 A at 230 V in operation. What is its operating resistance?
122945.e: R = U/I gives 230 V / 4 A, so 57.5 Ω.
122945.m: Resistance is voltage divided by current.

122946.q: Aluminium has about 0.028 Ω·mm²/m, copper 0.0178 Ω·mm²/m. What cross-section does an aluminium conductor of the same length need to have the same resistance as a copper conductor of 10 mm²?
122946.e: The same resistance requires A_Al = A_Cu · ρ_Al/ρ_Cu, so 10 · 0.028/0.0178, which gives about 15.7 mm².
122946.m: Metals that conduct less well need thicker conductors.

122947.q: A 12 V source supplies 2 Ω in series with a parallel combination of 4 Ω and 12 Ω. What current flows through the 4 Ω resistor?
122947.e: The parallel combination gives 4·12/16, so 3 Ω; together with 2 Ω that is 5 Ω and a total current of 2.4 A. There is a drop of 4.8 V across the 2 Ω resistor, leaving 7.2 V across the parallel combination; 7.2/4, so 1.8 A, flows through 4 Ω.
122947.m: With the junction and loop rules, networks can be solved step by step.

122948.q: A 100 Ω resistor is rated for at most 0.25 W. What is the highest voltage that may be applied?
122948.e: From P = U²/R it follows that U equals the square root of P·R, so the square root of 25 V², which gives 5 V.
122948.m: The power rating limits the voltage allowed across a resistor.

122949.q: A 7 W LED lamp replaces a 60 W filament bulb. How much energy do you save in 1000 hours of use?
122949.e: The difference in power is 53 W; 53 W · 1000 h gives 53,000 Wh, so 53 kWh.
122949.m: Energy-saving lamps lower energy use considerably.

122950.q: A heat pump gives out 12 kWh of heat from 3 kWh of electrical work. What is its coefficient of performance?
122950.e: The coefficient of performance is heat given out divided by electrical work put in: 12 kWh / 3 kWh gives 4. The extra energy comes from the surroundings.
122950.m: A heat pump delivers more heat than the electricity it uses.

122951.q: Why does the thin filament in a filament bulb glow, but not the supply wire?
a: The filament has a much larger resistance
Less current flows through the supply wire
The supply wire is always cooled
The filament has a higher voltage than the source
122951.e: The filament and the supply wire carry the same current; according to P = I²·R, heat is produced almost only where the resistance is large.
122951.m: With the same current, the larger resistance heats up more.

122952.q: A 100 Ω resistor with a mass of 2 g and c = 800 J/(kg·K) carries 0.1 A for 10 s. By how much does it heat up without giving off heat?
122952.e: The heat is 0.01 A² · 100 Ω · 10 s, so 10 J. From this ΔT = 10 J / (0.002 kg · 800 J/(kg·K)), so 6.25 K.
122952.m: Electrical heating raises the temperature of a component.

122953.q: Two D cells, each with 1.5 V and an internal resistance of 0.3 Ω, are connected in series to 2.4 Ω. What current flows?
122953.e: In series the voltages add up to 3 V and the internal resistances to 0.6 Ω; I = 3 V / (0.6 Ω + 2.4 Ω), so 1 A.
122953.m: In series, source voltages and internal resistances add up.

122954.q: Which medical device almost always uses superconducting magnet coils?
122954.e: An MRI scanner needs a very strong, even magnetic field. For this, superconducting coils are used, usually made of niobium-titanium and cooled with liquid helium.
122954.m: In an MRI scanner superconducting coils create the strong magnetic field.

a: The stages of development of plants and animals that recur every year
How flower colours are inherited in plants
The composition of soils in forests
Working out the age of trees
122955.e: Phenology studies when regular events such as leaf-out, flowering, fruit ripening or bird migration happen during the year. If these dates shift, it is an important sign of climate change.
122955.m: Phenology observes the timing of recurring natural events.

122956.q: Which observation is a typical phenological event in animals?
a: The first arrival of house martins in spring
The number of eggs per nest
The colour of a fox's fur
The weight of a roe deer in winter
122956.e: Phenology records not only plants but also dates in the animal kingdom, such as the return of migrating birds or the first flight of butterflies. Many of these dates have shifted in recent decades.
122956.m: The return of migrating birds is also a phenological event.

122958.q: What does the phenological calendar use instead of fixed calendar dates?
a: The development of certain indicator plants
The length of the nights alone
122958.e: The phenological calendar divides the year into ten seasons. Their start depends on indicator plants, such as hazel flowering for early spring.
122958.m: In the phenological calendar, indicator plants determine the seasons.

122959.q: In the phenological calendar, the flowering of which plant is the indicator for early spring?
122959.e: Hazel flowering, often as early as February, marks early spring. Elder indicates early summer, lime high summer and autumn crocus early autumn.
122959.m: Flowering hazel bushes announce early spring.

122960.q: Which phenological season is indicated by the start of apple blossom?
122960.e: In the phenological calendar, full spring begins with apple blossom. Before it come early spring and first spring, which begins with forsythia flowering.

122961.q: Which observation about the cherry blossom in Kyoto caused a stir in 2021?
a: It was the earliest since records began over 1200 years ago
It failed completely because of frost
It took place in autumn for the first time
It lasted twice as long as usual
122961.e: Kyoto has records of cherry blossom going back to the 9th century. In 2021, full bloom was on 26 March, earlier than ever before in this series.
122961.m: Kyoto's cherry blossom shows climate change in a data series more than a thousand years long.

122962.q: Why is a longer growing season not automatically an advantage for plants?
a: Early leaf-out increases the risk of late frost damage
Plants cannot carry out photosynthesis in autumn
A longer growing season always lowers the yield
The leaves become permanently smaller as a result
122962.e: If plants come into leaf early because of mild temperatures, a later cold snap can destroy young leaves and flowers. Late frosts like this hit fruit trees and vines hard in Switzerland in 2017, for example.
122962.m: Early leaf-out makes plants more vulnerable to late frost.

122963.q: In which directions do the ranges of many species typically shift as it gets warmer?
a: Towards the poles and to higher altitudes
Towards the equator and to lower altitudes
122963.e: As it gets warmer, suitable climate zones move towards the poles and up the mountains. Many species follow them, provided they can spread fast enough.
122963.m: With warming, species move towards the poles and up the mountains.

122964.q: In the mountains the temperature falls by about 0.65 °C per 100 metres of altitude. By roughly how many metres does a temperature zone move upwards if it gets 1.3 °C warmer?
122964.e: 1.3 °C divided by 0.65 °C per 100 m gives 2 times 100 m, so 200 m. To find the same conditions, a species would have to grow about 200 m higher.
122964.m: In the mountains, one degree of warming corresponds roughly to 150 metres of altitude.

122965.q: What do long-term observations of plants on European mountain summits show?
a: The number of plant species on the summits is increasing
The summits are losing all vascular plants
The number of species has stayed the same for 100 years
122965.e: Studies on hundreds of European summits show that more and more species from lower altitudes are moving up. This increase has accelerated in recent decades.
122965.m: More plant species grow on Europe's mountain summits today than in the past.

122966.q: What does the expression “escalator to extinction” mean for mountain species?
a: Species are pushed upwards until there is no habitat left above them
Species die out because ski lifts spread their seeds
Species move down into the valleys and crowd out others there
Species are carried to lower altitudes by avalanches
122966.e: As it gets warmer, cold-adapted species retreat higher and higher. When they reach the summit there is no cooler space left, and their habitat shrinks until it disappears.
122966.m: When it gets warmer, mountain species cannot escape beyond the summit.

122967.q: Which quantity describes how fast climate zones move across the landscape, for example in kilometres per year?
122967.e: Climate velocity (velocity of climate change) shows how far the same temperature conditions move over time. It is high on flat land and lower in the mountains, because short distances uphill are enough.
122967.m: Climate velocity measures how fast climate zones move.

122968.q: Which main tree species of the Swiss Plateau is considered particularly at risk at low altitudes because of drought and bark beetles?
122968.e: The spruce is a shallow-rooted tree of cool, damp places and was often planted on the Swiss Plateau outside its natural range. Drought stress weakens it, so pests can attack it more easily.
122968.m: At low altitudes, the spruce suffers especially from heat and drought.

122969.q: Why are many plants less able than many birds to follow the shifting climate?
a: They spread only slowly through seeds from generation to generation
They have no metabolism that reacts to warmth
They can only move towards the equator
122969.e: Plants are rooted in place and only move when seeds germinate in new places and produce seeds there in turn. For long-lived trees this can take decades, while birds can reach new areas in one season.
122969.m: Rooted plants move much more slowly than mobile animals.

122970.q: Which obstacle can stop species in an intensively used landscape from following their climate?
122970.e: Roads, settlements and intensive farming cut habitats into pieces. Species then find no corridors through which they can reach areas with a suitable climate.
122970.m: Fragmented landscapes slow down the movement of species.

122971.q: What is meant by a trophic mismatch?
a: A timing gap between a species' need for food and the food available
Two predators competing for the same prey
A lack of nutrients in the soil
122971.e: If predators and prey react differently to climate change, the peak of the food supply no longer coincides with the time of greatest need. Then, for example, there is not enough food for young birds.
122971.m: In a trophic mismatch, the timing of food needs and food supply no longer match.

122972.q: According to the match-mismatch hypothesis, what does the survival of fish larvae depend on strongly?
a: Whether they hatch at the time of the plankton bloom
Whether the lake freezes in winter
Whether there are many predatory fish
122972.e: The British fisheries biologist David Cushing used it to explain why the size of fish year classes varies. If the larvae hatch during the plankton bloom, they find enough food.
122972.m: Fish larvae survive better if they hatch during the plankton bloom.

122973.q: Which migratory bird became a textbook example in the Netherlands because it arrives too late when the caterpillar peak is early?
122973.e: The pied flycatcher spends the winter in West Africa and so can hardly return any earlier. Because the caterpillar peak in the oak woods comes earlier, its numbers fell where the peak was especially early.
122973.m: The pied flycatcher shows how migratory birds can miss their food peak.

122974.q: Why are long-distance migrants particularly vulnerable to a mismatch?
a: In their winter quarters they cannot sense how early spring is starting in the breeding area
They only breed every two years
They spend the winter in the breeding area
122974.e: In their winter quarters south of the Sahara they receive no signals about the weather in Europe. Short-distance migrants, which spend the winter closer, can adjust their return more easily.
122974.m: In Africa, long-distance migrants cannot tell when spring begins in Europe.

122975.q: Which food chain involving great tits in oak woods is often studied as an example of a mismatch?
a: Oak, winter moth caterpillar, great tit
122975.e: Leaf-out of the oak determines when winter moth caterpillars hatch. Great tits need lots of caterpillars for their nestlings at exactly that time, and with warming these dates shift by different amounts.
122975.m: Great tits feed their young on caterpillars that depend on oak leaf-out.

122976.q: Which environmental signal do many migratory birds respond to when timing their departure, while many plants hardly do?
122976.e: Day length (photoperiod) does not change with climate change. Plants and insects react more strongly to temperature, which is why the two rhythms can drift apart.
122976.m: Day length stays the same, even when the climate gets warmer.

122977.q: What effect did earlier plant growth in western Greenland have on young reindeer?
a: They missed the most nutritious food
They moved away to the south
122977.e: Because of warming, plant growth started earlier, but the reindeer calves were not born correspondingly earlier. So they missed the best food, and fewer young survived.
122977.m: Reindeer calves can also miss the best food because of climate change.

122978.q: Which mismatch threatens early-flowering plants and wild bees?
a: Plants flower before their pollinators are active
Bees eat the leaves instead of the pollen
122978.e: Flowering time and the emergence of bees are controlled by different signals. If plants flower too early, pollinators are missing, and the bees find less food later.
122978.m: If plants flower too early, they lack the right pollinators.

122979.q: In how many levels is the danger of forest fires given in Switzerland?
122979.e: The scale goes from level 1 (low danger) to level 5 (very high danger). At higher levels, fires are often banned in and near forests.
122979.m: Switzerland's forest fire danger scale has five levels.

122980.q: In which season is the risk of forest fires traditionally especially high on the southern side of the Alps in Ticino?
a: In late winter and early spring
122980.e: Before leaf-out there are lots of dry leaves on the ground, and the dry north foehn wind can quickly fan a fire. That is why fires are especially common in Ticino between December and April.
122980.m: In Ticino, forests often burn in late winter when the dry north foehn blows.

122981.q: Near which place in Valais did one of the largest forest fires in recent Swiss history happen in August 2003?
122981.e: In the hot summer of 2003, about 300 hectares of forest burned above Leuk. The area has since been used as a research site for recolonisation after fire.
122981.m: The Leuk forest fire of 2003 is an important research site.

122982.q: Which three factors make up the so-called fire triangle?
122982.e: A fire only burns when burnable material, oxygen and enough heat come together. If one of them is missing, it goes out.
122982.m: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat.

122983.q: Which internationally used index from Canada is used to assess the danger of forest fires from weather data?
122983.e: The Canadian Fire Weather Index combines temperature, humidity, wind and rainfall into a danger value. It is also used in Europe and in Switzerland.
122983.m: The Fire Weather Index estimates fire danger from weather data.

122984.q: What is the most common cause of forest fires in Switzerland?
122984.e: Most forest fires are caused by carelessness, for example campfires, cigarettes or flying sparks. Lightning causes a smaller share of fires, mainly in summer.
122984.m: Most forest fires in Switzerland are caused by people.

122985.q: Why do some pine species only open their cones after a forest fire?
a: The seeds then fall on open, nutrient-rich ground
The cones need soot as fertiliser
So that birds do not eat the seeds
122985.e: Resin seals the cones until the heat melts it. After the fire the seeds fall on ground without competition and with lots of ash as nutrients.
122985.m: Some pines only sow their seeds after a fire.

122986.q: Why can climate change make the forest fire season longer?
a: Warmer and drier periods start earlier and end later
Higher CO2 levels make wood unburnable
122986.e: Rising temperatures increase evaporation and dry out leaf litter and soil faster. So there are more days on which fires can start and spread.
122986.m: With climate change there are more days with a high risk of forest fires.

122987.q: What is meant by assisted migration?
a: Deliberately moving species to areas that will suit their climate in future
Returning zoo animals to their area of origin
Seeds being spread by the wind
122987.e: Because climate zones are shifting faster than some species can move, people bring them to new areas that will be suitable in future. The method is controversial.
122987.m: In assisted migration, people help species move to the climate that will suit them in future.

122988.q: Why was the critically endangered Florida torreya planted far north of where it occurs naturally?
a: Because its current habitat is becoming too warm for it
Because it bears fruit faster in the north
Because planting is forbidden in Florida
Because it needs snow to germinate
122988.e: The Florida torreya (Torreya taxifolia) occurs only in a small area. The group “Torreya Guardians” planted it in cooler regions further north, a well-known example of assisted migration.
122988.m: The Florida torreya was moved to cooler areas.

122989.q: Which risk is mentioned particularly often in connection with assisted migration?
a: The relocated species could become invasive in the new area
The species could get too little sunlight
The species could lose its colour
The species could no longer be transported
122989.e: A species that arrives in a new ecosystem can crowd out native species there or bring in diseases. That is why experts call for careful risk assessments.
122989.m: Relocated species can become a plague in the new area.

122990.q: What does assisted population migration mean in forestry?
a: Seed from warmer origins of the same species is used within its range
Whole forests are moved to other continents
Forest animals are moved into towns
Trees are only grown in nurseries
122990.e: The tree species stays the same, but trees are planted from populations already adapted to a warmer or drier climate. The risk is considered lower than when introducing new species.
122990.m: Other origins of the same tree species can also make forests fit for the climate.

122991.q: Why is assisted migration an issue especially for species that spread poorly?
a: They cannot shift their range fast enough
They are immune to climate change
122991.e: Species with heavy seeds or small remaining populations cannot manage the necessary move on their own. Without help they could die out, even though suitable habitats exist elsewhere.
122991.m: Slow species are more likely to need help when the climate changes quickly.

122992.q: What does the term assisted migration mean in plain words?
122992.e: It means supported or accompanied migration. The idea is always that people actively help a species shift its range.

122993.q: In the view of many experts, which condition should be met before assisted migration?
a: The species is seriously threatened without help and the risk in the target area has been checked
The species must be common in zoos
The target area must be as close to the equator as possible
The species must not produce seeds
122993.e: Because such interventions can hardly be reversed, they are usually seen as a last resort. Beforehand, the threat, the benefits and possible damage in the new ecosystem should be carefully assessed.
122993.m: Assisted migration is seen as a last resort after thorough checks.

122994.q: How does assisted migration differ from a classic reintroduction?
a: The species is brought to places where it did not occur before
The species is only kept in captivity
The species is brought back to its former area
The species is wiped out and replaced
122994.e: In a reintroduction, for example of the bearded vulture in the Alps, a species returns to its former range. Assisted migration, by contrast, targets areas outside the previous range.
122994.m: Reintroduction leads back, assisted migration leads to new areas.

122995.q: Which two federal bodies are the main partners behind the Swiss project “Test plantations of future-proof tree species”?
122995.e: The Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research WSL and the Federal Office for the Environment FOEN work with cantonal forest services and forest owners to test which tree species can cope with the future climate. The sites are spread across the whole of Switzerland.
122995.m: WSL and FOEN test trees for the forest of the future.

122996.q: Why are test plantations set up at the same time at many sites spread across Switzerland?
a: To compare tree species under different climate and soil conditions
To harvest as much wood as possible for sale
To give every canton the same number of trees
122996.e: Sites at different altitudes and in different regions already have conditions today that will only exist elsewhere in future. This makes it possible to estimate which species can survive where.
122996.m: Many different sites show where a tree species will thrive in future.

122997.q: Which region does the Douglas fir, which is being studied in Swiss test plantations, come from?
122997.e: The Douglas fir was brought to Europe from western North America in the 19th century. It grows fast and is considered more drought-tolerant than the spruce.
122997.m: The Douglas fir comes from western North America.

122998.q: Which mountains does the Atlas cedar, which is being tested as a possible tree species for drier sites, come from?
a: The Atlas Mountains in North Africa
122998.e: The Atlas cedar grows naturally in Morocco and Algeria and is adapted to drought. That is why researchers are interested in it as a possible addition to warmer Swiss forests.
122998.m: The Atlas cedar comes from the Atlas Mountains in North Africa.

122999.q: What principle lies behind growing several different tree species in a forest adapted to the climate?
122999.e: If one tree species fails because of drought or pests, other species can keep the forest going. That is why mixed forests are considered more resilient to an uncertain climate future.
122999.m: Mixed forests spread the risk over many tree species.

123000.q: In test plantations of future-proof tree species, what is recorded particularly carefully besides growth?
a: Survival and damage from drought, frost and pests
The colour of the bark in sunlight
123000.e: A tree of the future must not only withstand heat and drought but also survive late frosts and diseases. That is why survival rate, damage and growth are documented over many years.
123000.m: Trees of the future must withstand heat, frost and pests alike.

123001.q: Why do trials with tree species for the forest of the future take an especially long time?
a: Trees live very long and only react to site conditions over decades
Trees only grow in leap years
Seedlings may only be planted after 50 years
Measurements are only possible in winter
123001.e: A forest tree often stands in the same place for over 100 years. Whether it survives hot summers, late frosts and pests only becomes clear over a long time.
123001.m: Because trees live so long, forest trials need a lot of patience.

123002.q: Which tree species, widespread in Ticino since Roman times, is seen as a possible tree of the future north of the Alps too because it loves warmth?
123002.e: The sweet chestnut was probably promoted by the Romans and has shaped the southern side of the Alps for centuries. With warming, it could also become more important on the Swiss Plateau.
123002.m: The warmth-loving sweet chestnut could become more common on the Swiss Plateau.

123003.q: What does the CO2 fertilisation effect describe?
a: Greater plant growth due to more carbon dioxide in the air
Fertiliser being formed from carbon dioxide in the soil
Plants dying from too much CO2
123003.e: Carbon dioxide is the raw material of photosynthesis. If its concentration rises, many plants can take up more carbon and grow faster, as long as other factors do not limit them.
123003.m: More CO2 can boost plant growth.

123004.q: Which group of plants benefits more from higher CO2 in photosynthesis?
123004.e: C4 plants already concentrate CO2 internally around the enzyme Rubisco. C3 plants do not, which is why their photosynthesis increases more with extra CO2.
123004.m: C3 plants benefit more from extra CO2 than C4 plants.

123005.q: Which process is reduced in C3 plants by higher CO2 concentrations?
123005.e: Rubisco can bind oxygen instead of CO2, which leads to wasteful photorespiration. More CO2 pushes the oxygen away from the enzyme and so increases efficiency.

123006.q: How does the water use efficiency of plants often change with higher CO2?
a: It rises because the stomata open less wide
It falls because plants lose more water
It becomes zero because plants no longer need water
123006.e: With more CO2 in the air, the plant can manage with smaller stomatal openings. It loses less water for each amount of carbon it takes up.
123006.m: More CO2 makes plants use water more sparingly.

123007.q: How do many vegetable growers use the CO2 fertilisation effect deliberately?
a: They add CO2 to the air in the greenhouse
They remove the CO2 from the greenhouse air
They replace the air with pure oxygen
They only water with distilled water
123007.e: In closed greenhouses, CO2 is often added, for example from the heating. Tomatoes and cucumbers then grow faster and give a bigger yield.
123007.m: Greenhouses use extra CO2 for a bigger yield.

123008.q: What limits the CO2 fertilisation effect in many ecosystems in the long term?
a: A lack of nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus
123008.e: To grow more, plants also need more nutrients. If nitrogen or phosphorus is scarce, the effect levels off over time.
123008.m: Without enough nutrients, the CO2 fertilisation effect stays limited.

123009.q: Which consequence for nutrition do studies show for wheat and rice under raised CO2?
a: Lower levels of protein, zinc and iron
123009.e: With more CO2, plants make more carbohydrates, while minerals and proteins are diluted. This can harm nutrition in regions where the diet is based on rice.
123009.m: More CO2 can lower the nutrient content of cereals.

123010.q: Which observation from satellite data is partly attributed to the CO2 fertilisation effect?
a: A global greening of many land areas
A worldwide decrease in leaf area
123010.e: Since the 1980s, satellites have shown an increase in leaf area on many land areas. A large part of this is linked to rising CO2 levels, as well as to land use.
123010.m: Satellites show that the Earth has become greener in many regions.

123011.q: What do researchers mean when they talk about the tipping point of the Amazon rainforest?
a: Beyond a certain level of deforestation, more forest dies off by itself
The place where the Amazon flows into the sea
The year the last tree is cut down
The point at which the forest bears the most fruit
123011.e: If too much forest is lost, it rains less, and the remaining forest dries out. According to estimates, this could already begin at 20 to 25 per cent deforestation.
123011.m: At the tipping point, the Amazon would keep shrinking by itself.

123012.q: Into which type of vegetation could parts of the Amazon rainforest change after the tipping point is passed?
123012.e: Without forest, less water evaporates and it rains less. This favours drier, open vegetation, which is called savannisation.
123012.m: A tipped Amazon would partly become savannah.

123013.q: What is the transport of water vapour called, through which the rainforest carries moisture far inland?
123013.e: Trees release large amounts of water, which moves on as clouds and falls as rain again. These “flying rivers” even supply regions in southern Brazil with rain.
123013.m: The rainforest produces a large part of its own rain.

123014.q: What did a study by Luciana Gatti, published in “Nature” in 2021, show about south-eastern Amazonia?
a: It now releases more carbon than it absorbs
It absorbs twice as much CO2 as before
123014.e: Measurement flights over Amazonia showed that the heavily deforested south-east in particular has become a source of carbon. Fires and drought are important causes.
123014.m: Parts of Amazonia have turned from a carbon sink into a carbon source.

123015.q: Which country has the largest share of the Amazon rainforest?
123015.e: About 60 per cent of the Amazon rainforest lies in Brazil. The rest is spread across eight other countries and territories such as Peru, Colombia and French Guiana.
123015.m: Most of the Amazon rainforest lies in Brazil.

123016.q: What does hysteresis mean in connection with a tipping point?
a: After tipping, slightly reducing the cause is not enough to restore the old state
A system swings between two states every year
A system does not react to disturbances at all
A system always returns to its starting state immediately
123016.e: A system that has tipped can remain in a new stable state. To return, the pressure would often have to fall well below the original threshold.
123016.m: Ecosystems that have tipped do not simply return to their old state.

123017.q: Besides the Amazon rainforest, which parts of the climate system do researchers count as tipping elements?
a: Greenland's ice and the Atlantic ocean current
Phases of the moon and tides
The Earth's core and magnetic field
123017.e: Tipping elements are parts of the climate system that can tip into a new state if warming is strong. They include the Greenland ice sheet, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation and the Amazon rainforest.
123017.m: Greenland's ice and the Atlantic current are also considered tipping elements.

123018.q: Which mechanism makes the remaining rainforest dry out more after deforestation?
a: Less evaporation leads to less rain
More trees take oxygen out of the soil
A higher sea level floods the forest
123018.e: A large part of the rain in the Amazon region comes from water released by the trees themselves. If this is lost, it becomes drier, which encourages fires and weakens more forest.
123018.m: In the Amazon, fewer trees mean less rain.

a: The corals expel their symbiotic algae
123019.e: Under heat stress, corals expel their zooxanthellae, single-celled algae that give them colour and nutrients. What is left is the white limestone skeleton beneath the see-through tissue.
123019.m: During coral bleaching, corals lose the algae that give them colour.

123020.q: Which phylum of animals do corals belong to?
123020.e: Corals are related to jellyfish and sea anemones and have stinging cells. Reef-building stony corals live in colonies of many small polyps.

123021.q: What most often triggers coral bleaching?
a: Sea water that is too warm for weeks
Water that is too cold in winter
Too many fish on the reef
123021.e: If the water temperature stays above the normal summer maximum for a long time, the corals expel their algae. The US agency NOAA measures this build-up of heat stress in degree heating weeks.
123021.m: Sea water that stays too warm for a long time triggers coral bleaching.

123022.q: How have worldwide coral bleaching events developed since 1998?
a: They are happening more and more often
They now only affect the Atlantic
They only happen every hundred years
123022.e: There were global bleaching events in 1998, 2010, from 2014 to 2017 and again from 2023. The gaps are getting shorter because the oceans are warming.
123022.m: Global coral bleaching events are becoming more and more frequent.

123023.q: According to the 2018 IPCC special report, what proportion of tropical coral reefs is likely to be lost with 2 °C of warming?
123023.e: The IPCC report on 1.5 °C estimated a decline of 70 to 90 per cent at 1.5 °C. At 2 °C, more than 99 per cent of warm-water coral reefs would be lost.
123023.m: Even two degrees of warming would destroy almost all coral reefs.

123024.q: Which other effect of rising CO2 makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons?
123024.e: The sea absorbs CO2, forming carbonic acid and lowering the pH. As a result less carbonate is available for the aragonite skeleton.
123024.m: Ocean acidification makes it harder for corals to build their limestone.

123025.q: Why can bleached corals sometimes recover?
a: They can take up the algae again if the water cools down in time
They build new skeletons from sand
123025.e: Bleached corals are weakened but not dead straight away. If the temperature soon falls again, they can take up new zooxanthellae; if the stress lasts long, they starve.
123025.m: Bleached corals only survive if the heat stress ends quickly.

123026.q: Which largest coral reef system on Earth has suffered several mass bleaching events in quick succession since 2016?
123026.e: On the Great Barrier Reef off Australia there were mass bleaching events in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024, among others. The gaps are too short for a full recovery.
123026.m: The Great Barrier Reef is bleaching more and more often.

123027.q: How did the Swiss Army supply animals on alpine pastures with water in summer 2018?
a: With helicopters that flew water up
123027.e: Because springs and ponds dried up, the army's Super Puma helicopters flew water to alpine pastures that could not be reached by vehicle. This allowed cows to stay on the pastures.
123027.m: In summer 2018 the army flew water up to the Alps for cows.

123028.q: Which fish species died in large numbers in the High Rhine near Schaffhausen in summer 2018 because the water was too warm?
123028.e: Grayling need cool water rich in oxygen. When parts of the Rhine reached over 27 °C in August 2018, many fish died, as they had in the hot summer of 2003; in the canton of Zurich alone, about 1000 kg of dead fish were recovered.
123028.m: Grayling die when the Rhine gets too warm.

123029.q: What effect did the drought of 2018 have on shipping on the Rhine?
a: Because of low water, ships could only sail partly loaded
The ships had to stop because of ice
More ships sailed than ever before
123029.e: In autumn 2018 the water level at Kaub on the Middle Rhine fell to a record low. Cargo ships could carry only part of their load, which pushed up transport costs and fuel prices.
123029.m: When the water is low, Rhine ships can only carry a small load.

123030.q: Which measure did many cantons take around 1 August in summer 2018?
a: Bans on fireworks and open-air fires
A ban on watering gardens with rainwater
123030.e: Because of the high risk of forest fires, many cantons and municipalities banned fireworks and open-air fires. Many 1 August bonfires were also cancelled.
123030.m: In the hot summer of 2018, many 1 August bonfires did not take place.

123031.q: Which broadleaf tree species showed strikingly early brown leaves and early leaf fall in northern Switzerland after the drought of 2018?
123031.e: Especially on shallow soils, for example around Schaffhausen and in the Jura, beeches suffered badly from lack of water. In the following years many trees showed crown damage or died.
123031.m: In 2018 the beech suffered badly from the drought in northern Switzerland.

123032.q: Which pest benefited from the weakened spruces in the years after 2018?
123032.e: The European spruce bark beetle attacks weakened spruces because they produce less resin. After 2018 the amount of beetle-damaged wood in Switzerland rose sharply.
123032.m: Drought makes spruces vulnerable to the spruce bark beetle.

123033.q: Looking back, what was particularly characteristic of the 2018 drought in Central Europe?
a: It was the start of a dry period lasting several years, until about 2020
It only affected the southern side of the Alps
It came with record rainfall in summer
123033.e: In parts of Central Europe, 2019 and 2020 were also dry years, so the soils did not recover. Droughts lasting several years do particularly great damage to forests.
123033.m: In Central Europe, 2018 was followed by more dry years.

123034.q: Which Scandinavian country struggled with an unusually large number of forest fires in summer 2018, even north of the Arctic Circle?
123034.e: In 2018 many forests burned in Sweden, some even north of the Arctic Circle. The country asked other European countries for firefighting planes.
123034.m: In the hot summer of 2018, there were fires even in northern Sweden.

123035.q: What is meant by blue carbon?
a: Carbon stored in coastal and marine ecosystems
123035.e: The term covers carbon taken up by plants on coasts and in the sea. They store it mainly in their sediments.
123035.m: Blue carbon is the carbon stored in coastal ecosystems.

123036.q: Which three coastal ecosystems are at the centre of blue carbon research?
a: Mangroves, seagrass meadows and salt marshes
Coral reefs, the deep sea and icebergs
123036.e: These three habitats store a particularly large amount of carbon in the soil per area. Coral reefs are not included because building their limestone tends to release CO2.
123036.m: Mangroves, seagrass and salt marshes are the most important blue carbon stores.

123037.q: Why does carbon stay stored for a long time in mangrove and seagrass sediments?
a: The waterlogged sediments are low in oxygen, which slows breakdown
The salt turns carbon into stone
The tides pump the carbon into the atmosphere
123037.e: In soils low in oxygen, decomposers work only very slowly. Organic material therefore builds up over centuries to thousands of years.
123037.m: Lack of oxygen in the sediment preserves carbon.

123038.q: Why is blue carbon also linked to climate protection?
a: Coastal ecosystems take CO₂ out of the air and store it for a long time
It turns the sea water blue
Coastal plants make electricity from waves
Blue carbon replaces oil as a fuel
123038.e: Mangroves, seagrass meadows and salt marshes take up CO₂ and store the carbon in their sediments. Protecting them prevents this carbon from being released again.
123038.m: Coastal ecosystems are important carbon stores.

123039.q: Which plant forms extensive underwater meadows with large carbon stores in the Mediterranean?
123039.e: Neptune grass (Posidonia oceanica) occurs only in the Mediterranean. It forms thick mats of roots and rhizomes that grow over thousands of years and store a lot of carbon.
123039.m: Neptune grass stores a lot of carbon in the Mediterranean.

123040.q: Which statement about seagrasses is true?
a: They are flowering plants, not algae
123040.e: Seagrasses have roots and leaves and produce flowers and seeds under water. They are descended from land plants that returned to the sea.
123040.m: Seagrasses are true flowering plants in the sea.

123041.q: Which use has destroyed many mangrove forests in South-East Asia and Latin America?
123041.e: Large areas of mangroves were cleared for aquaculture. This not only destroys habitat but also releases the carbon stored in the soil.
123041.m: Shrimp farms have destroyed many mangroves.

123042.q: What are the breathing roots called that stick straight up out of the mud in many mangroves?
123042.e: The mud is very low in oxygen. Pneumatophores stick up into the air and supply the roots with oxygen through small openings.
123042.m: Mangroves breathe out of the mud through pneumatophores.

123043.q: How does the amount of carbon in soils worldwide compare with that of the atmosphere and vegetation together?
a: Soils store more than both together
Soils store exactly as much as the atmosphere
123043.e: The top metre of soil alone holds about 1500 billion tonnes of organic carbon. That is more than in the atmosphere and plants together.
123043.m: Soils are the largest carbon store on land.

123044.q: Which land ecosystems cover only about 3 per cent of the land area but store a particularly large amount of carbon?
123044.e: In wet peatlands low in oxygen, dead plant material hardly breaks down and builds up as peat. Peatlands store about twice as much carbon as the biomass of all forests.
123044.m: Despite their small area, peatlands are huge carbon stores.

123045.q: A soil contains 2.5 per cent organic carbon. Roughly what is its humus content if you convert using the factor 1.72?
123045.e: Humus is about 58 per cent carbon, so you multiply by about 1.72. 2.5 times 1.72 gives 4.3 per cent humus.
123045.m: You estimate humus content as carbon content times 1.72.

123046.q: Which initiative was launched at the 2015 Paris climate conference to raise soil carbon slightly every year?
123046.e: France launched the “4 per 1000” initiative. If the carbon stock of soils grew by 0.4 per cent a year, it could offset a large part of the annual rise in CO2.
123046.m: The “4 per 1000” initiative aims to put more carbon into soils.

123048.q: Which popular initiative of 1987 placed bogs and moorland landscapes in Switzerland under strict protection?
123048.e: The Rothenthurm initiative was accepted by the people in 1987, triggered by plans for a military training ground in a raised bog. Since then, bogs and moorland landscapes of special beauty and national importance have been protected in the Federal Constitution.
123048.m: Since the Rothenthurm initiative, bogs in Switzerland have been protected by the constitution.

123049.q: What happens when a peat soil is drained for farming, as in the Grosses Moos in the Seeland region?
a: The peat decomposes, releases CO2 and the ground sinks
The soil suddenly stores more carbon
123049.e: With oxygen, microorganisms break down the peat and CO2 escapes. As a result, the ground in the Grosses Moos has sunk by more than a metre since the Jura water corrections.
123049.m: Drained peatlands lose peat and become a source of CO2.

123051.q: Why can the CO2 fertilisation effect not simply cancel out the effects of climate change on plants?
a: Heat and drought can hold back growth more than extra CO2 boosts it
Plants do not take up CO2 at all
The effect only works at night
More CO2 makes all plants die immediately
123051.e: In drought, plants close their stomata, and in great heat their photosynthesis falls. Then the higher CO2 level is of little use.
123051.m: In heat and drought, even more CO2 hardly helps plants.

123052.q: Which country had the largest forest fire season by area in its recorded history in 2023, with smoke reaching Europe?
123052.e: In Canada more than 15 million hectares burned in 2023, far more than in any previous year. At times the smoke darkened the sky in New York and even reached Europe.
123052.m: Canada's 2023 forest fire season broke all records.

123053.q: What is being observed at the Alpine tree line as the climate warms?
a: In many places it is slowly moving upwards
It drops by 100 metres every year
It stays exactly the same everywhere
123053.e: Young trees now often grow above the former tree line where warmth and land no longer being used allow it. But because trees grow slowly, the tree line lags behind the climate.
123053.m: The tree line in the Alps is slowly moving upwards.

123054.q: Which record was measured at the port of Manaus during the drought in the Amazon region in October 2023?
a: The lowest level of the Rio Negro since measurements began
The highest flood of the Amazon for 100 years
The lowest air temperature in Brazil
123054.e: Water level measurements in Manaus go back more than 120 years. In 2023 the Rio Negro fell to a new low, river villages were cut off and river dolphins died in the overheated water; in 2024 the level fell even lower.
123054.m: The 2023 drought made the Rio Negro at Manaus fall to a record low.

123154.q: What is the thin layer called on which epithelial cells sit and which separates them from the tissue underneath?
123154.e: The basement membrane is a thin layer of extracellular material. It anchors the epithelium and separates it from the tissue below.
123154.m: Epithelial cells sit on a basement membrane.

123155.q: Which type of epithelium forms the human epidermis?
123155.e: The epidermis consists of many layers of cells, the top ones of which become horny and flake off. This protects the skin well against friction and drying out.
123155.m: The epidermis consists of stratified keratinised squamous epithelium.

123156.q: Which epithelium lines the bladder and adapts to the strong stretching as it fills?
123156.e: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) can change its height: when the bladder is empty it looks many-layered, when full it is flatter. It is found in the urinary tract.
123156.m: The bladder is lined with stretchy transitional epithelium.

123157.q: Which property is typical of epithelial tissue?
a: It has a great deal of intercellular substance
123157.e: Epithelia have no blood vessels. They are nourished by diffusion from the well-supplied tissue underneath.
123157.m: Epithelial tissue is supplied by diffusion without its own blood vessels.

123158.q: What do the cilia of the epithelium in the airways move along?
a: Mucus with dust towards the throat
123158.e: The cilia beat in a coordinated way and push the mucus with trapped particles and germs upwards. There it is swallowed or coughed up.
123158.m: Ciliated epithelium cleans the airways by moving mucus upwards.

123159.q: Which type of epithelium lines the alveoli and allows fast gas exchange because it is so thin?
123159.e: In the alveoli the wall is made only of very flat cells. This makes the diffusion path for oxygen and carbon dioxide very short.
123159.m: Thin simple squamous epithelium makes gas exchange in the lungs easier.

123160.q: What are the cell junctions called that seal neighbouring epithelial cells so tightly that hardly any substances get through between them?
123160.e: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) form a belt around the cells and seal the space between them. In this way the lining of the intestine, for example, controls which substances are taken up.
123160.m: Tight junctions seal epithelia against uncontrolled passage of substances.

123161.q: What is a malignant tumour that starts in epithelial tissue called?
123161.e: Carcinomas arise from epithelial cells, for example in the skin, lungs or intestine. They are the most common group of malignant tumours.
123161.m: A carcinoma is a malignant tumour of epithelial tissue.

123162.q: Which protein is the most common structural protein of connective tissue and makes tendons particularly strong under tension?
123162.e: Collagen forms tear-resistant fibres found in tendons, ligaments, bones and skin. It is the most common protein in the human body.
123162.m: Collagen fibres make tendons strong under tension.

123163.q: Which cells produce the fibres and ground substance in loose connective tissue?
123163.e: Fibroblasts are the typical cells of connective tissue. They make fibre proteins and components of the ground substance and are important in wound healing.
123163.m: Fibroblasts build the fibres of connective tissue.

123164.q: What is the whole of fibres and ground substance lying between the cells in connective tissue called?
123164.e: In connective tissue, the cells lie loosely scattered in a lot of intercellular substance. This extracellular matrix determines whether the tissue is firm, elastic or soft.
123164.m: Connective tissue consists largely of extracellular matrix.

123165.q: A lack of which vitamin disturbs the formation of stable connective tissue fibres and leads to the disease scurvy?
123165.e: Vitamin C is needed for an enzyme that stabilises the fibre proteins. Without it, bleeding gums, poor wound healing and bleeding occur.
123165.m: A lack of vitamin C causes scurvy.

123166.q: What are the cells called that store fat in fatty tissue?
123166.e: Adipocytes store fat in large droplets. Fatty tissue serves as an energy store, heat insulation and padding.

123167.q: Which fatty tissue can produce heat directly by burning fat, especially in babies?
123167.e: Brown fat cells contain a great many mitochondria with the protein thermogenin. As a result, energy is released as heat instead of as ATP.

123168.q: Which fibres make sure that skin or artery walls return to their shape after being stretched?
123168.e: Elastic fibres consist mainly of elastin and can be stretched like rubber. Their amount decreases with age, which is why the skin becomes more wrinkled.
123168.m: Elastic fibres make tissue stretchy and springy.

123169.q: Which two types of cell make up nervous tissue?
123169.e: Nerve cells (neurons) conduct and process signals. Glial cells support, nourish and insulate them.
123169.m: Nervous tissue consists of nerve cells and glial cells.

123170.q: Which glial cells form the myelin sheath around axons in the peripheral nervous system?
123170.e: Schwann cells wrap themselves several times around an axon and insulate it electrically. In the brain and spinal cord, other glial cells perform this task.
123170.m: In the peripheral nervous system, Schwann cells form the myelin.

123171.q: What are the uncovered points between two sections of myelin called, where the impulse jumps from point to point?
123171.e: The action potential only arises at the bare points between the sections of myelin. This saltatory conduction is much faster than continuous conduction.
123171.m: At the nodes of Ranvier, the impulse jumps along the axon.

123172.q: Which glial cells take on the role of immune and scavenger cells in the brain?
123172.e: Microglial cells remove pathogens, dead cells and waste products. They are the resident defence cells of the central nervous system.
123172.m: Microglia are the defence cells of the brain.

123173.q: What is the point of contact called where a nerve cell passes its signal on to another cell with the help of messenger substances?
123173.e: At a chemical synapse, neurotransmitters are released into a narrow gap. They bind to receptors on the next cell and trigger a response there.
123173.m: At synapses, a signal is transmitted with neurotransmitters.

123174.q: Which muscle tissue is striated but works involuntarily?
123174.e: Like skeletal muscle, heart muscle cells show striations. However, they are not controlled voluntarily but by the heart's own system for generating impulses.
123174.m: Heart muscle is striated and works involuntarily.

123175.q: Which two proteins slide past each other when a muscle contracts?
123175.e: The myosin heads pull on the actin filaments and push them towards each other. In this way the muscle shortens without the filaments themselves becoming shorter.
123175.m: During contraction, actin and myosin slide past each other.

123176.q: Which ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and trigger muscle contraction?
123176.e: Calcium binds to troponin and so frees the binding sites on the actin. Only then can the myosin heads grab hold.

123177.q: Which substance is needed so that the myosin heads can let go of the actin again?
123177.e: Only the binding of ATP releases the connection between myosin and actin. After death there is no ATP, which is why the muscles stay stiff in rigor mortis.
123177.m: Without ATP, a muscle cannot relax again.

123178.q: How do the multinucleated skeletal muscle fibres form during development?
a: By nuclear division without cell division
123178.e: Myoblasts with a single nucleus fuse into long muscle fibres with many nuclei. Such a structure is called a syncytium.
123178.m: Skeletal muscle fibres form by the fusion of many cells.

123179.q: What are the junctions between heart muscle cells called, through which the impulse spreads quickly from cell to cell?
123179.e: Intercalated discs contain mechanical anchoring junctions and gap junctions. The impulse flows directly into the neighbouring cell through these channels.
123179.m: Intercalated discs connect heart muscle cells mechanically and electrically.

123180.q: What usually distinguishes adult stem cells from embryonic stem cells?
a: They only form cells of their own tissue
They form all cell types of the body
