123180.e: Adult stem cells are usually multipotent: they renew a particular tissue, such as blood or skin. Embryonic stem cells, on the other hand, can form a great many cell types.
123180.m: Adult stem cells are usually limited to their own tissue.

123181.q: Which stem cells constantly replace all the blood cells in adults?
123181.e: Haematopoietic, that is blood-forming, stem cells produce red and white blood cells and platelets. In this way billions of new blood cells are formed every day.
123181.m: Haematopoietic stem cells are the source of all blood cells.

123182.q: Where are most blood-forming stem cells found in adults?
123182.e: In adults, blood formation takes place mainly in the red bone marrow of the pelvis, vertebrae, ribs and breastbone.
123182.m: In adults, blood is formed in the red bone marrow.

123183.q: Which disease has been treated for decades with the transplantation of blood-forming stem cells?
123183.e: In leukaemia, the diseased blood cells are destroyed and the blood system is rebuilt with healthy stem cells. The stem cells come from a donor or from the patient themselves.
123183.m: Stem cell transplants can save lives in leukaemia.

123184.q: Which two properties characterise every stem cell?
a: Self-renewal and the formation of specialised cells
123184.e: A stem cell can divide and in doing so form stem cells again. At the same time it can produce daughter cells that specialise.
123184.m: Stem cells renew themselves and supply specialised cells.

123185.q: Which cells can develop from mesenchymal stem cells?
123185.e: Mesenchymal stem cells are found, for example, in bone marrow and fatty tissue. They can develop into cells of the supporting tissues.
123185.m: Mesenchymal stem cells supply cells for bone, cartilage and fat.

123186.q: Why does the lining of the intestine need a particularly large number of stem cells?
a: Its cells are renewed every few days
123186.e: The cells of the intestinal lining are under heavy strain and are shed after a few days. Stem cells at the base of the lining constantly supply replacements.
123186.m: The lining of the intestine renews itself every few days.

123187.q: What is the special environment in a tissue called that keeps a stem cell in its stem cell state?
123187.e: In the niche, neighbouring cells and the matrix give signals that control the division and specialisation of the stem cell. If a daughter cell leaves the niche, it begins to specialise.
123187.m: The stem cell niche controls the behaviour of stem cells.

123188.q: How are blood-forming stem cells obtained from most donors today?
a: From the blood after a growth factor is given
By an operation on the liver
From a sample of the lining of the mouth
123188.e: A growth factor (G-CSF) draws the stem cells out of the bone marrow into the blood. There they are filtered out with a cell separator; less often, bone marrow is taken directly from the hip bone.
123188.m: Blood stem cells are usually collected from the donor's blood.

123189.q: What is meant by cell differentiation?
a: The specialisation of a cell for a task
The division of a cell into two identical cells
The programmed death of a cell
123189.e: In differentiation, a cell that is not very specialised develops into a particular cell type with its own shape and function, for example a nerve cell.

123190.q: Why do a liver cell and a nerve cell of the same person differ even though they have the same DNA?
a: Different genes are active in each
Only one of the two has mutations
123190.e: All body cells basically carry the same genetic material. But depending on the cell type, they switch different genes on or off.
123190.m: Cell types differ in their gene activity, not in their DNA.

123191.q: What are cells called that can develop into all cell types of the three germ layers?
123191.e: Pluripotent cells such as embryonic stem cells can form cells of all three germ layers. Multipotent cells are limited to a few cell types.
123191.m: Pluripotent cells can form a great many different cell types.

123192.q: Which researcher received the 2012 Nobel Prize in Medicine together with John Gurdon for reprogramming specialised body cells?
123192.e: In 2006 Shinya Yamanaka showed that a few genes are enough to return skin cells to a stem cell-like state. These cells are called induced pluripotent stem cells.
123192.m: Shinya Yamanaka discovered how to reprogramme body cells.

123193.q: What are proteins called that bind to DNA and control which genes are read?
123193.e: Transcription factors bind to control sections of the DNA and switch genes on or off. Certain combinations determine which cell type develops.
123193.m: Transcription factors switch genes on and off.

123194.q: Which chemical change to DNA often switches genes off permanently in specialised cells?
123194.e: Methyl groups on certain sections of DNA prevent genes from being read. Such epigenetic marks are passed on during cell division.
123194.m: DNA methylation can silence genes without changing the base sequence.

123195.q: What is the well-known image called that shows cell differentiation as a ball rolling down a slope with branching valleys?
123195.e: In 1957 the biologist Conrad Waddington described development as a ball rolling into one of several valleys. The further down it is, the more fixed the cell type.
123195.m: The epigenetic landscape illustrates how cells become committed.

123196.q: From which germ layer of the embryo does the nervous system develop?
123196.e: The outer germ layer forms the epidermis and the nervous system. The inner layer gives rise to the lining of the intestine and lungs, for example, and the middle layer to muscles and bones.
123196.m: The nervous system develops from the ectoderm.

123197.q: What is the aim of tissue engineering?
a: To make working tissue in the laboratory
123197.e: In tissue engineering, cells, carrier materials and growth factors are combined. This produces tissue intended to replace or repair damaged tissue.
123197.m: Tissue engineering grows replacement tissue from living cells.

123198.q: What is the supporting framework called on which the cells grow in tissue engineering?
123198.e: A scaffold gives the cells a three-dimensional shape. It is often made of biodegradable plastics or natural biomaterials.
123198.m: In tissue engineering, cells grow on a scaffold.

123199.q: Why are the patient's own cells preferred in tissue engineering?
123199.e: The body's own (autologous) cells are recognised by the immune system as its own. That is why no long-term medicines against rejection are needed.
123199.m: Autologous cells are not rejected by the immune system.

123200.q: Which tissue has been made from cultured cells since the 1980s, for example for people with extensive burns?
123200.e: From a small skin sample, skin cells can be multiplied in the laboratory into thin layers. These can be transferred onto large wounds.
123200.m: Cultured skin helps with severe burns.

123201.q: Which method builds up tissue structures layer by layer from cells and gel?
123201.e: In 3D bioprinting, “bio-inks” containing living cells are printed layer by layer. In this way shapes such as cartilage or blood vessels can be built up precisely.

123202.q: What is a bioreactor used for in tissue engineering?
a: It supplies growing tissue with nutrients in a controlled way
It breaks tissue down into single molecules
It stains tissue for the microscope
123202.e: In the bioreactor, temperature, oxygen, nutrients and often mechanical stimuli are regulated. This helps the cells develop properties typical of the tissue.
123202.m: A bioreactor creates ideal growing conditions for tissue.

123203.q: Which method removes cartilage cells, multiplies them in the laboratory and inserts them into a cartilage defect?
123203.e: In this procedure, healthy cartilage cells are taken from a part of the joint under little strain. After being multiplied, they fill the damage, for example in the knee.
123203.m: Cartilage damage can be treated with the patient's own cultured cartilage cells.

123204.q: What is one of the greatest difficulties in growing thick tissues and whole organs?
123204.e: Oxygen only reaches about 0.1 to 0.2 millimetres into tissue from a blood vessel by diffusion. Without a network of vessels, thick tissue dies on the inside.
123204.m: Grown organs need their own network of blood vessels.

123205.q: In which process are all the cells removed from a donor organ so that only the framework of matrix remains?
123205.e: The cells are washed out with mild detergents. The remaining framework can then be repopulated with the patient's cells.
123205.m: Decellularised organs serve as natural scaffolds.

a: A tiny organ-like tissue from cell culture
An artificial organ made of plastic
A benign tumour of an organ
A cell organelle in the cytoplasm
123206.e: Organoids are three-dimensional clusters of cells, often only a few millimetres in size. They reproduce the structure and some functions of a real organ.
123206.m: Organoids are mini-organs from the culture dish.

123207.q: From which cells are organoids usually grown?
123207.e: Organoids develop from adult stem cells of a tissue or from pluripotent stem cells. In a suitable environment the cells organise themselves.

123208.q: What can organoids from a patient's tumour tissue be used for?
123208.e: Tumour organoids can be used in the laboratory to test which medicine works. In this way treatment can be better adapted to the individual person.
123208.m: Tumour organoids help to find the right treatment.

123209.q: In which material are organoids usually embedded as they grow, to imitate the natural environment of the cells?
a: In a hydrogel made of matrix proteins
123209.e: A gel-like mixture of extracellular matrix proteins gives the cells support in three dimensions. Growth factors in the nutrient medium guide their development.
123209.m: Organoids grow in a gel that imitates the cell environment.

a: As big as a real organ
123210.e: Organoids are three-dimensional clusters of cells, often only a few millimetres in size. Without blood vessels they cannot grow larger, because nutrients do not reach the inside.
123210.m: Organoids are only a few millimetres in size.

123211.q: What are organoids called that reproduce parts of the human brain?
123211.e: Brain organoids develop layers of nerve cells like those found in early brain development. They are used to study, for example, malformations caused by the Zika virus.
123211.m: Brain organoids help us understand how the brain develops.

123212.q: What do most of today's organoids lack compared with real organs?
123212.e: Organoids usually consist of only a few cell types of an organ. Without blood vessels they stay small, and without immune cells some diseases are hard to model.
123212.m: Organoids usually lack blood vessels and immune cells.

123213.q: What advantage do human organoids have over many animal experiments?
a: They are made of human cells
They live for an unlimited time
123213.e: Medicines sometimes work differently in animals than in humans. Organoids made of human cells can partly avoid such differences.

123214.q: Organoids are seen as a possible alternative to animal experiments. What is the principle “Replace, Reduce, Refine” called, which a dedicated competence centre promotes in Switzerland?
123214.e: The 3R principle calls for animal experiments to be replaced, reduced and made gentler. In Switzerland, the Swiss 3R Competence Centre promotes such methods.
123214.m: The 3R principle aims to replace, reduce and refine animal experiments.

123215.q: What distinguishes a malignant tumour from a benign one?
a: It grows destructively into neighbouring tissue
It is always surrounded by a capsule
123215.e: Malignant tumours grow invasively, which means they break through tissue boundaries and destroy surrounding tissue. Benign tumours only push the tissue aside.
123215.m: Malignant tumours grow invasively into neighbouring tissue.

123216.q: What is a malignant tumour called that starts in connective or supporting tissue such as bone?
123216.e: Sarcomas arise from mesenchymal cells, for example from bone, cartilage, muscle or fatty tissue. They are much rarer than tumours of covering tissue.
123216.m: A sarcoma is a malignant tumour of connective or supporting tissue.

123217.q: What is a benign tumour called that arises from glandular tissue?
123217.e: Adenomas are benign growths of glandular epithelium, for example polyps in the large intestine. Some can become malignant over time.
123217.m: An adenoma is a benign tumour of a gland.

123218.q: What is the formation of new blood vessels called, by which a growing tumour supplies itself with oxygen?
123218.e: Once it reaches a size of a few millimetres, a tumour needs its own vessels. It sends out signalling substances such as VEGF that make vessels grow in.
123218.m: Tumours trigger angiogenesis to supply themselves.

123219.q: Which process do cancer cells avoid that normally makes damaged cells die in a controlled way?
123219.e: Apoptosis is programmed cell death. Cancer cells often switch off this self-destruction programme and survive despite damage to their genetic material.
123219.m: Cancer cells escape programmed cell death.

123220.q: What does the letter T stand for in the TNM classification of tumours?
a: Size and extent of the primary tumour
123220.e: T describes the original tumour, N the involvement of lymph nodes and M distant spread. Together they determine the stage and the treatment.
123220.m: The TNM classification describes how far a tumour has spread.

123221.q: Which malignant skin cancer starts in the pigment cells of the skin?
123221.e: Malignant melanoma arises from melanocytes. Heavy UV exposure and sunburn increase the risk; Switzerland has many cases compared with the rest of Europe.
123221.m: Melanoma arises from the pigment cells of the skin.

123222.q: What is the removal of a tissue sample that is examined under the microscope to identify a tumour with certainty called?
123222.e: In a biopsy, a small piece of tissue is removed. Only the examination of the cells shows for certain whether a tumour is benign or malignant.
123222.m: A biopsy provides tissue for a reliable diagnosis.

a: A secondary tumour far from the original tumour
A benign tumour with a capsule
A scar after a cancer operation
123223.e: Metastases form when cancer cells break away, travel through the body and grow again somewhere else. They consist of cells of the original tumour.
123223.m: Metastases are offshoots of a tumour in other parts of the body.

123224.q: By which two main routes do cancer cells spread through the body?
a: Through lymph vessels and blood vessels
123224.e: Cancer cells enter lymph vessels and reach lymph nodes. Through the blood vessels they reach distant organs such as the lungs, liver, bones or brain.
123224.m: Cancer cells spread through the lymph and the blood.

123225.q: What is the first lymph node in the drainage area of a tumour, which is specifically examined during operations, called?
123225.e: The sentinel lymph node is tracked down with a marker. If it is free of cancer cells, the other lymph nodes are usually not affected either.
123225.m: The sentinel lymph node shows whether a tumour has spread to the lymph nodes.

123226.q: What must cancer cells be able to do in order to form metastases?
a: Break away from the group of cells and move
123226.e: Normally cells stick firmly together. Cancer cells that spread release these connections, become mobile and enter blood or lymph vessels.
123226.m: To form metastases, cancer cells must become mobile.

123227.q: Why do some tumours spread preferentially to very particular organs?
a: Because the cancer cells find good conditions for growth there
Because these organs have no immune system
Because cancer cells from food collect there
Because these organs have no blood vessels
123227.e: The surgeon Stephen Paget compared cancer cells to seeds that only thrive in suitable soil. Certain organs offer them particularly favourable conditions.
123227.m: Metastases grow where the soil suits the cancer cells.

123228.q: Through which blood vessel do cells from a bowel tumour usually reach the liver first?
123228.e: Blood from the intestine flows first into the liver through the portal vein. That is why liver metastases are especially common in bowel cancer.
123228.m: Bowel cancer often spreads to the liver through the portal vein.

123229.q: What is the original tumour from which the secondary tumours start called?
123229.e: The primary tumour is the place where the cancer arose. Even metastases in the liver, in bowel cancer for example, consist of bowel cancer cells.
123229.m: Metastases come from the primary tumour.

123230.q: What is the actual cause of death in most cancer patients?
123230.e: A tumour that is confined to one place can often be removed by surgery. If, however, metastases have formed in vital organs, the disease is much harder to cure.
123230.m: Metastases are responsible for most cancer deaths.

123231.q: What are cancer cells called that can be detected in the blood and are looked for in a liquid biopsy, for example?
123231.e: Circulating tumour cells have broken away from the tumour and float in the blood. Detecting them can give clues about the spread and course of the disease.
123231.m: Circulating tumour cells are cancer cells in the blood.

a: A changed gene that drives cell growth excessively
A gene that stops cell division
A gene that only occurs in viruses
123232.e: Oncogenes arise by mutation from normal growth genes. Their product is permanently active and drives the cell to uncontrolled division.
123232.m: An oncogene acts like a stuck accelerator pedal for cell division.

123233.q: What is the normal, unchanged precursor of an oncogene called?
123233.e: Proto-oncogenes normally control growth and division. Only a mutation, multiplication or rearrangement turns them into oncogenes.
123233.m: A proto-oncogene can become an oncogene through mutation.

123234.q: Which tumour suppressor gene is called the “guardian of the genome” and is mutated in around half of all cancers?
123234.e: The protein p53 stops cell division when DNA is damaged or triggers cell death. If it fails, damaged cells can multiply unchecked.
123234.m: The TP53 gene protects the cell from damaged genetic material.

123235.q: Why does a mutated oncogene such as KRAS constantly drive the growth of a cell?
a: Its protein stays switched on all the time
123235.e: KRAS makes a switch protein that passes on growth signals. Because of the mutation it can no longer be switched off, much like a stuck accelerator pedal.
123235.m: Mutated oncogenes send growth signals all the time.

123236.q: What has happened in the Philadelphia chromosome, which occurs in one form of leukaemia?
a: One chromosome is present three times
123236.e: Chromosomes 9 and 22 exchange pieces. This creates a fusion gene whose protein is permanently active and makes the blood cells proliferate.
123236.m: The Philadelphia chromosome forms when two chromosomes exchange pieces.

123237.q: According to which hypothesis must both copies of a tumour suppressor gene usually fail for cancer to develop?
123237.e: In 1971 Alfred Knudson concluded from cases of retinoblastoma that two mutations are needed. If someone has already inherited a defective copy, a second hit is enough.
123237.m: Tumour suppressor genes usually need two hits.

123238.q: What is a tumour suppressor gene?
a: A gene that slows down uncontrolled cell division
A gene that drives cell growth excessively
A gene that only occurs in tumours
A gene that makes antibodies against tumours
123238.e: Tumour suppressor genes such as TP53 act like brakes on cell division. If they fail, damaged cells can multiply unchecked.
123238.m: Tumour suppressor genes are the brakes of cell division.

123239.q: What is the multiplication of a gene called, by which MYCN, for example, becomes overactive in neuroblastoma?
123239.e: In gene amplification, there are many copies of a gene. The cell then makes far too much protein, which drives growth.
123239.m: Gene amplification can turn a proto-oncogene into an oncogene.

123240.q: Why is a single mutated copy of an oncogene usually enough to have an effect?
a: Because the mutation increases the gene's function
Because the second allele is always missing
Because oncogenes lie in the mitochondria
Because the cell breaks down the gene immediately
123240.e: Oncogene mutations lead to a gain of function; the changed protein is overactive. The intact second copy cannot make up for this, so the effect is dominant.
123240.m: Oncogenes act dominantly because they increase a function.

123241.q: On which cells do classic cytostatic drugs have a particularly strong effect?
a: On cells with a lot of fat
123241.e: Cytostatic drugs disrupt DNA copying or cell division. Cancer cells often divide quickly and are therefore hit hard.
123241.m: Cytostatic drugs mainly attack cells that divide rapidly.

123242.q: Against which common side effect of chemotherapy are medicines such as ondansetron used?
123242.e: Ondansetron blocks serotonin receptors that trigger the urge to vomit. Such antiemetics make chemotherapy much more bearable.

123243.q: From the bark of which tree was the cancer drug paclitaxel originally obtained?
123243.e: Paclitaxel originally came from the bark of the Pacific yew. It prevents cancer cells from dividing. Today it is produced semi-synthetically.
123243.m: Paclitaxel originally came from the yew.

123244.q: Why do people lose their hair with many chemotherapies?
a: Hair root cells divide quickly and are damaged too
The medicines dissolve the hair chemically
The scalp is cooled during the treatment
The body needs the hair as an energy reserve
123244.e: Cytostatic drugs hit all cells that divide rapidly. Besides cancer cells, these include the cells of the hair roots. After treatment the hair usually grows back.
123244.m: Hair loss happens because hair root cells also divide quickly.

123245.q: From which chemical warfare agent were the first cytostatic drugs developed in the 1940s?
123245.e: It was observed that mustard gas greatly reduces the number of white blood cells. This led to the nitrogen mustard compounds that were used against lymphomas.
123245.m: The first chemotherapy drugs go back to mustard gas.

123246.q: What distinguishes a targeted cancer therapy such as imatinib, developed in Basel, from classic chemotherapy?
a: It specifically blocks a particular cancer protein
It is always used during surgery
It irradiates the tumour from outside
123246.e: Classic cytostatic drugs damage all cells that divide quickly. Imatinib, by contrast, specifically inhibits an overactive enzyme in leukaemia cells and so tends to spare healthy cells.
123246.m: Targeted cancer therapies attack a particular cancer protein.

123247.q: Why is chemotherapy sometimes given before a cancer operation?
a: To make the wound heal faster
123247.e: A smaller tumour can be removed more easily and more completely. Specialists call treatment before an operation neoadjuvant.
123247.m: Chemotherapy before an operation can shrink the tumour.

123248.q: What do many cytostatic drugs disrupt in cancer cells so that they can no longer divide?
123248.e: Before each division, a cell must copy its DNA. Many cytostatic drugs block this step, for example by depriving the cell of DNA building blocks.
123248.m: Cytostatic drugs prevent DNA copying before cell division.

123249.q: Why is chemotherapy usually given in cycles with breaks?
a: So that healthy tissue can recover
So that the tumour grows faster
Because otherwise the medicines go off
Because hospitals are closed at night
123249.e: Healthy dividing cells, for example in the bone marrow, are also damaged. During the breaks they can regenerate before the next cycle.
123249.m: Breaks between cycles protect healthy tissue.

123250.q: Which glial cells form an important part of the blood-brain barrier with their extensions?
123250.e: Astrocytes wrap their end feet around the blood capillaries in the brain. Together with the tightly connected vessel cells, they control which substances get into the brain.
123250.m: Astrocytes are important for the blood-brain barrier.

123251.q: At which point on a nerve cell is it decided whether an action potential is triggered?
123251.e: At the axon hillock, the incoming signals are added up. If the threshold is exceeded there, an action potential arises and travels along the axon.
123251.m: The axon hillock decides whether an action potential is triggered.

123252.q: What is the point of contact between a motor nerve fibre and a skeletal muscle fibre called?
123252.e: At the motor end plate, the nerve ending passes the impulse on to the muscle fibre. This special synapse triggers every voluntary movement.
123252.m: At the motor end plate, the nerve controls the muscle.

123253.q: Which neurotransmitter is released when a motor nerve stimulates a skeletal muscle?
123253.e: Acetylcholine binds to receptors in the muscle fibre membrane and opens ion channels. The arrow poison curare blocks these receptors and so paralyses the muscles.
123253.m: Acetylcholine transmits the signal from the nerve to the skeletal muscle.

123254.q: How does the electrical conductivity of a pure semiconductor change when you heat it?
123254.e: Heat frees more electrons from their bonds so that they can move freely. In metals it is the other way round: their resistance rises with temperature.
123254.m: A pure semiconductor conducts better when warm.

123255.q: What do you call the gap that an electron leaves in the crystal bond of a semiconductor, which moves like a positive charge?
123255.e: When an electron leaves its bond, a gap is left behind. Neighbouring electrons jump into it, so that the gap moves like a positive charge carrier.
123255.m: Holes are mobile positive charge carriers in a semiconductor.

123256.q: What is the conductivity of a completely pure, undoped semiconductor called?
123256.e: In intrinsic conduction, electrons and holes always form in pairs through heat or light. At room temperature it is very low in pure silicon.
123256.m: Pure semiconductors only conduct by intrinsic conduction.

123257.q: Which semiconductor material was mainly used for the first transistors around 1950?
123257.e: The first transistors at Bell Labs were made of germanium. Only later did the more robust and more common silicon take over.
123257.m: The early transistors were made of germanium.

123258.q: To which group does the compound semiconductor gallium arsenide belong?
123258.e: Gallium is in the third main group and arsenic in the fifth. On average the atoms therefore have as many outer electrons as silicon.
123258.m: Gallium arsenide is a III-V semiconductor.

123259.q: Where does the resistivity of semiconductors lie compared with other materials?
123259.e: Semiconductors conduct less well than metals, but much better than insulators such as glass. Their conductivity can also be changed on purpose.
123259.m: In conductivity, semiconductors lie between conductors and insulators.

123260.q: Which component uses the temperature dependence of a semiconductor to measure temperatures?
123260.e: A thermistor is made of semiconductor material whose resistance falls when it is heated. The temperature can be worked out from the resistance.
123260.m: An NTC resistor measures temperature through its semiconductor resistance.

123261.q: How many valence electrons does each atom have in the elemental semiconductors silicon and germanium?
123261.e: Silicon and germanium are in the fourth main group. Each atom forms covalent bonds with its neighbours.
123261.m: Silicon and germanium have four valence electrons.

123262.q: Which effect produces a transverse voltage in a current-carrying semiconductor plate in a magnetic field and is used for magnetic sensors?
123262.e: The Lorentz force pushes moving charge carriers sideways, creating a voltage across the current. In semiconductors it is especially large because there are few charge carriers.
123262.m: Hall sensors measure magnetic fields with a transverse voltage.

123263.q: What is meant by doping a semiconductor?
123263.e: In doping, small amounts of foreign atoms are built into the crystal lattice. Even a few of them change the conductivity greatly.
123263.m: Doping means deliberately building foreign atoms into a semiconductor.

123264.q: Which element is suitable for making silicon n-type?
123264.e: Phosphorus has one more outer electron than silicon. This electron is only weakly bound and can move freely.

123265.q: Which element is suitable for making silicon p-type?
123265.e: Boron has one outer electron fewer than silicon. A bond is therefore missing in the lattice, creating a hole as a positive charge carrier.

123266.q: What do you call foreign atoms that give an extra electron to the crystal?
123266.e: Donors donate an electron, which becomes a free charge carrier. What remains is a positive ion fixed in place.
123266.m: Donors give up electrons and create n-type conduction.

123267.q: In chip manufacturing, which process fires accelerated foreign atoms deliberately into the surface of a silicon wafer?
123267.e: In ion implantation, dopant atoms are ionised, accelerated and fired into the crystal. The depth they reach can be controlled precisely through their energy.
123267.m: Ion implantation introduces dopant atoms precisely.

123268.q: Why is an n-doped semiconductor electrically neutral overall despite having many free electrons?
a: Each free electron is matched by a positive foreign atom
The electrons leave the crystal immediately
123268.e: Each donor atom gives up one electron and itself becomes a positive ion. Positive and negative charges balance across the whole crystal.
123268.m: Even a doped semiconductor is neutral overall.

123269.q: How does heavier doping change the conductivity of a semiconductor?
123269.e: More foreign atoms provide more free charge carriers. This makes the semiconductor conduct better.
123269.m: The heavier the doping, the better the semiconductor conducts.

123270.q: What is the region at the boundary between the p and n regions called, where there are hardly any free charge carriers?
123270.e: Electrons from the n region and holes from the p region recombine at the boundary. What remains are fixed ions that form a space charge.
123270.m: A depletion region forms at a p-n junction.

123271.q: What happens to the depletion region when the p-n junction is reverse-biased?
123271.e: In reverse bias the charge carriers are pulled away from the boundary. The zone with few charge carriers grows and hardly any current flows.
123271.m: In reverse bias the depletion region widens.

123272.q: How must you connect a voltage source for a p-n junction to conduct?
a: Positive terminal to p, negative terminal to n
Positive terminal to n, negative terminal to p
123272.e: In forward bias the outside voltage pushes holes and electrons into the boundary zone. The barrier layer is broken down and current flows.
123272.m: A p-n junction conducts when plus is connected to the p region.

123273.q: What causes the built-in voltage at a p-n junction?
a: The fixed ions at the boundary
123273.e: After the mobile charge carriers have moved away, positive ions remain on the n side and negative ions on the p side. Their electric field slows further diffusion.
123273.m: Fixed ions create a built-in voltage at the p-n junction.

123274.q: When p and n regions are joined, what drives electrons across the boundary into the p region?
123274.e: There are many free electrons in the n region and hardly any in the p region. As with a scent in a room, the particles move from where the concentration is high to where it is low.
123274.m: Charge carriers diffuse at the p-n junction because of the difference in concentration.

123275.q: Which component makes use of the fact that the capacitance of a reverse-biased p-n junction depends on the voltage applied?
123275.e: The depletion region acts like the insulating layer of a capacitor. As the reverse voltage rises, it widens and the capacitance falls, which is used, for example, to tune receivers.
123275.m: A varactor diode is a voltage-controlled capacitor.

123276.q: Which current still flows in small amounts through a reverse-biased p-n junction?
a: A small reverse current of minority carriers
123276.e: Even in reverse bias there are a few minority charge carriers, which the field pulls across the boundary. This reverse current rises with temperature.
123276.m: A reverse-biased p-n junction lets through a tiny reverse current.

123277.q: What characteristic curve does a p-n junction show in forward bias?
a: The current rises sharply above a threshold
The current is proportional to the voltage
The current falls as the voltage rises
123277.e: Below the threshold voltage hardly any current flows. After that it rises almost exponentially, so the component does not follow Ohm's law.
123277.m: The forward characteristic of a p-n junction is strongly non-linear.

123278.q: What is the basic property of a semiconductor diode?
a: It only lets current through in one direction
123278.e: A diode conducts in the forward direction and blocks in the opposite direction. It acts like a valve for electric current.
123278.m: A diode is a valve for current.

123279.q: Which component was used as a rectifier before semiconductor diodes and worked with a heated cathode in a vacuum?
123279.e: In a vacuum tube diode, electrons leave the heated cathode and fly only to the anode, never the other way. Semiconductor diodes, by contrast, are smaller, more robust and need no heating.
123279.m: Before semiconductors, vacuum tubes served as diodes.

123280.q: What are the two terminals of a diode called?
123280.e: In the forward direction, current flows from the anode to the cathode. The cathode is usually marked with a ring on the component.
123280.m: A diode has an anode and a cathode.

123281.q: Which type of diode has a metal-semiconductor junction instead of a p-n junction and has a particularly low threshold voltage?
123281.e: The Schottky diode switches very quickly and conducts from about 0.2 to 0.4 volts. It is often used in switch-mode power supplies.
123281.m: Schottky diodes have a metal-semiconductor junction.

123282.q: What is a flyback diode connected in parallel with a relay coil for?
a: It protects against voltage spikes when switching off
It makes the relay pull in faster
It increases the current through the coil
123282.e: When switched off, the coil produces a high back voltage through self-induction. The diode lets the current die away and so protects the switching transistor.
123282.m: A flyback diode catches the induced voltage of a coil.

123283.q: Which diode turns incoming light into a measurable current and is used, for example, in light barriers?
123283.e: In a photodiode, light creates electron-hole pairs in the depletion layer. The resulting photocurrent is proportional to the light intensity.
123283.m: A photodiode turns light into a current.

123284.q: There is 0.7 V across a silicon diode and 2 A flows. How much power is turned into heat in the diode?
123284.e: Power is voltage times current: 0.7 V times 2 A gives 1.4 W. That is why diodes need heat sinks at large currents.
123284.m: The power loss of a diode is voltage times current.

123285.q: Which diode keeps a particular voltage constant in reverse bias and is used to stabilise voltages?
123285.e: The Zener diode is built so that its breakdown starts at a fixed voltage. With a series resistor it keeps a voltage stable.

123286.q: How is the light produced in a light-emitting diode?
a: Through the recombination of electrons and holes
123286.e: In the p-n junction, electrons fall into holes and give off energy as a photon. This way of producing light is called electroluminescence.
123286.m: In an LED, light is produced when electrons and holes recombine.

123287.q: What does the colour of the light from a light-emitting diode mainly depend on?
a: The band gap of the semiconductor
The length of the connecting wires
123287.e: The energy of the photons roughly equals the band gap of the material. Large band gaps give blue light, smaller ones red or infrared light.
123287.m: The band gap determines the colour of an LED.

123288.q: For which invention did Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura win the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014?
123288.e: In the 1990s the researchers developed powerful LEDs made of gallium nitride. Such light-emitting diodes had long been considered almost impossible to make.
123288.m: The blue LED was honoured with the Nobel Prize in 2014.

123289.q: How is white light produced in most white LEDs?
a: A blue LED with a yellow phosphor
A red LED with a green filter
An infrared LED with a mirror
A green LED with a filament
123289.e: Part of the blue light is converted into yellow light by a phosphor layer. Blue and yellow together look white to the eye.
123289.m: White LEDs combine blue light with a yellow phosphor.

123290.q: An LED has a band gap of 2.0 eV. Roughly what wavelength does its light have (with λ in nm ≈ 1240 / E in eV)?
123290.e: 1240 divided by 2.0 gives 620 nm. This corresponds to red to orange-red light.
123290.m: The smaller the band gap, the longer the wavelength of the LED light.

123291.q: A red LED (2.0 V, 20 mA) is to be run on 5 V. How large must the series resistor be?
123291.e: Across the resistor there is a drop of 5 V minus 2 V = 3 V. R = 3 V / 0.02 A = 150 Ω.
123291.m: An LED needs a series resistor to limit the current.

123292.q: What happens if you connect an LED the wrong way round (in reverse bias) to a small voltage?
a: It does not light up because hardly any current flows
It lights up in a different colour
It only shines in the infrared
123292.e: A light-emitting diode only lets current through in the forward direction. In reverse bias almost no current flows, so no light is produced.
123292.m: An LED only lights up in the forward direction.

123293.q: Why are LEDs much more efficient than classic filament bulbs?
a: They turn more energy directly into light instead of heat
They need no electricity at all
They only shine in the infrared range
They store light from the day
123293.e: A filament bulb gives off most of its energy as heat radiation. LEDs produce light directly in the semiconductor and need only a fraction of the power for the same brightness.
123293.m: LEDs are economical because they lose little energy as heat.

123294.q: What are light-emitting diodes called whose glowing layer consists of organic carbon compounds?
123294.e: OLEDs (organic light-emitting diodes) are thin and can form individually glowing pixels. They are used in many mobile phone and television screens.
123294.m: OLEDs are light-emitting diodes made of organic materials.

123295.q: What are the three terminals of a field-effect transistor called?
123295.e: In a field-effect transistor, the voltage at the gate controls the current between source and drain through an electric field. Almost no control current is needed.
123295.m: A field-effect transistor has a source, a gate and a drain.

123296.q: A bipolar transistor has a current gain of 100. What is the collector current with a base current of 0.2 mA?
123296.e: The collector current is current gain times base current: 100 times 0.2 mA gives 20 mA.
123296.m: In a bipolar transistor a small base current controls a large collector current.

123297.q: Which two main jobs do transistors do in electronic circuits?
123297.e: Transistors can amplify weak signals or switch on and off as electronic switches. In computer chips they work almost only as switches.

123298.q: Which type of transistor is the basic building block of almost all of today's computer chips?
123298.e: The metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor can be built very small and needs little control power. It is the most frequently manufactured device in history.
123298.m: MOSFETs are the heart of modern chips.

123299.q: What is the circuit technology called that combines n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs so that hardly any current is used at rest?
123299.e: In CMOS, one of the two transistors is switched off in every stable state. That is why current flows almost only while switching.

123300.q: What is the order of layers in an npn transistor?
123300.e: In an npn transistor a thin p-doped base lies between two n-doped regions. This creates two p-n junctions.
123300.m: An npn transistor has a p-layer between two n-layers.

123301.q: What is the observation called that the number of transistors on computer chips doubles about every two years?
123301.e: Gordon Moore, co-founder of Intel, described this trend in 1965. It was possible because transistors were built ever smaller.
123301.m: According to Moore's law the number of transistors doubles about every two years.

123302.q: Which physical effect turns light directly into electrical energy in a solar cell?
123302.e: Light creates electron-hole pairs in the semiconductor. The field at the p-n junction separates them so that a voltage is produced.
123302.m: Solar cells use the photovoltaic effect.

123303.q: What job does the p-n junction do in a solar cell?
a: It separates the electrons and holes produced
It stores the energy for the night
123303.e: Without the internal electric field, electrons and holes would recombine at once. Only their separation makes a current possible in the outside circuit.
123303.m: In a solar cell the p-n junction separates the charge carriers.

123304.q: Roughly what is the open-circuit voltage of a single silicon solar cell?
123304.e: A crystalline silicon cell delivers about 0.6 to 0.7 volts without a load. For higher voltages many cells are connected in series to form a module.
123304.m: A silicon solar cell delivers about 0.6 volts.

123305.q: A solar module with an area of 1.7 m² and an efficiency of 20 % receives 1000 W/m² of sunlight. What power does it deliver?
123305.e: The incoming power is 1000 W/m² times 1.7 m² = 1700 W. Of this, 20 % is used: 0.2 times 1700 W = 340 W.
123305.m: The power of a solar module is irradiance times area times efficiency.

123306.q: Why can a simple silicon solar cell never turn all sunlight into electricity?
a: Some photons have too little energy, and surplus energy becomes heat
Silicon does not conduct electricity at all
Sunlight contains no energy in the visible range
The cell stores part of the energy permanently
123306.e: Photons below the band gap are not used, and energy above the band gap is lost as heat. That is why the theoretical limit of a simple cell is about one third.
123306.m: Simple solar cells can use at most about one third of sunlight.

123307.q: Where was the first practically usable silicon solar cell presented in 1954?
a: At Bell Labs in the USA
123307.e: Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller and Gerald Pearson reached an efficiency of about 6 per cent. The first uses were soon found in satellites.
123307.m: The first silicon solar cell was made at Bell Labs in 1954.

123308.q: Which solar cell, which captures light with a dye rather like the green in leaves, was developed at EPFL in Lausanne?
123308.e: Michael Grätzel and Brian O'Regan presented the dye-sensitised solar cell in 1991. It imitates the principle of photosynthesis.
123308.m: Michael Grätzel's dye-sensitised solar cell comes from Lausanne.

123309.q: Which Swiss solar aircraft flew around the world in 2015 and 2016 without fuel?
123309.e: Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg took turns flying around the world in stages. About 17,000 solar cells on the wings powered the motors and batteries.
123309.m: Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world on solar energy alone.

123310.q: What do you call the operating point of a solar cell at which it delivers the greatest possible power?
123310.e: With no load no current flows, and in a short circuit there is no voltage, so both give no power. Inverters therefore keep the cell at the point of maximum power.
123310.m: At the maximum power point a solar cell delivers the most power.

a: It turns alternating current into direct current
It turns direct current into light
123311.e: Many devices such as mobile phones and computers need direct current. The rectifier uses diodes to let through only one direction of current.
123311.m: A rectifier turns alternating current into direct current.

123312.q: How many diodes does a bridge rectifier need?
123312.e: Four diodes are arranged so that both half-waves of the alternating current flow through the load in the same direction.
123312.m: A bridge rectifier consists of four diodes.

123313.q: What advantage does a bridge rectifier have over a half-wave rectifier with only one diode?
a: It uses both half-waves of the alternating current
It delivers a higher mains frequency
123313.e: Four diodes in a bridge circuit send both half-waves through the load in the same direction. The half-wave rectifier, by contrast, blocks every second half-wave.
123313.m: The bridge rectifier uses both half-waves.

123314.q: What does a half-wave rectifier with only one diode deliver at its output?
a: Both half-waves in the same direction
123314.e: The diode only lets the positive half-waves through and blocks the negative ones. Half the energy is lost and the voltage pulses strongly.
123314.m: A half-wave rectifier only uses one half-wave.

123315.q: Which component smooths the pulsing voltage after a rectifier?
123315.e: The reservoir capacitor charges up at the voltage peaks and gives off charge in between. Only a small residual ripple remains.
123315.m: A reservoir capacitor smooths the rectified voltage.

123316.q: What is the peak value of the Swiss mains voltage of 230 V (RMS value)?
123316.e: For a sine-wave voltage, the peak value is the RMS value times the square root of 2: 230 V times 1.414 gives about 325 V. A smoothing capacitor charges almost to this value.
123316.m: The peak value of the mains voltage is about 325 volts.

123317.q: At what frequency does the voltage pulse after a bridge rectifier on the 50 Hz mains?
123317.e: Each of the two half-waves gives a bump in the voltage. So there are two per cycle, which is 2 times 50 = 100 bumps per second.
123317.m: A bridge rectifier doubles the pulse frequency.

123318.q: Roughly how much voltage is lost in a bridge rectifier with silicon diodes, since the current always flows through two diodes?
123318.e: In each half-wave, two diodes conduct in series. Each needs about 0.7 V, so together about 1.4 V.
123318.m: About two diode voltages are lost in a bridge rectifier.

a: Many components on a single piece of semiconductor
A wiring harness in a car
123319.e: Transistors, resistors and connections are made together on one chip. This makes circuits small, cheap and reliable.
123319.m: An integrated circuit combines many components on one chip.

123320.q: What is the rule of thumb called that says the number of transistors on a chip doubles about every two years?
123320.e: Gordon Moore, co-founder of Intel, described this development in 1965. It continued for decades and made computers ever more powerful.
123320.m: According to Moore's law the number of transistors doubles about every two years.

123321.q: Why is the silicon for chips deliberately mixed with foreign atoms such as boron or phosphorus?
123321.e: This doping creates extra free electrons or holes in the silicon. Only then can diodes and transistors be built.
123321.m: Doping turns silicon into a controllable semiconductor.

123322.q: Which process uses light to transfer the structures of a chip onto the wafer?
123322.e: A light-sensitive resist is exposed through a mask and then developed. The uncovered areas are etched, doped or coated.
123322.m: Chip structures are made with photolithography.

123323.q: Why is light with a very short wavelength used for the finest chip structures?
a: The shorter the wavelength, the finer the structures that can be imaged
Short-wave light is cheaper to produce
123323.e: Because of diffraction, light cannot image structures much smaller than its wavelength. That is why extreme ultraviolet is used today.
123323.m: Shorter wavelengths allow finer chip structures.

123324.q: Why are chips made in clean rooms?
a: Because even tiny dust particles destroy structures
Because silicon would otherwise melt immediately
Because the workers are exposed to radiation
Because chips can only be made in the dark
123324.e: The structures on a chip are much smaller than a grain of dust. A single particle can break a connection and make the chip useless.
123324.m: Clean rooms protect chips from dust.

123325.q: Which microprocessor came onto the market in 1971 as the first commercially available single-chip processor?
123325.e: The Intel 4004 was a 4-bit processor with about 2,300 transistors. It was originally developed for a desktop calculator.
123325.m: The Intel 4004 from 1971 is considered the first microprocessor.

123326.q: What is the thin slice of silicon called on which many chips are made at the same time?
123326.e: A wafer is a round, very pure disc of silicon. Hundreds of identical chips are made on it and cut out at the end.
123326.m: Chips are made by the hundred on a wafer.

123327.q: What is the atomic number of silicon?
123327.e: Silicon has 14 protons in its nucleus and is directly below carbon in the periodic table. Germanium, with atomic number 32, is below it.

123328.q: Which element is more common than silicon in the Earth's crust?
123328.e: Silicon makes up about a quarter of the mass of the Earth's crust, which makes it the second most common element. Only oxygen is more common.
123328.m: After oxygen, silicon is the most common element in the Earth's crust.

123329.q: Which raw material is silicon mainly obtained from?
123329.e: Quartz sand or quartz rock is reduced with carbon in an electric arc furnace. This produces raw silicon, which is then purified further.

123330.q: Which process is used to pull large single crystals of silicon from a melt for chip making?
123330.e: A seed crystal is dipped into the molten silicon and slowly pulled out while turning. A cylindrical single crystal grows, which is cut into slices.
123330.m: Silicon single crystals are made by the Czochralski process.

123331.q: What is the diameter of the largest silicon wafers commonly used in mass production today?
123331.e: Modern chip factories process wafers 300 mm across. Larger discs hold more chips and lower the cost per chip.
123331.m: Modern silicon wafers are 300 millimetres across.

123332.q: Roughly at what temperature does silicon melt?
123332.e: Silicon melts at about 1414 °C. To make single crystals, it is melted in crucibles made of quartz glass.
123332.m: Silicon melts at about 1410 degrees Celsius.

123333.q: In which crystal structure are the atoms in silicon arranged?
123333.e: Each silicon atom is bonded to four neighbours in the shape of a tetrahedron. This arrangement matches that of diamond, which is made of carbon.
123333.m: Silicon crystallises in the diamond structure.

123334.q: Which Californian industrial area is named after the semiconductor material?
123334.e: From the 1950s many semiconductor companies were founded south of San Francisco Bay. The name refers to silicon.
123334.m: Silicon Valley is named after silicon.

123335.q: What does the band gap of a solid describe?
a: The energy gap between the valence band and the conduction band
The width of a circuit track
123335.e: Electrons need at least the energy of the band gap to get from the valence band into the conduction band. Only there can they conduct electricity.
123335.m: The band gap separates the valence and conduction bands.

123336.q: Why does pure silicon conduct electricity only poorly at room temperature?
a: Only a few electrons can overcome the band gap
Its atoms are too far apart
123336.e: The band gap of silicon is about 1.1 eV. The heat energy at room temperature is only rarely enough to lift an electron into the conduction band.
123336.m: Silicon has a band gap of about 1.1 electronvolts.

123337.q: How do metals differ from semiconductors in their band structure?
a: They have a very large band gap
They only have an empty conduction band
123337.e: In metals the highest occupied band is only partly filled or overlaps with the next one. Electrons can therefore move without an energy threshold.
123337.m: Metals conduct because they have no band gap.

123338.q: Which material has a particularly large band gap of about 5.5 eV and is therefore considered an insulator?
123338.e: With such a large band gap, practically no electrons can reach the conduction band at room temperature. Pure diamond therefore hardly conducts electricity.
123338.m: Diamond is an insulator because of its large band gap.

123339.q: Up to what wavelength can germanium, with its band gap of about 0.67 eV, absorb light (λ in nm ≈ 1240 / E in eV)?
123339.e: 1240 divided by 0.67 gives about 1850 nm. Light with a longer wavelength has too little energy and passes through germanium, which is why germanium suits infrared photodiodes.
123339.m: Germanium absorbs light up to a wavelength of about 1850 nanometres.

123340.q: What mainly determines the colour of the light given off by a light-emitting diode?
a: The size of the semiconductor's band gap
The colour of the plastic casing
The length of the connecting wires
123340.e: In the LED an electron falls back across the band gap and gives off the energy as a photon. A larger band gap gives more energetic, that is bluer, light.
123340.m: The band gap determines the colour of an LED.

123341.q: Which material with a large band gap of about 3.3 eV is increasingly used in the power electronics of electric cars?
123341.e: Silicon carbide withstands high voltages and temperatures and switches with low losses. This improves things like inverters and chargers.
123341.m: Silicon carbide is a semiconductor with a large band gap for high power.

123342.q: How many joules is one electronvolt, the usual unit for band gaps?
123342.e: One electronvolt is the energy an electron gains when it passes through 1 volt. It equals the elementary charge times 1 volt, so about 1.6 · 10⁻¹⁹ joules.
123342.m: One electronvolt is about 1.6 times ten to the power of minus 19 joules.

123343.q: What does Moore's law say in its well-known form?
a: The number of transistors on chips doubles about every two years
The price of chips doubles every year
The clock speed halves every ten years
123343.e: Gordon Moore observed that the number of components per chip doubles regularly. He spoke of a rule of thumb, not a law of nature.
123343.m: According to Moore's law the number of transistors doubles about every two years.

123344.q: In which year did Gordon Moore publish his famous article on the growth in the number of components on chips?
123344.e: The article appeared in 1965 in the journal Electronics. At that time Moore still predicted a doubling every year; in 1975 he corrected this to about two years.
123344.m: Gordon Moore put forward his observation in 1965.

123345.q: Why have the clock speeds of processors hardly risen since the mid-2000s?
a: The chips would get too hot
The speed of light has been reached
Higher frequencies are banned by law
123345.e: In the past, making transistors smaller also allowed the voltage to be lowered, so the power per area stayed the same. Since that no longer works, a higher frequency would produce too much heat. That is why several processing cores are used instead.
123345.m: Heat limits the clock speed of modern processors.

123346.q: By what factor does the number of transistors grow in 10 years if it doubles every two years?
123346.e: In 10 years there are 5 doublings. 2 to the power of 5 gives 32.
123346.m: Five doublings give a factor of 32.

123347.q: In 1971 a chip had about 2,300 transistors. How many would a chip have had in 2011 if the number doubled every two years?
123347.e: From 1971 to 2011 is 40 years, so 20 doublings. 2,300 times 2 to the power of 20 gives about 2.4 billion.
123347.m: Exponential growth leads to huge numbers within a few decades.

123348.q: Which physical limit makes it harder to keep Moore's law going with very small transistors?
a: Quantum effects such as electrons tunnelling
The speed of light in copper
The air pressure in the clean room
123348.e: When insulating layers are only a few atoms thick, electrons can tunnel through them. This causes leakage currents and heat.
123348.m: Quantum effects set limits to making transistors smaller.

123349.q: What kind of growth does Moore's law describe?
123349.e: With a fixed doubling time, a quantity grows exponentially. In equal time intervals it is not the same amount that is added, but the same factor.

123350.q: How can the computing power of chips be increased when transistors hardly get any smaller?
a: By stacking chips and using specialised chips
By a higher mains voltage in the house
By using copper as the semiconductor material
123350.e: Instead of only shrinking, people turn to 3D stacking, chiplets and special chips, for example for graphics or artificial intelligence. This strategy is called “More than Moore”.
123350.m: “More than Moore” relies on new designs, not just smaller transistors.

123351.q: On a Walter-Lieth climate diagram, what amount of precipitation corresponds to 10 °C on the temperature axis?
123351.e: In the Walter-Lieth diagram, temperature and precipitation are scaled in the ratio 1 to 2. So one mark of 10 °C corresponds to 20 mm of precipitation.
123351.m: In the Walter-Lieth diagram, one degree Celsius corresponds to two millimetres of precipitation.

123352.q: In a Walter-Lieth diagram, what does it mean if the precipitation curve lies above the temperature curve?
123352.e: If precipitation lies above the temperature curve, more water falls than can evaporate according to the rule of thumb. Such months are called humid.
123352.m: If the precipitation curve is on top, the month is humid.

123353.q: How is the arid period usually shown in a Walter-Lieth climate diagram?
123353.e: Arid periods are marked with dots (often yellow or red). Humid periods have vertical hatching, and very wet months over 100 mm are filled in black.
123353.m: In the Walter-Lieth diagram, arid months are dotted.

123354.q: How does the precipitation scale in the Walter-Lieth diagram change above 100 mm?
a: It is shortened to a tenth.
123354.e: So that very wet months do not burst the diagram, the scale above 100 mm is squeezed to a tenth. This perhumid zone is filled in black.
123354.m: Above 100 mm, the precipitation scale in the Walter-Lieth diagram is squeezed.

123355.q: Which two monthly values does a Walter-Lieth climate diagram show as curves?
a: Hours of sunshine and cloud cover
123355.e: The temperature curve and the precipitation curve are drawn on top of each other on a scale of 1 to 2. This shows humid and arid months at a glance.
123355.m: The Walter-Lieth diagram shows monthly temperature and monthly precipitation.

123356.q: A month has a mean temperature of 15 °C and 25 mm of precipitation. How should it be classified according to Walter-Lieth?
123356.e: On the 1 to 2 scale, 15 °C corresponds to 30 mm. Since 25 mm is less than 30 mm, the precipitation curve lies below the temperature curve: the month is arid.
123356.m: If precipitation in mm is less than twice the temperature, the month is arid.

123357.q: Which two annual values usually appear at the top of a Walter-Lieth climate diagram?
a: Mean annual temperature and annual precipitation
Hours of sunshine and wind strength
123357.e: Besides the name of the station and its altitude above sea level, the mean annual temperature and the total annual precipitation are given. This makes it quick to compare stations.
123357.m: At the top, a climate diagram gives the mean annual temperature and annual precipitation.

123358.q: What is a climate called in which, according to the climate diagram, all twelve months are humid?
123358.e: If all months are humid, it is called a fully humid climate, as on the Swiss Plateau, for example. If some months are arid, it is called semi-humid or semi-arid.
123358.m: A climate with only humid months is called fully humid.

123359.q: For stations in the southern hemisphere, which month does the time axis of a Walter-Lieth diagram usually begin with?
123359.e: So that summer lies in the middle of the diagram as in the northern hemisphere, the axis begins with July for southern hemisphere stations. This makes diagrams from both hemispheres directly comparable.
123359.m: For stations in the southern hemisphere, the Walter-Lieth diagram begins with July.

123360.q: Which features are considered together when dividing the Earth into ecozones?
a: Climate, soils, vegetation and land use
123360.e: Ecozones are large areas with a similar climate, similar soils and similar vegetation. A well-known division is the one into nine ecozones by the geographer Jürgen Schultz.
123360.m: Ecozones combine climate, soil, plant life and land use.

123361.q: According to Schultz, which ecozone do the Sahara and the Arabian Desert belong to?
123361.e: The great deserts around the tropics lie under the subtropical high pressure with sinking, dry air. Schultz groups them with the neighbouring semi-deserts as tropical and subtropical drylands.
123361.m: The Sahara and the Arabian Desert belong to the tropical and subtropical drylands.

123362.q: Which ecozone does the Swiss Plateau belong to?
123362.e: The Swiss Plateau has precipitation all year round, warm summers and cool winters. Its natural vegetation would be deciduous broadleaf forest, typical of the humid mid-latitudes.
123362.m: The Swiss Plateau lies in the humid mid-latitudes.

123363.q: Which ecozone is mainly characterised by coniferous forest, the taiga?
123363.e: The boreal zone stretches as a broad belt across North America, Scandinavia and Siberia. Long, cold winters and short summers favour conifers such as spruce, pine and larch.
123363.m: The taiga is the coniferous forest of the boreal zone.

123364.q: Which ecozone does the Mediterranean region belong to?
123364.e: In the Mediterranean region the summers are hot and dry, and rain falls mainly in winter. This combination is typical of the subtropics with winter rain.
123364.m: The Mediterranean region belongs to the subtropics with winter rain.

123365.q: Which ecozone has the highest plant biomass per area?
123365.e: Warmth all year round and plenty of rain allow growth without a break in the ever-humid tropics. The rainforests therefore store a great deal of biomass per hectare.
123365.m: The ever-humid tropics have the most biomass per area.

123366.q: Which ecozone do the tundra and the polar cold deserts belong to?
123366.e: The polar and subpolar zone covers the treeless areas at high latitudes. It includes ice sheets, cold deserts and the tundra.
123366.m: Tundra and cold deserts lie in the polar and subpolar zone.

123367.q: Which ecozone do the steppes of Central Asia and the prairies of North America belong to?
123367.e: Steppes and prairies lie in the mid-latitudes but get too little precipitation for closed forest. That is why grasses dominate.
123367.m: Steppes and prairies are grasslands of the dry mid-latitudes.

123368.q: Which ecozone do most of Africa's savannahs belong to?
123368.e: Savannahs have a rainy season in summer and a marked dry season. These alternating wet and dry conditions are typical of the tropics with summer rain.
123368.m: Savannahs belong to the tropics with summer rain.

123369.q: Which elements mainly build up as oxides in laterite?
123369.e: With intense tropical weathering, soluble substances are washed out. What remains are iron and aluminium oxides, which hardly dissolve.
123369.m: Laterite is rich in iron and aluminium oxides.

123370.q: Why are tropical red soils often poor in nutrients despite the lush rainforest?
a: Long, intense weathering has washed out the nutrients
They are young and hardly weathered
123370.e: Over a very long time, even silica and almost all nutrients were washed out. This process is called ferrallitisation. What is left are iron and aluminium oxides.
123370.m: Tropical red soils are poor in nutrients because of long washing out.

123371.q: Where does the name “laterite” come from?
a: from the Latin word for brick
from the Greek word for red
from the name of a geologist
123371.e: “Later” means brick in Latin. In India the material was cut into blocks and dried in the air into a brick-like building material.
123371.m: Laterite is named after the Latin word for brick.

123372.q: What causes the red colour of many laterites?
123372.e: Iron oxides such as haematite colour the soil red, goethite more yellowish brown. They are left behind when other substances are washed out.
123372.m: The red colour of laterite comes from iron oxides.

123373.q: What happens to exposed lateritic material if it dries out repeatedly?
a: It hardens into a hard crust.
It breaks down into fine sand.
123373.e: After deforestation and erosion, laterite material at the surface can harden irreversibly. Such crusts make farming and reforestation very difficult.
123373.m: Laterite that dries out can become a hard crust.

123374.q: Which important aluminium ore forms, like laterite, through tropical weathering?
123374.e: Bauxite is a weathering product of tropical climates that is especially rich in aluminium. Most of the world's aluminium is obtained from it.
123374.m: Bauxite is the most important ore for aluminium.

123375.q: In which climate do laterites mainly form?
123375.e: High temperatures and lots of water greatly speed up chemical weathering. Over a long time this produces deeply weathered soils poor in nutrients.
123375.m: Laterite forms through intense weathering in the hot, humid tropics.

123376.q: Why can heavily weathered tropical soils hold on to fertiliser only poorly?
a: Their clay minerals have only a few binding sites for nutrients
123376.e: In such soils the clay mineral kaolinite, which has a small cation exchange capacity, dominates. In addition, humus breaks down quickly in the warmth.
123376.m: Heavily weathered tropical soils hold on to nutrients poorly.

123377.q: What does “short-circuited” mean for the nutrient cycle of the rainforest?
a: Nutrients go from the leaf litter almost directly back into the plants.
Nutrients are stored in the soil for a long time.
Nutrients reach the sea via rivers.
Nutrients come mainly from the rain.
123377.e: Dead material is broken down quickly and the nutrients released are immediately taken up again by roots. The detour via a store in the soil is largely skipped.
123377.m: In the short-circuited cycle, nutrients go straight back into the plants.

123378.q: Which partners help rainforest trees take up nutrients directly from the leaf litter?
123378.e: Mycorrhizal fungi form a symbiosis with the roots. Their fine network of fungal threads takes up nutrients from decomposed leaf litter and passes them on to the tree.
123378.m: Mycorrhizal fungi supply rainforest trees with nutrients from the leaf litter.

123379.q: Why is a field cleared by slash-and-burn in the rainforest often productive for only a few years?
a: The nutrients in the ash are quickly washed out.
The ash poisons the soil permanently.
It no longer rains after clearing.
123379.e: Burning releases the nutrients in the biomass as ash. But the soil, which stores little, cannot hold them, and heavy rain washes them away.
123379.m: After slash-and-burn, the nutrients in the ash are quickly lost.

123380.q: How does the layer of leaf litter in the tropical rainforest compare with that in a broadleaf forest in Switzerland?
123380.e: Warmth and moisture let bacteria, fungi and termites break down the leaf litter very quickly. That is why hardly any thick layer of leaves builds up.
123380.m: In the rainforest the leaf litter is thin because it decomposes quickly.

123381.q: Where are most of the fine roots of many rainforest trees?
a: in the top layer of soil
123381.e: Because the nutrients come from the leaf litter, many trees have very shallow roots. The dense network of roots catches released nutrients immediately.
123381.m: Rainforest trees take up nutrients with shallow fine roots.

123382.q: What especially speeds up the breakdown of leaf litter in the tropical rainforest?
a: warmth and moisture all year round
123382.e: Decomposers work fastest at high temperatures in damp conditions. In the rainforest there is no cold season to slow down decomposition.
123382.m: Warmth and moisture speed up decomposition in the rainforest.

123383.q: Which type of farming imitates the layered structure and the nutrient cycle of the rainforest?
123383.e: In agroforestry, trees, shrubs and crops grow together in several layers. Falling leaves and roots keep the nutrients in the system.
123383.m: Agroforestry uses trees to keep nutrients in the soil.

123384.q: What is meant by a pyrophyte?
a: a plant growing on volcanic ash
123384.e: Pyrophytes survive fires or even benefit from them, for example by germinating after a fire. The Greek “pyr” means fire.
123384.m: Pyrophytes are adapted to regular fires.

123385.q: Which Mediterranean tree protects itself from fire with especially thick bark?
123385.e: The thick layer of cork insulates the living tissue against heat. This way the cork oak survives fires that kill other trees.
123385.m: The cork oak protects itself from fire with thick cork bark.

123386.q: What is special about the serotinous cones of some pine species?
a: They only open through the heat of a fire.
They fall off every year in spring.
They only grow on the roots.
123386.e: Resin keeps the cones sealed for years. Only heat melts it, and the seeds fall on freshly exposed ground with little competition.
123386.m: Serotinous cones only release their seeds after a fire.

123387.q: Which Australian trees often sprout again after a fire from buds under the bark?
123387.e: Many eucalyptus trees have dormant buds protected under the bark. After a fire they sprout again along the trunk and branches.
123387.m: Eucalyptus trees sprout again after fires from protected buds.

a: a woody swelling at the base of the stem
a leaf with a wax layer
123388.e: The lignotuber stores reserves and carries many buds. If the shoot burns down, the plant sprouts again from it.
123388.m: A lignotuber lets a plant sprout again after a fire.

123389.q: Which signal from a fire makes the seeds of some plants germinate?
123389.e: When plant material burns, substances called karrikins are produced. They tell the seeds that light and space are available after the fire.
123389.m: Substances in smoke can make seeds germinate.

123390.q: Which Californian tree needs regular fires so that its seedlings can germinate on open ground?
123390.e: Its very thick, fibrous bark protects the trunk. Fire removes leaf litter and competition so that the seeds can germinate on mineral soil.
123390.m: The giant sequoia depends on regular forest fires.

123391.q: In which biome are pyrophytes especially widespread because of frequent grass fires?
123391.e: In the savannah's dry season the dry grass burns regularly. Trees with thick bark and grasses with protected buds survive this.
123391.m: In the savannah, many plants are adapted to fire.

123392.q: Why do plants in sclerophyll forest have hard, leathery leaves?
a: They protect against water loss in the dry summer.
They protect against frost in summer.
They fall off more easily in autumn.
123392.e: A thick cuticle and firm tissue reduce evaporation. This lets the evergreen leaves survive hot summers with little rain.
123392.m: Hard leaves protect plants from losing water in summer.

123393.q: In which season does most precipitation fall in sclerophyll regions?
123393.e: In summer, sclerophyll regions lie under the subtropical high pressure, and in winter they get rain from low-pressure systems. That is why the summers are dry.
123393.m: In sclerophyll regions it rains mainly in winter.

123394.q: In which region does the species-rich fynbos grow?
a: in the Cape region of South Africa
123394.e: Fynbos is a sclerophyll shrub vegetation of the Cape region. It is considered one of the most species-rich plant regions in the world.
123394.m: Fynbos is the sclerophyll vegetation of the Cape region.

123395.q: Which evergreen tree is typical of Mediterranean sclerophyll forest?
123395.e: The holm oak has small, leathery, evergreen leaves. It used to form large forests all around the Mediterranean.
123395.m: The holm oak is a typical tree of Mediterranean sclerophyll forest.

123396.q: What is the low, patchy shrub heath called that often develops around the Mediterranean after deforestation and grazing?
123396.e: In many places, sclerophyll forest was pushed back by clearing, fire and grazing. This produced the dense maquis and the even more open garrigue with thyme and rosemary.
123396.m: Garrigue is a low shrub heath around the Mediterranean.

123397.q: Which crop is especially typical of the sclerophyll regions around the Mediterranean?
123397.e: The olive tree is itself a sclerophyll plant and copes well with dry summers. The limit of where it is grown roughly follows the Mediterranean climate.
123397.m: The olive tree is a typical crop of the Mediterranean climate.

123398.q: Which code in the Köppen classification stands for the climate of sclerophyll regions?
123398.e: C stands for a warm temperate climate, s for a dry summer. Cs is therefore the typical Mediterranean climate with winter rain.
123398.m: In the Köppen system, the Mediterranean climate has the code Cs.

123399.q: What is the transition belt between taiga and tundra with scattered, low trees called?
123399.e: In the forest tundra, the coniferous forest becomes more and more open towards the north. In the end only a few stunted trees remain before the open tundra begins.
123399.m: The forest tundra links the taiga and the tundra.

123400.q: What is the top layer of soil above the permafrost called, which thaws in summer?
123400.e: Only the top few tens of centimetres thaw in summer. Below that, the ground stays permanently frozen.
123400.m: Above the permafrost, only the active layer thaws in summer.

123401.q: Which plants are typical of the Arctic tundra?
123401.e: Only low plants that can cope with cold and a short growing season grow in the tundra. Dwarf willows and dwarf birches hardly reach knee height.
123401.m: The tundra is dominated by mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs.

a: slow flowing of soil over frozen ground
salt being washed out by rain
123402.e: In summer the active layer is waterlogged because the water cannot seep into the permafrost. On a slope it slowly slides downhill.
123402.m: Solifluction is soil flowing over the permafrost.

123403.q: Why is the ground of the tundra often waterlogged despite low precipitation?
a: The permafrost stops water seeping away.
The plants give off a lot of water.
123403.e: The frozen ground acts like a barrier. In addition, little water evaporates at low temperatures, so many marshes and pools form.
123403.m: Permafrost stops water seeping away and makes the tundra waterlogged.

123404.q: Why do many tundra plants grow flat and cushion-shaped on the ground?
a: It is warmer and more sheltered from the wind there.
123404.e: Just above the ground the air is warmer and the wind weaker. In winter the snow cover also protects the low plants.
123404.m: Growing low protects tundra plants from cold and wind.

123405.q: Which gases can be released when permafrost thaws?
123405.e: Permafrost contains large amounts of old plant remains. If they thaw, microorganisms break them down and release greenhouse gases, which can increase warming.
123405.m: Thawing permafrost can release methane and carbon dioxide.

123406.q: What is a hill with an ice core called, which bulges up in permafrost areas?
123406.e: A pingo forms when a growing body of ice develops in the ground and lifts the surface. Pingos can be several dozen metres high.
123406.m: A pingo is a hill with an ice core in the permafrost.

123407.q: What is typical of a cold desert?
a: Cold prevents almost all plant growth.
It always lies below sea level.
It consists only of sand dunes.
123407.e: In cold deserts it is too cold and too dry for a closed cover of plants. They are found in polar regions and in the highest mountains.
123407.m: In cold deserts, the cold prevents almost all plant growth.

123408.q: Which is the largest desert on Earth if cold deserts are included?
123408.e: Desert refers to very low precipitation. The interior of Antarctica gets extremely little precipitation, and it is larger in area than the Sahara.
123408.m: Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth.

123409.q: Why are the Dry Valleys of Antarctica largely free of ice and snow?
a: Very dry downslope winds make moisture evaporate
The sun shines there all year round
Warm sea water flows through the valleys
123409.e: In the McMurdo Dry Valleys, cold, extremely dry winds blow down from the glaciers. Snow turns straight into vapour, and mountains hold back the ice sheet.
123409.m: Dry downslope winds keep the Antarctic Dry Valleys free of ice.

123410.q: Which living things survive in cold deserts partly inside rocks?
123410.e: Endolithic organisms live in fine cracks and pores in rock. There they are protected from wind, drying out and strong radiation.

123411.q: Which group of plants has only two native species on the Antarctic continent?
123411.e: On the Antarctic Peninsula, only Antarctic hair grass and Antarctic pearlwort grow as flowering plants. Mosses and lichens, by contrast, have many more species.
123411.m: Antarctica has only two native flowering plants.

123412.q: Which type of weathering is especially typical of cold deserts?
123412.e: Water gets into cracks in the rock and expands when it freezes. Frequent freezing and thawing breaks the rock into scree.
123412.m: Frost shattering breaks rock apart through freezing water.

123413.q: What are the stone rings and polygons sorted by frost on the ground in cold regions called?
123413.e: Repeated freezing and thawing lifts and sorts stones in the soil. Coarse stones move outwards and form rings or networks.
123413.m: Patterned ground forms through repeated freezing and thawing.

123414.q: Why does so little precipitation fall in polar cold deserts?
a: Cold air can hold hardly any water vapour.
The sun evaporates any rain immediately.
The wind always blows the clouds towards the equator.
The sea there is too warm.
123414.e: The amount of water vapour air can hold falls sharply as the temperature drops. In addition, sinking air in high pressure often dominates over the poles.
123414.m: Very cold air contains little water vapour and brings hardly any precipitation.

123415.e: The Greek “xeros” means dry. Xerophytes have features that save or store water.
123415.m: Xerophytes are plants of dry places.

123416.q: What is the dense hair on the leaves of plants in dry, sunny places for?
a: It holds a layer of moist air and reflects light.
It acts as a water pipe.
123416.e: The hairs slow the wind right at the leaf surface, so moist air stays there. Light-coloured hairs also reflect sunlight and prevent overheating.
123416.m: Dense leaf hairs reduce evaporation and overheating.

123417.q: What is special about the CAM metabolism of many desert plants?
a: The plants do not carry out photosynthesis.
123417.e: At night it is cool and evaporation is low, so CAM plants take up CO2 then and store it as malic acid. During the day the stomata stay closed.
