123785.m: World shops sell fair trade goods and inform people about trade.

123786.q: Which Swiss women's group campaigned for fairer banana prices with campaigns from the 1970s onwards?
123786.e: The Banana Women from Frauenfeld drew attention to the poor pay on banana plantations. They are considered pioneers of fair trade in Switzerland.
123786.m: The Banana Women were pioneers of fair trade in Switzerland.

123787.q: For which product does Fairtrade have a particularly high market share in Switzerland?
123787.e: In Switzerland a very large proportion of the bananas sold carry a Fairtrade label. This puts Switzerland among the leaders for fair bananas.
123787.m: In Switzerland, fair trade is especially widespread for bananas.

123788.q: Which two countries does most of the world's harvested cocoa come from?
123788.e: Together the two West African countries supply well over half of the cocoa. Low incomes and child labour are big problems there.
123788.m: Most cocoa comes from Ivory Coast and Ghana.

123789.q: Which title can municipalities and towns receive if they actively promote fair trade?
123789.e: Fair Trade Towns meet criteria such as fair products in the administration, shops and restaurants. Several municipalities in Switzerland hold this title.
123789.m: A Fair Trade Town actively supports fair trade.

123790.q: What is a plant protection product against fungal diseases such as mildew called?
123790.e: Fungicides stop fungi from growing. They are used a lot in vineyards and orchards, for example.

123791.q: Which organisms are herbicides aimed at?
123791.e: Herbicides control weeds that compete with crops for light, water and nutrients. By quantity they are one of the largest groups of pesticides.

123792.q: Which goal did the Confederation set itself with the 2017 action plan on plant protection products?
a: To halve the risks of plant protection products
To only import pesticides from now on
123792.e: The action plan aims to reduce the risks to people, waters and beneficial insects significantly. This includes alternatives to chemical plant protection and less spray drift.
123792.m: The Confederation's action plan aims to halve pesticide risks.

123793.q: What is the required minimum period between the last use of a pesticide and the harvest called?
123793.e: The pre-harvest interval makes sure that residues fall below the permitted maximum levels by harvest time. It is set for each product and each crop.
123793.m: After spraying, the pre-harvest interval must be kept before harvesting.

123795.q: Which plants does the natural insecticide pyrethrum come from?
123795.e: Pyrethrum is obtained from the dried flowers of certain chrysanthemums. It acts as a nerve poison on insects and is allowed in organic farming with restrictions.
123795.m: Pyrethrum is an insecticide made from chrysanthemum flowers.

123796.q: What is it called when a long-lasting substance such as DDT builds up in living things, increasing along the food chain?
123796.e: Birds of prey at the end of the food chain had such high DDT levels that their eggshells became thin. The concentration rises from level to level.
123796.m: Long-lasting poisons build up along the food chain.

123797.q: Why do pesticides often lose their effect when used frequently?
a: The pesticides become stronger in light
The plants turn them into fertiliser
123797.e: With every use, a few resistant individuals survive. Through selection their genes spread until the population is resistant.
123797.m: Frequent use of pesticides breeds resistant pests.

123798.q: In integrated plant protection, what does the “damage threshold” mean?
a: The level of infestation at which control makes economic sense
The highest amount of pesticide allowed per year
The temperature at which pests die
The distance between a field and a body of water
123798.e: Below the damage threshold, the loss of yield is smaller than the cost of treatment. This way pesticides are only used when needed.
123798.m: Integrated plant protection only sprays once the damage threshold is reached.

123799.q: Which receptors in the nervous system of insects do neonicotinoids bind to?
123799.e: Neonicotinoids occupy the acetylcholine receptors and overstimulate the nerve cells. Insects are much more sensitive than mammals.
123799.m: Neonicotinoids disrupt signal transmission in the insect nervous system.

123800.q: What does it mean that neonicotinoids work “systemically”?
a: They are taken up by the plant and spread to all its parts
They only work on the leaf surface
They break down immediately after spraying
They only work in the soil
123800.e: Systemic substances get into stems, leaves, pollen and nectar. This protects the whole plant but also reaches pollinators.
123800.m: Systemic insecticides are found throughout the whole plant.

123801.q: In what form were neonicotinoids often applied in farming?
a: As a seed treatment on the seed
As an additive in animal feed
123801.e: In seed treatment, the grain is coated with the active substance. When sowing, contaminated dust can be produced, which can endanger bees.
123801.m: Neonicotinoids were often applied directly to the seed.

123802.q: What effect of the neonicotinoid imidacloprid on bumblebee colonies did a study published in “Science” in 2012 show?
a: The colonies produced far fewer new queens
The bumblebees grew twice as big
The bumblebees became immune to mites
123802.e: Bumblebee colonies exposed to realistic amounts of imidacloprid grew more slowly and raised about 85 per cent fewer queens. As a result they found fewer new colonies the following year.
123802.m: Neonicotinoids can also weaken wild bees such as bumblebees.

123803.q: Which active substance was the first commercially very successful neonicotinoid?
123803.e: Imidacloprid came on the market in the 1990s and quickly became one of the best-selling insecticides in the world.
123803.m: Imidacloprid was the first big neonicotinoid.

123804.q: Which measure did the EU decide on in 2018 for three widely used neonicotinoids?
a: A requirement to use them in organic farming
123804.e: The ban affected imidacloprid, clothianidin and thiamethoxam, after the food safety authority EFSA had confirmed risks to bees. Switzerland followed with similar restrictions.
123804.m: In 2018 the EU banned three neonicotinoids from fields.

123805.q: What effect of even small amounts of neonicotinoids has been proved in honeybees?
a: They find their way back to the hive less well
123805.e: Sublethal doses do not kill the bees immediately but disturb learning and orientation. Foraging bees then return less often, which weakens the colony.
123805.m: Even small amounts of neonicotinoids disturb bees' sense of direction.

123806.q: What did a study by the University of Neuchâtel, published in 2017, show about honey samples from all over the world?
a: Only honey from Europe was contaminated
123806.e: The researchers examined 198 honey samples from every continent except Antarctica. The levels were mostly below the limits for humans, but in a range that is worrying for bees.
123806.m: Neonicotinoids can be detected in honey all over the world.

123807.q: Why do plants treated with glyphosate die?
a: They can no longer make important amino acids
They can no longer absorb light
123807.e: Glyphosate blocks an enzyme that plants need for certain amino acids. Without these building blocks they can no longer make proteins and die.
123807.m: Glyphosate shuts down the production of important amino acids in plants.

123808.q: Why does the main way glyphosate works not affect people and animals directly?
a: Animals do not have the blocked metabolic pathway
Animals immediately turn it into sugar
123808.e: Animals get aromatic amino acids from their food instead of making them themselves. However, other possible effects are being discussed, for example on gut bacteria.
123808.m: Glyphosate targets a metabolic pathway that only plants and microorganisms have.

123809.q: How is glyphosate classified by its effect on plants?
123809.e: Glyphosate works on almost all green plants it hits. That is why it is used before sowing or after harvesting.
123809.m: Glyphosate kills almost every plant it touches.

123810.q: Which US company brought glyphosate onto the market in the 1970s under the name Roundup?
123810.e: Monsanto later also developed genetically modified plants that tolerate glyphosate. The patent on the active substance expired long ago.
123810.m: Glyphosate was originally marketed by Monsanto.

123811.q: Which German company took over Monsanto in 2018?
123811.e: With the takeover, Bayer inherited many lawsuits in the USA over alleged cancer risks from Roundup. The court cases cost the company billions.
123811.m: Since 2018, Monsanto has belonged to Bayer.

123812.q: How did the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classify glyphosate in 2015?
123812.e: The IARC placed glyphosate in Group 2A. Authorities such as EFSA, however, concluded that no cancer risk had been proved when it is used correctly.
123812.m: Expert bodies disagree about the cancer risk of glyphosate.

123813.q: For how many years did the European Commission extend the approval of glyphosate in 2023?
123813.e: Because the member states could not agree, the Commission decided. The new approval applies until 2033 and includes some conditions.
123813.m: Glyphosate remains approved in the EU until 2033 for now.

a: Genetically modified varieties that survive glyphosate treatment
Varieties that only grow with glyphosate
Plants that break down glyphosate in the soil
123814.e: Such soya, maize or cotton varieties carry a gene for an insensitive enzyme. The field can be sprayed without harming the crop, which increased glyphosate use.
123814.m: Glyphosate-tolerant plants survive spraying, but weeds do not.

123815.q: What is the main goal of regenerative agriculture?
a: Building up humus and soil health
Making maximum use of mineral fertiliser
123815.e: Regenerative agriculture aims not only to protect the soil but to improve it. More humus stores water, nutrients and carbon.
123815.m: Regenerative agriculture builds fertile soil back up.

123816.q: What is sowing without ploughing or other tillage beforehand called?
123816.e: In direct drilling, the seed is placed in untilled soil. Soil life and structure are preserved and erosion falls.
123816.m: Direct drilling protects the soil because it is not ploughed.

123817.q: Which soil problem arises when heavy machinery drives on wet farmland?
123817.e: The pressure squeezes the pores in the soil together so that water and air get in less well. Roots and soil organisms often suffer for years.
123817.m: Heavy machinery on wet soil compacts it.

123818.q: Why is building up humus considered a contribution to climate protection?
a: Humus stores carbon that was previously in the air as CO2
Humus cools the Earth's surface by several degrees
Humus produces oxygen like a forest
123818.e: Plants take up CO2 through photosynthesis and release part of it into the soil as organic matter. If this becomes stable humus, the carbon stays stored for a long time.
123818.m: More humus in the soil means less CO2 in the atmosphere.

123819.q: What does the “4 per 1000” initiative, launched at the 2015 Paris climate conference, call for?
a: Raising the carbon content of soils by 0.4 per cent a year
Cutting pesticide use by 4 per cent a year
Planting forest on four in every thousand hectares
Limiting meat consumption to 4 kilos a year
123819.e: Such an increase in soil carbon could offset a significant part of annual CO2 emissions. The initiative was started by France.
123819.m: The 4 per 1000 initiative relies on soils as carbon stores.

123820.q: What is grazing called in which many animals graze a small area for only a short time and then move on?
123820.e: In mob grazing, the grass is used briefly and intensively and then left to rest for a long time. This is meant to encourage root growth and humus formation.
123820.m: Mob grazing lets pastures rest for a long time after brief use.

123821.q: Why should farmland in regenerative agriculture be covered for as much of the year as possible?
a: To protect it from erosion and drying out
So that nobody can walk on it
So that birds cannot find worms
123821.e: Bare soil is carried away by rain and wind and heats up a lot. Plants or mulch protect it and feed the soil life.

123822.q: What is the very fertile dark earth enriched with charcoal called, which people in the Amazon region created centuries ago?
123822.e: Terra preta was created from charcoal, pottery fragments and organic waste. Today biochar is used on this model to improve soils.
123822.m: Terra preta shows how charcoal can make soils permanently more fertile.

123823.q: Which soil animal is considered an important indicator of healthy, living soil?
123823.e: Earthworms loosen the soil, create pores for water and air and mix in organic material. Lots of worms suggest gentle farming.
123823.m: Lots of earthworms show that soil is healthy.

123824.q: What is meant by vertical farming?
a: Growing plants on floors stacked on top of each other in buildings
123824.e: Vertical farms stack growing areas in halls or tower blocks. Light, temperature and nutrients are completely controlled.

123825.q: What is growing plants without soil, with the roots standing in a nutrient solution, called?
123825.e: In hydroponics, a circulating solution supplies all the nutrients. Many vertical farms work on this principle.
123825.m: In hydroponics, plants grow in nutrient solution instead of soil.

123826.q: Why is the yield per area of ground much higher in vertical farms than in a field?
a: Crops are harvested on several floors and all year round
The plants grow ten times bigger there
They are only harvested once a year
123826.e: Several growing levels stacked on top of each other multiply the area. On top of that there are many harvests a year, because weather and seasons play no part.
123826.m: Stacked floors and harvests all year round give high yields per area of ground.

123827.q: Which system combines fish farming with growing plants in one cycle?
123827.e: Bacteria turn the fish's waste into nutrients that the plants take up. In doing so, the plants clean the water for the fish.
123827.m: Aquaponics links fish and plants in one cycle.

123828.q: Which colours of light do LED lamps in vertical farms mainly use?
123828.e: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light, while green light is reflected more. That is why many facilities glow purple-pink.
123828.m: For photosynthesis, plants mainly use red and blue light.

123829.q: What is considered the biggest disadvantage of vertical farming?
a: The high energy use for light and air conditioning
The large amount of land needed
123829.e: Because sunlight is replaced by artificial light, running the farm needs a lot of electricity. This makes the products expensive, and their climate impact depends on the source of the electricity.
123829.m: Vertical farms need a lot of energy because they replace the sun.

123830.q: Which plants are especially suitable for vertical farming?
123830.e: Lettuces and herbs grow fast, stay small and are almost entirely eaten. Staple foods such as cereals would be far too expensive to grow indoors.
123830.m: Vertical farming mainly grows lettuces and herbs.

123831.q: Why does vertical farming often need much less water than growing outdoors?
a: The water is reused in a closed cycle
The plants are smaller and drink nothing
The building collects fog from the city
123831.e: Evaporated water is condensed and excess nutrient solution is fed back. So hardly any water is lost.
123831.m: Closed cycles make vertical farming save water.

123832.q: Which advantage of vertical farming is particularly interesting for cities?
123832.e: Vertical farms can stand in the middle of cities. Lettuces and herbs reach the shops fresh and without long lorry journeys.
123832.m: Vertical farming brings growing close to the city.

123931.q: In which part of the cell does glycolysis take place?
123931.e: The enzymes of glycolysis are dissolved in the cytoplasm. That is why it can also take place in cells without mitochondria.
123931.m: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm.

123932.q: Which end product is formed from one molecule of glucose in glycolysis?
123932.e: Glucose, with six carbon atoms, is split into two C3 units and oxidised to two pyruvate molecules.
123932.m: Glycolysis makes two pyruvate from one glucose.

123933.q: How many ATP does the cell gain net from one molecule of glucose in glycolysis?
123933.e: Glycolysis uses 2 ATP at the start and later forms 4 ATP. That leaves a net 2 ATP per glucose.
123933.m: Glycolysis yields a net 2 ATP per glucose.

123934.q: What is the main purpose of converting pyruvate into lactate when oxygen is lacking?
a: It produces a lot of extra ATP
123934.e: Glycolysis needs NAD+ as an electron acceptor. Without oxygen, it is only made available again through the formation of lactate.
123934.m: Lactate formation keeps glycolysis going by recovering NAD+.

a: No, it also works without oxygen
Yes, it always needs a lot of oxygen
Yes, but only in the nucleus
123935.e: Glycolysis is anaerobic. That is why yeasts during fermentation or muscles short of oxygen can also gain energy from it.

123936.q: What happens to the pyruvate from glycolysis when there is enough oxygen?
a: It is broken down further in the mitochondria
It is stored in the nucleus
123936.e: With oxygen, pyruvate enters the mitochondria. There it is completely broken down to carbon dioxide and water via the citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain.
123936.m: With oxygen, pyruvate is broken down further in the mitochondria.

123937.q: Why do red blood cells depend entirely on glycolysis for their energy?
a: They have no contact with glucose
They do not need to transport oxygen
123937.e: Mature erythrocytes have neither a nucleus nor mitochondria. They therefore lack the citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain.
123937.m: Red blood cells only gain ATP through glycolysis.

123938.q: Where does the citric acid cycle take place in human cells?
123938.e: The enzymes of the citric acid cycle are in the matrix of the mitochondria. Only succinate dehydrogenase sits in the inner membrane.
123938.m: The citric acid cycle takes place in the matrix of the mitochondria.

123939.q: With which molecule does acetyl-CoA react at the start of the citric acid cycle to form citrate?
123939.e: Citrate synthase links the C2 unit from acetyl-CoA with the C4 molecule oxaloacetate to form citrate with six carbon atoms.
123939.m: Acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate together form citrate.

123940.q: After which biochemist is the citric acid cycle also named?
123940.e: Hans Adolf Krebs described the cycle in the 1930s. That is why it is also called the Krebs cycle.
123940.m: After Hans Krebs, the citric acid cycle is also called the Krebs cycle.

123941.q: How many molecules of carbon dioxide are released per turn of the citric acid cycle?
123941.e: In two oxidative decarboxylations, one CO2 is split off each time. This corresponds to the two carbon atoms from the acetyl-CoA fed in.
123941.m: Each turn of the citric acid cycle releases two carbon dioxide.

123942.q: Which reducing equivalents does one turn of the citric acid cycle supply?
123942.e: Three dehydrogenases transfer hydrogen to NAD+, and succinate dehydrogenase to FAD. The electrons then go into the respiratory chain.
123942.m: One turn of the citric acid cycle supplies three NADH and one FADH2.

123943.q: What are the substances NADH and FADH2 formed in the citric acid cycle used for?
a: They supply electrons for the respiratory chain
123943.e: NADH and FADH2 hand their electrons over to the respiratory chain. There most of the ATP is gained from them.
123943.m: NADH and FADH2 bring electrons to the respiratory chain.

123944.q: Which enzyme complex links glycolysis with the citric acid cycle?
123944.e: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, splitting off CO2. This step cannot be reversed.
123944.m: Pyruvate dehydrogenase turns pyruvate into acetyl-CoA.

123945.q: Why does the citric acid cycle quickly come to a standstill without oxygen, even though it does not use oxygen itself?
a: NAD+ and FAD are no longer regenerated
Citrate breaks down immediately without oxygen
123945.e: The respiratory chain only oxidises NADH and FADH2 with oxygen as the final acceptor. Without it, the cycle runs out of oxidised coenzymes.
123945.m: The citric acid cycle needs oxygen indirectly, because the respiratory chain recovers its coenzymes.

123946.q: In which structure are the complexes of the respiratory chain located?
123946.e: The enzyme complexes are built into the inner mitochondrial membrane. Its folds, the cristae, increase the surface area.
123946.m: The respiratory chain lies in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

123947.q: Which substance is the final electron acceptor of the respiratory chain?
123947.e: At complex IV the electrons are transferred to oxygen. Together with protons, this produces water.
123947.m: Oxygen takes up the electrons at the end of the respiratory chain.

123948.q: Which enzyme uses the backflow of protons into the mitochondrial matrix to make ATP?
123948.e: ATP synthase works like a tiny turbine. When protons flow back through it, it turns and joins ADP and phosphate to form ATP.
123948.m: ATP synthase makes ATP using the proton gradient.

123949.q: What do complexes I, III and IV of the respiratory chain pump across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
123949.e: The energy from electron transfer is used to pump protons into the intermembrane space. This creates an electrochemical gradient.
123949.m: The respiratory chain pumps protons out of the matrix.

123950.q: Which complex of the respiratory chain does the poison cyanide inhibit?
123950.e: Cyanide binds to cytochrome c oxidase, complex IV. The electrons can no longer be transferred to oxygen, and cellular respiration comes to a halt.
123950.m: Cyanide blocks cytochrome c oxidase and therefore cellular respiration.

123951.q: Which mobile molecule transfers electrons from complexes I and II to complex III?
123951.e: Ubiquinone, also called coenzyme Q10, is fat-soluble and moves freely in the membrane. It shuttles electrons to complex III.
123951.m: Ubiquinone transports electrons within the membrane.

123952.q: According to current estimates, roughly how many ATP does the complete oxidation of one glucose molecule yield?
123952.e: Older textbooks give 36 to 38 ATP. Because the flow of protons has been measured more precisely, the figure today is around 30 to 32 ATP.
123952.m: A completely respired glucose yields around thirty ATP.

123953.q: Which molecules supply the electrons that flow through the respiratory chain?
123953.e: NADH and FADH2 are formed mainly in the citric acid cycle. They hand their electrons to the respiratory chain, whose energy is used to make ATP.
123953.m: NADH and FADH2 feed electrons into the respiratory chain.

123954.q: Where does the beta-oxidation of fatty acids mainly take place in humans?
123954.e: The fatty acids are broken down step by step in the mitochondria. Very long-chain fatty acids are first shortened in the peroxisomes.
123954.m: Beta-oxidation takes place in the mitochondria.

123955.q: Which product of beta-oxidation is then broken down further in the citric acid cycle?
123955.e: Beta-oxidation breaks fatty acids down into acetyl-CoA. This is broken down further into carbon dioxide in the citric acid cycle of the mitochondria.
123955.m: Fatty acids produce acetyl-CoA for the citric acid cycle.

123956.q: By how many carbon atoms is a fatty acid shortened in each round of beta-oxidation?
123956.e: Each round splits off a C2 unit as acetyl-CoA. The remaining chain starts the next round.
123956.m: Beta-oxidation shortens the fatty acid by two carbon atoms per round.

123957.q: How many molecules of acetyl-CoA are produced when palmitic acid with 16 carbon atoms is broken down completely?
123957.e: 16 carbon atoms divided by 2 gives 8 acetyl-CoA. Only 7 rounds are needed for this, because the last step yields two acetyl-CoA.
123957.m: Palmitic acid is broken down into eight acetyl-CoA.

123958.q: Where do the fatty acids broken down in beta-oxidation come from?
123958.e: Fats consist of glycerol and three fatty acids. When they are split, the fatty acids enter the mitochondria and are broken down there.
123958.m: Beta-oxidation breaks down fatty acids from split fats.

123959.q: Where do the coenzymes NADH and FADH2 loaded in beta-oxidation hand over their electrons?
123959.e: NADH and FADH2 deliver their electrons to the respiratory chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane. There most of the ATP is formed with them.
123959.m: The respiratory chain uses the electrons from beta-oxidation.

123960.q: When does the body rely particularly heavily on beta-oxidation?
a: During fasting and long endurance exercise
123960.e: When carbohydrate stores are low, the body increasingly draws on its fat reserves. The fatty acids are then broken down in beta-oxidation.
123960.m: During fasting and endurance sport, the body burns more fat.

123961.q: In which organ are ketone bodies formed?
123961.e: The liver cells form ketone bodies in their mitochondria, especially during fasting. They then release them into the blood.
123961.m: Ketone bodies are formed in the liver.

123962.q: Which ketone body is given off in the breath and has a fruity smell?
123962.e: Acetone forms through the spontaneous decarboxylation of acetoacetate. It is volatile and is breathed out.
123962.m: Acetone gives the breath a fruity smell in ketosis.

123963.q: From which nutrient does the liver mainly form ketone bodies during fasting?
123963.e: During fasting, fatty acids are brought from the fatty tissue to the liver and broken down into acetyl-CoA. From this the liver builds the ketone bodies.
123963.m: Ketone bodies are made from fat.

123964.q: Why does the liver release ketone bodies into the blood during fasting?
a: As a source of energy for other organs
123964.e: The liver forms ketone bodies but cannot use them itself. In this way they are available as fuel for the heart, muscles and brain.
123964.m: The liver exports ketone bodies but does not use them itself.

123965.q: Which organ, which hardly uses fatty acids, covers a large part of its energy needs from ketone bodies during prolonged starvation?
123965.e: Fatty acids hardly cross the blood-brain barrier, but ketone bodies do. In this way the body saves glucose and spares the muscle proteins.
123965.m: During long fasting, the brain uses ketone bodies as a source of energy.

123966.q: What is the dangerous metabolic derailment called in which ketone bodies build up in the blood because of a lack of insulin?
123966.e: Without insulin, fatty acids are broken down on a massive scale and ketone bodies are formed. These acids lower the pH of the blood dangerously.
123966.m: A lack of insulin can lead to dangerous ketoacidosis.

123967.q: Which hormone situation promotes the formation of ketone bodies?
a: Little insulin and a lot of glucagon
A lot of insulin and little glucagon
A lot of insulin and a lot of glucagon
A lot of insulin after a meal
123967.e: Low insulin and high glucagon promote lipolysis and beta-oxidation in the liver. As a result, more ketone bodies are formed.
123967.m: More ketone bodies are formed when insulin is low and glucagon is high.

123968.q: Why does the body form more ketone bodies on a low-carbohydrate, ketogenic diet?
a: Without carbohydrates it breaks down more fat
Ketone bodies are found directly in vegetables
Protein is fermented into ketone bodies in the intestine
It then stores particularly large amounts of glycogen
123968.e: Without carbohydrates, the insulin level falls and the glycogen stores empty. The liver then breaks down more fatty acids and forms ketone bodies from them.
123968.m: Few carbohydrates put the body into ketosis.

123969.q: Why do people with ketoacidosis breathe very deeply and quickly?
a: To breathe out carbon dioxide and reduce the acid
Because the lungs form ketone bodies
123969.e: Carbon dioxide acts as an acid in the blood. If more of it is breathed out, the acidity falls. This deep breathing is called Kussmaul breathing.
123969.m: Kussmaul breathing is a response to metabolic acidosis.

123970.q: What does a permanently positive energy balance mean?
a: More energy is taken in than used
More energy is used than taken in
Intake and use are the same
123970.e: Excess energy is stored mainly as fat. In the long run, body weight therefore increases.
123970.m: Anyone who takes in more energy than they use gains weight.

123971.q: Which component makes up the largest part of daily energy use in adults who are not very active?
123971.e: With little exercise, the basal metabolic rate makes up around 60 to 70 per cent of total energy use. Activity and digestion share the rest.
123971.m: The basal metabolic rate is usually the biggest item in energy use.

123972.q: Which physical law forms the basis of every energy balance of the body?
123972.e: The first law states that energy is not lost but only converted. Energy taken in is used, stored or given off as heat.
123972.m: Energy is not lost in the body; it is only converted.

123973.q: A person has a basal metabolic rate of 1600 kcal and a PAL value of 1.5. What is their total energy use per day?
123973.e: Total energy use is the basal metabolic rate times the PAL value: 1600 kcal × 1.5 = 2400 kcal.
123973.m: Basal metabolic rate times PAL value gives total energy use.

123974.q: What does indirect calorimetry measure in order to determine energy use?
a: Oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide output
123974.e: From the gas exchange of breathing, you can calculate how much energy the body uses. For this the person wears a breathing mask, for example.
123974.m: Indirect calorimetry calculates energy use from the breathing gases.

123975.q: What respiratory quotient does the pure burning of carbohydrates have?
123975.e: With glucose, exactly one molecule of carbon dioxide is produced for each molecule of oxygen used. The ratio of CO2 output to O2 uptake is therefore 1.0.
123975.m: For carbohydrates, the respiratory quotient is one.

123976.q: For a week, someone takes in 500 kcal a day less than they use. How big is the energy deficit after this week?
123976.e: 7 days × 500 kcal = 3500 kcal. The body covers this deficit mainly from its energy stores.
123976.m: A daily deficit adds up over the week.

123977.q: How is the body mass index calculated?
a: Body mass in kg divided by the square of height in m
Body mass in kg divided by height in cm
Waist measurement divided by hip measurement
123977.e: The BMI has the unit kg per square metre. So the height is squared.
123977.m: For the BMI, you divide the weight by the height squared.

123978.q: What is the BMI of a person with a body mass of 72 kg and a height of 1.80 m (rounded)?
123978.e: 1.80 m × 1.80 m = 3.24 m². 72 kg ÷ 3.24 m² gives around 22.2 kg/m².
123978.m: You get the BMI by dividing the weight by the height squared.

123979.q: A person weighs 90 kg and is 1.75 m tall. Which WHO category does their BMI fall into?
123979.e: 1.75 m × 1.75 m = 3.0625 m². 90 kg ÷ 3.0625 m² gives around 29.4, which is in the range from 25 to under 30.
123979.m: A BMI between 25 and 30 counts as overweight.

123980.q: Which BMI range counts as normal weight for adults according to the WHO?
123980.e: The WHO classifies adults with a BMI of 18.5 or more and under 25 as normal weight. Above that, overweight begins.
123980.m: Normal weight is a BMI between 18.5 and 25.

123981.q: From what BMI does the WHO speak of obesity in adults?
123981.e: A BMI of 30 or more counts as obesity. This is further divided into three classes.
123981.m: A BMI of 30 or more is called obesity.

123982.q: Which Belgian scholar developed the basis of the body mass index in the 19th century?
123982.e: The statistician Adolphe Quetelet found that the weight of adults increases roughly with the square of their height. The BMI used to be called the Quetelet index.
123982.m: The BMI goes back to Adolphe Quetelet.

123983.q: What is an important weakness of the body mass index?
a: It does not distinguish between muscle and fat mass
It can only be determined in a laboratory
It is only valid for children
It does not take body weight into account
123983.e: Very muscular athletes can have a high BMI without carrying much fat. The BMI does not show how fat is distributed either.
123983.m: The BMI says nothing about muscle content or fat distribution.

123984.q: How is the BMI assessed in children and teenagers?
a: With percentiles by age and sex
With the same fixed limits as for adults
Not at all, it cannot be calculated for them
123984.e: Because body shape changes a great deal during growth, the BMI is compared with children of the same age and sex. Percentile curves are used for this.
123984.m: In children, the BMI is assessed with percentile curves.

123986.q: Which distribution of fat is considered particularly bad for health?
a: A lot of fat in the abdomen around the organs
A lot of fat on the hips and thighs
A lot of fat on the forearms
Evenly distributed fat under the skin
123986.e: Visceral belly fat is metabolically active and releases substances that promote inflammation. It increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
123986.m: Belly fat is particularly bad for health.

123987.q: Which metabolic disease is a common consequence of obesity?
123987.e: Being overweight promotes insulin resistance in the body's cells. This can develop into type 2 diabetes mellitus.
123987.m: Obesity increases the risk of type 2 diabetes.

123988.q: Which hormone does fatty tissue produce to tell the brain how large the fat reserves are?
123988.e: Leptin has a satiating effect in the hypothalamus. In obesity the leptin level is high, but the brain often responds to it less strongly.
123988.m: Leptin from fatty tissue tells the brain about the fat reserves.

123989.q: Which joint disease is encouraged by severe overweight, especially in the knees?
123989.e: The extra load wears down the joint cartilage faster. That is why osteoarthritis of the knee is more common in obesity.
123989.m: Being overweight strains the knee joints and promotes osteoarthritis.

123990.q: Which breathing disorder during sleep occurs more often in obesity?
123990.e: Fatty tissue on the neck can narrow the upper airways during sleep. This leads to repeated pauses in breathing.
123990.m: Obesity encourages pauses in breathing at night.

123991.q: What is the surgery called that, in severe obesity, creates a gastric bypass, for example?
123991.e: Bariatric operations make the stomach smaller or shorten the path of food. They are an option in severe obesity when other measures are not enough.
123991.m: Bariatric surgery treats severe obesity with an operation.

123992.q: What is meant by activity energy expenditure?
a: Energy use beyond the basal metabolic rate
The energy use of the brain alone
123992.e: Activity energy expenditure covers the energy for movement, work, sport and other extra effort. Together with the basal metabolic rate, it gives total energy use.
123992.m: Activity energy expenditure is energy use above the basal metabolic rate.

123993.q: What does the unit 1 MET mean?
a: Energy use at rest while sitting
The energy in one gram of fat
123993.e: 1 MET corresponds roughly to resting energy use, around 1 kcal per kg of body mass per hour. An activity of 8 MET therefore uses eight times as much.
123993.m: One MET corresponds to energy use at rest.

123994.q: A person weighing 70 kg jogs for an hour at 8 MET. Roughly how much energy do they use if 1 MET is around 1 kcal per kg per hour?
123994.e: 8 kcal per kg per hour × 70 kg × 1 h = 560 kcal.
123994.m: You estimate energy use as MET times body mass times time.

123995.q: Roughly what share of the energy is converted into mechanical work during muscle activity?
123995.e: The efficiency of the muscles is around 20 to 25 per cent. The rest is released as heat, which is why we get warm during sport.
123995.m: Muscles convert most of the energy into heat.

123996.q: What is the increased oxygen consumption after intense exercise called?
123996.e: After exercise the body has to refill stores, break down lactate and cool down. For this it uses more oxygen than at rest for a while.
123996.m: After intense sport, oxygen consumption stays raised for a while.

123997.q: Which activity has the highest activity energy expenditure per hour?
123997.e: In cross-country skiing, the arms and legs work at the same time at high intensity. Energy use is therefore very high.
123997.m: Endurance sport using many muscles uses a particularly large amount of energy.

123998.q: Which energy store supplies ATP particularly quickly in the first seconds of a sprint?
123998.e: Creatine phosphate transfers its phosphate group directly to ADP. However, the supply only lasts for a few seconds of maximum effort.
123998.m: Creatine phosphate supplies energy in the first seconds of a sprint.

123999.q: How does the activity energy expenditure of a person change if they become heavier while doing the same activity?
a: It rises because more mass has to be moved
It falls because fat saves energy
It always stays exactly the same
123999.e: When walking or climbing stairs, you have to move your own body weight. More mass needs more energy for this.
123999.m: Anyone who weighs more uses more energy for the same movement.

124000.q: Roughly what energy value does alcohol (ethanol) have?
124000.e: Ethanol supplies around 7 kcal or 29 kJ per gram. Alcoholic drinks are therefore high in energy.
124000.m: Alcohol supplies almost as much energy as fat.

124001.q: Why is the physiological energy value of protein lower than its physical energy value?
a: The nitrogen is excreted as urea, which still contains energy
Protein is not broken down in the body at all
Protein burns hotter in the body
124001.e: In a calorimeter, protein burns completely. The body, however, excretes the nitrogen as urea, which still contains energy.
124001.m: With urea, the body loses part of the energy in protein.

124002.q: Which device is used to determine the physical energy value of a food?
124002.e: The sample is burned completely in pure oxygen in the bomb calorimeter. The energy value is worked out from how much the surrounding water warms up.
124002.m: In a bomb calorimeter, the energy value is measured by burning.

124003.q: How many kilojoules are equal to one kilocalorie?
124003.e: A calorie is the heat that warms one gram of water by about one degree. One kilocalorie is equal to 4.184 kilojoules.
124003.m: One kilocalorie is just over four kilojoules.

124004.q: A snack contains 10 g of fat, 30 g of carbohydrates and 5 g of protein. Roughly how much energy does it supply (9, 4 and 4 kcal per gram)?
124004.m: You calculate the energy value by multiplying each nutrient by its value and adding them up.

124005.q: Why does fibre supply the body with only a little energy?
a: It is not digested in the small intestine
It is burned in the stomach straight away
124005.e: Our digestive enzymes cannot split fibre. Only gut bacteria in the large intestine ferment part of it, which is why it supplies only around 2 kcal per gram.
124005.m: Fibre supplies only a little energy.

124006.q: Roughly how large is diet-induced thermogenesis on a mixed diet?
a: Around 10 per cent of total energy use
Around 50 per cent of total energy use
Around 1 per cent of total energy use
Around 30 per cent of total energy use
124006.e: Digesting, absorbing and processing nutrients costs energy. On a mixed diet this is about ten per cent of daily energy use.
124006.m: Digestion uses around a tenth of the daily energy.

124007.q: Which nutrient has the strongest diet-induced thermogenesis?
124007.e: With protein, around 20 to 30 per cent of the energy taken in is used for processing it. With fat the share is smallest.
124007.m: Protein costs the most energy to process.

124008.q: How does the body quickly produce extra heat using the skeletal muscles when it is cold?
a: By widening the blood vessels in the skin
124008.e: When shivering, the muscles contract rapidly and without coordination. The energy is turned almost completely into heat.
124008.m: Shivering is a quick source of heat in the cold.

124009.q: What is the production of heat in the cold that happens without shivering called?
124009.e: In non-shivering thermogenesis, energy is released directly as heat in the metabolism. It is particularly important in newborn babies.
124009.m: The body can also produce heat without shivering.

124010.q: Which hormones increase the basal metabolic rate and therefore the body's heat production?
124010.e: Thyroxine and triiodothyronine increase the metabolic activity of many cells. People with an overactive thyroid often sweat and hardly feel cold.
124010.m: Thyroid hormones fire up the metabolism.

124011.q: What does the abbreviation NEAT stand for in the energy balance?
a: Energy used in everyday movement without sport
124011.e: NEAT means non-exercise activity thermogenesis. It includes walking, standing, climbing stairs or fidgeting.
124011.m: Everyday movement without sport also uses energy.

124012.q: Why is 2,4-dinitrophenol, which used to be sold as a slimming product, life-threatening?
a: It uncouples the respiratory chain and can cause fatal overheating
It blocks the digestion of fat in the intestine
124012.e: The substance lets protons flow back past ATP synthase. The energy is released as heat instead of as ATP, and body temperature can rise dangerously.
124012.m: Uncouplers turn energy into heat instead of ATP.

124013.q: Which region of the brain controls body temperature and therefore heat production?
124013.e: The body's temperature centre is in the hypothalamus. It compares the actual temperature with the set point and starts heat production or cooling.
124013.m: The hypothalamus is the body's thermostat.

124014.q: Which protein makes heat production possible in brown fat?
124014.e: UCP1 lets protons flow back into the mitochondrial matrix without making ATP. The energy of the gradient is thus turned directly into heat.
124014.m: Thermogenin turns brown fat into a heater.

124015.q: Why is brown fat brownish in colour?
a: It contains a great many mitochondria
It stores a lot of melanin
It contains a lot of bile pigment
It has a poor blood supply
124015.e: The numerous mitochondria contain iron-containing cytochromes. Together with the good blood supply, this produces the brownish colour.
124015.m: The many mitochondria colour brown fat.

124016.q: Where is there a particularly large amount of brown fat in newborn babies?
a: Between the shoulder blades and on the neck
In the soles of the feet
In the lens of the eye
In the bone marrow of the fingers
124016.e: Newborn babies can hardly shiver yet. The brown fat in the back and neck area therefore protects them from getting cold.
124016.m: Newborn babies keep warm with brown fat in the neck.

124017.q: How do brown fat cells differ in structure from white fat cells?
a: They contain many small fat droplets instead of one large one
They contain no fat at all
They are much bigger than white fat cells
124017.e: White fat cells have a single large fat droplet. Brown fat cells are multilocular, so the mitochondria can reach the fatty acids quickly.
124017.m: Brown fat cells have many small fat droplets.

124018.q: Through which part of the nervous system is brown fat activated in the cold?
a: Through the sympathetic nervous system with noradrenaline
Through the parasympathetic nervous system with acetylcholine
Through the motor nerves of the arms
124018.e: Cold stimuli lead to the release of noradrenaline at the brown fat cells. This starts lipolysis and switches on UCP1.
124018.m: In the cold, the sympathetic nervous system switches on brown fat.

124019.q: What are fat cells in white fat called that take on heat-producing properties because of cold?
124019.e: With prolonged cold, cells with UCP1 and many mitochondria can form in white fat. They are called beige or brite fat cells.
124019.m: White fat can partly turn beige and produce heat.

124020.q: Which imaging method made active brown fat in adults visible?
a: A normal X-ray of the lungs
124020.e: Active brown fat takes up a lot of glucose. In PET-CT with labelled glucose it therefore lights up brightly, especially after exposure to cold.
124020.m: Active brown fat shows up in PET-CT.

124021.q: What do hibernating animals such as marmots use their brown fat for in particular?
a: To warm up quickly when they wake
124021.e: When waking from hibernation, the body temperature has to rise a great deal. Brown fat supplies a lot of heat quickly for this.
124021.m: Hibernating animals heat themselves up with brown fat.

124022.q: What is produced from the pyruvate of glycolysis in the alcoholic fermentation of yeast?
124022.e: Without oxygen, yeasts convert pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide makes bread dough rise, for example.
124022.m: Yeast turns pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

124023.q: Which organ covers most of its energy needs at rest by breaking down fatty acids?
124023.e: The heart muscle is rich in mitochondria and works non-stop. At rest, most of its ATP comes from beta-oxidation.
124023.m: The heart mainly burns fatty acids.

124024.q: What is the combination of abdominal obesity, high blood pressure, unfavourable blood fats and insulin resistance called?
124024.e: When these risk factors occur together, it is called metabolic syndrome. It clearly increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.
124024.m: Metabolic syndrome combines several metabolic risk factors.

124025.q: Why does the body store energy for the long term mainly as fat rather than as glycogen?
a: Fat is stored without water and is much more energy-dense
Fat can be broken down faster than glycogen
The body cannot store glycogen at all
Fat contains more oxygen than glycogen
124025.e: Glycogen binds a lot of water and supplies little energy per gram of stored weight. Fat is compact and therefore the ideal long-term store.
124025.m: Fat is the body's most compact energy store.

124026.q: Why are the physiological and physical energy values of carbohydrates almost the same?
a: They are broken down completely to carbon dioxide and water in the body
They are not used by the body at all
They contain nitrogen, which is excreted
They do not burn in the calorimeter
124026.e: In the body, as in the calorimeter, carbohydrates end up only as carbon dioxide and water. No waste product containing energy is left over.
124026.m: Nutrients that are broken down completely give the body almost all their energy value.

124027.q: Which substance is formed at the end of the respiratory chain when oxygen takes up electrons and protons?
124027.e: At the last complex of the respiratory chain, oxygen, electrons and protons combine to form water. The carbon dioxide, by contrast, is produced earlier in the citric acid cycle.
124027.m: The respiratory chain turns oxygen into water.

124028.q: Why do many cancer cells use a particularly large amount of glucose?
a: They break down glucose heavily by glycolysis even with oxygen
They need glucose for their cell wall
They pass glucose on to healthy cells
124028.e: Many tumour cells rely heavily on glycolysis and form lactate even when there is enough oxygen. This quickly supplies energy and building blocks for their growth.
124028.m: Cancer cells often rely heavily on glycolysis even with oxygen.

124029.q: How does the basal metabolic rate usually respond to a long and severe reduction in calories?
a: It always stays exactly the same
124029.e: The body adapts to the shortage and saves energy, partly because body mass is lost. This makes further weight loss harder.
124029.m: During strict fasting, the body saves energy.

124030.q: Which SI unit of energy appears on nutrition tables next to the kilocalorie?
124030.e: The joule is the SI unit of energy. On packaging, the energy content is given in kilojoules and in kilocalories.
124030.m: The energy content of food is given in kilojoules.

124031.q: How is the RMS value of an alternating voltage defined?
a: As the DC voltage that converts the same power in a resistor
As the highest value the voltage reaches
As the average voltage over one cycle
As the voltage at the moment of switching on
124031.e: The RMS value compares the heating effect. An alternating voltage with an RMS value of 230 V heats a resistor just as much as 230 V DC.
124031.m: The RMS value equals the DC voltage with the same power.

124032.q: By what factor do you divide the peak value of a sinusoidal voltage to get the RMS value?
124032.e: For sinusoidal quantities, Urms = Umax divided by the square root of 2. The RMS value is therefore about 71 per cent of the peak value.
124032.m: For a sine wave, the RMS value is the peak value divided by the square root of two.

124033.q: A sinusoidal voltage has a peak value of 100 V. What is its RMS value?
124033.m: You get the RMS value of a sine wave by dividing the peak value by 1.414.

124034.q: What is the RMS value of a symmetrical square-wave voltage that jumps between +12 V and -12 V?
124034.e: The voltage has a magnitude of 12 V at every moment. The power in a resistor is therefore the same as with 12 V DC.
124034.m: For a symmetrical square wave the RMS value and the peak value are equal.

124035.q: What is special about a meter labelled “True RMS”?
a: It measures the RMS value correctly even for non-sinusoidal signals
It always shows the peak value
124035.e: Simple meters calculate with a form factor that is only correct for sine waves. True RMS meters work out the real root mean square.
124035.m: A True RMS meter measures the real RMS value of any waveform.

124036.q: What is the arithmetic mean of a sinusoidal voltage over a whole cycle?
124036.e: The positive and negative half-waves are equally large and cancel out. That is why the RMS value is needed for power.
124036.m: The mean of a sinusoidal voltage over one cycle is zero.

124037.q: The mains voltage has an RMS value of 230 V. Roughly what is its peak value?
124037.e: For a sine wave, peak value = RMS value times the square root of 2. 230 V times 1.414 gives about 325 V.
124037.m: The mains voltage reaches peaks of about 325 V.

124038.q: Which mains frequency is usual in the USA?
124038.e: North America uses 60 Hz, Europe 50 Hz. Devices with a clock or a motor must be designed for this.
124038.m: In North America the power grid runs at 60 hertz.

124039.q: Which country has two different mains frequencies, 50 Hz in the east and 60 Hz in the west?
124039.e: In the 19th century eastern and western Japan bought generators from different countries. To this day the grids are linked through frequency converters.

124040.q: What happens to the mains frequency if suddenly more electricity is used than produced?
124040.e: The missing power is taken from the rotational energy of the generators. They slow down and the frequency falls.
124040.m: If power is missing in the grid, the frequency falls.

124041.q: How do power stations in the interconnected grid react within seconds to a falling mains frequency?
124041.e: This automatic reaction is called primary control. Power stations across the whole interconnected grid immediately deliver a little more power until the frequency is stable. Later, secondary and tertiary control take over.
124041.m: Primary control stabilises the frequency within seconds.

124042.q: What is the angular frequency of the 50 Hz grid?
124042.e: ω = 2 × π × f. So 2 × 3.1416 × 50 Hz gives about 314 per second.
124042.m: The angular frequency is two pi times the frequency.

124043.q: Why is the mains frequency the same everywhere in the whole continental European interconnected grid?
a: All the generators turn in sync with each other
Each country measures the frequency again itself
The frequency is sent out by radio
The electricity meters set the frequency
124043.e: The synchronous generators are electrically coupled through the grid. They run in step and form a single synchronous area.
124043.m: An interconnected grid has the same frequency everywhere.

124044.q: In the first moment after a power station fails, what softens the drop in the mains frequency?
a: The inertia of the rotating generators
124044.e: The heavy rotating machines store kinetic energy. This instantaneous reserve is fed into the grid at once.
124044.m: Rotating masses support the mains frequency in the first few seconds.

124045.q: By how many degrees are the three voltages in a three-phase grid out of phase with each other?
124045.e: The three windings in the generator are offset by a third of a circle. That is why the voltages are shifted by 360 ÷ 3 = 120 degrees.
124045.m: The three phases of three-phase current are 120 degrees apart.

124046.q: By what factor is the voltage between two line conductors larger than the voltage between a line conductor and the neutral?
124046.e: Because of the 120-degree phase shift, the difference between two phase voltages is the square root of 3 times as large. 230 V × 1.732 is about 400 V.
124046.m: The line voltage is the square root of three times larger than the phase voltage.

124047.q: How many line conductors does a three-phase grid have?
124047.e: The line conductors are called L1, L2 and L3. There is usually also a neutral conductor and a protective earth conductor.
124047.m: A three-phase grid has three line conductors.

124048.q: How large is the current in the neutral conductor of a star connection when all phases are loaded exactly equally?
124048.e: Three equal currents that are 120 degrees apart always add up to zero. No current flows in the neutral conductor.
124048.m: With a balanced load no current flows in the neutral conductor.

124049.q: What are the two basic connections of three-phase loads called?
124049.e: In a star, each phase winding lies between a line conductor and the star point; in a delta, between two line conductors. The windings therefore get different voltages.
124049.m: Three-phase loads are connected in star or in delta.

124050.q: Which property makes three-phase current especially suitable for electric motors?
a: It produces a rotating magnetic field in three coils
It has a higher frequency than alternating current
It only flows in one direction
124050.e: Three offset coils with offset currents produce a magnetic field that rotates. This rotating field pulls the rotor round with it.
124050.m: Three-phase current produces a rotating field that drives motors.

124051.q: What real power does a balanced three-phase load take with a line voltage of 400 V, a line current of 10 A and cos phi = 1?
124051.e: P = √3 × U × I × cos phi = 1.732 × 400 V × 10 A × 1, which gives about 6928 W.
124051.m: Three-phase power is calculated with the factor of the square root of three.

124052.q: Which Swiss company took part in the first long-distance transmission of three-phase current from Lauffen am Neckar to Frankfurt in 1891?
124052.e: AEG and Maschinenfabrik Oerlikon supplied the system for the electrical exhibition in Frankfurt. The line was about 175 km long.
124052.m: The first long-distance three-phase transmission was built with Swiss involvement.

124053.q: What is characteristic of a synchronous motor?
a: The rotor turns at exactly the speed of the rotating field
The rotor always turns a little more slowly than the rotating field
The rotor turns twice as fast as the rotating field
The rotor needs no magnetic field
124053.e: The magnetised rotor is carried along by the rotating field like a compass needle. It therefore runs in step, that is synchronously.
124053.m: A synchronous motor turns in step with the rotating field.

124054.q: At what speed does a synchronous motor with two pole pairs run on the 50 Hz mains?
124054.e: n = 60 × f ÷ p = 60 × 50 ÷ 2 = 1500 revolutions per minute.
124054.m: The speed of a synchronous motor depends on the frequency and the number of pole pairs.

124055.q: What is the speed of the rotating field of a machine with one pole pair on the 50 Hz mains?
124055.e: With one pole pair, the field makes one revolution per mains cycle, so 50 per second. That is 50 × 60 = 3000 per minute.
124055.m: With one pole pair the field turns fifty times a second.

124056.q: Why does a simple synchronous motor connected to a fixed grid not start by itself?
a: The heavy rotor cannot follow the fast rotating field from a standstill
It has no windings in the stator
It only works with direct current
124056.e: The rotating field changes direction so quickly that the stationary rotor is only pulled back and forth. A starting aid or a frequency converter is needed.
124056.m: A synchronous motor needs help to start.

124057.q: How is the rotor of a synchronous motor magnetised?
a: By permanent magnets or a winding excited with direct current
Only by induction from the rotating field
124057.e: The rotor needs its own fixed magnetic field. This is provided by permanent magnets or an exciter winding with direct current.
124057.m: The rotor of a synchronous motor has its own magnetic field.

124058.q: Which machine is fitted as the generator in most large power stations?
124058.e: The speed of the synchronous machine is firmly linked to the mains frequency. That is why hydroelectric and nuclear power stations mostly produce their electricity with synchronous generators.
124058.m: Power station generators are mostly synchronous machines.

124059.q: What must match before a synchronous generator in a power station is connected to the grid?
a: Voltage, frequency and phase must match the grid
The generator must be at a standstill
The generator must turn twice as fast as the grid
The generator must deliver direct current
124059.e: During synchronisation, voltage, frequency and phase are matched. Otherwise large equalising currents would flow when connecting.
124059.m: A generator is only connected once it is in step with the grid.

124060.q: Why do clocks with a small synchronous motor keep accurate time as long as the mains frequency is right?
a: Their speed is firmly linked to the mains frequency
They do not count the voltage peaks
124060.e: The synchronous motor turns exactly in step with the mains frequency. That is why grid operators even out frequency deviations over the course of the day.
124060.m: Synchronous clocks count the oscillations of the grid.

124061.q: What happens if a synchronous motor is loaded too heavily?
a: It falls out of step and stops
It turns faster than the rotating field
124061.e: If the load torque exceeds the pull-out torque, the rotor can no longer follow the field. It loses synchronism and must be switched off.
124061.m: When overloaded, the synchronous motor loses synchronism.

124062.q: What is called slip in an induction motor?
a: The relative difference between the speed of the rotating field and the rotor
124062.e: Slip is (n_field minus n_rotor) ÷ n_field. It is usually given in per cent.
124062.m: Slip describes how much more slowly the rotor turns than the rotating field.

124063.q: A rotating field turns at 1500 per minute and the rotor at 1440 per minute. What is the slip?
124063.m: Slip is the difference in speed divided by the speed of the field.

124064.q: What is the most common type of rotor in an induction motor called?
124064.e: The rotor consists of aluminium or copper bars short-circuited at the ends by rings. It looks like a hamster wheel.
124064.m: The squirrel-cage rotor is robust and needs no sliding contacts.

124065.q: Why can the rotor of an induction motor never quite reach the speed of the rotating field?
a: Without a difference in speed no current would be induced in the rotor
Because the friction in the bearing is too great
Because the rotor is made of plastic
124065.e: Induction only occurs if the field moves relative to the rotor. Without rotor current there would be no torque.
124065.m: An induction motor needs slip to produce torque.

124066.q: What in the stator of a three-phase induction motor produces the turning of the rotor?
a: A rotating magnetic field from three currents out of phase
A permanent magnet that turns along with it
An electrostatic field between two plates
124066.e: Alternating currents shifted in time flow through the three windings in the stator. This creates a rotating magnetic field that induces currents in the rotor and pulls it along.
124066.m: The rotating field in the stator drives the induction motor.

124067.q: What is star-delta starting used for in larger induction motors?
a: It lowers the high starting current
It reverses the direction of rotation
124067.e: When starting in star connection, each winding only gets the phase voltage. The starting current falls to about a third, and then the motor is switched to delta.
124067.m: Star-delta starting protects the grid when switching on.

124068.q: How do you reverse the direction of rotation of a three-phase induction motor?
a: Swap the neutral and earth conductors
124068.e: Swapping two phases changes the order of the voltages. The rotating field, and with it the motor, then runs the other way.
124068.m: Swapping two line conductors reverses the direction of rotation.

124069.q: Which device can adjust the speed of an induction motor smoothly?
124069.e: The frequency converter produces a voltage with a variable frequency. This changes the speed of the rotating field and the motor.
124069.m: A frequency converter controls the speed through the frequency.

124070.q: How large is the starting current of an induction motor switched on directly, typically?
a: About five to eight times the rated current
Exactly the same as the rated current
About a hundred times the rated current
124070.e: At a standstill the slip is at its maximum and a very high current is induced in the rotor. The current only falls as the speed rises.
124070.m: Induction motors draw several times their rated current when switched on.

124071.q: The transmission voltage is increased tenfold for the same power. How do the line losses change?
124071.e: The current falls to a tenth. Because the losses grow with I², they fall to (1/10)² = 1/100.
124071.m: Line losses decrease with the square of the current.

124072.q: At what frequency does a transformer on the 50 Hz mains mainly hum?
124072.e: Through magnetostriction, the sheets change length at every peak of magnetisation, whatever its direction. That happens twice per cycle.
124072.m: A transformer on the 50 Hz mains hums at 100 hertz.

124073.q: Roughly what efficiency do large power transformers achieve?
124073.e: Large transformers have no moving parts and very well optimised cores. Their losses are below one per cent.
124073.m: Large transformers work almost without losses.

124074.q: An ideal transformer converts 230 V and 1 A on the primary side into 23 V. What current flows on the secondary side?
124074.e: In an ideal transformer the power stays the same: 230 V × 1 A = 230 W. This gives I = 230 W ÷ 23 V = 10 A.
124074.m: If the voltage is lowered, the current rises in the same ratio.

124075.q: What is special about an autotransformer?
a: The primary and secondary sides share a common winding
It has no iron core at all
124075.e: In an autotransformer the secondary voltage is taken from a tap on the winding. This saves copper but does not separate the circuits.
124075.m: An autotransformer manages with a single winding.

124076.q: What is an isolating transformer for?
a: It isolates the circuit electrically from the mains
It turns alternating current into direct current
It stores energy for power cuts
124076.e: There is no conducting connection between the primary and secondary windings. Anyone touching a conductor does not form a circuit to earth, which increases safety.
124076.m: An isolating transformer protects through electrical isolation.

124077.q: What are large power transformers in substations usually cooled and insulated with?
124077.e: The windings sit in a tank of insulating oil. The oil carries the heat to the cooling fins and insulates at the same time.
124077.m: Large transformers stand in an oil bath.

124078.q: What advantage does HVDC offer when connecting two grids?
a: It can link grids with different frequencies or not in sync
It increases the frequency of both grids
It only works within one grid
124078.e: The DC link decouples the two AC grids. They therefore do not have to run in sync.
124078.m: HVDC can even connect grids that do not run in step.

124079.q: Which semiconductor components are used in modern HVDC converter stations?
124079.e: Older systems use thyristors, newer ones mainly IGBTs. They switch very large currents and voltages.
124079.m: HVDC stations work with high-power semiconductors.

124080.q: To which island did the world's first commercial HVDC link lead?
124080.e: The Swedish company ASEA connected the island of Gotland to the mainland with an undersea cable. This was the start of commercial HVDC technology.
124080.m: The first commercial HVDC link led to Gotland.

124081.q: What is the main disadvantage of HVDC?
a: The lines must be made of gold
124081.e: Complex converters are needed at both ends. That is why HVDC only pays off over large distances, for undersea cables or for linking grids.
124081.m: Because of the expensive stations, HVDC only pays off over long distances.

124082.q: How many conductors does a bipolar HVDC link need?
124082.e: One conductor carries a positive and the other a negative voltage relative to earth. Three-phase current, by contrast, needs three conductors.
124082.m: A bipolar HVDC line manages with two conductors.

124083.q: What does the converter station at the receiving end of an HVDC line do?
a: It turns direct current back into alternating current
It turns alternating current into direct current
It stores the electricity in batteries
124083.e: There the station works as an inverter and feeds alternating current into the grid. The rectifier is at the start of the line.
124083.m: At the end of an HVDC link alternating current is produced again.

124084.q: Which effect, which pushes alternating current to the surface of a conductor, plays no role in HVDC?
124084.e: With direct current the current spreads evenly over the whole cross-section. The conductor is therefore used better.
124084.m: Direct current uses the whole cross-section of the conductor.

124085.q: Why are HVDC systems built with the rectifier and inverter at the same place, with no long-distance line at all?
a: To link two neighbouring grids that do not run in step
To transmit electricity over long distances
124085.e: Such a back-to-back link connects two neighbouring AC grids. The DC section is only a few metres long and decouples the grids.
124085.m: An HVDC back-to-back link connects neighbouring grids.

124086.q: Besides operating the lines, what job does Swissgrid have?
a: It keeps generation and consumption in balance
124086.e: Swissgrid obtains balancing power and so keeps the mains frequency stable. Selling electricity is done by the energy suppliers.
124086.m: Swissgrid keeps the Swiss grid in balance.

124087.q: Which federal law required an independent national grid company for the transmission grid?
124087.e: The Electricity Supply Act governs the opening of the electricity market. It states that the transmission grid must be run by an independent company.
124087.m: The Electricity Supply Act is the basis for Swissgrid.

124088.q: According to the law, who must own the majority of Swissgrid?
a: Cantons and municipalities, directly or indirectly
124088.e: The Electricity Supply Act requires the majority of capital and voting rights to lie with cantons and municipalities, either directly or through their energy companies.
124088.m: Swissgrid is mostly owned by the Swiss public sector.

124089.q: In which association does Swissgrid work together with the other European transmission system operators?
124089.e: In the ENTSO-E association, Europe's transmission system operators coordinate planning and operation. Swissgrid is a member.
124089.m: Swissgrid is part of the European association of grid operators.

124090.q: Which grid level is Swissgrid's transmission grid in Switzerland?
124090.e: The Swiss power grid is divided into seven grid levels. Extra-high voltage forms grid level 1, and households are connected to grid level 7.
124090.m: The transmission grid is the top grid level.

124091.q: Which independent authority in Switzerland supervises grid usage charges and therefore Swissgrid too?
a: The Financial Market Supervisory Authority FINMA
124091.e: ElCom is the regulatory authority for electricity. Among other things it checks grid tariffs and the security of supply.
124091.m: ElCom regulates the Swiss electricity market.

124092.q: How are the costs of Swissgrid's transmission grid mainly paid for?
a: Through grid usage charges on the electricity bill
124092.e: The costs are passed on through grid tariffs to the distribution system operators and finally to the end customers. They are part of the price of electricity.
124092.m: The transmission grid is paid for through the electricity bill.

124093.q: In which unit is reactive power given?
124093.e: The unit var stands for volt-ampere reactive. It distinguishes reactive power from real power in watts.
124093.m: Reactive power is given in var.

124094.q: A load has a real power of 3 kW and a reactive power of 4 kvar. What is the apparent power?
124094.e: S = square root of (P² + Q²) = square root of (9 + 16) = square root of 25 = 5 kVA.
124094.m: Apparent, real and reactive power form a right-angled triangle.

124095.q: What is the power factor cos phi with a real power of 8 kW and an apparent power of 10 kVA?
124095.e: cos phi = P ÷ S = 8 kW ÷ 10 kVA = 0.8.
124095.m: The power factor is real power divided by apparent power.

124096.q: Which components cause reactive power in AC circuits?
124096.e: In coils and capacitors energy is stored in fields and given back again. Current and voltage are shifted relative to each other.
124096.m: Coils and capacitors swing reactive power back and forth.

124097.q: What is used to compensate for the inductive reactive power of large motors?
124097.e: Capacitors take up reactive power with the opposite sign. In this way the reactive currents largely cancel out.
124097.m: Capacitors balance out inductive reactive power.

124098.q: How does the current in an ideal coil behave compared with the voltage?
a: It lags the voltage by 90 degrees
It leads the voltage by 90 degrees
It is in phase with the voltage
124098.e: Through self-induction the coil resists every change in current. That is why the current only reaches its maximum a quarter of a cycle after the voltage.
124098.m: In a coil the current comes late.

124099.q: How does the current in an ideal capacitor behave compared with the voltage?
a: It leads the voltage by 90 degrees
It lags the voltage by 90 degrees
It is in phase with the voltage
124099.e: The capacitor must first be charged before there is a voltage across it. The charging current is greatest when the voltage passes through zero.
124099.m: In a capacitor the current leads.

124100.q: Why is a lot of reactive power in the grid unwanted?
a: It loads the lines with current without doing useful work
124100.e: Reactive currents flow back and forth and heat the lines. Lines and transformers have to be built larger to cope.
124100.m: Reactive power loads the grid without any benefit.

124101.q: In which unit is apparent power given?
124101.e: Apparent power is the product of RMS voltage and RMS current. Its unit is the volt-ampere.
124101.m: Apparent power is given in volt-amperes.

124102.q: Between which forms of energy does the energy swing back and forth in an electrical oscillating circuit?
a: The electric field of the capacitor and the magnetic field of the coil
124102.e: The charged capacitor discharges through the coil and builds up a magnetic field. This collapses and charges the capacitor again the other way round.
124102.m: In an oscillating circuit the energy alternates between capacitor and coil.

124103.q: How does the natural frequency of an oscillating circuit change if you quadruple the capacitance?
124103.e: The frequency is inversely proportional to the square root of C. The square root of 4 is 2, so the frequency falls to half.
124103.m: Four times the capacitance means half the frequency.

124104.q: Why does the oscillation in a real oscillating circuit gradually die away?
a: The ohmic resistance turns energy into heat
124104.e: With every swing back and forth, energy is lost as heat in the wires. The amplitude therefore decreases; this is called damping.

124105.q: What is an adjustable oscillating circuit used for in a classic radio receiver?
124105.e: A variable capacitor changes the natural frequency of the circuit. It then responds strongly only to the station with that frequency.
124105.m: An oscillating circuit selects the station you want on the radio.

124106.q: How does the impedance of a series oscillating circuit behave at its resonant frequency?
a: It is at its minimum and equals the ohmic resistance
It is zero ohms, even with losses
It is the same as at any other frequency
124106.e: At resonance the reactances of the coil and the capacitor cancel out. Only the ohmic part remains.
124106.m: At resonance a series circuit lets the most current through.

124107.q: How does the impedance of an ideal parallel oscillating circuit behave at resonance?
a: It equals exactly the resistance of the coil
124107.e: In the parallel circuit at resonance the current only swings between the coil and the capacitor. Hardly any current flows in from outside, so the circuit blocks.
124107.m: A parallel oscillating circuit blocks at its resonant frequency.

124108.q: How can the oscillation in an oscillating circuit be kept going permanently?
a: Through feedback that supplies energy in the right rhythm
By charging it more strongly once
124108.e: A real oscillating circuit loses energy with every oscillation. A feedback circuit with an amplifier supplies this energy again in time with the oscillation.
124108.m: Feedback cancels out the damping of an oscillation.

124109.q: At what speed do electromagnetic waves travel in a vacuum?
124109.e: All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum. It is almost exactly 300,000 km per second.
124109.m: Electromagnetic waves are as fast as light.

124110.q: How are the electric and magnetic fields arranged in an electromagnetic wave?
a: At right angles to each other and to the direction of travel
Parallel to each other and to the direction of travel
Both along the direction of travel
124110.e: Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves. The two fields oscillate across the direction of travel and are perpendicular to each other.

124111.q: Which physicist predicted the existence of electromagnetic waves in theory with his equations?
124111.e: Maxwell summed up electricity and magnetism in four equations. From these followed waves that travel at the speed of light.
124111.m: Maxwell predicted electromagnetic waves in theory.

124112.q: What distinguishes electromagnetic waves from sound waves?
a: They need no medium and also travel through a vacuum
124112.e: The fields create each other and need no carrier. That is why sunlight reaches us through empty space.
124112.m: Electromagnetic waves can cross a vacuum too.

124113.q: Which kind of electromagnetic radiation has the highest frequency?
124113.e: The spectrum ranges from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, light and ultraviolet to X-rays and gamma rays. Gamma radiation has the most energy.
124113.m: Gamma radiation has the highest frequency in the spectrum.

124114.q: How long is a simple dipole antenna tuned to a wave, compared with the wavelength?
124114.e: In a half-wave dipole a standing wave forms with a current maximum in the middle. That is why it radiates especially well.
124114.m: A dipole antenna is usually half a wavelength long.

124115.q: At which university did Heinrich Hertz carry out his famous experiments with electromagnetic waves?
124115.e: Hertz was a professor in Karlsruhe when he carried out his experiments there. Afterwards he moved to Bonn.
124115.m: Heinrich Hertz did his research in Karlsruhe.

124116.q: What did Hertz use to produce electromagnetic waves in his experiments?
124116.e: An induction coil produced a high voltage across a spark gap. The rapid discharges gave off waves, which Hertz detected with a receiving loop.
124116.m: Hertz produced waves with electric sparks.

124117.q: What did Hertz discover along the way during his spark experiments?
a: That ultraviolet light makes it easier for sparks to jump
124117.e: Hertz observed that UV light helps sparks to form. This was an early sign of the photoelectric effect.
124117.m: Hertz was an early observer of the photoelectric effect.

124118.q: In which city was Heinrich Hertz born?
124118.e: Heinrich Rudolf Hertz was born in Hamburg. There, among other things, the Heinrich Hertz Tower reminds people of him.

124119.q: How old was Heinrich Hertz when he died?
124119.e: Hertz died after a serious illness in early 1894 in Bonn. He was only 36 years old.

124120.q: Under which famous physicist did Heinrich Hertz study in Berlin?
124120.e: Helmholtz supported Hertz and encouraged him to study fast electrical oscillations.
124120.m: Heinrich Hertz was a student of Hermann von Helmholtz.

124121.q: Which relative of Heinrich Hertz later won the Nobel Prize in Physics?
124121.e: Gustav Hertz was honoured together with James Franck for the Franck-Hertz experiment. The experiment confirmed separate energy levels in atoms.
124121.m: Gustav Hertz was also an important physicist.

124122.q: A 46 ohm heating resistor is connected to an alternating voltage with an RMS value of 230 V. What power does it convert?
124122.e: With the RMS value you calculate as with DC voltage: P = U² ÷ R = 230 V × 230 V ÷ 46 ohms = 1150 W.
124122.m: With the RMS value, power can be calculated as for direct current.

124123.q: Which emergency measure is triggered automatically when the mains frequency drops sharply, to prevent a widespread power cut?
a: An increase in the mains voltage
124123.e: If the reserves are not enough, groups of consumers are automatically disconnected from the grid. This allows the balance to be restored.
124123.m: When the frequency drops sharply, consumers are deliberately switched off.

124124.q: What does a transformer draw when nothing is connected to its secondary side?
a: Only a small no-load current for magnetisation
No current at all, not even a magnetising current
124124.e: With no load, the primary winding acts like a coil with a large reactance. Only a small current flows, which magnetises the core and covers the iron losses.
124124.m: An unloaded transformer needs only a little current.

124125.q: What does the (n-1) criterion require when operating the transmission grid?
a: The grid must cope with the failure of any single element without interrupting supply
A power station may never feed more than one line
There may only be one line per canton
Every line is switched off once a year
124125.e: If a line or a transformer fails, the remaining equipment must be able to take over the load. This keeps the supply secure.
124125.m: The grid must be able to cope with any single failure.

124126.q: What does the quality factor of an oscillating circuit tell you?
