a: How weakly it is damped and how sharp its resonance is
How high its operating voltage may be
How many turns the coil has
124126.e: A circuit with a high quality factor loses little energy per oscillation. Its resonance curve is narrow and tall.
124126.m: A high quality factor means little damping and sharp resonance.

124127.q: Roughly what wavelength does a 900 MHz mobile phone signal have?
124127.m: The higher the frequency, the shorter the wavelength.

124128.q: What does an electromagnetic wave carry, for example the light from the Sun to the Earth?
124128.e: Electromagnetic waves carry energy through space, even through a vacuum. No matter is carried along.

124129.q: Which inventor used the waves studied by Hertz shortly afterwards for wireless telegraphy?
124129.e: Marconi built on Hertz’s findings and transmitted signals over ever greater distances. This developed into radio.
124129.m: Marconi turned Hertzian waves into radio technology.

124130.e: Pharmacognosy is the study of medicinal substances from living things, that is from plants, fungi, animals or microorganisms. It is a classic subject in pharmacy degrees.
124130.m: Pharmacognosy studies medicinal substances from nature.

124131.q: In pharmacognosy, what are dried plant parts called that serve as the starting material for medicines?
124131.e: In pharmacy, “drug” originally simply meant a dried natural raw material. The word probably comes from the Dutch “droog”, meaning dry.
124131.m: A crude drug is a dried plant part.

124132.q: Which Latin term means the root in the names of crude drugs?
124132.e: Radix means root, folium leaf, cortex bark and semen seed. For example, valerian root is called “Valerianae radix”.
124132.m: Radix is the Latin name for root.

124133.q: What is a herbal tea called for which boiling water is poured over the crude drug and left to steep?
124133.e: For an infusion, boiling water is poured over the crude drug. A decoction, by contrast, is boiled, and a macerate is made with cold water.
124133.m: An infusion is made by pouring hot water over the plant.

124134.q: What is a preparation called in which a hard crude drug such as bark or root is boiled in water?
124134.e: Hard plant parts release their substances poorly when hot water is just poured over them. That is why they are prepared by boiling, in Latin a decoction.
124134.m: A decoction is made by boiling.

124135.q: In pharmacy, what is a tincture?
a: An extract of a crude drug made with ethanol
124135.e: Tinctures are liquid extracts, usually made with a mixture of ethanol and water. Alcohol dissolves many substances well and makes the extract keep.
124135.m: A tincture is an alcoholic plant extract.

124136.q: In Switzerland, which work, together with the Pharmacopoea Helvetica, sets out the quality requirements for crude drugs?
124136.e: Switzerland applies the European Pharmacopoeia (Pharmacopoea Europaea). The Pharmacopoea Helvetica adds national rules to it.
124136.m: The pharmacopoeia sets out what good crude drugs must be like.

124137.q: What is treating illnesses with plants, plant parts and preparations made from them called?
124137.e: The Greek “phyton” means plant. Phytotherapy uses herbal medicines whose effect is based on the substances they contain.

124138.q: What distinguishes secondary plant substances from products of primary metabolism?
a: They are not directly needed for growth and energy production
They are only made at night
124138.e: Every cell needs primary substances such as sugars, amino acids and fats to live. Secondary substances carry out special tasks such as defence, attraction or protection.
124138.m: Secondary plant substances do not serve basic metabolism but special tasks.

124139.q: Which task do many secondary plant substances carry out for the plant?
a: Building the cell wall from cellulose
124139.e: Many secondary substances are bitter, poisonous or antimicrobial. Plants, which cannot run away, use them to protect themselves from animals, fungi and bacteria.

124140.q: What is the group of natural substances containing nitrogen, usually basic, called, to which caffeine and nicotine belong?
124140.e: Alkaloids contain nitrogen, usually in a ring, and often react as bases. Many of them have a strong effect on the nervous system.
124140.m: Alkaloids are plant substances containing nitrogen.

124141.q: Glucosinolates, which release hot mustard oils when chewed, are typical of which plant family?
124141.e: Mustard, cabbage, radish and cress belong to the crucifers. When the tissue is damaged, the enzyme myrosinase splits the glucosinolates into hot mustard oils.
124141.m: Cabbage and mustard protect themselves with mustard oils.

124142.q: Which substance makes chilli peppers hot?
124142.e: Capsaicin stimulates heat and pain receptors (TRPV1) and so produces the burning feeling. Piperine, on the other hand, makes black pepper hot.

124143.q: How can you recognise saponins when you shake a plant solution with water?
124143.e: Saponins are soap-like glycosides that lower surface tension. The name comes from the Latin “sapo”, meaning soap.

124144.q: Which poisonous gas can cyanogenic glycosides such as amygdalin from bitter almonds release?
124144.e: Amygdalin is split by enzymes, producing hydrogen cyanide (prussic acid). That is why larger amounts of bitter almonds are poisonous.
124144.m: Bitter almonds can release hydrogen cyanide.

124145.q: Which secondary plant substance is produced by the grapevine when a fungus attacks the plant?
124145.e: Resveratrol inhibits fungi and is produced in greater amounts by the vine after an infection. It also occurs in grape skins and red wine.
124145.m: Among other things, the grapevine fights off fungi with resveratrol.

124146.q: From which basic building blocks are terpenes formally built?
a: From isoprene units with 5 carbon atoms
124146.e: Terpenes can be described as several isoprene units (C5H8) joined together. This rule is called the isoprene rule.
124146.m: Terpenes are made of isoprene building blocks.

124147.q: How many carbon atoms does the basic skeleton of a monoterpene have?
124147.e: A monoterpene consists of two isoprene units of 5 carbon atoms each. 2 times 5 gives 10 carbon atoms.

124148.q: What are terpenes with 15 carbon atoms called?
124148.e: “Sesqui” means one and a half: one and a half monoterpenes, that is three isoprene units of 5 carbon atoms. That gives 15 carbon atoms.

124149.q: Which natural substance is a polyterpene made of very many isoprene units?
124149.e: The milky sap of the rubber tree contains cis-polyisoprene. Natural rubber is made from it.

124150.q: Which class of terpenes does beta-carotene, with 40 carbon atoms, belong to?
124150.e: 40 carbon atoms correspond to eight isoprene units or four monoterpene units. That is why carotenoids count as tetraterpenes.

124151.q: Which terpene gives peppermint its cooling taste?
124151.e: Menthol is a monoterpene alcohol from peppermint oil. It stimulates the cold receptors of the skin and therefore feels cooling.
124151.m: Menthol from peppermint is a terpene.

124152.q: What do many terpenes do for plants?
a: They act as scents and defensive substances
They are building material for the cell wall
124152.e: Many terpenes smell strongly, scare off herbivores or attract pollinators. Essential oils from mint or conifers contain many terpenes.
124152.m: Terpenes often serve plants as scents and defensive substances.

124153.q: Which solvent is distilled from the resin of pine trees and consists mainly of monoterpenes such as pinene?
124153.e: Distilling pine resin produces turpentine, and rosin is left behind. The word “terpene” comes from turpentine.

124154.q: Where does the name “flavonoids” come from?
a: From the name of a chemist
124154.e: Many flavonoids are yellow plant pigments. That is why the group was named after the Latin word for yellow.
124154.m: Flavonoids are named after the colour yellow.

124155.q: What job do flavonoids do in the leaves of many plants?
a: They anchor the plant in the soil
They carry sugar to the roots
124155.e: Flavonoids in the outer layers of the leaf absorb UV light. In this way they protect the genetic material and the photosynthesis machinery of the cells.
124155.m: In leaves, flavonoids work like a sunscreen.

124156.q: Which flavonoids colour many flowers and fruits red, purple or blue?
124156.e: Anthocyanins are water-soluble pigments in the vacuole. They colour cherries, blueberries and red cabbage, for example.
124156.m: Anthocyanins colour plants red to blue.

124157.q: Why can red cabbage juice be used as an acid-base indicator?
a: Its anthocyanins change colour with the pH
It only conducts electricity in acids
124157.e: The structure of anthocyanins changes depending on the pH, and so does their colour. In acid the juice turns red, in alkali green to yellow.
124157.m: Red cabbage juice shows the pH with its colour.

124158.q: Which flavonol is found in particularly large amounts in onions, especially in the skins?
124158.e: Quercetin is one of the most common flavonols in food. Because of pigments like this, onion skins dye Easter eggs yellowish brown.

124159.q: In which legume are isoflavones such as genistein found in particularly large amounts?
124159.e: Isoflavones occur almost only in legumes, most of all in the soya bean. They are also called phytoestrogens.
124159.m: The soya bean contains a lot of isoflavones.

124160.q: What are the coloured flavonoids in many flowers for?
124160.e: Pigments such as anthocyanins make flowers visible to insects and birds. Some flavonoids also form UV patterns that bees can see but people cannot.
124160.m: Flavonoids make flowers stand out to pollinators.

124161.q: Which flavonoids are found in particularly large amounts in green tea?
124161.e: Green tea contains many catechins such as epigallocatechin gallate. When it is fermented into black tea, most of them are turned into theaflavins.
124161.m: Green tea is rich in catechins.

124162.q: How did tannins get their name?
a: They were used to tan animal hides into leather
124162.e: Tannins link up the proteins of the hide, which then becomes durable leather. In the past, oak and spruce bark were mainly used for this.
124162.m: Tannins are used to turn hide into leather.

124163.q: What effect do tannins have on skin and mucous membranes?
124163.e: Tannins bind proteins in the top layers of cells and make them denser. This creates a protective layer, and the mucous membrane tightens.

124164.q: What causes the furry feeling in the mouth after unripe fruit or strong black tea?
a: Tannins bind proteins in the saliva and on the mucous membrane
124164.e: Tannins make the proteins in saliva clump together, so it no longer lubricates well. This feels dry and furry.
124164.m: Tannins make your mouth feel furry.

124165.q: Why does red wine usually taste drier and harsher than white wine?
a: It contains more tannins from skins and seeds
It is stored at a lower temperature
124165.e: For red wine, the juice ferments together with the skins and seeds. Many tannins pass into the wine, giving it a harsh, furry feel.
124165.m: Red wine contains many tannins from the grape skins.

124166.q: What job do tannins do for the plant itself?
a: They protect against herbivores and pathogens
They store energy for the winter
124166.e: Tannins taste harsh and bind proteins, including the digestive enzymes of animals and the enzymes of fungi. That is why many animals avoid plant parts rich in tannins.
124166.m: Tannins protect plants from being eaten.

124167.q: Which bark is a classic tannin-rich crude drug of European folk medicine, used for example for sitz baths and compresses?
124167.e: Oak bark contains plenty of tannins and is used externally for mild skin inflammation. It was also used in the past for tanning leather with bark.
124167.m: Oak bark is rich in tannins.

124168.q: Which ink used to be made from tannin-rich oak galls and iron salts?
124168.e: Oak galls are growths on oak leaves caused by gall wasps. Their tannins form a dark, long-lasting ink with iron salts.
124168.m: Iron gall ink is made from oak galls and iron.

124169.q: Which dried berries are traditionally used for mild diarrhoea because of their tannins?
124169.e: Dried bilberries contain tannins that have an astringent effect on the lining of the gut. Fresh bilberries are not suitable for this.
124169.m: Dried bilberries are a traditional remedy for mild diarrhoea.

124170.q: By which process are most essential oils obtained from plants?
124170.e: Hot steam carries the volatile scent substances with it. After cooling, the oil separates from the water.
124170.m: Essential oils are usually obtained by steam distillation.

124171.q: How are essential oils from citrus peel usually obtained?
124171.e: The oils are in oil glands just under the surface of the peel. Pressing mechanically without heat leaves the scent substances unchanged.

124172.q: How can you tell an essential oil from a fatty oil on paper?
a: It evaporates and leaves no lasting grease mark
It sets the paper on fire immediately
124172.e: Essential oils are volatile and evaporate completely. Fatty oils such as olive oil do not evaporate and leave a see-through mark.
124172.m: Essential oils evaporate without a trace.

124173.q: What is scented plant water such as rose water called, which is produced alongside the essential oil during steam distillation?
124173.e: The hydrosol contains small amounts of dissolved scent substances. Well-known examples are rose water and orange blossom water.
124173.m: The hydrosol is the scented water from distillation.

124174.q: In which structures do members of the mint family such as peppermint and sage store their essential oil?
a: In glandular hairs on the leaf surface
In the vessels of the wood
124174.e: Members of the mint family have glandular scales in which the oil collects under a cuticle. If you rub the leaf, they burst and give off a scent.
124174.m: Plants of the mint family store oil in glandular hairs.

124175.q: What has clove oil long been used for in dentistry?
a: Against toothache, because it numbs locally
Against tooth decay, because it contains fluoride
124175.e: Clove oil contains a lot of eugenol. This substance numbs locally and is antiseptic, so it is used for toothache and in dental cements.

124176.q: Which substance gives thyme oil its strong antiseptic effect?
124176.e: Thymol is a phenol from the group of monoterpenes and works against bacteria and fungi. That is why thyme is used in cough medicines.

124177.q: What is chamomile mainly used for in folk medicine?
a: Against inflammation, for example as tea or a steam bath
As a remedy for broken bones
124177.e: Chamomile flowers contain an essential oil with anti-inflammatory substances. That is why chamomile tea, rinses and steam baths are used for inflammation.

124178.q: What is eucalyptus oil often used for?
a: For inhaling when you have a cold
As a substitute for cooking oil when frying
124178.e: Eucalyptus oil contains mainly cineole, which clears the airways. That is why it is inhaled for colds or used in chest rubs.
124178.m: Inhaling eucalyptus oil helps against colds.

124179.q: Which Latin plant name does the name “salicylic acid” come from?
124179.e: In willow bark, the precursor salicin was found, from which salicylic acid is formed. Salix is the Latin genus name of the willows.
124179.m: Salicylic acid is named after the willow.

124180.q: What is the precursor in willow bark called that is turned into salicylic acid in the body?
124180.e: Salicin is a glycoside. In the gut and liver it is converted into salicyl alcohol and then into salicylic acid.

124181.q: Which group of medicines does acetylsalicylic acid belong to?
124181.e: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs relieve pain, reduce fever and reduce inflammation without having a cortisone structure. Ibuprofen and diclofenac belong to the same group.
124181.m: Acetylsalicylic acid is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug.

124182.q: Why is low-dose acetylsalicylic acid prescribed to prevent heart attacks?
a: It stops blood platelets from clumping together
124182.e: In the blood platelets, the substance blocks the production of thromboxane, which encourages clumping. Because platelets have no nucleus, the effect lasts their whole lifetime.
124182.m: A little aspirin inhibits the blood platelets.

124183.q: How does acetylsalicylic acid work against pain and inflammation?
a: It blocks cyclooxygenase and so the production of prostaglandins
It blocks the sodium channels of nerves
124183.e: Acetylsalicylic acid transfers an acetyl group to the enzyme cyclooxygenase and blocks it permanently. As a result fewer prostaglandins, which pass on pain and inflammation, are produced.

124184.q: What is salicylic acid used for in skin products such as wart plasters?
124184.e: Salicylic acid is keratolytic: it loosens the bonds between horny skin cells. This makes it possible to remove calluses, corns and warts.

124185.q: What role does salicylic acid play in the plant itself?
a: It is a signal substance for defence against pathogens
It is the most important storage sugar
124185.e: After an infection, the salicylic acid level rises and switches on defence genes. In this way the whole plant can become more resistant (systemic acquired resistance).
124185.m: Salicylic acid is a defence signal in the plant.

124186.q: Why are children and teenagers with viral infections usually not given acetylsalicylic acid?
a: Because of the risk of Reye's syndrome
Because it does not work in children
124186.e: In children with viral infections, a link with the rare but dangerous Reye's syndrome has been observed. It damages the liver and brain.
124186.m: Aspirin is avoided in children with fever because of Reye's syndrome.

124187.q: How is salicylic acid for medicines mostly obtained today?
124187.e: In the past willow bark was used; today salicylic acid is made chemically, cheaply and pure, in large quantities. Acetylsalicylic acid is made from it.
124187.m: Salicylic acid is now made industrially.

124188.q: From which plant is the active substance artemisinin obtained?
124188.e: Artemisinin comes from Artemisia annua, sweet wormwood (annual mugwort). The plant has long been used in traditional Chinese medicine.

124189.q: Which disease are artemisinin and its derivatives mainly used against?
124189.e: Artemisinin derivatives kill the malaria parasites (plasmodia) in the blood very quickly. Today they are part of standard treatment.

124190.q: Which researcher received a Nobel Prize in 2015 for discovering artemisinin?
124190.e: The Chinese pharmacologist Tu Youyou received the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Her group had discovered artemisinin in the 1970s.

124191.q: Which change to the extraction method brought Tu Youyou her decisive success?
a: Extracting at a low temperature instead of boiling
124191.e: An old Chinese text described soaking the wormwood in cold water and squeezing it. Tu Youyou then extracted it with ether at a low temperature and got an effective extract, because heat destroys the active substance.

124192.q: Why does artemisinin work especially well against malaria parasites in red blood cells?
a: It reacts with iron from the blood pigment and forms harmful radicals
It makes the red blood cells bigger
124192.e: The parasites break down haemoglobin in the red blood cells, which releases iron. This splits artemisinin's peroxide bridge, producing radicals that damage the parasite.
124192.m: Artemisinin is activated by iron in the parasite.

124193.q: Why are people also trying to get yeasts to make artemisinin?
a: The amount in the plant is low and varies
124193.e: Sweet wormwood contains only a little artemisinin, and harvests vary. Genetically modified yeasts can make a precursor, which is converted chemically into artemisinin.
124193.m: Yeasts can make a precursor of artemisinin.

124194.q: Why is artemisinin given against malaria in combination with a second active substance?
a: To prevent resistance and kill the remaining parasites
Because on its own it is poisonous
Because otherwise it does not get into the blood
124194.e: Artemisinins work fast but stay in the body only briefly. A longer-acting partner gets rid of the remaining parasites and makes resistance harder, which is why the WHO recommends combination therapies.
124194.m: Against malaria, artemisinin is always given in combination.

124195.q: Which derivative of artemisinin is injected for severe malaria?
124195.e: Artesunate dissolves in water and can therefore be given intravenously. For severe malaria it is now the first-choice medicine.
124195.m: Artesunate is injected for severe malaria.

124196.q: From the bark of which tree was paclitaxel originally isolated?
124196.e: Paclitaxel was found in the bark of Taxus brevifolia in a screening programme run by the US National Cancer Institute. This yew grows in western North America.
124196.m: Paclitaxel originally comes from the Pacific yew.

124197.q: What is paclitaxel used for in medicine?
a: As a cytostatic drug in cancer treatment
124197.e: Paclitaxel stops cell division and so hits fast-growing cancer cells in particular. It is used for breast and lung cancer, among others.

124198.q: How does paclitaxel act on the cell?
a: It stabilises the microtubules and so blocks cell division
It blocks protein production at the ribosomes
124198.e: Normally the microtubules of the spindle are constantly built up and broken down. Paclitaxel prevents them from breaking down, the spindle freezes and mitosis gets stuck.

124199.q: Why was the bark of the Pacific yew not enough as a source of paclitaxel?
a: It contains very little of the substance, and harvesting it kills the trees
It is too hard to grind
The substance breaks down immediately in sunlight
The trees only grow in Antarctica
124199.e: One treatment would have needed the bark of several trees, and yews die when their bark is stripped. That is why other ways of making it were sought.
124199.m: Yew bark was too scarce as a source.

124200.q: From which renewable starting material is paclitaxel made semi-synthetically?
a: From substances in the needles of the European yew
124200.e: The needles contain the precursor 10-deacetylbaccatin III. They can be harvested without killing the tree and converted chemically into paclitaxel.
124200.m: Yew needles provide a precursor for paclitaxel.

124201.q: Why does paclitaxel have a particularly strong effect on cancer cells?
a: Cancer cells have no cell membrane
Cancer cells take up no sugar
124201.e: Paclitaxel blocks cell division. Cells that divide often, such as cancer cells, are therefore hit especially hard.
124201.m: Paclitaxel mainly hits cells that divide often.

124202.q: Which side effect often occurs during chemotherapy with paclitaxel, because healthy cells also divide quickly?
124202.e: Paclitaxel hits all cells that divide quickly, including the cells of the hair roots. The hair usually grows back after the treatment ends.

124203.q: What is the group of active substances called to which paclitaxel and docetaxel belong?
124203.e: The group is named after the genus Taxus, the yew. Docetaxel is a semi-synthetic relative of paclitaxel.

124204.q: On which island did the Netherlands set up large cinchona plantations in the 19th century?
124204.e: Seeds of cinchona trees were taken out of the Andes and planted on Java. This broke the South American monopoly, and the Netherlands soon supplied most of the world's production.
124204.m: Cinchona was later grown mainly on Java.

124205.q: For centuries, quinine was the most important remedy against which disease?
124205.e: Quinine kills malaria parasites in the blood. Synthetic medicines were only added in the 20th century.
124205.m: Quinine was the classic malaria medicine.

124206.q: In which drink does quinine give the bitter taste?
124206.e: Tonic water contains a small amount of quinine as a bitter substance. The amount is much smaller than in a medicinal dose.
124206.m: Tonic water tastes bitter because of quinine.

124207.q: What can you see if you shine UV light on tonic water?
124207.e: Quinine is a fluorescent substance. It absorbs UV light and gives off visible blue light.
124207.m: Quinine glows blue under UV light.

124208.q: Which region do cinchona trees originally come from?
124208.e: Cinchona trees grow wild in the mountain forests of the Andes, for example in Peru and Ecuador. In German they are called “China bark trees”, but the name has nothing to do with China.
124208.m: Cinchona trees come from the Andes.

124209.q: What was cinchona bark called in Europe in the 17th century, because members of a religious order spread it?
124209.e: Jesuits brought the bark from Peru to Europe and made sure it spread. That is why it was also called Jesuits' powder.
124209.m: Cinchona bark used to be called Jesuits' bark.

124210.q: Why may tonic water contain only a little quinine?
a: Because quinine has side effects in larger amounts
Because quinine makes the drink freeze
124210.e: At higher doses quinine is a medicine. Too much of it can cause ringing in the ears, dizziness and problems with vision, which is why the amount in drinks is limited.
124210.m: Quinine is only harmless in small amounts.

124211.q: Which synthetic malaria medicine was developed using quinine as a model?
124211.e: Like quinine, chloroquine is a quinoline derivative. It was very widely used in the 20th century; today many parasites are resistant to it.
124211.m: Chloroquine is a synthetic successor to quinine.

124212.q: Which plant genus does digitoxin come from?
124212.e: Digitoxin is obtained from foxglove species (Digitalis). The name Digitalis comes from the Latin “digitus”, meaning finger.

124213.q: Which group of active substances does digitoxin belong to?
124213.e: Cardiac glycosides consist of a sugar part and a steroid-like aglycone. They act specifically on the heart muscle.

124214.q: How does digitoxin act on the heart muscle?
a: It increases the force with which the heart contracts
It makes the heart beat faster
124214.e: Digitoxin increases the force of contraction (positive inotropic) and slows the heart rate. It used to be a main medicine for heart failure.
124214.m: Digitoxin strengthens the pumping power of the heart.

124215.q: Which transport protein does digitoxin block in heart muscle cells?
124215.e: Blocking the pump raises sodium in the cell, which lets more calcium in. More calcium means a stronger contraction.

124216.q: Why is the common foxglove considered a dangerous poisonous plant?
a: Its substances disturb the heart rhythm
Its roots give off hydrogen cyanide
124216.e: Foxglove contains cardiac glycosides such as digitoxin. Just a few leaves can cause nausea and dangerous heart rhythm problems.
124216.m: Foxglove is very poisonous because of its heart poisons.

124217.q: Why must digitoxin be dosed particularly precisely?
a: The effective dose and the toxic dose are very close together
It is destroyed in the stomach immediately
124217.e: Digitoxin has a narrow therapeutic range. Even a slight overdose can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems.
124217.m: Digitoxin has a narrow therapeutic range.

124218.q: Digitoxin has a half-life of about one week. What does that mean?
a: After about a week, half of it has been broken down
It only works for half a week
After a week it has all been excreted
You have to take it every half week
124218.e: The half-life shows the time after which only half of a substance is left in the body. Digitoxin is broken down slowly by the liver and so stays effective for a long time.
124218.m: Because of its long half-life, digitoxin stays in the body for a long time.

124219.q: Which striking problem with vision is a typical sign of digitalis poisoning?
124219.e: With an overdose, people see colours wrongly, often yellowish. Nausea and heart rhythm problems come on top.
124219.m: Digitalis poisoning can make people see yellow.

124220.q: Why is the foxglove called Digitalis, from the Latin word for finger?
a: Its flowers fit over a fingertip like a sewing thimble
It only grows a finger's breadth tall
Its leaves are divided like fingers
It was described by a doctor called Finger
124220.e: The tube-shaped flowers can be slipped over a fingertip like a thimble. The Latin name Digitalis comes from “digitus”, finger.

a: How people of different cultures use and understand plants
The effect of fertiliser on cereals
124221.e: Ethnobotany combines botany and ethnology. It documents knowledge of plants, for example about medicinal plants, food, fibres or rituals.
124221.m: Ethnobotany studies the relationship between people and plants.

124222.q: Which US biologist is considered the “father of ethnobotany” because of his research in the Amazon region?
124222.e: Richard Evans Schultes lived for years among indigenous peoples of South America. He documented thousands of useful and medicinal plants.
124222.m: Richard Evans Schultes shaped modern ethnobotany.

a: Using traditional knowledge about plants without consent and a fair share of the profits
Cutting down trees in the forest
124223.e: Some companies patented substances based on indigenous knowledge without involving the communities they came from. This is criticised as biopiracy.
124223.m: Biopiracy uses other people's plant knowledge without fair compensation.

124224.q: Which international agreement regulates access to genetic resources and the fair sharing of the benefits?
124224.e: The Nagoya Protocol is part of the Convention on Biological Diversity. Switzerland has ratified it too.
124224.m: The Nagoya Protocol regulates the fair sharing of benefits.

124225.q: Which arrow poison of indigenous peoples of South America led to muscle-relaxing drugs for anaesthesia?
124225.e: Curare paralyses the muscles by blocking the transmission of signals from nerve to muscle. Its active substance tubocurarine was used in anaesthesia.
124225.m: Curare went from arrow poison to an aid in anaesthesia.

124226.q: Which mountain plant does folk medicine, including in the Alpine region, use externally for bruises?
124226.e: Arnica (mountain arnica) contains anti-inflammatory substances. It is only used externally, because it can be poisonous if taken internally.
124226.m: Arnica helps with bruises when used externally.

124227.q: Which well-known substance against malaria comes from the bark of a South American tree?
124227.e: Indigenous peoples of the Andes used the bark of the cinchona tree against fever. Its active substance quinine was long the most important malaria medicine and also gives tonic water its bitter taste.
124227.m: Quinine from cinchona bark works against malaria.

124228.q: From the bark of which tree does the starting substance for aspirin come, which was already used against pain in the past?
124228.e: Willow bark contains salicin, which already helped against fever and pain in folk medicine. Acetylsalicylic acid, known as aspirin, was developed from it.
124228.m: Aspirin goes back to a substance from willow bark.

124229.q: Which anti-cancer substance was obtained from the Madagascar periwinkle, which was known in folk medicine?
124229.e: Researchers studied the Madagascar periwinkle because of its use in folk medicine. They found the vinca alkaloids vinblastine and vincristine, which are used against leukaemias.
124229.m: Vincristine comes from the Madagascar periwinkle.

124328.q: Which food group forms the broad base of the Swiss food pyramid?
124328.e: The bottom level of the pyramid shows drinks such as water and unsweetened tea. They should be consumed in the largest amounts every day.
124328.m: Unsweetened drinks form the base of the pyramid.

124329.q: Which organisation publishes the Swiss food pyramid together with the federal government?
124329.e: The pyramid comes from the Swiss Society for Nutrition (SGE) and is supported by the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office (FSVO).
124329.m: The SGE is the specialist body behind the Swiss food pyramid.

124330.q: Roughly what amount counts as one portion of vegetables in the Swiss food pyramid?
124330.e: One portion of vegetables is around 120 grams, about a handful. This makes it easy to estimate the recommended daily portions.
124330.m: One portion of vegetables is about a handful.

124331.q: On which level of the Swiss food pyramid are potatoes and pulses found as well as cereals?
a: On the level of starchy foods
On the level of vegetables and fruit
124331.e: Cereal products, potatoes and pulses together form the group that mainly supplies starch and therefore energy.
124331.m: In the pyramid, potatoes and pulses belong to the starchy foods.

124332.q: Which kind of nuts does the Swiss food pyramid recommend for the small daily portion?
124332.e: Nuts supply unsaturated fatty acids, vitamin E and fibre. Salt or a sugar coating would reduce this benefit.
124332.m: A handful of unsalted nuts fits into a daily diet.

124333.q: Which cereal products does the Swiss food pyramid prefer?
124333.e: Wholegrain products contain more fibre, vitamins and minerals than white flour, because the outer layers of the grain are kept.
124333.m: For cereals, wholegrain is the better choice.

124334.q: How many portions of milk and dairy products are recommended each day according to the Swiss food pyramid?
124334.e: Three portions a day, such as a glass of milk, a yoghurt and a piece of cheese, cover a large part of the calcium requirement.
124334.m: Three portions of dairy products a day help the bones.

124335.q: Which principle does the shape of the food pyramid illustrate?
a: The higher the level, the smaller the recommended amount
The higher the level, the more important the food
Each level should be eaten in equal amounts
Main meals are at the top, snacks at the bottom
124335.e: The area of each level shows its share of the amount. At the bottom are the groups for large amounts, at the top those for small amounts.
124335.m: In the pyramid, the recommended amount decreases towards the top.

124336.q: Which food serves as the reference with the value 100 in the glycaemic index?
124336.e: The rise in blood sugar after glucose (dextrose) is set at 100. Other foods are compared with it.
124336.m: Glucose is the standard of the glycaemic index, with a value of 100.

124337.q: What does the glycaemic index of a food show?
a: How much it makes blood sugar rise compared with glucose
How many calories it contains per 100 grams
How much sugar it contains per portion
How quickly it is digested in the stomach
124337.e: The area under the blood sugar curve after an amount containing 50 g of usable carbohydrates is measured and compared with glucose.
124337.m: The glycaemic index describes the effect of carbohydrates on blood sugar.

124338.q: From what value is a glycaemic index usually considered high?
124338.e: The usual classification is: low up to 55, medium 56 to 69, high from 70.
124338.m: A glycaemic index of 70 or more counts as high.

124339.q: How do you calculate the glycaemic load of a portion?
a: GI times grams of carbohydrate divided by 100
GI divided by grams of carbohydrate
124339.e: The glycaemic load also takes into account the amount of carbohydrate actually eaten in a portion.
124339.m: The glycaemic load combines the GI with the amount of carbohydrate in a portion.

124340.q: A portion contains 30 g of carbohydrates and has a GI of 70. What is the glycaemic load?
124340.m: For the glycaemic load, you multiply the GI by the carbohydrates and divide by a hundred.

124341.q: Which sugar has a particularly low glycaemic index?
124341.e: Fructose (fruit sugar) is mostly converted in the liver and makes blood sugar rise only a little. Its GI is around 20.
124341.m: Fruit sugar makes blood sugar rise only a little.

124342.q: How does the glycaemic index of pasta change if it is cooked al dente instead of soft?
124342.e: With a shorter cooking time the starch is less broken down and is digested more slowly. Blood sugar therefore rises more slowly.
124342.m: Pasta cooked al dente has a lower glycaemic index.

124343.q: Which component of a meal usually lowers its effect on blood sugar?
124343.e: Fibre, fat and protein slow down stomach emptying and the uptake of glucose into the blood.
124343.m: Fibre slows down the rise in blood sugar.

124344.q: Which hormone does the pancreas release mainly after meals with a high glycaemic index?
124344.e: When blood sugar rises quickly, the beta cells of the pancreas release a lot of insulin so that the cells take up glucose.
124344.m: Insulin lowers blood sugar after eating.

124345.q: Which of these amino acids is not essential for humans?
124345.e: The body can make glycine, the simplest amino acid, itself from serine. This is not possible with lysine, leucine and valine.
124345.m: The body can make glycine itself.

124346.q: How many proteinogenic amino acids are built into proteins in humans according to the standard genetic code?
124346.e: The standard code has 20 proteinogenic amino acids. Of these, 8 are considered essential in adults, or 9 including histidine.
124346.m: Human proteins are made of twenty standard amino acids.

124347.q: What does it mean that an amino acid is essential?
a: The body cannot make it itself
The body does not need it at all
124347.e: Essential amino acids must be taken in with food because the body cannot make them. If one of them is missing, the body cannot build certain proteins.
124347.m: Essential amino acids must come from food.

124348.q: Which food group supplies a particularly large amount of plant protein?
a: Pulses such as lentils and beans
Fruit such as apples and pears
Cooking oils such as rapeseed oil
124348.e: Lentils, beans, peas and chickpeas contain a lot of protein. Together with cereals, they supply all the essential amino acids in good amounts.
124348.m: Pulses are important sources of plant protein.

124349.q: Which three essential amino acids are called branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs)?
124349.e: Leucine, isoleucine and valine have a branched side chain and are metabolised mainly in muscle.
124349.m: Leucine, isoleucine and valine are the branched-chain amino acids.

124350.q: From which essential amino acid does the body make the messenger substance serotonin?
124350.e: Tryptophan is converted via 5-hydroxytryptophan into serotonin, from which melatonin is later also formed.
124350.m: Serotonin is made from the amino acid tryptophan.

124351.q: Which essential amino acid must people with phenylketonuria strictly limit?
124351.e: In phenylketonuria, the breakdown of phenylalanine is disturbed. It builds up and, if untreated, damages the brain. Newborns are tested for it.
124351.m: Phenylketonuria requires a diet low in phenylalanine.

124352.q: Why is combining maize and beans good from a nutritional point of view?
a: Their amino acids complement each other
Maize supplies the missing vitamin B12
124352.e: Maize is low in lysine and tryptophan, while beans supply a lot of lysine. Together they give a more complete pattern of amino acids.
124352.m: Different plant proteins complement each other's amino acids.

124353.q: What characterises a saturated fatty acid chemically?
a: It has no carbon double bond
It has exactly one double bond
It contains nitrogen in the chain
124353.e: In saturated fatty acids, all the carbon atoms in the chain are bonded to the maximum number of hydrogen atoms; there are no double bonds.
124353.m: Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds.

124354.q: Which saturated fatty acid with 16 carbon atoms is common in palm oil and many animal fats?
124354.e: Palmitic acid (C16:0) is one of the most common fatty acids of all. Oleic acid and linoleic acid, by contrast, are unsaturated.
124354.m: Palmitic acid is a common saturated fatty acid with 16 carbon atoms.

124355.q: Which cooking fat contains a particularly high proportion of saturated fatty acids?
124355.e: Coconut fat consists of around 90 per cent saturated fatty acids, mainly lauric acid. That is why it is solid at room temperature.
124355.m: Coconut fat is rich in saturated fatty acids.

124356.q: Why are fats with many saturated fatty acids usually solid at room temperature?
a: The straight chains can pack closely together
They have shorter chains than oils
They have a stronger ionic charge
124356.e: Without double bonds the chains are straight and pack tightly together. This raises the melting point.
124356.m: Straight fatty acid chains pack tightly, which is why saturated fats are solid.

124357.q: According to current knowledge, which blood value does a high intake of saturated fatty acids raise in particular?
124357.e: Many saturated fatty acids increase LDL cholesterol, which is considered a risk factor for cardiovascular disease.
124357.m: A lot of saturated fat pushes LDL cholesterol up.

124358.q: What is the general molecular formula of saturated monocarboxylic acids?
124358.e: Saturated fatty acids are unbranched carboxylic acids of the form CnH2nO2, for example stearic acid C18H36O2.
124358.m: Saturated fatty acids follow the formula CnH2nO2.

124359.q: Which saturated fatty acid with 18 carbon atoms is found in large amounts in beef tallow and cocoa butter?
124359.e: Stearic acid (C18:0) is saturated. Oleic acid also has 18 carbon atoms, but one double bond.
124359.m: Stearic acid is the saturated fatty acid with 18 carbon atoms.

124360.q: According to nutrition research, which swap is more likely to lower the risk of cardiovascular disease?
a: Replacing saturated with unsaturated fatty acids
Replacing unsaturated with saturated fatty acids
124360.e: Anyone who replaces saturated fats with rapeseed or olive oil, for example, lowers their LDL cholesterol. Replacing them with sugar does not bring this benefit.
124360.m: Unsaturated plant oils are a good replacement for saturated fats.

124361.q: How does a trans fatty acid differ from the usual natural unsaturated fatty acid?
a: The double bond is in the trans configuration
124361.e: Natural unsaturated fatty acids usually have cis double bonds. In trans, the hydrogen atoms are on opposite sides and the chain stays straight.
124361.m: Trans fatty acids have a straight double bond in the trans position.

124362.q: In which industrial process were large amounts of trans fatty acids formed in the past?
124362.e: In the partial hydrogenation of plant oils, some double bonds are not saturated but rearranged. This produces trans fatty acids.
124362.m: Partially hydrogenated fats were the main source of trans fatty acids.

124363.q: How do trans fatty acids affect blood fats?
a: They raise LDL and lower HDL
They lower LDL and raise HDL
They do not affect blood fats
124363.e: Trans fatty acids worsen the ratio of LDL to HDL cholesterol in two ways and so increase the risk of heart attack.
124363.m: Trans fatty acids harm the cholesterol profile twice over.

124364.q: How has Switzerland regulated trans fatty acids in plant oils and fats since 2008?
a: With a maximum value per 100 g of fat
With a complete ban on hydrogenated fats
Not at all, only with recommendations
124364.e: Since 2008, plant oils and fats in Switzerland may contain no more than 2 grams of trans fatty acids per 100 grams of fat.
124364.m: In Switzerland, no more than two per cent trans fatty acids are allowed in fat.

124365.q: Which country was the first to introduce a legal limit for trans fatty acids?
124365.e: Denmark was the first country to limit industrial trans fatty acids, in 2003. Switzerland followed in 2008.
124365.m: Denmark led the way in limiting trans fatty acids.

124366.q: Where do trans fatty acids also occur naturally in small amounts?
a: In the milk and meat of ruminants
124366.e: Bacteria in the rumen of cows, sheep and goats form trans fatty acids. That is why butter and beef contain small amounts.
124366.m: Milk fat from ruminants also contains a little trans fat.

124367.q: Which organisation has set the goal of banishing industrial trans fatty acids from food worldwide?
124367.e: The World Health Organization (WHO) calls on countries to eliminate industrially produced trans fatty acids, for example through limits.
124367.m: The WHO wants to remove industrial trans fatty acids from all food.

124368.q: Which foods typically contained a lot of trans fatty acids before the limits were introduced?
a: Fried foods and puff pastry made with hydrogenated fats
124368.e: Partially hydrogenated fats were used for frying oils, puff pastry, biscuits and margarines because they kept for a long time and were easy to shape.
124368.m: Pastries and fried foods used to be typical sources of trans fat.

124369.e: The body needs micronutrients only in small amounts, and they supply no energy. Carbohydrates, fats and protein are macronutrients.
124369.m: Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients without energy content.

124370.q: According to the WHO, which micronutrient deficiency is the most common worldwide?
124370.e: Iron deficiency affects a great many people worldwide, especially children and women, and is the most common cause of anaemia.
124370.m: Iron deficiency is the most widespread nutrient deficiency in the world.

124371.q: Which vitamin do people on a vegan diet usually need to take as a supplement?
124371.e: Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods, as it is made by microorganisms. Vegans therefore need a supplement.
124371.m: On a vegan diet, vitamin B12 is needed as a supplement.

124372.q: Which vitamin does the body need for blood clotting?
124372.e: Vitamin K is needed for making several clotting factors in the liver. That is why newborns are given it as a precaution.
124372.m: Without vitamin K, blood does not clot well.

124373.q: Which disease is caused by a severe lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine)?
124373.e: Beriberi used to occur mainly where people ate almost nothing but polished white rice, because thiamine is in the husk.
124373.m: Beriberi is the result of thiamine deficiency.

124374.q: For which function is the trace element iron mainly needed in the blood?
124374.e: Iron forms the centre of the haem group in the haemoglobin of the red blood cells and binds oxygen there.

124375.q: What is a micronutrient deficiency called that exists despite enough calories?
124375.e: The term “hidden hunger” describes people who get enough to fill them up but too few vitamins or minerals such as iron, iodine or vitamin A.
124375.m: Hidden hunger is a lack of micronutrients despite a full plate.

124376.q: Which B vitamin is important for closing the neural tube in early embryonic development?
124376.e: Folic acid (vitamin B9) is needed for cell division. A deficiency increases the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida.
124376.m: Folic acid is essential for cell division in the embryo.

124377.q: Why is vitamin D not really a typical vitamin?
a: The body can make it itself with sunlight
It is only needed in the brain
124377.e: Vitamins normally have to be taken in with food. However, the skin makes vitamin D itself with sunlight, which is why it acts more like a hormone.
124377.m: The body can make vitamin D itself with sunlight.

124378.q: Which radiation does the skin need to make vitamin D?
124378.e: UVB radiation converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin into a precursor of vitamin D3.
124378.m: The skin needs UVB light to make vitamin D.

124379.q: Why does the skin hardly make any vitamin D in Switzerland in winter?
a: The sun is too low, so too little UVB arrives
The air is too dry in winter
The days are longer in winter
124379.e: When the sun is low, the path through the atmosphere is long and the ozone layer filters out most of the UVB.
124379.m: In the Swiss winter, the UVB light is hardly enough for vitamin D.

124380.q: Which disease do children get from a severe lack of vitamin D?
124380.e: Without enough vitamin D, too little calcium is built into the bones. They stay soft and become deformed. Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C, night blindness by a lack of vitamin A.
124380.m: A severe lack of vitamin D causes rickets in children.

124381.q: In which organ is the active hormone form calcitriol made?
124381.e: The liver first forms calcidiol, which the kidney then converts into active calcitriol.
124381.m: The kidney activates vitamin D into the hormone calcitriol.

124382.q: What task does vitamin D perform in the intestine?
a: It promotes the uptake of calcium
124382.e: Calcitriol increases the production of transport proteins that bring calcium from the intestine into the blood.
124382.m: Vitamin D makes sure calcium from food is taken up.

124383.q: Which food is one of the few good natural sources of vitamin D?
124383.e: Oily fish such as herring, salmon or mackerel contain significant amounts of vitamin D. Most other foods supply very little.
124383.m: Oily sea fish supplies natural vitamin D.

124384.q: A supplement contains 20 micrograms of vitamin D. How many international units (IU) is that if 1 µg is 40 IU?
124384.m: One microgram of vitamin D equals forty international units.

124385.q: Which group of people routinely receives vitamin D drops from birth in Switzerland?
a: Women pregnant for the first time
124385.e: Breast milk contains little vitamin D and babies should not be in strong sun. That is why a daily dose of vitamin D is recommended for babies.
124385.m: Babies in Switzerland are given vitamin D drops as a precaution.

124386.q: Which disease was the introduction of iodised table salt in Switzerland mainly meant to fight?
124386.e: A lack of iodine leads to an enlarged thyroid (goitre, struma). Goitre used to be very widespread in the Alpine region.
124386.m: Iodised salt has made goitre almost disappear in Switzerland.

124387.q: In which decade was iodised table salt introduced in Switzerland?
124387.e: In the 1920s Switzerland was one of the first countries with iodised table salt. The canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden led the way.
124387.m: Switzerland has been iodising its salt for around a hundred years.

124388.q: Why can the supply of iodine become low despite iodised household salt?
a: Many processed foods are made with non-iodised salt
Iodine evaporates immediately when the packet is opened
Iodised salt is banned in Switzerland
The body stores iodine for decades
124388.e: We take in a large part of our salt through bread, cheese and ready meals. If non-iodised salt is used there, iodine intake falls.
124388.m: For enough iodine, bakeries and industry should also use iodised salt.

124389.q: Roughly how much iodine does iodised table salt contain in Switzerland?
124389.e: The iodine content is around 25 milligrams per kilogram of salt. With a few grams of salt a day, part of the iodine requirement is covered in this way.
124389.m: Even a tiny amount of iodine in salt clearly improves the supply.

124390.q: Why are the soils in the Alpine region particularly low in iodine?
a: Glaciers and rain have washed the iodine out
The Alps are made of pure granite without salts
Cows take all the iodine out of the soil
The thin air breaks down iodine
124390.e: After the Ice Ages, meltwater and rain washed the easily dissolved iodine out of the soils. Plants and animals therefore contain little of it.
124390.m: Washed-out Alpine soils supply little iodine.

124391.q: Which severe developmental disorder can a serious lack of iodine during pregnancy cause in the child?
124391.e: Missing thyroid hormones disturb the growth of the brain and body. Cretinism used to be common in the Alpine region.
124391.m: A lack of iodine before birth can seriously damage brain development.

124392.q: Which company produces table salt in Switzerland and is responsible for iodising it?
124392.e: Swiss Saltworks extracts salt at Schweizerhalle, Riburg and Bex, among other places, and supplies iodised table salt.
124392.m: Swiss Saltworks supplies the country with iodised salt.

124393.q: In what form is iodine added to table salt?
a: As potassium iodide or potassium iodate
As tincture of iodine with alcohol
124393.e: Iodine is added as a potassium salt, because in this form it is stable, tasteless and easy to dose.
124393.m: Table salt is enriched with potassium compounds of iodine.

124394.q: What is fluoridated table salt for?
124394.e: Fluoride hardens tooth enamel and inhibits the bacteria that cause decay. Fluoridated salt therefore works against tooth decay through the diet.
124394.m: Fluoride in salt protects teeth against decay.

124395.q: Which compound forms in tooth enamel when fluoride is built in?
124395.e: Fluoride replaces hydroxide ions in hydroxyapatite. The fluorapatite produced is more resistant to acid.
124395.m: Fluorapatite makes tooth enamel more resistant to acid.

124396.q: In which decade was fluoridated table salt introduced in Switzerland?
124396.e: In 1955 the canton of Zurich became the first authority in the world to allow the sale of fluoridated table salt. The other cantons followed later.
124396.m: Switzerland was a pioneer of fluoridated table salt.

124397.q: Roughly how much fluoride does fluoridated table salt contain in Switzerland?
124397.e: The content is around 250 milligrams of fluoride per kilogram of salt, that is 0.025 per cent.
124397.m: Fluoridated salt contains only a tiny amount of fluoride.

124398.q: Which city fluoridated its drinking water instead of salt for decades?
124398.e: For decades Basel added fluoride to its drinking water. In 2003 the canton switched to fluoridated salt.
124398.m: Basel fluoridated its drinking water until 2003.

124399.q: What can too high an intake of fluoride cause while the teeth are developing?
a: Bleeding gums from a vitamin deficiency
124399.e: Too much fluoride while the enamel is forming leads to fluorosis: white to brownish spots on the permanent teeth.
124399.m: Too much fluoride in children can cause spots on the teeth.

124400.q: How can you tell in the shop whether table salt contains fluoride?
a: From the note “with fluoride” or “fluoridated” on the packet
From the green colour of the salt
124400.e: Fluoridated salt looks and tastes like ordinary salt. Only the label on the packet shows the additive.
124400.m: Whether salt is fluoridated is written on the packaging.

124401.q: What effect does fluoride have in addition to hardening tooth enamel?
a: It promotes the remineralisation of early damage
124401.e: Fluoride helps to put calcium and phosphate back into damaged areas of enamel and inhibits the metabolism of decay bacteria.
124401.m: Fluoride helps to repair early enamel damage.

124402.q: How many levels does the Nutri-Score scale have?
124402.e: The scale goes from A (dark green) via B, C and D to E (red).
124402.m: The Nutri-Score has five levels from A to E.

124403.q: In which country was the Nutri-Score developed and first introduced?
124403.e: The Nutri-Score comes from French nutrition researchers and was first introduced in France as a voluntary label.
124403.m: The Nutri-Score originally comes from France.

124404.q: Is the Nutri-Score compulsory for food in Switzerland?
124404.e: In Switzerland, manufacturers may use the Nutri-Score voluntarily. The FSVO supports it as a guide.
124404.m: In Switzerland, the Nutri-Score is a voluntary label.

124405.q: Which component gives positive points for a better rating in the Nutri-Score?
124405.e: Fibre, protein and the shares of fruit, vegetables and pulses improve the rating. Energy, sugar, saturated fats and salt make it worse.

124406.q: On which reference amount is the Nutri-Score calculated?
124406.e: Because all products refer to 100 g or 100 ml, they can be compared regardless of portion size.
124406.m: The Nutri-Score always refers to 100 grams or 100 millilitres.

124407.q: What is the Nutri-Score most useful for?
a: Comparing similar products in one category
124407.e: The Nutri-Score helps, for example, when comparing different breakfast cereals. It does not judge whether a food fits into a balanced diet.
124407.m: The Nutri-Score works best for comparing products of the same kind.

124408.q: What colour is grade A on the Nutri-Score?
124408.e: A is dark green and stands for the best nutritional composition. E is red.
124408.m: A dark green A is the best Nutri-Score grade.

124409.q: Which criticism of the Nutri-Score is often made?
a: It does not take into account the degree of processing or additives
It can only be read in English
It only applies to fresh fruit
124409.e: The algorithm is based on nutritional values. How heavily a product is processed or which additives it contains is not included.
124409.m: The Nutri-Score says nothing about the degree of processing.

124410.q: What does the biological value of a dietary protein show?
a: How much body protein can be made from it
How many calories the protein supplies
How quickly the protein is digested
How much fat is in the food
124410.e: The more similar the amino acid pattern is to the body's own protein, the more body protein can be built from 100 g of dietary protein.
124410.m: Biological value measures how well dietary protein becomes body protein.

124411.q: Which food serves as the reference with a biological value of 100?
124411.e: The whole hen's egg was set as the reference with a value of 100 because of its favourable amino acid pattern.
124411.m: The egg is the reference for biological value.

124412.q: Which combination reaches one of the highest known biological values, around 136?
124412.e: Potatoes and egg in a ratio of about 35 to 65 complement each other so well that they exceed the value of egg alone. So rösti with a fried egg is a protein-rich combination.
124412.m: Potatoes with egg make a particularly high-quality protein combination.

124413.q: What mainly determines the biological value of a protein?
124413.e: The essential amino acid that is in shortest supply relative to need limits the building of body protein.
124413.m: The scarcest essential amino acid limits the biological value.

124414.q: A dietary protein has a biological value of 80. In theory, how much body protein can be built from 50 g of it?
124414.e: A value of 80 means 80 g of body protein per 100 g of dietary protein. 50 g × 0.8 = 40 g.
124414.m: The biological value shows what percentage can become body protein.

124415.q: Why does gelatine have a very low biological value?
a: It lacks the essential amino acid tryptophan
It is not digested in the stomach
124415.e: Gelatine made from collagen contains practically no tryptophan. Without this essential amino acid, the body can hardly build body protein from it.

124416.q: What do modern measures of protein quality such as DIAAS take into account in addition to the amino acid pattern?
a: How well the amino acids are digested
How much fat the food contains
124416.e: A protein is only as useful as the amount the body can absorb from it in the small intestine. That is why DIAAS includes the digestibility of each essential amino acid.
124416.m: Digestibility also counts for protein quality.

124417.q: Why is the combination of milk and cereals, for example in Bircher muesli, a good one?
a: Milk protein supplies the lysine that cereals lack
Cereals greatly increase the calcium content of milk
124417.e: Milk protein is rich in lysine and so makes up for the weakness of cereal protein.
124417.m: Milk and cereals together make high-quality protein.

124418.q: What does the 16:8 method mean in intermittent fasting?
a: Fasting for 16 hours, eating for 8 hours
Fasting for 16 days, eating for 8 days
16 grams of fat, 8 grams of sugar
124418.e: With 16:8, you eat nothing for 16 hours every day. The meals fall within a window of 8 hours.
124418.m: With 16:8, you only eat within eight hours a day.

124419.q: Someone fasting with the 16:8 method eats their last meal at 7 pm. When is the earliest they may have their first meal the next day?
124419.e: 7 pm plus 16 hours gives 11 am the next day.
124419.m: For the fasting window, you count the hours from the last meal.

124420.q: What does the 5:2 method mean in intermittent fasting?
a: Eating normally on 5 days, greatly reduced on 2 days
Eating for 5 hours, fasting for 2 hours
124420.e: On two non-consecutive days a week, you eat only about 500 to 600 kcal, and normally on the other five days.
124420.m: With 5:2, you partly fast on two days of the week.

124421.q: What is the cellular recycling process called that is stepped up during fasting?
124421.e: In autophagy, cells break down their own components and reuse them. Yoshinori Ohsumi received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for researching it.
124421.m: Autophagy is the self-recycling of cell components.

124422.q: Which energy sources does the liver increasingly make from fatty acids during prolonged fasting?
124422.e: When the glycogen stores are used up, ketone bodies such as acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are formed from fatty acids; the brain can also use them.
124422.m: During fasting, the liver makes ketone bodies from fat.

124423.q: What have studies shown so far about weight loss through intermittent fasting?
a: It is similar to that from an equal reduction in calories
It is always twice as large as with any diet
It is completely independent of the number of calories
124423.e: Many comparative studies find that intermittent fasting brings about a similar amount of weight loss to a classic reduction in calories. The energy balance remains decisive.
124423.m: Even with intermittent fasting, the energy balance is what counts for losing weight.

124424.q: Which hormone level typically drops clearly during the fasting phases?
124424.e: Without food, blood sugar stays low and the release of insulin falls. Glucagon, by contrast, rises.
124424.m: During fasting phases, the insulin level is low.

124425.q: Which group of people should only try intermittent fasting after consulting a doctor?
a: People with diabetes who take medication
Adults with a healthy body weight
124425.e: With medicines that lower blood sugar, longer fasting can lead to dangerously low blood sugar. Children and people with eating disorders should not fast either.
124425.m: Anyone taking diabetes medication should only fast under medical supervision.

124426.q: Which mineral is present in the largest amount in the human body?
124426.e: An adult contains around one kilogram of calcium, almost all of it in bones and teeth. Iron, zinc and iodine are trace elements with only a few grams or less.
124426.m: Calcium is the most common mineral in the body.

124427.q: What is the form of intermittent fasting called in which you alternately eat for one day and fast for one day?
124427.e: In alternate-day fasting, eating days and fasting days alternate. Therapeutic fasting, by contrast, lasts several days in a row.
124427.m: In alternate-day fasting, eating days and fasting days alternate.

124428.q: Which Swiss nuclear power station has the greatest electrical output?
124428.e: With about 1,200 megawatts, Leibstadt produces the most of all Swiss nuclear power stations and alone covers a large part of the country’s consumption.
124428.m: Leibstadt is the most powerful nuclear power station in Switzerland.

124429.q: In which decade did the Leibstadt nuclear power station start operating?
124429.e: Leibstadt was put into operation in the mid-1980s as the youngest of the Swiss nuclear power stations.
124429.m: Leibstadt is the youngest nuclear power station in Switzerland.

124430.q: What is the tall cooling tower of the Leibstadt nuclear power station for?
a: It releases the waste heat from the condenser into the air
It protects the reactor from plane crashes
It produces extra electricity with wind
124430.e: The condenser’s cooling water is cooled in the tower by evaporation. This means less warm water has to be fed into the Rhine.
124430.m: The cooling tower releases waste heat into the air through evaporation.

124431.q: What is the white plume above the Leibstadt cooling tower made of?
124431.e: The warm, moist air from the cooling tower cools down outside and the water vapour condenses into tiny droplets. The cooling circuit has no contact with the reactor water.
124431.m: The cloud above a cooling tower is condensed water vapour.

124432.q: A power station with an output of 1,200 MW runs for 8,000 hours a year. How much electrical energy does it supply?
124432.m: Energy is power multiplied by time.

124433.q: Where in the Leibstadt nuclear power station is heat converted into mechanical energy?
124433.e: The steam flows through the turbine, expands and makes it turn. The connected generator converts the rotation into electricity.
124433.m: The steam turbine converts heat into rotation.

124434.q: What is special about Unit 1 of the Beznau nuclear power station?
a: It is the oldest nuclear power station still running in the world
It is the largest reactor in Europe
It runs on thorium instead of uranium
It is the only one built underground
124434.e: Beznau 1 started operating in 1969 and is considered the oldest commercially operated nuclear reactor in the world that still produces electricity.
124434.m: Beznau 1 is the oldest power reactor still running in the world.

124435.q: Which type of reactor is used at the Beznau nuclear power station?
124435.e: Both Beznau units separate a high-pressure primary circuit from the steam circuit of the turbine.
124435.m: Beznau works with pressurised water reactors.

124436.q: How many reactor units does the Beznau nuclear power station have?
124436.e: Beznau consists of the two almost identical units Beznau 1 and Beznau 2.

124437.q: Where exactly is the Beznau nuclear power station?
a: On an island in the River Aare in the canton of Aargau
On the shore of Lake Geneva
In a side valley of the Valais
124437.e: The plant stands near Döttingen on an artificial island between the Aare and a canal of the Beznau hydroelectric power station.
124437.m: Beznau is on an island in the Aare.

124438.q: Why does the Beznau nuclear power station sometimes have to reduce its output in hot summers?
a: The Aare must not get too warm, to protect the fish
The solar panels then supply too much electricity
The fuel rods melt in the heat
The staff are on holiday in summer
124438.e: If the Aare is already warm, the extra warm cooling water would exceed the limits. To protect fish such as grayling, the output is reduced.
124438.m: When the Aare is warm, Beznau must release less waste heat.

124439.q: Which company operates the Beznau nuclear power station?
124439.e: Beznau belongs to Axpo, which is largely owned by the cantons of north-eastern Switzerland.
124439.m: The Beznau nuclear power station is operated by Axpo.

124440.q: A reactor unit with a thermal output of 1,130 MW delivers 365 MW of electrical power. Roughly how high is its efficiency?
124440.e: η = 365 MW / 1,130 MW ≈ 0.32, so about 32 per cent. The rest is released as waste heat.
124440.m: Efficiency is the useful output divided by the input.

124441.q: How is part of the waste heat from the Beznau nuclear power station put to good use?
a: As district heating for municipalities in the lower Aare valley
124441.e: Through the Refuna district heating network, homes and businesses in the region are supplied with heat from Beznau.
124441.m: Besides electricity, Beznau also supplies district heating.

124442.q: Why is the water in the primary circuit of a pressurised water reactor kept under high pressure?
a: So that it does not boil despite about 300 °C
124442.e: The high pressure raises the boiling point so much that the water in the reactor stays liquid.
124442.m: High pressure prevents boiling in the primary circuit.

124443.q: Roughly how high is the pressure in the primary circuit of a pressurised water reactor?
124443.e: About 150 to 160 bar is typical, roughly 150 times air pressure.
124443.m: The primary circuit of a pressurised water reactor is at about 150 bar.

124444.q: Which component in a pressurised water reactor transfers heat from the primary to the secondary circuit?
124444.e: In the steam generator, the hot primary water flows through thousands of tubes and makes the secondary water boil without mixing with it.
124444.m: The steam generator keeps the two circuits separate.

124445.q: What advantage do the separate circuits of a pressurised water reactor bring?
a: The turbine steam is not radioactively contaminated
124445.e: The radioactive primary water stays inside the containment. The turbine and condenser only come into contact with the clean secondary steam.
124445.m: Separate circuits keep the turbine free of radioactivity.

124446.q: Which type of reactor is the most common among power reactors worldwide?
124446.e: About two thirds of all power reactors worldwide are pressurised water reactors. They are also used in submarines and aircraft carriers.
124446.m: The pressurised water reactor is the most widespread reactor type in the world.

124447.q: What does the pressuriser do in a pressurised water reactor?
a: It keeps the pressure in the primary circuit constant
It holds the fuel rods together
124447.e: In the pressuriser there is a cushion of steam above the water. Heaters and spray water are used to control the pressure.
124447.m: The pressuriser controls the pressure in the primary circuit.

124448.q: Besides cooling, what role does the water in the core of a light water reactor play?
a: As a moderator, it slows the neutrons down
124448.e: Fast neutrons are slowed down by collisions with hydrogen nuclei. Slow neutrons split uranium-235 much more effectively.
124448.m: Water cools the reactor and slows the neutrons.

124449.q: From where are the control rods inserted into the core of a pressurised water reactor?
a: Not at all, it has none
124449.e: The control rods hang above the core. In an emergency shutdown they drop in by gravity.
124449.m: In a pressurised water reactor, the control rods drop into the core from above.

124450.q: To what percentage is uranium-235 typically enriched in the fuel of a light water reactor?
124450.e: Natural uranium contains only about 0.7 per cent uranium-235. For light water reactors it is enriched to a few per cent.
124450.m: Light water reactors need slightly enriched uranium.

124451.q: What happens to the water in the core of a boiling water reactor?
a: It turns to steam directly in the core
124451.e: In a boiling water reactor, the coolant boils inside the pressure vessel. The steam goes to the turbine without an intermediate circuit.
124451.m: In a boiling water reactor, the water boils directly in the reactor.

124452.q: Roughly how high is the operating pressure in a boiling water reactor?
124452.e: At about 70 bar, water boils at about 286 °C. This pressure is much lower than in a pressurised water reactor.
124452.m: A boiling water reactor works at about 70 bar.

124453.q: How many water and steam circuits between reactor and turbine does a boiling water reactor have?
124453.e: The steam from the reactor drives the turbine directly, is condensed and pumped back. So there is only one circuit.
124453.m: A boiling water reactor manages with a single circuit.

124454.q: Why does the turbine of a boiling water reactor also have to be shielded against radiation?
a: The steam comes directly from the reactor core
The steam is mixed with plutonium
124454.e: A boiling water reactor has no intermediate circuit. The steam from the core is slightly radioactive during operation, so the turbine is part of the controlled area.
124454.m: In a boiling water reactor, steam from the core goes directly to the turbine.

124455.q: What do the control rods in a nuclear reactor do?
a: They capture neutrons and so control the chain reaction
They supply the fuel for fission
They produce the steam for the turbine
124455.e: Control rods are made of materials that strongly absorb neutrons, such as boron or cadmium. The deeper they are in the core, the fewer fissions take place.
124455.m: Control rods regulate the chain reaction by capturing neutrons.

124456.q: Which Swiss nuclear power station, now shut down, worked with a boiling water reactor?
124456.e: The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was permanently shut down at the end of 2019 and is being dismantled.
124456.m: Mühleberg was a boiling water reactor and has been shut down since 2019.

124457.q: Which type of reactor was in the Fukushima Daiichi units that were damaged in 2011?
124457.e: After the earthquake and tsunami, the cooling failed. Several boiling water reactors suffered core meltdowns and hydrogen explosions.

124458.q: What happens to the reactivity of a boiling water reactor when more steam bubbles form in the core?
124458.e: Steam slows neutrons down less well than liquid water. More bubbles mean less moderation and therefore fewer fissions. This can also be used to control the output.
124458.m: More steam bubbles lower the output of a boiling water reactor.

124459.q: In which decade was the Grande Dixence dam completed?
124459.e: Construction took about ten years. The dam was finished in the early 1960s.
124459.m: The Grande Dixence was completed in the early 1960s.

124460.q: Which reservoir is held back by the Grande Dixence?
124460.e: The dam in the Val des Dix holds back the Lac des Dix in the canton of Valais.
124460.m: The Grande Dixence holds back the Lac des Dix.

124461.q: How does a gravity dam like the Grande Dixence withstand the water pressure?
a: Through the arch effect against the rock walls
124461.e: The dam is so heavy that its weight and the friction on the rock take up the horizontal water pressure. An arch dam, by contrast, directs the forces sideways into the valley sides.
124461.m: A gravity dam holds back the water with its mass.

124462.q: How does water from other valleys in the Valais, for example from the Zermatt area, reach the Lac des Dix?
a: Through pumping stations and about 100 km of tunnels
Through open channels through the villages
Through a pipeline from Lake Geneva
124462.e: A widely branched network of tunnels and pumping stations collects glacier water from several valleys in the Valais and channels it to the reservoir.
124462.m: Tunnels and pumps bring glacier water from many valleys to the Grande Dixence.

124463.q: Roughly what hydrostatic pressure is there at the bottom of a reservoir with a water depth of 280 m, if ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s²?
124463.e: p = ρ · g · h = 1000 · 9.81 · 280 Pa ≈ 2.75 MPa. Since 1 bar = 100,000 Pa, that is about 27 bar.
124463.m: Water pressure increases linearly with depth.

124464.q: What world record did the Bieudron power station, part of the Grande Dixence, hold when it opened?
a: The greatest head of any hydroelectric power station
The largest reservoir in the world
124464.e: At Bieudron, the water falls about 1,880 metres onto the turbines. That was a world record.
124464.m: Bieudron uses a head of almost 1,900 metres.

124465.q: Roughly how much potential energy does 1 m³ of water (1000 kg) have at a height of 1000 m, if g = 9.81 m/s²?
124465.e: E = m · g · h = 1000 kg · 9.81 m/s² · 1000 m = 9.81 MJ. Divided by 3.6 MJ per kWh, that gives about 2.7 kWh.
124465.m: Potential energy is calculated from mass, gravitational acceleration and height.

124466.q: Why is a storage lake like the Lac des Dix important for Switzerland’s electricity supply?
a: It stores summer water for producing electricity in winter
It mainly supplies drinking water for Geneva
It cools the nuclear power stations
It is used only for tourism
124466.e: In summer, meltwater fills the lake. In winter, when demand is high, the water is sent through the turbines.
124466.m: Storage lakes shift hydropower from summer to winter.

124467.q: What is the output of the Nant de Drance pumped storage power station?
124467.e: Six machine units of 150 MW each make 900 MW, about as much as a large nuclear power station.
124467.m: Nant de Drance has an output of 900 megawatts.

124468.q: Between which two reservoirs does Nant de Drance work?
a: Lac d'Emosson and Lac du Vieux Emosson
Lac des Dix and Lac de Moiry
Lake Geneva and Lac de Joux
124468.e: The water is moved back and forth between the lower Lac d'Emosson and the higher Lac du Vieux Emosson.
124468.m: Nant de Drance links the two Emosson lakes.

124469.q: Why was the dam of the Lac du Vieux Emosson raised for Nant de Drance?
a: To be able to store more water
To keep avalanches away from the village
To build a road over it
To make the lake deeper for boats
124469.e: With the higher dam, the upper reservoir holds much more water. This lets the power station run at full output for longer.
124469.m: A larger upper reservoir increases the storage capacity of a pumped storage plant.

124470.q: What does a pumped storage power station do when there is too much electricity in the grid?
a: It pumps water into the upper reservoir
It lets water flow into the lower reservoir
124470.e: Surplus electricity drives pumps that pump water uphill. When needed, it flows back and drives turbines.
124470.m: A pumped storage plant stores electricity as the potential energy of water.

124471.q: Roughly how high is the overall efficiency of a modern pumped storage power station?
124471.e: Losses in pumps, turbines, generators and lines mean that about 80 per cent of the energy used is recovered.
124471.m: A pumped storage plant gives back about four fifths of the energy.

124472.q: A pumped storage power station uses 100 MWh of electricity for pumping. How much electricity does it give back at 80 % efficiency?
124472.e: 100 MWh · 0.80 = 80 MWh. The remaining 20 MWh are lost.
124472.m: Storing energy always loses part of it.

124473.q: What task does Nant de Drance especially perform in the electricity grid?
a: It balances fluctuations in wind and solar power
It supplies constant baseload power like a run-of-river plant
It produces electricity from the tides
124473.e: The machines can switch between pumping and generating within minutes and so stabilise the grid.
124473.m: Pumped storage plants are the big battery of the electricity grid.

124474.q: Apart from power stations, where are gas turbines mainly used?
a: In the engines of passenger aircraft
In heat pumps of family houses
124474.e: A jet engine is a gas turbine: air is compressed, burnt with fuel and expanded in the turbine. The exhaust jet and the fan produce the thrust.

124475.q: In what order does the air flow through the main parts of a gas turbine?
124475.e: The air is first compressed, then fuel is burnt in the combustion chamber, and the hot gases drive the turbine.
124475.m: Compress, burn, expand is the sequence in a gas turbine.

124476.q: Where was the world’s first gas turbine power station for generating electricity put into operation in 1939?
124476.e: The company Brown Boveri built the plant, with about 4 MW, for the town of Neuchâtel. Today it is considered a technical monument.
124476.m: The world’s first gas turbine power station was in Neuchâtel.

124477.q: What uses up a large part of a gas turbine’s own turbine output?
124477.e: The turbine and compressor sit on the same shaft. The compressor often needs more than half of the turbine output.
124477.m: The compressor eats up a large part of the turbine output.

124478.q: Roughly what temperature do the exhaust gases of a gas turbine have?
124478.e: The hot exhaust gases still contain a lot of usable energy, which is used again in combined cycle power stations.
124478.m: The exhaust gases of a gas turbine are still several hundred degrees hot.

124479.q: Why are gas turbines well suited as reserve power stations, for example in Birr AG?
a: They can be started up within minutes
They run only when the sun shines
124479.e: Gas turbines reach full output very quickly and are therefore suitable for bridging shortages in the electricity supply.
