124479.m: Gas turbines step in quickly when electricity is scarce.

124480.q: Which quantity do engineers try to increase to improve the efficiency of gas turbines?
a: The temperature at the turbine inlet
The length of the exhaust pipe
124480.e: The hotter the gas when it enters the turbine, the greater the theoretically achievable efficiency. This requires cooled blades made of special alloys.
124480.m: Higher turbine inlet temperatures make gas turbines more efficient.

124481.q: Which fuel is increasingly being tested in gas turbines as a more climate-friendly option for the future?
124481.e: Hydrogen burns to water vapour without CO2. Modern gas turbines are therefore designed for mixtures of hydrogen and natural gas.
124481.m: Gas turbines can also run on hydrogen.

124482.q: What is the component called in which the exhaust gases of the gas turbine turn water into steam?
124482.e: In the heat recovery steam generator, the hot exhaust gases flow through bundles of tubes in which water turns into steam.
124482.m: The heat recovery steam generator turns exhaust heat into steam.

124483.q: Why does a combined cycle gas and steam power station reach a higher efficiency than a gas turbine alone?
a: The hot exhaust gases of the gas turbine produce steam for a second turbine
It burns twice as much natural gas
The steam turbine produces extra fuel
124483.e: The exhaust gases of the gas turbine are still several hundred degrees hot. In a combined cycle plant they produce steam that drives a steam turbine, so about 60 per cent of the fuel energy becomes electricity.
124483.m: A combined cycle plant uses the waste heat of the gas turbine a second time.

124484.q: A gas turbine has an efficiency of 38 %. The steam turbine uses 35 % of the remaining energy. Roughly how high is the overall efficiency?
124484.m: In a combined cycle plant, the output of the second stage from the leftover heat is added.

124485.q: A combined cycle power station receives 1,000 MW of fuel power and has an efficiency of 60 %. How much waste heat is produced?
124485.e: Electrical: 1,000 MW · 0.6 = 600 MW. Waste heat: 1,000 MW minus 600 MW = 400 MW.
124485.m: Whatever does not become electricity becomes waste heat.

124486.q: Roughly how much CO2 does a combined cycle gas and steam power station emit per kilowatt hour compared with a hard coal power station?
124486.e: Natural gas contains more hydrogen and less carbon than coal, and the efficiency is higher. Together this roughly halves the CO2 emissions per kWh.
124486.m: Gas power stations emit about half as much CO2 per kilowatt hour as coal power stations.

124487.q: Why can combined cycle gas and steam power stations be controlled more flexibly than nuclear power stations?
a: They can change their output quickly and start fast
124487.e: Gas turbines reach their output in a short time. Combined cycle plants can therefore balance fluctuating demand or gaps in renewable energy.
124487.m: Combined cycle plants react quickly to changes in demand.

124488.q: What is meant by combined heat and power?
a: Producing electricity and usable heat at the same time
124488.e: With combined heat and power, the waste heat from electricity production is used for heating or as process heat.
124488.m: Combined heat and power uses electricity and waste heat together.

124489.q: What overall efficiency can combined heat and power plants achieve?
124489.e: Because the heat is used as well as the electricity, most of the fuel energy can be put to use.
124489.m: With combined heat and power, the fuel is used almost completely.

124490.q: What is a small, compact combined heat and power plant, for example for a housing estate, called?
124490.e: A block heat and power plant (CHP unit) usually consists of a combustion engine with a generator, whose waste heat goes into the heating network.
124490.m: A block heat and power plant produces electricity and heat on site.

124491.q: Which technology can make combined heat and power possible even without a flame?
124491.e: Fuel cells convert the chemical energy of, for example, hydrogen or natural gas electrochemically into electricity. The heat produced can be used for heating.
124491.m: Fuel cells also supply electricity and heat at the same time.

124492.q: A plant produces 35 kWh of electricity and 50 kWh of usable heat from 100 kWh of fuel energy. How high is the overall efficiency?
124492.e: (35 kWh + 50 kWh) / 100 kWh = 0.85, so 85 per cent.
124492.m: For overall efficiency, electricity and heat are counted together.

124493.q: A block heat and power plant supplies 35 kW of electricity and 50 kW of heat. What is its power to heat ratio, the ratio of electrical to thermal output?
124493.e: Power to heat ratio = electrical output / thermal output = 35 / 50 = 0.7.
124493.m: The power to heat ratio compares a plant’s electricity and heat.

124494.q: What does it mean when a combined heat and power plant is run in heat-led mode?
a: It adjusts its output to the heat demand
It runs only when the electricity price is high
It produces only heat, no electricity
It is powered by solar heat
124494.e: Heat-led plants produce as much as is needed for heat. The electricity is a by-product.
124494.m: Heat-led plants follow the heating demand.

124495.q: Why does combined heat and power suit Switzerland’s electricity supply well?
a: It supplies electricity mainly in winter, when heating is also needed
It only works in summer heat
124495.e: Heat is needed mainly in winter. That is exactly when electricity is scarce too, and the plants supply both.
124495.m: Combined heat and power supplies winter electricity when it is most in demand.

124496.q: What was the name of the geothermal project in Basel that aimed to obtain electricity and heat from hot rock?
124496.e: The Deep Heat Mining project was meant to make hot deep rock artificially permeable and use it as a heat exchanger.
124496.m: Deep Heat Mining was Basel’s deep geothermal project.

124497.q: In which year did the Basel geothermal project trigger a noticeable earthquake?
124497.e: In December 2006, the ground shook during the water injection. The quake was clearly felt throughout the city.
124497.m: The Basel geothermal earthquake happened in 2006.

124498.q: Roughly what magnitude did the strongest earthquake of the Basel geothermal project have?
124498.e: The earthquake reached a magnitude of about 3.4. It mainly caused minor damage to buildings, such as cracks.
124498.m: The Basel earthquake had a magnitude of about 3.4.

124499.q: Roughly how deep was the drilling for the Basel geothermal project?
124499.e: The borehole went about 5 kilometres deep, where the granite is about 200 °C hot.
124499.m: In Basel they drilled about five kilometres deep.

124500.q: Which method was meant to make the rock in Basel permeable?
a: Water was pumped in under high pressure
The rock was melted with lasers
124500.e: In hydraulic stimulation, water under high pressure opens existing cracks. This is what caused the earthquakes.
124500.m: Hydraulic stimulation forces water into hot rock.

124501.q: What happened to the Basel geothermal project after the earthquakes?
a: Since then it has supplied electricity for all of Basel
124501.e: After a risk analysis, the Basel government decided at the end of 2009 to stop the project for good.
124501.m: The Basel geothermal project was stopped because of the earthquakes.

124502.q: The temperature rises by 3 °C per 100 m and is 10 °C at the surface. How warm is it at a depth of 4,000 m?
124502.m: The temperature underground rises roughly linearly with depth.

124503.q: In which geological structure does Basel lie, which increases the risk of earthquakes?
a: In the Molasse basin of central Switzerland
In the Jura mountains near Geneva
124503.e: The Upper Rhine Graben is tectonically active. As early as 1356, a strong earthquake destroyed large parts of Basel.
124503.m: Basel lies on the tectonically active Upper Rhine Graben.

124504.q: Which Swiss city also experienced an earthquake linked to a geothermal project in 2013?
124504.e: During the deep drilling in St Gallen, gas flowed in. The countermeasures caused a noticeable earthquake, and the project was later abandoned.
124504.m: The St Gallen geothermal project was also accompanied by an earthquake.

124505.q: What is the main advantage of solar plants in the Alps compared with the Swiss Plateau?
a: They supply much more electricity in winter
124505.e: In the mountains you are often above the fog, the air is clearer and snow reflects extra light. This increases production in winter.
124505.m: Alpine solar plants help to reduce the winter electricity gap.

124506.q: Why does snow increase the electricity production of alpine solar plants?
a: It reflects a lot of sunlight onto the modules
It raises the height of the sun
It clears clouds from the air
124506.e: Fresh snow has a high albedo and reflects most of the light. Bifacial modules use this light on their back.
124506.m: Snow throws a lot of light back onto the solar modules.

a: Modules that use light on both front and back
Modules that supply electricity and heat
Modules that turn to follow the sun
124507.e: Bifacial modules also have active cells on the back and can therefore use reflected light.
124507.m: Bifacial modules catch light from both sides.

124508.q: How does the cold in the mountains affect the efficiency of solar cells?
124508.e: Silicon solar cells lose voltage when warm. Low temperatures therefore improve their efficiency.
124508.m: Cold solar cells work more efficiently.

124509.q: Why are alpine solar modules often mounted very steeply?
a: So that snow slides off and the low winter sun is used well
So that ibexes can sleep underneath
So that they get less light
124509.e: Steep modules stay free of snow and face the low winter sun almost at a right angle.
124509.m: Steep modules stay free of snow in winter.

124510.q: On which dam in the canton of Glarus was one of the first large alpine solar plants in Switzerland built?
124510.e: On the Muttsee dam at about 2,500 m above sea level, the AlpinSolar project covered a large wall with solar modules.
124510.m: The Muttsee dam carries a large alpine solar plant.

124511.q: What is the temporary support scheme for large alpine solar plants, decided by Parliament in 2022, called?
124511.e: With the Solarexpress, large plants are to be built quickly and receive part of their investment costs from the federal government.
124511.m: The Solarexpress supports large solar plants in the Alps.

124512.q: A plant has 1,000 m² of module area, the irradiance is 1,000 W/m² and the efficiency 20 %. What output does it supply?
124512.m: Solar output comes from area, irradiance and efficiency.

124513.q: Which source of electricity has grown the most in Switzerland in recent years?
124513.e: Thanks to many roof and façade installations, solar power production has risen sharply and now supplies a noticeable share.
124513.m: Photovoltaics is growing especially fast in Switzerland.

124514.q: Which energy source supplied the second-largest share of Swiss electricity production in 2024?
124514.e: In 2024, the nuclear power stations contributed about 28 per cent of domestic production, hydropower just under 60 per cent.
124514.m: Nuclear energy is Switzerland’s second most important source of electricity.

124515.q: In which season does Switzerland typically depend on electricity imports?
124515.e: In winter, consumption is high while run-of-river power stations and solar plants produce less.
124515.m: In winter, Switzerland usually imports electricity.

124516.q: What does the supply mix on the electricity bill show, in contrast to the production mix?
a: Which sources the electricity sold by the supplier to its customers comes from
How much electricity was produced in Switzerland in total
How much electricity a household has used
Which power stations abroad are standing still
124516.e: Electricity labelling uses guarantees of origin to show which sources the supplied electricity comes from. The production mix, by contrast, describes the power stations in Switzerland.
124516.m: The supply mix describes where the electricity you buy comes from.

124517.q: What is the name of the grid junction in Aargau where the electricity grids of Switzerland, Germany and France were connected for the first time in 1958?
124517.e: The European interconnected grid began with the Star of Laufenburg. Since then, Switzerland has been an important hub for electricity exchange.
124517.m: The Star of Laufenburg is considered the birthplace of the European interconnected grid.

124518.q: At what frequency is the Swiss electricity grid operated?
124518.e: As throughout the European interconnected grid, the grid frequency is 50 hertz. The SBB use their own grid for their railway power supply.
124518.m: The Swiss electricity grid runs at 50 hertz.

124519.q: What did the Energy Act, approved by the people in 2017, lay down about nuclear energy?
a: No more general licences will be granted for new nuclear power stations
All nuclear power stations had to shut down immediately
Two new nuclear power stations must be built
Nuclear power will be imported from France from now on
124519.e: With the Energy Strategy 2050, the construction of new nuclear power stations was ruled out. Existing plants may keep running as long as they are safe.
124519.m: Since the Energy Act of 2017, no new nuclear power stations may be approved.

124520.q: How does a run-of-river power station differ from a storage power station?
a: It uses the flowing water without a large storage lake
It uses only rainwater from the roof
124520.e: Run-of-river power stations on rivers such as the Rhine or the Aare produce according to the water flow, mainly in summer. Storage power stations can shift production in time.
124520.m: Run-of-river power stations supply electricity as the river happens to flow.

124521.q: How many nuclear reactor units were operating in Switzerland in 2025?
124521.e: Beznau 1 and 2, Gösgen and Leibstadt were in operation. Mühleberg has been shut down since 2019 (as of 2025).
124521.m: Switzerland has four operating nuclear reactor units (as of 2025).

124522.q: What does the field of phytopathology deal with?
a: The growth of fungi in soils
124522.e: Phytopathology is the science of plant diseases, their causes, how they develop and how to control them. The name is made up of the Greek “phyton” (plant) and “pathos” (suffering).
124522.m: Phytopathology is the study of plant diseases.

124523.q: In phytopathology, which three factors make up the so-called disease triangle?
124523.e: A disease only breaks out when a susceptible host plant, a pathogen able to cause disease and favourable environmental conditions come together. If one of the three is missing, the plant stays healthy.
124523.m: A plant disease only develops when host, pathogen and environment match.

124524.q: What is the yellowing of leaves called that is caused by a lack of chlorophyll?
124524.e: In chlorosis, too little chlorophyll is made or it is broken down, so the leaves turn yellowish. Causes can be pathogens but also a lack of nutrients.
124524.m: Yellow leaves due to lack of chlorophyll are called chlorosis.

124525.q: In phytopathology, what is dead, usually brown plant tissue called?
124525.e: A necrosis is dead tissue that often turns brown or black. Many fungal and bacterial diseases show up as such spots.
124525.m: Dead, brown plant tissue is called necrosis.

124526.q: Why can rust fungi hardly be grown on culture media in the laboratory?
124526.e: Rust fungi depend on living cells of their host. Such pathogens are called obligate biotrophs. They cannot multiply on dead culture media.
124526.m: Rust fungi need living host tissue.

124527.q: The grey mould Botrytis cinerea kills plant cells and feeds on the dead tissue. What is this way of life called?
124527.e: Necrotrophic pathogens release enzymes and toxins that kill the tissue and then live on it. Botrytis attacks strawberries and grapes, among others.
124527.m: Necrotrophic pathogens kill tissue and feed on it.

124528.q: Which defence reaction of plants makes cells around an infection site die on purpose?
124528.e: In the hypersensitive response, the cells around the infection site die quickly. Biotrophic pathogens find no more living tissue there and cannot spread.
124528.m: With the hypersensitive response, the plant sacrifices a few cells to stop the pathogen.

124529.q: Which plant disease caused a great famine in Ireland in the 1840s?
124529.e: A fungus-like pathogen destroyed the potato harvests for several years. Because many people lived almost only on potatoes, about a million people died and many emigrated.
124529.m: Potato blight caused the great famine in Ireland.

124530.q: Which rules are used to prove that a particular microorganism causes a disease?
124530.e: The pathogen must be present in every diseased plant, be able to be isolated, cause the same disease in a healthy plant and be isolated from it again. These rules also apply in phytopathology.
124530.m: Koch's postulates prove which pathogen causes a disease.

124531.q: Which 19th-century famine was caused by potato late blight?
a: The famine after the eruption of Tambora
124531.e: From 1845, the pathogen Phytophthora infestans destroyed several potato harvests in Ireland. About a million people died, and over a million emigrated.
124531.m: Potato late blight caused the Irish famine from 1845.

124532.q: Why is the cause of potato late blight not considered a true fungus, even though it looks like one?
a: It is more closely related to brown algae than to fungi
It is not made of cells
124532.e: Phytophthora belongs to the water moulds (oomycetes). These are more closely related to brown algae than to true fungi, and their cell walls contain cellulose instead of chitin.
124532.m: The cause of late blight is a water mould, not a true fungus.

124533.q: Which two crops are mainly attacked by late blight?
124533.e: Potato and tomato both belong to the nightshade family and serve as hosts for the pathogen. In tomatoes it is also called tomato blight.
124533.m: Late blight attacks potatoes and tomatoes.

124534.q: Which weather most encourages an epidemic of late blight?
a: Damp and mild for several days
124534.e: The pathogen needs wet leaves and high humidity for its sporangia to germinate. In wet, warm summers a whole field can die within a few days.
124534.m: Wet, mild weather encourages late blight.

124535.q: How can late blight typically be recognised on the underside of the leaf?
a: By a whitish growth of spores at the edge of brown patches
By black fruiting bodies like peppercorns
124535.e: On the upper side, brown patches appear and spread quickly. On the underside, in damp conditions, the pathogen forms a fine white coating of sporangium-bearing threads.
124535.m: Brown patches with a white edge on the underside of the leaf suggest late blight.

124536.q: Which metal is used in organic potato growing against late blight?
124536.e: Copper products work preventively against oomycetes and are approved in organic farming. Because copper builds up in the soil, the permitted amounts are limited.
124536.m: In organic farming, potatoes are protected with limited amounts of copper.

124537.q: How does late blight often survive from one season to the next?
a: Through infected seed potatoes and waste heaps
124537.e: Infected tubers that are planted or dumped on heaps sprout in spring and produce new spores. Healthy seed potatoes are therefore an important precaution.
124537.m: Healthy seed potatoes stop late blight surviving the winter.

124538.q: How do the spores of late blight get from infected leaves to the tubers in the soil?
a: With the roots of neighbouring plants
124538.e: Rain washes the spores off the leaves into the soil, where they infect the tubers. Earthing up the ridges well protects the tubers.
124538.m: Rain washes late blight spores down to the tubers.

124539.q: Roughly by how much did Ireland's population fall through death and emigration during the Great Famine?
124539.e: Through hunger, disease and emigration, Ireland lost about a fifth to a quarter of its population within a few years. It was one of the worst famines in 19th-century Europe.
124539.m: Ireland lost about a quarter of its population through the famine.

124540.q: What was the main cause of the Great Famine in Ireland?
a: A volcanic eruption darkened the sky
A drought dried out the fields
124540.e: A large part of the poor rural population lived almost only on potatoes. When the pathogen destroyed the harvests, the most important food was missing.
124540.m: A potato disease caused the Irish famine.

124541.q: Roughly how many people died during the Great Famine in Ireland?
124541.e: Estimates suggest about a million deaths from hunger and disease. Many died of typhus and other epidemics that struck weakened people.
124541.m: About a million people died in the Irish famine.

124542.q: What is the Great Famine called in Irish?
124542.e: “An Gorta Mór” means “the great hunger”. The term is still used in Ireland today for this period.
124542.m: The Irish call the famine “An Gorta Mór”.

124543.q: Why were the Irish potato fields particularly vulnerable to the disease?
a: Almost everywhere the same variety was grown, propagated from tubers
The potatoes were only grown in winter
They were fertilised only with salt
The fields were all high in the mountains
124543.e: Potatoes are propagated from tubers, which are genetically the same as the parent plant. Because mainly the “Lumper” variety was grown, there was no genetic diversity against the pathogen.
124543.m: Lack of genetic diversity made the Irish potatoes vulnerable.

124544.q: What consequence did the Great Famine have for Ireland's population?
a: Mass emigration, mainly to North America
A rapid rise in the number of births
The founding of many new large cities
124544.e: More than a million people emigrated during and shortly after the famine, many of them to the USA and Canada. Ireland's population fell sharply and never returned to its former level.
124544.m: The famine drove many Irish people to emigrate to America.

124545.q: Which state did Ireland belong to at the time of the Great Famine?
124545.e: Since the Act of Union of 1801, Ireland had been part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. The relief policy of the government in London is still viewed critically today.
124545.m: During the famine, Ireland belonged to the United Kingdom.

124546.q: What happened to many farm goods from Ireland, such as grain and cattle, during the Great Famine?
a: They were all given to the poor
They could only be stored in churches
124546.e: Many goods belonging to large landowners were sold abroad despite the hunger. The poor population could not afford this food.
124546.m: Despite the famine, grain and cattle left Ireland as exports.

124547.q: How does an infection with powdery mildew show on leaves?
a: As a white coating that can be wiped off, usually on the upper side
As orange rust pustules on the underside
As black sooty patches after an aphid attack
As see-through holes in the leaf
124547.e: The fungus grows on the leaf surface and forms a floury network with spores. That is where the name “powdery mildew” comes from.
124547.m: Powdery mildew forms a white, floury coating on the leaves.

124548.q: Which group of fungi do the powdery mildews belong to?
124548.e: The powdery mildews form the order Erysiphales within the sac fungi. So they are true fungi, unlike the organisms that cause downy mildew.

124549.q: Why is powdery mildew often called a “fair-weather fungus”?
a: It does not need wet leaves to infect
It only grows in sunshine in winter
It dies immediately when it is cloudy
It only attacks ornamental plants on balconies
124549.e: The spores of powdery mildew germinate without water droplets on the leaf; high humidity is often enough. That is why it also spreads during warm, dry periods.
124549.m: Powdery mildew also thrives in dry, warm weather.

124550.q: With which structures do powdery mildew fungi take nutrients from plant cells?
124550.e: The fungal network lies on the surface and sends feeding organs, the haustoria, into the epidermal cells. The host cells stay alive.
124550.m: Mildew fungi draw nutrients from living cells with haustoria.

124551.q: Which element has long been used in wine growing against powdery mildew of the vine?
124551.e: Wettable sulphur works well against powdery mildew of the vine and is also allowed in organic farming. Against downy mildew, however, sulphur hardly helps.
124551.m: Powdery mildew of the vine is traditionally sprayed with sulphur.

124552.q: By what other name is powdery mildew of the vine known in wine growing?
124552.e: The name Oidium comes from the asexual form of the fungus. Today the pathogen is called Erysiphe necator.
124552.m: Winegrowers also call powdery mildew of the vine Oidium.

124553.q: Why do mildew-resistant cereal varieties often become susceptible again after a few years?
a: The fungus changes and overcomes the resistance
The variety loses its genes through fertiliser
The soil becomes too acidic over time
The grains get bigger every year
124553.e: Cereal mildew produces huge numbers of spores and multiplies quickly. New forms arise that get round a variety’s defences. That is why breeders constantly have to develop new resistant varieties.
124553.m: Mildew fungi can overcome the resistance of cereal varieties.

124554.q: How are most powdery mildew fungi suited to their host plants?
a: They are specialised on particular host plants
They only live on dead leaves
124554.e: A mildew from roses does not usually spread to cucumbers. Many species are even limited to single varieties or genera.
124554.m: Powdery mildew fungi are mostly host-specific.

124555.q: What else do winegrowers call downy mildew of the vine?
124555.e: In wine growing, downy mildew is often called Peronospora. Oidium, on the other hand, is powdery mildew, and grey mould is caused by Botrytis.
124555.m: Downy mildew of the vine is called Peronospora in wine growing.

124556.q: From which region was downy mildew of the vine brought into Europe in the 19th century?
124556.e: The pathogen probably came to Europe with American vines that were introduced to fight phylloxera. European vines had no defence against it.
124556.m: Downy mildew comes from North America.

124557.q: How can you recognise an early downy mildew infection on the upper side of a vine leaf?
124557.e: The spots look like translucent oil stains. In damp conditions, a white layer of spores forms on the underside of these areas.
124557.m: Oil spots on vine leaves are a sign of downy mildew.

124558.q: Through which openings do the zoospores of downy mildew enter the vine leaf?
a: Through the leaf veins on the upper side
124558.e: The zoospores, which have flagella, swim in a film of water to the stomata on the underside of the leaf. That is why infection needs wet conditions.
124558.m: The zoospores of downy mildew enter through the stomata.

124559.q: Which mixture was developed in the Bordeaux area in the 19th century against downy mildew?
124559.e: The so-called Bordeaux mixture was one of the first effective plant protection products ever. It goes back to the botanist Pierre-Marie-Alexis Millardet.
124559.m: Bordeaux mixture is made of copper sulphate and lime.

124560.q: Which weather condition is decisive for an infection with downy mildew of the vine?
124560.e: Without a film of water on the leaf, the zoospores cannot swim. In rainy summers the risk of infection is therefore especially high.

124561.q: Why are vines often sprayed against downy mildew several times a season?
a: Because every rainfall allows new infections
Because the pathogen is only active in winter
Because the sprays make the grapes sweeter
Because otherwise the vines produce no flowers
124561.e: The pathogen needs wet leaves to get in. In rainy summers, new infections keep happening, and the leaves have to be protected again.
124561.m: With downy mildew, rain keeps bringing new infections.

124562.q: Which plant disease caused a famine in Ireland in the 19th century and is related to downy mildew of the vine?
124562.e: Late blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans. This pathogen belongs to the same group as the organism that causes downy mildew of the vine.
124562.m: Potato blight and downy mildew of the vine have related pathogens.

124564.q: What are plant protection products that work specifically against mites called?
124564.e: Mites belong to the arachnids, not the insects. That is why there are special products against them, the acaricides.

124565.q: Why does the herbicide glyphosate act on plants but hardly directly on animals?
a: It blocks a metabolic pathway that only plants have
It only acts on the chlorophyll in the leaf
Animals excrete it immediately through the skin
It breaks down into sugar in animals
124565.e: Glyphosate blocks an enzyme that plants use to make certain amino acids. Animals do not have this metabolic pathway and get these amino acids from their food.
124565.m: Glyphosate blocks a metabolic pathway that only plants have.

124566.q: Because of which group of animals were several neonicotinoids banned for outdoor use in the EU and in Switzerland?
124566.e: Neonicotinoids act on insects’ nerve receptors and also harm pollinators. That is why three of these active substances were banned outdoors.
124566.m: Neonicotinoids were restricted to protect bees.

124567.q: Which Swiss chemist received the Nobel Prize in 1948 for discovering the insect-killing effect of DDT?
124567.e: Paul Hermann Müller worked for the Basel company Geigy and discovered that DDT kills insects. DDT was later banned in many countries because it lasts so long in the environment.
124567.m: Paul Hermann Müller discovered the insecticidal effect of DDT.

124568.q: What is the legally set maximum amount of a pesticide that a food may contain called?
124568.e: Each active substance and each food has its own maximum residue level. Food inspectors check that it is respected.
124568.m: The maximum residue level limits pesticide residues in food.

124570.q: How were the Drinking Water Initiative and the Pesticide Initiative decided in the Swiss popular vote of June 2021?
a: Only the Pesticide Initiative was accepted
124570.e: Both popular initiatives wanted to strongly restrict the use of pesticides. The people and the cantons rejected them in June 2021.
124570.m: In 2021 Switzerland rejected the Drinking Water and Pesticide Initiatives.

124572.q: Which principle shapes integrated pest management?
a: Chemicals only as much as necessary, preventive measures first
Spraying chemicals only according to a fixed calendar
124572.e: Integrated pest management combines preventive, biological, mechanical and chemical measures. Chemicals are only used when other methods are not enough.
124572.m: In integrated pest management, chemicals come last.

124573.q: What is the level of infestation at which control becomes worthwhile economically called?
124573.e: Below this threshold, control costs more than the damage would. That is why the infestation is first checked and counted.
124573.m: Control only pays off above the economic threshold.

124574.q: Which preventive measure stops soil-borne pests and diseases building up in a field?
124574.e: If a different crop grows every year, specialised pathogens and pests no longer find a host and die out. Crop rotation is a key part of integrated pest management.
124574.m: A good crop rotation takes away the basis for pests and diseases.

124575.q: What do farmers and winegrowers use forecasting models such as the Swiss platform Agrometeo for?
a: To find the right time for a treatment
To predict market prices for wine
124575.e: The models use weather data to calculate when infections or pest flights are to be expected. That way, crops are only treated when there really is a risk.
124575.m: Forecasting models help to use plant protection in a targeted way.

124576.q: Why are flower strips planted at the edge of fields in integrated pest management?
a: To encourage beneficial insects such as hoverflies and lacewings
To attract pests and poison them
124576.e: Many beneficial insects need nectar and pollen as food, while their larvae eat aphids. Flower strips therefore increase natural pest control.
124576.m: Flower strips encourage beneficial insects in the field.

124577.q: What are pheromone traps mainly used for in integrated pest management?
a: To monitor the flight of pests
124577.e: The traps use sex attractants to lure males of certain species. The numbers caught show when control is needed.
124577.m: Pheromone traps show when pests are flying.

124578.q: How does the mating disruption technique used against grape moths in Swiss vineyards work?
a: Lots of sex attractant stops males from finding the females
Loud noises drive the moths away
Light traps lure all insects away
A poison kills the caterpillars in the berries
124578.e: Dispensers release large amounts of pheromone in the vineyard, so the males cannot find the scent trail of the females. Without mating there are no harmful caterpillars.
124578.m: Mating disruption stops grape moths from mating.

124579.q: Why should you switch between active substances with different modes of action in integrated pest management?
a: To avoid resistance in pests and pathogens
Because otherwise active substances evaporate immediately
So that the plants grow faster
Because the law forbids it for every crop
124579.e: If the same active substance is always used, resistant individuals survive and multiply. Switching modes of action slows down this selection.
124579.m: Switching active substances slows down the development of resistance.

124580.q: Why is plant resistance based on many genes usually longer-lasting than resistance based on just one gene?
a: The pathogen would have to develop many adaptations at once
Many genes make the plant bigger
Many genes prevent any mutation in the pathogen
Many genes make pesticides more effective
124580.e: A pathogen cannot overcome resistance from many genes, each with a small effect, with a single mutation. Resistance from just one gene, on the other hand, is often broken quickly.
124580.m: Resistance from many genes is hard for pathogens to overcome.

124581.q: What is an important aim of breeding crops for resistance?
a: Getting plants with as few genes as possible
124581.e: Varieties that fight off diseases themselves need fewer sprays. That protects the environment and saves money, even though pathogens never disappear completely.

124582.q: Where do the resistance genes that breeders cross into crops often come from?
a: From wild relatives of the crop
124582.e: Wild species have developed alongside pathogens over a long time and often carry defence genes. For example, resistance from wild potatoes was crossed into cultivated potatoes.
124582.m: Wild relatives are an important source of resistance genes.

124583.q: What is it called when a pathogen overcomes a variety’s resistance that used to work?
124583.e: Through mutations, a pathogen can lose the feature by which the plant recognises it. Then the variety suddenly becomes susceptible.
124583.m: In a resistance breakdown, the pathogen overcomes the variety’s defences.

124584.q: What does the abbreviation PIWI stand for in grape varieties?
124584.e: PIWI varieties are bred to be much more resistant to mildew diseases. They need far fewer pesticides.

124585.q: Which fungus-resistant red wine variety was bred by the Swiss research institute Agroscope?
124585.e: Divico is much more resistant to downy and powdery mildew than traditional varieties. Merlot, Cornalin and Humagne Rouge are older, susceptible varieties.
124585.m: Divico is a Swiss-bred PIWI grape variety.

124586.q: Why do breeders like to combine several resistance genes against the same pathogen in one variety?
a: The pathogen then has to overcome several hurdles at once
The variety then no longer needs pollinators
124586.e: Several stacked resistance genes make it hard for the pathogen to break through the defences. The resistance therefore lasts longer.
124586.m: Several resistance genes together make the defence longer-lasting.

124587.q: Which technique uses DNA features to select plants with resistance genes while they are still seedlings?
124587.e: With molecular markers you can tell in the lab whether a plant carries a resistance gene, without infecting it first. This saves a lot of time in breeding.
124587.m: Marker-assisted selection finds resistance genes directly in the genome.

124588.q: What is the genetic engineering transfer of genes from the same species or a crossable species called?
124588.e: In cisgenesis, for example, resistance genes from wild potatoes are built directly into a potato variety. In transgenesis, by contrast, the genes come from unrelated species.
124588.m: In cisgenesis, the transferred genes come from crossable species.

124589.q: What kind of pathogen is Xylella fastidiosa?
124589.e: Xylella fastidiosa is a Gram-negative bacterium. It is considered one of the most dangerous plant pathogens in the world.

124590.q: In which plant tissue does Xylella fastidiosa live?
124590.e: The bacterium multiplies in the xylem and blocks the vessels. The plant can then no longer transport water and dries out.
124590.m: Xylella blocks the xylem of plants.

124591.q: Which insect is considered the main carrier of Xylella fastidiosa in Europe?
124591.e: The meadow spittlebug sucks xylem sap and takes up the bacteria. When it feeds on the next plant, it passes on the pathogen.
124591.m: The meadow spittlebug spreads Xylella fastidiosa.

124592.q: In which Italian region did Xylella fastidiosa cause a large die-off of olive trees from 2013?
124592.e: Millions of olive trees died in Apulia, including centuries-old ones. The outbreak was the first major detection of the bacterium in Europe.
124592.m: Xylella fastidiosa destroyed many olive trees in Apulia.

124593.q: How can you recognise plants that are badly infected with Xylella fastidiosa?
a: Leaves dry up and branches die
The fruit becomes twice as big
124593.e: The bacterium blocks the water pipes. The leaves turn brown from the edge and dry up, and whole branches or trees die.

124594.q: What is the most important measure when Xylella fastidiosa is found in a new area?
a: Removing infected and nearby host plants
124594.e: Infected plants cannot be cured in the field. That is why infected plants and host plants in a zone around them are removed.
124594.m: The only thing that helps against Xylella is removing infected plants.

124595.q: What status does Xylella fastidiosa have in Switzerland?
a: Priority quarantine organism that must be reported
124595.e: Quarantine organisms are especially dangerous pests whose introduction must be prevented. A suspected case must be reported to the cantonal plant protection service.
124595.m: Xylella fastidiosa must be reported in Switzerland.

124596.q: What does the Latin species name “fastidiosa” mean in the bacterium Xylella fastidiosa?
124596.e: The name refers to the fact that the bacterium can only be grown in the lab on special nutrient media and very slowly. “Xylella” refers to the xylem.
124596.m: “Fastidiosa” means demanding, because the bacterium is hard to grow.

124597.q: How do parasitic wasps fight the European corn borer in Swiss maize fields?
a: They lay their eggs in the pest’s eggs
They eat the adult moths in flight
They sting the maize plants with poison
They pass a fungal disease to the maize
124597.e: The tiny parasitic wasps parasitise the eggs of the corn borer. Instead of a caterpillar, a new wasp hatches from them.
124597.m: Parasitic wasps develop inside the eggs of the corn borer.

124598.q: Which bacterium makes a protein that specifically kills caterpillars and is used as a biological insecticide?
124598.e: The Bt toxin is activated in the alkaline gut of caterpillars and destroys the gut wall. It is harmless to humans and most other animals.
124598.m: Bacillus thuringiensis provides a biological product against caterpillars.

124599.q: Which beneficial organism is often used in greenhouses against the two-spotted spider mite?
124599.e: The predatory mite eats spider mites and their eggs and multiplies quickly. It is released in greenhouses on purpose.
124599.m: Predatory mites eat spider mites in greenhouses.

124600.q: What kind of living thing was successfully used in Australia against introduced, rampant prickly pears (Opuntia)?
a: A moth whose caterpillars ate the cacti
A virus that attacked the cacti
A kind of goat that eats cacti
A fungus that destroyed the roots
124600.e: The caterpillars of the cactus moth Cactoblastis cactorum ate their way through the prickly pears that had overgrown huge areas of grazing land. The example is a classic of biological control.
124600.m: A moth freed Australia from rampant prickly pears.

124602.q: Which pathogen is used in fruit growing as a biological product against codling moth caterpillars?
124602.e: The codling moth granulovirus only attacks the caterpillars of this moth species. It is harmless to beneficial insects, bees and humans.
124602.m: A granulovirus helps against the codling moth.

124603.q: Which organisms are used in the garden against the soil-dwelling larvae of the vine weevil?
124603.e: The tiny roundworms enter the larvae and kill them with the help of bacteria. They are applied with the watering water.
124603.m: Nematodes fight vine weevil larvae in the soil.

124604.q: What is meant by classical biological pest control?
a: Introducing a natural enemy from the home region of an introduced pest
124604.e: Introduced species often have no natural enemies in their new home. In the classical method, a specialised enemy is brought in from the region of origin.
124604.m: Classical biological control brings in natural enemies from the pest’s homeland.

124605.q: What is the importance of the tobacco mosaic virus in the history of biology?
a: It was the first virus to be discovered
It was the first bacterium to be discovered
It was the first cloned organism
It was the first known prion
124605.e: At the end of the 19th century, researchers showed that the cause of mosaic disease is smaller than bacteria. This was the beginning of virology.
124605.m: The tobacco mosaic virus was the first virus to be discovered.

124606.q: Which Russian researcher showed in 1892 that the cause of tobacco mosaic disease passes through bacterial filters?
124606.e: Ivanovsky filtered the sap of diseased tobacco plants through porcelain filters that hold back bacteria. The sap was still infectious.
124606.m: Ivanovsky proved that the tobacco mosaic agent passes through bacterial filters.

124607.q: Why was the discovery of the tobacco mosaic virus at the end of the 19th century so important?
a: It was the first virus to be discovered
It was the first bacterium to be discovered
It was the first known mould
It was the first remedy against plant diseases
124607.e: Researchers such as Ivanovsky and Beijerinck showed that the agent even passes through bacterial filters. So the tobacco mosaic virus became the first known virus.
124607.m: The tobacco mosaic virus was the first virus to be discovered.

124608.q: What shape and what genetic material does the tobacco mosaic virus have?
124608.e: The virus consists of a strand of RNA with many identical coat proteins arranged around it in a spiral. This forms a rigid rod.
124608.m: The tobacco mosaic virus is a rod-shaped RNA virus.

124609.q: What did the crystallisation of the tobacco mosaic virus in 1935 show?
a: Viruses can be crystallised like chemical substances
Viruses can multiply without a host
124609.e: Wendell Stanley showed that a virus can be crystallised like a chemical substance. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this in 1946.
124609.m: The tobacco mosaic virus can be crystallised like a chemical substance.

124610.q: Which scientist, known for X-ray images of DNA, later studied the structure of the tobacco mosaic virus?
124610.e: Using X-ray diffraction, Rosalind Franklin worked out how the RNA lies inside the protein coat. Her work contributed a lot to understanding virus structures.
124610.m: Rosalind Franklin also studied the structure of the tobacco mosaic virus.

124611.q: How is the tobacco mosaic virus mainly spread?
a: Mechanically via hands, tools and plant sap
Only through root contact in water
124611.e: The virus is very stable and gets into the plant through small wounds. Tobacco products can also contain infectious viruses, which is why hand washing is important in horticulture.
124611.m: The tobacco mosaic virus is mainly spread mechanically.

124612.q: What did experiments in the 1950s show when the RNA and the coat protein of the tobacco mosaic virus were separated and then mixed again?
a: The parts assembled themselves into infectious viruses
The parts turned into fungal spores
124612.e: Heinz Fraenkel-Conrat and Robley Williams showed that the virus builds itself. This principle is called self-assembly.
124612.m: The tobacco mosaic virus can assemble itself from its building blocks.

124613.q: What is the scientific name of the Japanese beetle?
124613.e: Popillia japonica comes from Japan and belongs to the scarab beetles. Leptinotarsa decemlineata is the Colorado potato beetle, Melolontha melolontha the cockchafer.
124613.m: The scientific name of the Japanese beetle is Popillia japonica.

124614.q: In which canton was the Japanese beetle first found in Switzerland in 2017?
124614.e: The beetle spread from northern Italy, where it has been present since 2014, into southern Switzerland. Later there were also finds north of the Alps.
124614.m: The Japanese beetle first reached Switzerland in Ticino.

124615.q: How can you tell the Japanese beetle apart from the similar native garden chafer?
a: By white tufts of hair on the sides and at the end of the abdomen
By red dots on the wing cases
124615.e: The Japanese beetle has five white tufts of hair on each side and two at the end of the abdomen. The garden chafer does not have these tufts.
124615.m: White tufts of hair give away the Japanese beetle.

124616.q: What colours does an adult Japanese beetle have?
a: A metallic green head and copper-brown wing cases
124616.e: The head and the shield behind it shine metallic green, and the wing cases are copper-coloured. The beetle is about one centimetre long.
124616.m: The Japanese beetle has a green head and copper-brown wings.

124617.q: What damage do the larvae of the Japanese beetle cause?
a: They eat the roots of lawns and meadows
They eat fruit on the tree
They suck blood from grazing animals
124617.e: The grubs live in the soil and feed on grass roots. Infested lawn turns brown and can be lifted like a carpet.
124617.m: Japanese beetle larvae eat the roots of grass.

124618.q: How do adult Japanese beetles damage plant leaves?
a: By skeletonising, leaving only the leaf veins
By spinning webs round the leaves
By rolling and mining the leaves
124618.e: The beetles eat away the leaf tissue between the veins, leaving a fine skeleton. They attack several hundred plant species, including vines, fruit trees and roses.
124618.m: Japanese beetles skeletonise the leaves of many plants.

124619.q: Why is watering lawns sometimes banned in areas infested with the Japanese beetle?
a: Because eggs and larvae need moist soil
Because the beetles drink water and become poisonous
Because otherwise the lawn grows too fast
124619.e: The females prefer to lay their eggs in moist lawns. Dry soil in summer makes it harder for the larvae to develop.
124619.m: Dry lawns slow down the spread of the Japanese beetle.

124620.q: What should you do in Switzerland if you find a Japanese beetle outside known infested areas?
a: Report the find to the cantonal plant protection service
Let it go because it is protected
Take it to the nearest forest
124620.e: The Japanese beetle is a quarantine organism whose spread must be prevented. Early reports help to fight new outbreaks quickly.
124620.m: Finds of the Japanese beetle must be reported to the plant protection service.

124621.q: Which country was the Japanese beetle brought into at the beginning of the 20th century, where it caused great damage?
124621.e: The beetle was discovered around 1916 in the eastern USA, probably brought in with plant material. There it has no natural enemies, and it spread widely.
124621.m: Outside Asia, the Japanese beetle first spread in the USA.

124720.q: In which unit is relative VO2max usually given?
a: ml per minute per kg of body weight
Litres per kg of body weight
124720.e: So that people of different weights can be compared, oxygen uptake is divided by body weight. This gives the unit ml/(min·kg).
124720.m: Relative VO2max is given in millilitres per minute per kilogram.

124721.q: An athlete weighs 70 kg and has an absolute VO2max of 4.2 l/min. What is her relative VO2max?
124721.m: For relative VO2max, you divide absolute VO2max by body weight.

124722.q: Which athletes typically reach the highest relative VO2max values?
124722.e: Cross-country skiing uses a very large amount of muscle mass over a long time. Top athletes in this sport therefore reach exceptionally high values of oxygen uptake.
124722.m: Endurance athletes such as cross-country skiers have particularly high VO2max values.

124723.q: Which factor mainly limits VO2max in healthy, trained people?
a: The pumping capacity of the heart
The strength of the breathing muscles
124723.e: In healthy people, the main limit is the transport of oxygen by the cardiovascular system. Cardiac output determines how much oxygen-rich blood reaches the muscles.
124723.m: VO2max is limited mainly by the performance of the heart.

124724.q: Which adaptation of the heart through endurance training increases VO2max?
124724.e: Endurance training enlarges the heart and its stroke volume. As a result it pumps more oxygen-rich blood into the muscles per minute, and VO2max rises.
124724.m: Endurance training increases stroke volume and therefore VO2max.

124725.q: How does VO2max typically change with increasing age in adulthood?
124725.e: From young adulthood, VO2max slowly falls, partly because the maximum heart rate decreases. Regular endurance training can slow down this decline.

124726.q: Which field test estimates endurance capacity from the distance you can run in 12 minutes?
124726.e: In the Cooper test, you run as far as possible in 12 minutes. VO2max can be roughly estimated from the distance.
124726.m: The Cooper test measures the distance run in 12 minutes.

124727.q: Which method is used to measure VO2max directly?
124727.e: In spiroergometry, you breathe into a mask during an exercise test. A device analyses the breathing gases and so measures oxygen uptake directly.
124727.m: Spiroergometry measures oxygen uptake through the breathing gases.

124728.q: What does the anaerobic threshold describe?
a: The highest workload at which blood lactate stays steady
The point at which breathing stops completely
The workload at maximum heart rate
The lowest workload at which you sweat
124728.e: At the anaerobic threshold, the production and breakdown of lactate are only just balanced. If the workload is increased further, lactate in the blood keeps rising.
124728.m: At the anaerobic threshold, lactate production and breakdown are only just in balance.

124729.q: What is measured in a stepwise lactate test to determine the anaerobic threshold?
a: The lactate concentration in the blood
The blood sugar in the urine
The cholesterol level in the blood
124729.e: At each stage of the test, a drop of blood is usually taken from the earlobe. The threshold can be read from the course of the lactate values.
124729.m: The anaerobic threshold is often determined from blood lactate.

124730.q: Which form of training improves the anaerobic threshold in a particularly targeted way?
a: Longer runs at a pace just at the threshold
Short maximum sprints of five seconds
Pure strength training with heavy weights
124730.e: In threshold training, you run for 20 to 40 minutes at a pace that is just possible without lactate rising. In this way the body learns to break down more lactate.
124730.m: Training close to the threshold pushes the threshold upwards.

124731.q: What happens during a workload clearly above the anaerobic threshold?
124731.e: Above the threshold, more lactate is produced than broken down. It builds up, and the workload can only be kept up for a limited time.
124731.m: Above the anaerobic threshold, lactate builds up in the blood.

124732.q: Roughly how long can a well-trained person keep up a workload at the anaerobic threshold?
124732.e: At the threshold the workload is high, but the metabolism is still in balance. Trained people can therefore keep it up for roughly half an hour to an hour.
124732.m: A workload at the anaerobic threshold can be kept up for about half an hour to an hour.

124733.q: How does targeted endurance training affect the anaerobic threshold?
a: It shifts towards a higher performance
It shifts towards a lower performance
124733.e: Through training, the body can break down more lactate and supply more energy aerobically. That is why the threshold is afterwards at a higher speed or power.
124733.m: Endurance training shifts the anaerobic threshold towards higher performance.

124734.q: Which test tries to determine the anaerobic threshold from a kink in the heart rate curve?
124734.e: The Italian Francesco Conconi described a kink after which the heart rate no longer rises in a straight line with speed. The method is scientifically disputed, because the kink does not appear in everyone.
124734.m: The Conconi test looks for the threshold from a kink in the pulse curve.

124735.q: How does breathing change when you raise the workload clearly above the threshold?
124735.e: More acid in the blood is buffered by breathing out more carbon dioxide. That is why breathing rises more steeply than the workload, which is used as the ventilatory threshold.
124735.m: Above the threshold, breathing rises disproportionately.

124736.q: What is the threshold called that is determined by breathing gas analysis instead of blood samples?
124736.e: In spiroergometry, the ventilatory thresholds can be recognised from changes in breathing and carbon dioxide output. No blood lactate measurement is needed for this.
124736.m: The ventilatory threshold is determined from the breathing gases.

a: Performance rises above the starting level after recovery
The body replaces muscle with fat
Heart rate rises above its maximum during training
124737.e: After exercise the body not only recovers but builds its reserves up a little above the previous level. This raised level is called supercompensation.
124737.m: In supercompensation, performance rises above the starting level after recovery.

124738.q: In which order do the phases take place in the supercompensation model?
124738.e: First, performance falls because of the load. Then the body recovers and rises briefly above the starting level.
124738.m: Load and fatigue are followed by recovery and supercompensation.

124739.q: According to the model, what happens if the next training stimulus comes far too late?
a: Performance falls back to the starting level
124739.e: Supercompensation only lasts for a limited time. If no new stimulus comes, the gain is lost again.
124739.m: If the next stimulus comes too late, the training gain is lost again.

124740.q: According to the model, what happens if new strong stimuli are always applied before recovery?
124740.e: If you train again before the body has recovered, the fatigue adds up. Performance then decreases instead of increasing.
124740.m: Breaks that are too short between hard training sessions lower performance.

124741.q: Which energy store is often given as an example of supercompensation?
124741.e: After being emptied by long endurance exercise and followed by a carbohydrate-rich diet, the glycogen stores fill up beyond their previous level. This is considered a well-documented example of supercompensation.
124741.m: Muscle glycogen is a textbook example of supercompensation.

124742.q: Why is the supercompensation model considered highly simplified?
a: Different body systems recover at different speeds
The body cannot recover after training at all
Training has no effect on performance
124742.e: Energy stores, muscle structures, tendons and the nervous system take different amounts of time to recover. A single curve cannot show this accurately.
124742.m: The supercompensation model is a simplification because systems recover at different speeds.

124743.q: According to the stimulus threshold rule, which stimuli trigger an adaptation of the body?
124743.e: Below-threshold stimuli cause no adaptation, and stimuli that are too strong can do harm. Only stimuli that are strong enough, above the threshold, produce a training effect.
124743.m: Only training stimuli above the threshold cause adaptation.

124744.q: Why must the training load be increased over time?
a: Familiar stimuli become too weak after adaptation
Otherwise the body forgets the technique
Otherwise the risk of injury rises sharply
Otherwise the pulse would stay too high permanently
124744.e: After adaptation, the same stimulus is no longer big enough for the body. That is why the principle of progressive overload calls for new, slightly higher stimuli.
124744.m: Further progress needs gradually increasing loads.

124745.q: Which nutritional strategy before a marathon makes deliberate use of supercompensation?
124745.e: In carb-loading, a lot of carbohydrates are eaten in the days before the competition and training is reduced. As a result the stores are particularly full on race day.
124745.m: Carb-loading fills up the carbohydrate stores particularly well before a competition.

a: Planned alternation of effort and recovery
Continuous effort at the same pace
124746.e: In interval training, phases of effort and breaks follow each other according to a fixed plan. In this way you can train at high intensities for longer in total.
124746.m: Interval training alternates between effort and recovery according to a plan.

124747.q: In the interval method, what is the incomplete break called after which you already start the next effort?
124747.e: In the rewarding break, you only recover partly, usually until the pulse has fallen to a certain value. The first part of recovery is the fastest and is therefore the most worthwhile.
124747.m: In the interval method, you take incomplete, rewarding breaks.

124748.q: A Tabata protocol consists of 8 rounds, each with 20 seconds of effort and 10 seconds of rest. How long does it last in total?
124748.e: One round lasts 20 + 10 = 30 seconds. 8 × 30 seconds gives 240 seconds, which is 4 minutes.
124748.m: A classic Tabata workout lasts four minutes.

124749.q: What is true of intensive interval training compared with extensive interval training?
124749.e: Extensive interval training works with medium intensity and many repetitions. Intensive interval training uses higher intensities with fewer repetitions.
124749.m: Intensive interval training means higher intensity with fewer repetitions.

124750.q: What does the abbreviation HIIT stand for?
124750.e: HIIT stands for high-intensity interval training. Short, very hard efforts alternate with recovery phases.
124750.m: HIIT stands for high-intensity interval training.

124751.q: How does the repetition method differ from the interval method?
a: By having no breaks at all
By training only on a bike
124751.e: In the repetition method, you recover almost completely before the next effort. This allows each repetition to be done at very high intensity.
124751.m: The repetition method works with complete breaks.

124752.q: In classic interval training, how can you tell that the rewarding break is over?
124752.e: In the Freiburg interval training method, the next effort starts when the pulse has fallen to about 120 to 130 beats per minute.
124752.m: The pulse shows when the rewarding break is over.

124753.q: What is the Swedish “speed play” called, in which changes of pace across country are freely chosen?
124753.e: Fartlek means speed play in Swedish. You change the pace playfully depending on the terrain and how you feel.
124753.m: Fartlek is playful running training with free changes of pace.

a: The intervals first get longer and then shorter again
All intervals are exactly the same length
You only run uphill and never downhill
The breaks are always longer than the effort
124754.e: One example is 200, 400, 600, 400, 200 metres. The length of the sections rises and falls again like a pyramid.
124754.m: In pyramid intervals, the lengths of the sections rise and fall again.

a: A hormone of the adrenal gland
124755.e: Lactate is formed when glucose is broken down and a lot of energy has to be supplied quickly. It is the anion, or salt, of lactic acid.
124755.m: Lactate is the salt of lactic acid.

124756.q: Where is a small blood sample usually taken in a lactate test in sport?
124756.e: A drop of capillary blood is enough to measure lactate. It is usually taken from the earlobe or the fingertip.
124756.m: A drop of blood from the earlobe is enough for the lactate test.

124757.q: How is a typical stepwise lactate test set up?
a: The workload increases in steps, with a measurement after each step
You run once as fast as possible and measure afterwards
You only measure at rest before breakfast
The workload decreases in steps until you stop
124757.e: On the treadmill or bike ergometer, the workload is raised in fixed steps. Lactate is measured after each step, and this gives the lactate performance curve.
124757.m: In the stepwise lactate test, the workload is increased step by step.

124759.q: Which lactate value is often called the aerobic threshold?
124759.e: At the aerobic threshold, lactate begins to rise above the resting value for the first time. Many models assume a value of around 2 mmol/l for this.
124759.m: The aerobic threshold is often at about 2 mmol/l of lactate.

124760.q: What does a shift to the right of the lactate performance curve between two tests show?
a: A fault in the measuring device
124760.e: A shift to the right means that the same lactate value is only reached at a higher speed. So the body works more economically at the same performance.
124760.m: A lactate curve shifted to the right shows better endurance.

124761.q: Why is a lactate test repeated several times over a season?
a: To check progress and adjust training zones
To fill the muscles with lactate
124761.e: If the lactate performance curve changes, the right training intensities change too. Repeated tests show the success of training and allow the training zones to be set again.
124761.m: Repeated lactate tests make training progress visible.

124762.q: What can happen in a lactate test if the glycogen stores are empty beforehand?
a: The lactate values come out lower and suggest better fitness
The lactate values rise extremely high
The test cannot be carried out at all
The heart rate stays at its resting value
124762.e: With little glycogen, less glucose can be broken down, so less lactate is formed. The curve seems to shift to the right even though fitness is not better.
124762.m: Empty glycogen stores can distort a lactate test.

124763.q: What is meant by overtraining syndrome?
a: A lasting drop in performance from training without enough recovery
Brief tiredness after a single hard training session
Muscle gain from a great deal of strength training
Better performance from training every day
124763.e: In overtraining syndrome, the balance between training load and recovery is wrong over a long period. Performance falls despite, or because of, the training and does not recover in a few days.
124763.m: Overtraining happens when too little recovery follows the training load.

124764.q: What is a short-term overload called, after which performance recovers within days to weeks?
124764.e: In functional overreaching, you deliberately train hard. After recovery, performance is often even better, unlike with real overtraining.
124764.m: Functional overreaching is a short-term overload you can recover from.

124765.e: Typical signs are tiredness, poor sleep, irritability and falling motivation. These signs remain despite short breaks.
124765.m: Lasting tiredness and poor sleep can point to overtraining.

124766.q: What is the principle called by which the body becomes fitter than before after training and enough recovery?
124766.e: After training, the body is tired at first. During recovery it builds its reserves up beyond the old level. Without recovery, overtraining threatens.
124766.m: Supercompensation needs both training load and recovery.

124767.q: What is the most important measure in overtraining syndrome?
a: Clearly reducing training and allowing recovery
Taking part in several competitions in quick succession
124767.e: Only a clear reduction in the load allows the body to recover. Sleep, a balanced diet and reducing stress also help.
124767.m: In overtraining, less training and more recovery help most.

124768.q: How does overtraining often affect the immune system?
a: The immune system stays completely unaffected
124768.e: Permanent overload weakens the body's defences. Overtrained athletes therefore often suffer more from colds and other infections.
124768.m: Overtraining makes you more prone to infections.

124769.q: How long does recovery from real overtraining syndrome often take?
124769.e: Severe overtraining needs a lot of time to heal. That is why prevention through good training planning is so important.
124769.m: Recovery from overtraining syndrome can take months.

124770.q: Which simple measurement in the morning can be a warning sign of overtraining?
a: A resting pulse that is raised for several days
124770.e: Many athletes measure their resting pulse after waking up. If it is clearly above the usual value for several days, this can point to insufficient recovery.
124770.m: A raised resting pulse in the morning can point to overload.

124771.q: What is an example of active recovery?
a: An afternoon nap on the sofa
124771.e: In active recovery, you move gently without putting strain on the body. Blood flow is stimulated, while sauna, massage and sleep count as passive measures.
124771.m: Gentle movement at low intensity is active recovery.

124772.q: Why do people often jog gently to cool down after intense exercise?
a: The blood flow helps to break down lactate
It makes the muscles stronger immediately
It raises the pulse to its maximum
124772.e: Light movement keeps blood flow high. As a result lactate is broken down faster than when standing completely still.
124772.m: A gentle cool-down jog speeds up the breakdown of lactate.

124773.q: Why are drinks with a little salt recommended after a lot of sweating?
a: Sodium is lost with the sweat too
124773.e: Sweat is not just water; it also contains electrolytes, especially sodium. A slightly salty drink helps to replace both.
124773.m: After heavy sweating, the body needs water and salt.

124774.q: With which kind of muscle work does muscle soreness develop particularly easily?
124774.e: Eccentric work means that the muscle is lengthened under tension, for example when running downhill. This causes a particularly large number of micro-injuries.
124774.m: Braking movements such as running downhill easily cause muscle soreness.

124775.q: When does muscle soreness usually reach its peak?
a: Around 24 to 72 hours after the exercise
124775.e: Muscle soreness appears with a delay, which is why it is called DOMS, delayed onset muscle soreness. The pain is usually strongest one to three days after the exercise.
124775.m: Muscle soreness is usually worst one to three days after training.

124776.q: Which nutrients after training mainly support refilling the glycogen stores?
124776.e: Glycogen is the storage form of glucose. Carbohydrates supply the material for it, often combined with some protein for muscle repair.

124777.q: Which measure uses cold water to reduce the feeling of pain and inflammatory reactions after exercise?
124777.e: In cold water immersion, for example in an ice bath, the blood vessels narrow. Many athletes feel less pain afterwards, but the effect on adaptation is disputed.
124777.m: An ice bath is a form of cold water immersion for recovery.

124778.q: What is the increased oxygen uptake after the end of intense exercise called?
124778.e: EPOC stands for excess post-exercise oxygen consumption. After exercise, the body still uses more oxygen to refill stores and restore balance.
124778.m: After intense exercise, oxygen uptake stays raised for a while.

124779.q: What is meant by periodisation in sport?
a: Dividing the training year into sections with goals
124779.e: In periodisation, training is divided into periods with different focuses. The aim is to reach peak form at the right time.
124779.m: Periodisation divides training into sections with different goals.

124780.q: What is the smallest planning unit in periodisation called, which usually covers about a week?
124780.e: Microcycles usually last a few days to a week. Several microcycles together form a mesocycle.
124780.m: A microcycle is the smallest training unit.

124781.q: How long does a mesocycle typically last?
124781.e: A mesocycle brings together several training weeks with a common focus. It often ends with a week of reduced load.
124781.m: A mesocycle covers several training weeks.

124782.q: Which three periods does Lev Matveyev's classic periodisation distinguish?
124782.e: Matveyev divided the training year into a preparation period, a competition period and a transition period. This model shaped training theory for a long time.
124782.m: Classic periodisation has preparation, competition and transition.

a: Reducing the training volume before a competition
Increasing the volume shortly before the race
124783.e: In tapering, the volume is reduced before an important competition, while the intensity is partly kept. In this way the body recovers and reaches peak form.
124783.m: Tapering means less training before an important competition.

a: Training blocks concentrate on a few target abilities
All abilities are always trained at the same time
Training takes place in only one block a year
There are no competitions during the season
124784.e: In block periodisation, described among others by Vladimir Issurin, each block focuses on only a small number of abilities. The blocks follow one another in a planned sequence.
124784.m: Block periodisation trains a few abilities in a targeted way in each block.

a: Two competition peaks in one year
124785.e: In double periodisation, there are two preparation and competition periods per year. One example is athletes with an indoor and an outdoor season.
124785.m: Double periodisation plans two peaks a year.

124786.q: What is the aim of the transition period after the season?
a: Physical and mental recovery while staying active
Increasing competition performance to the maximum
Taking part in as many extra competitions as possible
124786.e: After the competition period, the training load is greatly reduced. You stay active with varied, easy exercise and recharge your energy for the new season.
124786.m: The transition period is for recovery after the season.

124787.q: What does heart rate variability describe?
a: The variation in the intervals between heartbeats
The difference between resting and maximum heart rate
How loud the heart sounds are
The difference in pulse between the two arms
124787.e: The heart does not beat like a metronome. The time intervals between consecutive beats vary slightly, and this variation is called HRV.
124787.m: Heart rate variability measures how much the intervals between heartbeats vary.

124788.q: What does a resting HRV that is high compared with your own normal value usually indicate?
124788.e: A well-rested body reacts flexibly, and the intervals between beats vary more. Low values compared with your normal value, on the other hand, can point to stress or strain.
124788.m: A high resting HRV usually indicates good recovery.

124789.q: Through which cranial nerve does the parasympathetic nervous system mainly act on the heart?
124789.e: The vagus nerve slows the heartbeat and causes variations from beat to beat. Many HRV measures therefore reflect its activity.
124789.m: The vagus nerve calms the heart.

124790.q: What do many athletes use to measure their heart rate variability in everyday life?
a: A blood pressure cuff on the leg
124790.e: Chest straps and many smartwatches record the intervals between heartbeats very accurately. An app then calculates the HRV from them.
124790.m: Chest straps and smartwatches can measure HRV.

124791.q: Between which peaks on an ECG are the heartbeat intervals for HRV usually measured?
124791.e: The R wave is the highest and most clearly visible spike on the ECG. The interval between two R waves is called the RR interval.
124791.m: For HRV, the intervals between R waves are measured.

124792.q: When should HRV ideally be measured for planning training?
a: In the morning after waking, at rest
At any random time of day
124792.e: HRV values react strongly to movement, food and stress. The same conditions every morning make the measurements comparable from day to day.
124792.m: HRV is best measured in the morning under the same conditions.

124793.q: How does drinking alcohol the evening before usually affect HRV during the night?
124793.e: Alcohol puts strain on the body and dampens parasympathetic recovery during sleep. That is why HRV is usually lower than normal afterwards.

124794.q: How does the heart rate change during inhalation in respiratory sinus arrhythmia?
124794.e: When you breathe in, the influence of the parasympathetic nervous system decreases and the pulse rises. When you breathe out, it falls again, which contributes to HRV.
124794.m: When you breathe in, the heart rate rises slightly.

124795.q: Above which town is Magglingen, the headquarters of the Federal Office of Sport, located?
124795.e: Magglingen lies at the southern foot of the Jura, high above Lake Biel. The town of Biel is directly below it.

124796.q: Which federal department does the Federal Office of Sport (FOSPO) belong to?
a: Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport
Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research
Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications
124796.e: Sport is part of the DDPS, which even has sport in its name. FOSPO is one of its federal offices.

124797.q: Which sports promotion programme for children and young people is run by the Federal Office of Sport?
124797.e: Jugend+Sport, or J+S for short, supports sports courses and camps in clubs and schools. It is the federal government's most important programme for children's and youth sport.
124797.m: Jugend+Sport is the federal sports promotion programme for young people.

124798.q: What is Magglingen, the home of the Federal Office of Sport, called in French?
124798.e: Magglingen lies on the language border in the Biel region, where German and French are spoken. The French name of the village is Macolin.
124798.m: Magglingen is called Macolin in French.

124799.q: Which university belongs to the Federal Office of Sport?
a: Swiss Federal Institute of Sport Magglingen
124799.e: The SFISM trains PE teachers and coaches, among others, and carries out research. It is part of the Federal Office of Sport itself.
124799.m: The Swiss Federal Institute of Sport Magglingen belongs to the Federal Office of Sport.

124800.q: In which place in Ticino does the Federal Office of Sport run a national youth sports centre?
124800.e: The Centro sportivo nazionale della gioventù in Tenero lies on Lake Maggiore. Many sports camps and training courses take place there.
124800.m: The national youth sports centre of the Confederation is in Tenero.

124801.q: Under what name was the federal school in Magglingen originally founded?
124801.e: The Federal Gymnastics and Sports School, or ETS for short, was the forerunner of today's Federal Office of Sport. The federal office and the sports university developed from it.
124801.m: The Federal Office of Sport grew out of the Federal Gymnastics and Sports School.

124802.q: Which federal law is the Confederation's promotion of sport mainly based on today?
124802.e: The Sport Promotion Act covers Jugend+Sport, school sport and elite sport, among other things. The Federal Office of Sport puts it into practice.
124802.m: Federal sports promotion is based on the Sport Promotion Act.

124803.q: Which deep abdominal muscle acts like a natural corset around the trunk?
124803.e: The transverse abdominal muscle, musculus transversus abdominis, wraps around the abdomen like a belt. It increases the pressure in the abdomen and so stabilises the spine.
124803.m: The transverse abdominal muscle stabilises the trunk like a corset.

124804.q: What is the static exercise called in which you hold your body straight on your forearms and toes?
124804.e: The plank, also called the forearm plank, trains all the trunk muscles. It is important that your head, back and legs form a straight line.
124804.m: The plank is a classic exercise for core stability.

124805.q: Which exercise mainly strengthens the back muscles of the trunk?
a: Back extensions lying on your front
124805.e: For back extensions you lie on your front and lift your upper body, or your arms and legs, slightly. The muscles along the spine do the work.
124805.m: Back extensions lying on your front strengthen the back muscles.

124806.q: Why is a stable trunk important for many sports?
a: It transfers force between the legs and arms
It lowers the maximum heart rate
124806.e: In throws, jumps or strikes, the force flows from the legs through the trunk to the arms. An unstable trunk lets energy go to waste.
124806.m: A stable trunk transfers force from the legs to the arms.

124807.q: Which English term is often used in training for the trunk muscles?
124807.e: Core means the centre. It refers to the muscles of the abdomen, back, hips and pelvis that stabilise the body in the middle.
124807.m: The trunk muscles are often called the core in training.

124808.q: Which poor posture is encouraged by weak abdominal muscles and a pelvis tilted forwards?
124808.e: When the pelvis tilts forwards, the curve of the lower spine increases. Strong abdominal and buttock muscles counteract this.
124808.m: Weak abdominal muscles can encourage a hollow back.

124809.q: Which breathing muscle forms the upper boundary of the abdominal cavity and helps stabilise the trunk?
124809.e: The diaphragm separates the chest from the abdomen. Together with the abdominal muscles, it builds up pressure in the abdomen that supports the spine.
124809.m: The diaphragm helps with breathing and with stabilising the trunk.

124810.q: Which muscles does the side plank train in particular?
a: The side muscles of the trunk
124810.e: In the side plank you hold your body sideways on one forearm. Above all, the oblique abdominal muscles and the quadratus lumborum work hard.
124810.m: The side plank strengthens the side muscles of the trunk.

124811.q: Why is a resting ECG often done during sports medical examinations?
a: To detect heart disease and rhythm disorders
To measure the strength of the leg muscles
To measure the exact size of the lungs
