124811.e: The ECG records the electrical activity of the heart. It can reveal certain heart conditions that may become dangerous during sport.
124811.m: A resting ECG can uncover dangerous heart problems in athletes.

124812.q: Which organisation publishes the worldwide list of prohibited substances and methods in sport every year?
124812.e: The World Anti-Doping Agency, WADA for short, draws up the prohibited list. National bodies and sports federations base their tests on it.
124812.m: WADA decides which substances are banned in sport.

a: A narrowing of the airways caused by physical exertion
An inflammation of the heart valves caused by sport
A hardening of the muscles after training
Feeling dizzy when standing up quickly
124813.e: In exercise-induced asthma, the bronchial tubes narrow during or after sport, often in cold, dry air. A good warm-up and medicine prescribed by a doctor help.
124813.m: Exercise-induced asthma is a narrowing of the airways caused by exertion.

124814.q: What should you do if an athlete collapses on the pitch and is no longer breathing normally?
a: Call 144, start chest compressions and use a defibrillator
Sit them up and give them water
Wait until they wake up by themselves
Drive them to hospital by car straight away
124814.e: In cardiac arrest, every minute counts. Calling for help, starting chest compressions at once and using a defibrillator greatly increase the chance of survival.
124814.m: In cardiac arrest: call for help, press, defibrillate.

124815.q: What is the name of Switzerland's national anti-doping foundation?
124815.e: Swiss Sport Integrity is the independent body for fighting doping and ethical violations in Swiss sport. It carries out doping tests.
124815.m: Swiss Sport Integrity fights doping in Swiss sport.

124816.q: What is a broken bone called that develops without an accident through repeated overuse?
124816.e: In a stress fracture, also called a fatigue fracture, many small loads cause fine cracks in the bone. Runners are often affected in the metatarsals or shin.
124816.m: Repeated overuse can lead to a stress fracture.

124817.q: What danger is there if you drink far too much plain water during a long run?
a: A dangerous lack of sodium in the blood
Low blood sugar due to a lack of protein
124817.e: Too much water dilutes the blood, while sodium is lost in sweat at the same time. This hyponatraemia can cause confusion and, in extreme cases, be life-threatening.
124817.m: Too much plain water during long exercise can lead to a lack of sodium.

124818.q: Why do many endurance athletes train at altitude for a while?
a: The lack of oxygen stimulates the production of red blood cells
The air at altitude contains more oxygen
124818.e: At altitude, the partial pressure of oxygen is lower. The body reacts by making more red blood cells and can then transport more oxygen.
124818.m: Altitude training encourages the production of red blood cells.

124819.q: Which particles were fired at the metal foil in Rutherford’s scattering experiment?
124819.e: Alpha particles from a radioactive source served as projectiles. They are positively charged and comparatively heavy.
124819.m: Rutherford fired alpha particles at the foil.

124820.q: Which metal was the very thin foil made of in Rutherford’s classic experiment?
124820.e: Gold can be hammered into extremely thin foils, only a few hundred layers of atoms thick. Gold nuclei also have a large charge, which makes the scattering easy to see.
124820.m: A gold foil was used in the Rutherford experiment.

124821.q: What did Rutherford conclude from the fact that most particles passed through the foil almost undisturbed?
a: The atom consists mostly of empty space
124821.e: If almost all particles get through without being deflected, hardly any hits anything solid. So the atom must be largely empty.
124821.m: The atom consists mostly of empty space.

124822.q: What did Rutherford conclude from the fact that a few particles were strongly deflected or even bounced back?
a: There is a tiny, positively charged, massive nucleus
The electrons are heavier than the alpha particles
The positive charge is spread evenly through the atom
124822.e: Such strong deflection is only possible if the positive charge and almost all the mass are concentrated in a very small space. Rutherford called this region the atomic nucleus.
124822.m: The scattering experiment revealed a small, positively charged atomic nucleus.

124823.q: Which atomic model was disproved by Rutherford’s scattering experiment?
124823.e: In Thomson’s model, the plum pudding model, the positive charge is spread over the whole atom. This could not explain the large deflection angles.
124823.m: The scattering experiment disproved Thomson’s plum pudding model.

124824.q: Roughly how many times larger is the diameter of an atom than that of its nucleus?
124824.e: Atoms have a diameter of about 10⁻¹⁰ m, nuclei about 10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻¹⁴ m. That gives a ratio of about 10⁴ to 10⁵.
124824.m: The nucleus is ten thousand to a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom.

124825.q: Which force deflects the alpha particles in Rutherford’s experiment?
a: The electric repulsion of the nucleus
The magnetic force of the electrons
124825.e: The alpha particle and the nucleus are both positively charged. The Coulomb force repels the alpha particle and deflects it onto a hyperbolic path.
124825.m: Coulomb repulsion deflects the alpha particles.

124826.q: Why were only very few alpha particles strongly deflected in Rutherford’s experiment?
a: Only a few passed very close to one of the tiny nuclei
The gold foil was too thick in most places
The electrons caught almost all the particles
124826.e: The nucleus takes up only a tiny part of the atom. An alpha particle is strongly repelled only if it heads almost straight at a nucleus, and that is rare.
124826.m: Strong deflections are rare because the nucleus is so small.

124827.q: Which two researchers carried out the scattering experiments under the direction of Ernest Rutherford?
124827.e: Hans Geiger and his student Ernest Marsden counted the scattered alpha particles on a fluorescent screen. Rutherford interpreted the results.
124827.m: Geiger and Marsden carried out the scattering experiment for Rutherford.

124828.q: What did Niels Bohr postulate for the electrons in an atom?
a: They move on allowed orbits without radiating
They are spread evenly in the nucleus
They constantly give off light on their orbits
They stand completely still in the atom
124828.e: According to classical physics, an orbiting electron should radiate constantly and fall into the nucleus. Bohr therefore proposed stationary orbits on which no radiation is produced.
124828.m: In Bohr’s model, electrons orbit on fixed paths without losing energy.

124829.q: According to Bohr, when does an atom emit light?
a: When an electron jumps to a lower orbit
When an electron circles on its orbit
When an electron jumps to a higher orbit
124829.e: When it jumps to a lower energy level, the energy difference is released as a photon. The frequency of the light equals this difference divided by Planck’s constant.
124829.m: An atom emits light when an electron jumps to a lower level.

124830.q: Where does Bohr’s atomic model reach its limits?
a: With atoms that have several electrons
With the spectrum of the hydrogen atom
With the size of the hydrogen atom
With the ionisation energy of hydrogen
124830.e: For hydrogen, the model gives surprisingly good values. For atoms with several electrons and for many fine details of spectra it fails; there you need quantum mechanics.
124830.m: Bohr’s model works well for hydrogen but not for atoms with several electrons.

124831.q: What energy does the hydrogen electron have at level n = 2 in Bohr’s model?
124831.e: The energy is proportional to 1/n². For n equal to 2, the ground state energy is divided by 4.
124831.m: The energy levels in hydrogen decrease with 1 over n².

124832.q: What energy does the photon have that is emitted when the hydrogen electron moves from n = 3 to n = 2?
124832.e: ΔE is 13.6 eV · (1/4 minus 1/9), which equals 13.6 eV · 5/36, so about 1.89 eV. This photon is in the red part of visible light.
124832.m: The photon energy equals the difference between two energy levels.

124833.q: Roughly how large is the Bohr radius?
124833.e: The Bohr radius is about 5.29 · 10⁻¹¹ m. This is the radius of the innermost orbit in the hydrogen atom.
124833.m: The Bohr radius is about five hundredths of a nanometre.

124834.q: In Bohr’s model, how many times larger is the orbit radius for n = 3 than for n = 1?
124834.e: The orbit radii grow with n². For n equal to 3, this gives 3² equals 9.
124834.m: In Bohr’s model, the orbit radii grow with the square of the principal quantum number.

124835.q: According to Bohr’s quantum condition, which quantity is a whole-number multiple of h/(2π)?
a: The orbital angular momentum of the electron
124835.e: Bohr required that the angular momentum can only take the values n · ħ. The allowed orbits and energies follow from this.
124835.m: According to Bohr, the electron’s angular momentum is quantised.

124836.q: What is the series of hydrogen lines called whose transitions end in the ground state n = 1?
124836.e: Transitions to the ground state release a particularly large amount of energy. The lines of the Lyman series are therefore in the ultraviolet.
124836.m: The Lyman series ends in the ground state and lies in the ultraviolet.

124837.q: What is meant by the mass defect of an atomic nucleus?
a: The nucleus is lighter than its individual nucleons together
The nucleus is heavier than its nucleons together
Some of the electrons are missing from the atom
The nucleus has too few neutrons
124837.e: If you weigh all the protons and neutrons separately and compare them with the finished nucleus, some mass is missing. This difference is called the mass defect.
124837.m: An atomic nucleus is lighter than the sum of its building blocks.

124838.q: In which unit are masses often given in nuclear and particle physics?
124838.e: Because mass and energy are equivalent, you divide an energy by c² and get a mass. For example, the proton has a mass of about 938 MeV/c².
124838.m: Particle masses are often given in MeV/c².

124839.q: According to E = m·c², how much energy would be released if 1 gram of mass were converted completely (c = 3 · 10⁸ m/s)?
124839.e: E = 0.001 kg · (3 · 10⁸ m/s)² = 0.001 · 9 · 10¹⁶ J = 9 · 10¹³ J. That is about 25 million kilowatt hours.
124839.m: Even one gram of mass corresponds to an enormous amount of energy.

124840.q: A mass defect is 1.0 · 10⁻²⁹ kg. What energy does this correspond to (c = 3.0 · 10⁸ m/s)?
124840.e: E is 1.0 · 10⁻²⁹ kg · (3.0 · 10⁸ m/s)². That gives 1.0 · 10⁻²⁹ · 9.0 · 10¹⁶ J, which equals 9.0 · 10⁻¹³ J.
124840.m: Even tiny masses correspond to large energies because c² is very large.

124841.q: How is the atomic mass unit u defined?
a: As one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
As the mass of a hydrogen atom
As one sixteenth of the mass of an oxygen atom
As the mass of an electron
124841.e: Since 1961, the atomic mass unit has been based on carbon-12. One atom of this isotope has exactly 12 u.
124841.m: The atomic mass unit is one twelfth of the mass of a C-12 atom.

124842.e: The neutron is about 0.14 % heavier than the proton. That is why a free neutron can decay into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino.
124842.m: The neutron is a little heavier than the proton.

124843.q: Looking at the masses, why is energy released when a uranium nucleus splits?
a: The products together are lighter than the starting particles
The products together are heavier than the starting particles
The mass stays exactly the same
124843.e: The fission products together have less mass than the uranium nucleus and the neutron had before. The missing mass is released as energy.
124843.m: In nuclear fission, missing mass is converted into energy.

124844.q: Roughly how much mass does the Sun lose every second through nuclear fusion?
124844.e: The Sun radiates about 3.8 · 10²⁶ W. Divided by c², that gives a mass loss of about 4 · 10⁹ kg per second.
124844.m: Every second, the Sun converts millions of tonnes of mass into energy.

124845.q: Around which elements is the maximum binding energy per nucleon found?
124845.e: The curve of binding energy per nucleon rises from the light nuclei and reaches its maximum at iron and nickel. After that it slowly falls again.
124845.m: Iron and nickel are among the most tightly bound nuclei.

124846.q: Roughly how large is the maximum binding energy per nucleon?
124846.e: The most tightly bound nuclei reach just under 8.8 MeV per nucleon. Most medium and heavy nuclei lie between about 7.5 and 8.8 MeV.
124846.m: The binding energy per nucleon is at most just under 9 MeV.

124847.q: Which nuclear building blocks make up the nucleus of deuterium, heavy hydrogen?
124847.e: Deuterium is an isotope of hydrogen. Its nucleus, the deuteron, is only weakly bound, with about 2.2 MeV.
124847.m: The deuteron consists of one proton and one neutron.

124848.q: Why can energy be obtained from very heavy nuclei by fission?
a: The fission products have a greater binding energy per nucleon
The fission products have a smaller binding energy per nucleon
Heavy nuclei have no binding energy
Neutrons bring all the energy with them
124848.e: Medium-heavy nuclei are more tightly bound than very heavy ones. In the change to more tightly bound nuclei, the difference is released as energy.
124848.m: Fission pays off because medium-heavy nuclei are more tightly bound.

124849.q: Which force holds protons and neutrons together in the atomic nucleus?
124849.e: The strong interaction acts between all nucleons and, over short distances, is much stronger than the electric repulsion of the protons. That is why the nucleus stays together.
124849.m: The strong interaction holds the atomic nucleus together.

124850.q: Roughly what range does the nuclear force between nucleons have?
124850.e: The nuclear force only acts over distances of a few femtometres. A nucleon therefore only feels its direct neighbours.
124850.m: The nuclear force has a very short range.

124851.q: Why is the binding energy per nucleon smaller for very light nuclei than for medium-heavy ones?
a: Many nucleons lie at the surface and have fewer neighbours
Electric repulsion is greatest for them
Gravity is too weak for them
124851.e: The nuclear force only acts between direct neighbours. In small nuclei, a large share of the nucleons lies at the surface and is less tightly bound. The liquid drop model describes this effect.
124851.m: Nucleons at the surface of the nucleus are less tightly bound.

124852.q: The total binding energy of a helium-4 nucleus is about 28.3 MeV. How large is the binding energy per nucleon?
124852.e: Helium-4 has 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so 4 nucleons. 28.3 MeV : 4 gives about 7.1 MeV.
124852.m: For the binding energy per nucleon, you divide by the number of nucleons.

124853.q: According to the law of radioactive decay, how does the number of nuclei that have not yet decayed decrease over time?
124853.e: The law of decay is N(t) equals N₀ · e^(−λt). In equal time intervals, the same fraction of the remaining nuclei always decays.
124853.m: Radioactive nuclei decay according to an exponential law.

124854.q: After 12 hours, only 1/16 of the nuclei of a radioactive sample are left. What is the half-life?
124854.e: 1/16 is (1/2)⁴, so 4 half-lives have passed. 12 h : 4 gives 3 h.
124854.m: From the remaining fraction, you can work out the number of half-lives.

124855.q: What does the curve N(t) of radioactive decay look like in a graph with a logarithmic N axis?
124855.e: Taking the logarithm of N(t) gives ln N equals ln N₀ minus λt. That is a straight line with a negative slope.
124855.m: An exponential decay appears as a straight line on a semi-logarithmic graph.

124856.q: What can be said about the moment a single radioactive nucleus decays?
a: It is random and cannot be predicted
It is exactly after one half-life
It depends on the age of the nucleus
124856.e: Radioactive decay is a random process. The law of decay only applies statistically to a large number of nuclei.
124856.m: When a single nucleus decays is pure chance.

124857.q: What does the unit becquerel stand for?
a: An absorbed energy of one joule per kilogram
124857.e: The becquerel is the unit of activity. A sample with 1 Bq has on average one decay per second.
124857.m: One becquerel means one decay per second.

124858.q: After how many half-lives is less than 1 % of a radioactive sample left for the first time?
124858.e: After 6 half-lives, 1/64, about 1.56 %, is left. After 7 half-lives it is 1/128, about 0.78 %.
124858.m: After seven half-lives, less than one per cent is left.

124859.q: How strongly does the half-life of radioactive nuclei depend on temperature and pressure?
a: It depends strongly on the weather
124859.e: The decay takes place in the nucleus and is practically unaffected by outside conditions. That is why it is well suited as a natural clock.
124859.m: Half-lives are practically independent of temperature and pressure.

124860.q: A sample has an activity of 6,400 Bq. What is its activity after 4 half-lives?
124860.e: The activity halves just like the number of nuclei. 6,400 : 2⁴ is 6,400 : 16, so 400 Bq.
124860.m: The activity halves with every half-life.

124861.q: How is the half-life T½ related to the decay constant λ?
124861.e: If you set N equal to N₀/2 in the law of decay, then e^(−λT½) equals 1/2. From this, T½ equals ln 2 divided by λ.
124861.m: Half-life and decay constant are inversely proportional.

124862.q: What unit does the decay constant λ have in the SI system?
124862.e: The exponent of e^(−λt) must be a number without units. That is why λ has the unit of an inverse time.
124862.m: The decay constant has the unit one per second.

124863.q: A nuclide has the decay constant λ = 0.0693 per year. What is its half-life (ln 2 ≈ 0.693)?
124863.e: T½ is ln 2 divided by λ. 0.693 : 0.0693 per year gives 10 years.
124863.m: You get the half-life by dividing ln 2 by the decay constant.

124864.q: How is the mean lifetime τ of a nuclide related to the decay constant?
124864.e: The mean lifetime is the average time until a nucleus decays. For exponential decay, it is the reciprocal of the decay constant.
124864.m: The mean lifetime is the reciprocal of the decay constant.

124865.q: A nuclide has a half-life of 5 hours. What is its decay constant (ln 2 ≈ 0.693)?
124865.e: λ is ln 2 divided by T½. 0.693 : 5 h gives about 0.139 per hour.
124865.m: The decay constant is ln 2 divided by the half-life.

124866.q: A sample contains 5 · 10⁹ nuclei with λ = 1 · 10⁻³ per second. What is its activity?
124866.e: The activity is A equals λ · N. 1 · 10⁻³ per second times 5 · 10⁹ gives 5 · 10⁶ decays per second.
124866.m: The activity is the product of decay constant and number of nuclei.

124867.q: What does a large decay constant mean for a nuclide?
a: It decays quickly and has a short half-life
It decays slowly and has a long half-life
It does not decay at all
124867.e: The larger λ, the greater the probability of decay per unit of time. The half-life is correspondingly short.
124867.m: A large decay constant means fast decay.

124868.q: How does the mean lifetime of a nuclide compare with its half-life?
a: It is about 1.44 times as long
It is exactly half as long
It is about 0.69 times as long
124868.e: τ equals T½ divided by ln 2. Because 1 : 0.693 gives about 1.44, the mean lifetime is about 44 % longer.
124868.m: The mean lifetime is longer than the half-life.

124869.q: Which isotope does radiocarbon dating use?
124869.e: Living things take in carbon from their surroundings, including a small share of radioactive C-14. After death, this decays without being replaced.
124869.m: Radiocarbon dating measures the decay of carbon-14.

124870.q: Roughly what share of the carbon in living organisms is made up of C-14 atoms?
124870.e: There is only about one C-14 atom for every trillion or so carbon atoms. That is why dating needs very sensitive measuring methods.
124870.m: Carbon-14 makes up only a tiny part of carbon.

124871.q: How is carbon-14 formed in the atmosphere?
a: Neutrons from cosmic rays convert nitrogen-14
Oxygen decays into carbon in sunlight
Volcanoes release it from inside the Earth
124871.e: Cosmic rays produce neutrons in the upper atmosphere. When one hits a nitrogen-14 nucleus, carbon-14 is formed and a proton is released.
124871.m: Carbon-14 is formed from nitrogen in the atmosphere.

124872.q: Who developed radiocarbon dating and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it?
124872.e: The American chemist Willard Libby developed the method. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.

124873.q: Why is carbon-14 suitable for dating finds?
a: It decays with a known half-life
It glows in a different colour depending on its age
It keeps forming in dead organisms
It only occurs in very old objects
124873.e: After an organism dies, no new carbon is taken in. The C-14 present decays with a half-life of about 5,700 years, so the age can be calculated from what is left.
124873.m: C-14 decays steadily and therefore serves as a clock for finds.

124874.q: Up to roughly what age can radiocarbon dating be used?
124874.e: After about nine half-lives, so little C-14 is left that it can hardly be measured. Other methods are used for older samples.
124874.m: Radiocarbon dating only reaches back a few tens of thousands of years.

124875.q: Which sample can be dated using radiocarbon dating?
a: Charcoal from a Stone Age fireplace
A lump of granite from the Alps
A bronze axe made of metal
124875.e: The method only works for material that was once alive, and only for a few tens of thousands of years. Dinosaurs are far too old, and rock and metal contain no carbon taken in biologically.

124876.q: Who first interpreted the experimental results of Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann physically as nuclear fission?
124876.e: After bombarding uranium with neutrons, Hahn and Strassmann found the much lighter barium. Lise Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch explained this as the nucleus bursting apart.
124876.m: Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained nuclear fission physically.

124878.q: Roughly how much energy is released when a single uranium-235 nucleus splits?
124878.e: About 200 MeV are released per fission. That is millions of times more per atom than in a chemical reaction.
124878.m: One uranium fission releases about 200 MeV.

124879.q: Roughly what share of natural uranium is uranium-235?
124879.e: Natural uranium is over 99 % uranium-238. For many reactors, the share of uranium-235 is therefore enriched to a few per cent.
124879.m: Natural uranium contains only very little uranium-235.

124880.q: What is meant by spontaneous fission?
a: A nucleus splits without any outside trigger
A nucleus splits after being hit by neutrons
A molecule breaks apart when heated
An electron breaks away from an atom
124880.e: Very heavy nuclei can occasionally split into two fragments by themselves. This process is a rare form of radioactive decay.
124880.m: In spontaneous fission, a nucleus splits by itself.

124881.q: Uranium-235 captures a neutron and splits into barium-141 and krypton-92. How many neutrons are released?
124881.e: Before, there are 235 + 1 = 236 nucleons. 236 minus 141 minus 92 gives 3 free neutrons.
124881.m: In nuclear reactions, the number of nucleons is conserved.

124882.q: In what form is most of the energy of a nuclear fission released at first?
a: As kinetic energy of the fission fragments
As kinetic energy of the electrons
124882.e: The two positively charged fragments repel each other and fly apart at high speed. Their kinetic energy is converted into heat in the fuel.
124882.m: The fission fragments carry most of the fission energy.

124883.q: Which fissile nuclide is formed in a reactor from uranium-238 by neutron capture and two beta decays?
124883.e: After capturing a neutron, uranium-238 becomes uranium-239. Two beta-minus decays turn this into plutonium-239, which is itself fissile.
124883.m: Plutonium-239 is formed from uranium-238 in a reactor.

124884.q: What is a nuclear chain reaction?
a: Neutrons from fissions trigger further fissions
Electrons jump to higher orbits one after another
Alpha particles are scattered by a foil
Protons fuse into helium in a chain
124884.e: Each fission releases several neutrons. If these hit further fissile nuclei, the process keeps itself going.
124884.m: In a chain reaction, fission neutrons trigger new fissions.

124885.q: What does a multiplication factor k = 1 mean in a reactor?
a: The chain reaction runs at constant output
The output grows like an avalanche
No fissions take place at all
124885.e: With k equal to 1, each fission triggers exactly one more on average. The reactor is critical and the output stays the same.
124885.m: A critical reactor has a constant output.

124886.q: What is a state with a multiplication factor k greater than 1 called?
124886.e: Then each fission triggers more than one more on average. The number of fissions grows from generation to generation.
124886.m: In a supercritical state, the number of fissions increases.

124887.q: What is meant by critical mass?
a: The minimum mass for a self-sustaining chain reaction
The mass at which a nucleus decays
The largest mass of an atomic nucleus
The mass of all neutrons in the reactor
124887.e: If there is too little fissile material, too many neutrons escape to the outside. Only from the critical mass upwards do enough remain to keep the chain going.
124887.m: Below the critical mass, a chain reaction stops.

124888.q: Which elements are often used in control rods to absorb neutrons?
124888.e: Boron and cadmium capture neutrons very effectively. If the control rods are moved deeper into the core, the output falls.
124888.m: Control rods made of boron or cadmium swallow neutrons.

124889.q: What happens when all control rods are fully inserted into the reactor core during an emergency shutdown?
124889.e: The control rods capture so many neutrons that each fission triggers less than one new one on average. The reactor becomes subcritical and the chain reaction dies out. However, the decay heat must still be cooled.
124889.m: Inserted control rods stop the chain reaction.

124890.q: Under whose leadership was the first controlled, self-sustaining chain reaction achieved in Chicago?
124890.e: Enrico Fermi led the construction of the Chicago Pile-1 reactor. In it, a controlled chain reaction was achieved for the first time.
124890.m: Enrico Fermi ran the world’s first nuclear reactor.

124891.q: In a thought model, each fission triggers exactly 2 new fissions. Starting with one, how many fissions are there in the 10th generation?
124891.e: The number doubles in each generation. In the 10th generation there are 2¹⁰, so 1024 fissions.
124891.m: With a factor greater than one, a chain reaction grows exponentially.

124892.q: Which fusion provides most of the Sun’s energy?
124892.e: In the Sun’s core, four hydrogen nuclei are fused into one helium nucleus through the proton-proton chain. This releases energy.
124892.m: The Sun gets its energy from fusing hydrogen into helium.

124893.q: Which fusion reaction is easiest to achieve on Earth?
124893.e: The reaction of deuterium and tritium has the highest reaction probability at comparatively low temperatures. That is why research reactors rely on it.
124893.m: Fusion reactors use deuterium and tritium.

124894.q: Which particle is produced alongside a helium nucleus in the fusion of deuterium and tritium?
124894.e: Deuterium (1 proton, 1 neutron) and tritium (1 proton, 2 neutrons) together make 2 protons and 3 neutrons. The helium nucleus contains 2 protons and 2 neutrons, leaving one neutron, which carries most of the energy.
124894.m: D-T fusion produces helium and a fast neutron.

124895.q: Why does nuclear fusion need extremely high temperatures?
a: The nuclei must overcome their electric repulsion
The electrons must join the nucleus
Only then is gravity switched off
124895.e: Atomic nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. Only at very high speeds do they get close enough for the nuclear force to act.
124895.m: High temperatures help nuclei overcome Coulomb repulsion.

124896.q: Roughly how hot is the core of the Sun?
124896.e: The Sun’s core is about 15 million kelvin. Together with the enormous pressure, this is enough for hydrogen fusion.
124896.m: The Sun’s core is about 15 million kelvin hot.

124897.q: From which element is tritium to be bred in future fusion power stations?
124897.e: Tritium is radioactive and hardly occurs in nature. In a breeding blanket, fusion neutrons are meant to convert lithium into tritium and helium.
124897.m: Tritium for fusion power stations is to be bred from lithium.

124898.q: What keeps the extremely hot plasma in a tokamak away from the walls?
124898.e: The plasma consists of charged particles. Strong magnetic fields force these onto ring-shaped paths, so the plasma, at over 100 million degrees, does not touch the wall.
124898.m: A tokamak holds the fusion plasma in place with magnetic fields.

124899.q: At which Swiss university is fusion research carried out with the TCV tokamak?
124899.e: The Swiss Plasma Center at EPFL runs the Tokamak à configuration variable. Among other things, it is used to study the shape of the plasma.
124899.m: EPFL in Lausanne runs the TCV tokamak.

124900.q: In which country is the ITER fusion reactor being built?
124900.e: ITER is being built in Cadarache in southern France. Several countries are financing and building the project together.
124900.m: ITER is being built in southern France.

124901.q: Which type of reactor is ITER?
124901.e: A tokamak encloses the plasma in a ring-shaped magnetic field. The word comes from Russian.

124902.q: What is ITER’s goal for the energy balance of the plasma?
a: Ten times more fusion power than heating power
As much fusion power as heating power
A hundred times more electricity than a nuclear power station
Half as much fusion power as heating power
124902.e: ITER is meant to produce about 500 MW of fusion power from about 50 MW of heating power. That corresponds to a gain factor Q of 10.
124902.m: ITER is meant to produce ten times more fusion power than is needed for heating.

124903.q: What does the Latin word “iter”, to which the name ITER alludes, mean?
124903.e: Iter is Latin for way. The name is meant to express that ITER should pave the way to producing energy from fusion.

124904.q: Roughly what plasma temperature is ITER meant to reach?
124904.e: On Earth there is none of the enormous pressure inside the Sun. That is why the plasma in ITER must be much hotter than the Sun’s core.
124904.m: The ITER plasma is meant to reach about 150 million degrees Celsius.

124905.q: Why does ITER use superconducting magnet coils?
a: They produce strong fields with almost no electrical losses
124905.e: Below a critical temperature, superconductors have no electrical resistance. This allows the huge currents for confining the plasma to flow without large heat losses.
124905.m: Superconducting coils produce strong magnetic fields without resistance losses.

124906.q: How many members support the international ITER project (as of 2025)?
124906.e: The members are the EU, China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA. The EU counts as one member.
124906.m: Seven members support the ITER project.

124907.q: Will ITER feed electricity into the public grid?
a: No, it is an experimental facility
Yes, for a whole large city
124907.e: ITER is meant to show that fusion is technically possible and does not produce electricity for the grid. Only a successor power station, often called DEMO, is meant to supply electricity.
124907.m: ITER is an experiment, not a power station.

124908.q: Which quantity is given in sieverts?
a: The equivalent dose or effective dose
The activity of a radiation source
124908.e: The sievert takes into account how harmful a radiation is for humans. It is the unit for equivalent dose and effective dose.
124908.m: Sieverts measure the biological effect of radiation.

124909.q: What does the unit gray indicate?
124909.e: One gray equals one joule of absorbed radiation energy per kilogram. The different biological effects of the types of radiation are not yet included.
124909.m: The gray measures the absorbed dose.

124910.q: What radiation weighting factor does alpha radiation have?
124910.e: Alpha particles give off their energy over a very short distance and badly damage tissue. That is why their absorbed dose is weighted with a factor of 20.
124910.m: Alpha radiation is weighted with a factor of 20.

124911.q: A tissue absorbs a dose of 2 mGy from alpha radiation. How large is the equivalent dose?
124911.e: The equivalent dose is the absorbed dose times the weighting factor. 2 mGy · 20 gives 40 mSv.
124911.m: The equivalent dose is the absorbed dose times the weighting factor.

124912.q: Roughly how high is the average annual radiation dose of the population in Switzerland?
124912.e: The Federal Office of Public Health gives an average dose of about 6 mSv per year for Switzerland. It comes from natural sources and medical examinations.
124912.m: In Switzerland, each person receives on average a few millisieverts per year.

124913.q: Which source contributes most to the radiation dose of the population in Switzerland?
124913.e: Radon is a radioactive noble gas from the ground that can build up in houses. It makes up the largest part of the average dose.
124913.m: Radon is the most important source of radiation in Switzerland.

124914.q: What annual limit for the effective dose applies in Switzerland to people exposed to radiation at work?
124914.e: The Radiological Protection Ordinance limits the effective dose for occupationally exposed people to 20 mSv per year. They include, for example, people working in radiology and nuclear facilities.
124914.m: For people exposed to radiation at work, the limit is 20 mSv per year.

124915.q: What annual limit applies in Switzerland to the public for radiation from artificial sources, excluding medicine?
124915.e: For people not exposed at work, the limit is 1 mSv per year. Natural radiation and medical uses are not included.
124915.m: For the public, the dose limit is 1 mSv per year.

124916.q: Who is the unit sievert named after?
124916.e: Rolf Sievert was a Swedish medical physicist and a pioneer of radiation protection. The unit honours his work on the biological effects of radiation.
124916.m: The sievert is named after the Swede Rolf Sievert.

124917.q: What is the technical term from Greek for the science of soil?
124917.e: Soil science is also called pedology, from the Greek “pedon” for soil. Petrology, on the other hand, is the study of rocks, and pomology the study of fruit growing.
124917.m: Pedology is the science of soil.

124918.q: Which factor mainly decides whether a soil over limestone or over granite develops to be acidic or alkaline?
124918.e: The parent rock provides the minerals from which the soil forms. Limestone has an alkaline effect, while granite contains hardly any lime, so soils on it tend to become acidic.
124918.m: The parent rock shapes the properties of a soil.

124919.q: Which factor is NOT one of the classic soil-forming factors?
124919.e: The classic soil-forming factors are parent rock, climate, relief, organisms and time. Air pressure does not play a role of its own.
124919.m: Soils form from rock, climate, relief, living things and time.

124920.q: What is the particle size fraction with particles smaller than 0.002 millimetres called?
124920.e: Particles under 2 micrometres count as clay. Silt is a bit coarser, sand coarser still.
124920.m: Clay consists of the finest soil particles.

124921.q: Which simple field method estimates the soil type by rubbing moist soil between your fingers?
124921.e: In the finger test you check whether the soil feels rough, floury or sticky and whether it can be rolled out. This lets you estimate the amount of sand, silt and clay.
124921.m: The finger test is used to estimate soil type in the field.

124922.q: Which letter is used in a soil profile for the unweathered or barely weathered parent rock?
124922.e: At the top of a soil profile there is often an organic layer (O), below it the humus-rich topsoil (A), the subsoil (B) and at the very bottom the parent rock (C).
124922.m: The C horizon is the parent rock.

124923.q: What is a soil mixture with roughly balanced amounts of sand, silt and clay called?
124923.e: Loam is a mixture of sand, silt and clay. Loess, on the other hand, is a silt-rich sediment deposited by the wind.
124923.m: Loam is a mixture of sand, silt and clay.

124924.q: What does a dark, almost black colour in the topsoil usually show?
124924.e: Humus colours the topsoil dark. Light colours tend to point to sand, lime or washed-out horizons.
124924.m: Dark topsoil usually contains a lot of humus.

124925.q: How does a soil type differ from a soil texture class?
a: It describes the sequence of horizons
It describes only the particle size
It describes only the pH value
124925.e: The soil texture class depends on the distribution of particle sizes. The soil type groups together soils with a similar development and a similar sequence of horizons.
124925.m: The soil type describes the development and horizons of a soil.

124926.q: What is the soil in river valleys called that is regularly flooded and gets fresh sediment each time?
124926.e: Alluvial soils form from river deposits. During floods they are covered with water and get new material, which is why they are often layered.
124926.m: Alluvial soils form from river deposits.

124927.q: Which soil type shows a pale, washed-out bleached horizon below the topsoil?
124927.e: In a podzol, iron, aluminium and humus are carried downwards by acidic seepage water. What is left is an ash-grey bleached horizon, with a rusty brown accumulation horizon below it.
124927.m: A podzol has a grey bleached horizon.

124928.q: Which especially fertile soil type with a very thick humus horizon is typical of steppes such as those in Ukraine?
124928.e: Chernozem, or black earth, forms under steppe grass on loess. The dark humus horizon can be very thick and makes the soil extremely fertile.
124928.m: Black earth is a very fertile steppe soil.

124929.q: Which soil type is the most common under meadows and broadleaf forests in the Swiss Plateau?
124929.e: Brown earths form in a temperate, humid climate. The brown colour comes from iron oxides released during weathering.
124929.m: Brown earth is a typical soil of the Swiss Plateau.

124930.q: Why are soils high up in the Alps usually very shallow?
a: Cold and a short growing season slow down soil formation
The wind blows all the soil away every year
There is no parent rock in the Alps
124930.e: Soil formation needs weathering, living things and time. In the cold these processes are slow, and many areas only became free of ice after the Ice Age.
124930.m: In cold mountain areas, soils form only slowly.

124931.q: Which substances give tropical soils such as ferralsols their typical red colour?
124931.e: In the humid tropics many substances are washed out, while iron and aluminium oxides stay behind. Iron oxides in particular colour these soils red.
124931.m: Iron oxides colour tropical soils red.

124932.q: Why are tropical rainforest soils often poor in nutrients despite the lush vegetation?
a: Heavy rain washes out nutrients, and most are stored in the plants
They consist almost entirely of lime
The soil is frozen all year
124932.e: High temperatures and lots of rain lead to fast decomposition and strong leaching. The nutrients circulate quickly and are mostly bound up in the biomass.
124932.m: In the rainforest, the nutrients are mainly stored in the plants.

124933.q: Which mineral group do clay minerals belong to because of their structure?
124933.e: Clay minerals are sheet silicates: they consist of stacked layers of silicon-oxygen tetrahedra and aluminium or magnesium octahedra.

124934.q: What is the clay mineral kaolinite mainly used for?
124934.e: Kaolinite is the main component of kaolin, the white china clay. It hardly swells and stays light-coloured when fired.
124934.m: Kaolinite is the raw material for porcelain.

124935.q: Which clay mineral swells strongly and is the main component of bentonite?
124935.e: Montmorillonite belongs to the smectites. Water can be stored between its three-layer packets, which is why it swells so much.
124935.m: Montmorillonite swells strongly when it takes up water.

124936.q: Why do some clay soils swell up in rain and get deep cracks in dry weather?
a: Their clay minerals store water between their layers
They contain lots of quartz sand
124936.e: Swelling clay minerals such as montmorillonite take up water between their layers and expand. When they dry out they shrink, and shrinkage cracks form. In illite, potassium ions prevent swelling.
124936.m: Swelling clay minerals make soils swell and shrink.

124937.q: Why can clay minerals store nutrients such as calcium, magnesium and potassium?
a: They contain a lot of nitrogen
124937.e: Clay minerals carry negative charges and therefore bind positively charged ions. These cations can be exchanged for others and so made available to plants.
124937.m: Negatively charged clay minerals hold on to cations.

124938.q: What is the measure called that shows how many cations a soil can bind in an exchangeable way?
124938.e: The cation exchange capacity (CEC) measures how many exchangeable cations a soil can store. Soils rich in clay and humus have a high CEC.
124938.m: Clay-rich soils have a high cation exchange capacity.

124939.q: From which minerals do clay minerals mainly form through chemical weathering?
124939.e: Feldspars and micas weather under the influence of water and acids and turn into clay minerals. Quartz, on the other hand, is very resistant to weathering.
124939.m: Clay minerals mainly form from weathered feldspars and micas.

124940.q: Which clay-rich rock is planned in Switzerland as the host rock for a deep geological repository for radioactive waste?
124940.e: Opalinus Clay is very dense and can seal cracks itself by swelling. That is why Nagra plans to use it as the host rock for the deep repository.
124940.m: Opalinus Clay is meant to enclose radioactive waste safely.

124941.q: What is meant by soil fertility?
a: The lasting ability to allow plant growth
The amount of water after rain
The share of stones in the subsoil
The number of earthworms per hectare
124941.e: Soil fertility describes a soil’s ability to offer plants good growing conditions over the long term. This includes nutrients, water, air, structure and soil life.
124941.m: A fertile soil allows good plant growth over the long term.

124942.q: What is the benefit of a green manure sown between two main crops?
a: It protects against erosion and nutrient loss
124942.e: The green manure plants cover the soil, hold on to nutrients and later provide organic matter. In this way they protect against soil being washed away and nutrients being leached out.
124942.m: Green manure protects and feeds the soil.

124943.q: Which three main nutrients do the letters NPK on fertiliser bags stand for?
124943.e: N stands for nitrogen, P for phosphorus and K for potassium (Latin “kalium”). Plants need these three in large amounts.
124943.m: NPK stands for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

124944.q: Why do legumes such as clover increase the fertility of a soil?
a: Their nodule bacteria fix nitrogen from the air
They loosen the soil with thorns
They remove lime from the soil
They store salt in their roots
124944.e: Rhizobia live in the root nodules of legumes and fix nitrogen from the air. This nitrogen later also benefits the following crops.
124944.m: Clover brings nitrogen into the soil with nodule bacteria.

124945.q: Which naturalist published a whole book in the 19th century on the importance of earthworms for soil formation?
124945.e: In his last book, Charles Darwin described how earthworms mix soil and form humus. He showed that over the years they move entire layers of soil.
124945.m: Darwin recognised the great importance of earthworms.

124946.q: What is the dark, very fertile soil in the Amazon region called that people enriched with charcoal and waste?
124946.e: Terra preta was formed from charcoal, bones, pottery shards and organic waste from earlier settlements. It is still much more fertile than the surrounding tropical soils.
124946.m: Terra preta is fertile soil made by people.

124947.q: What effect does driving heavy machines on wet soil have on soil fertility?
124947.e: Heavy machines squeeze wet soil together. Large pores are lost, water drains away less well and roots get less air.
124947.m: Heavy machines on wet soil compact it.

124948.q: In which pH range do most field crops grow best?
124948.e: At a slightly acidic to neutral pH, most nutrients are easily available and soil life is active. In strongly acidic or alkaline soils, some nutrients are taken up poorly.
124948.m: Most crops like slightly acidic to neutral soil.

124949.q: Which compounds from traffic, industry and farming contribute to soil acidification through rain?
124949.e: Sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and ammonia get into the soil with rain or as dust. There they form acids or release acid as they are converted.
124949.m: Sulphur and nitrogen inputs acidify soils.

124950.q: Which metal is dissolved as an ion in strongly acidified soils and damages the fine roots of trees?
124950.e: If the pH value drops a lot, aluminium ions are released from the clay minerals. They are poisonous to plant roots.
124950.m: In acidic soils, poisonous aluminium is released.

124951.q: Which measure is used in farming and forestry against soil acidification?
124951.e: Liming means spreading calcium carbonate, which neutralises acid. This makes the pH value rise again.
124951.m: Lime raises the pH value of acidic soils.

124952.q: What happens to the pH value of a lime-rich soil when acid rain falls, as long as there is still lime present?
a: It changes a lot every day
124952.e: Lime neutralises incoming acids, so the soil is buffered. Only when the lime is used up does the pH value drop noticeably.

124953.q: Why do soils on limestone in the Jura acidify more slowly than soils on granite?
124953.e: Limestone contains calcium carbonate, which neutralises acids. Granite contains hardly any lime and can only buffer acids weakly.

124954.q: Which nitrogen compound comes mainly from livestock farming in Switzerland and contributes to the acidification of forest soils?
124954.e: Ammonia escapes mainly from slurry and manure. When it is converted to nitrate in the soil, acid is released.
124954.m: Ammonia from livestock farming acidifies soils.

124955.q: Which nutrients are especially lost through leaching as soil acidification progresses?
a: Basic cations such as calcium and magnesium
124955.e: Acid pushes calcium, magnesium and potassium off the exchange sites. These basic cations are then washed out with the seepage water.
124955.m: Acidification washes calcium and magnesium out of the soil.

124956.q: Which natural source contributes to soil acidification through root respiration and decomposition?
124956.e: Roots and microorganisms give off carbon dioxide. Dissolved in soil water it forms carbonic acid, which slowly dissolves lime and acidifies the soil.
124956.m: Carbon dioxide in soil water forms carbonic acid.

a: Organic remains are converted into humic substances
Organic remains turn completely into gas
124957.e: In humification, new, stable humic substances form from dead plants and animals. They colour the soil dark and last a long time.
124957.m: In humification, humus forms from organic remains.

124958.q: What is the opposite process called, in which organic matter is broken down completely into carbon dioxide, water and mineral salts?
124958.e: In mineralisation, organic substances are completely broken down and the nutrients are released again as inorganic ions. Humification, on the other hand, builds up stable humic substances.
124958.m: Mineralisation releases nutrients from organic matter.

124959.q: Which humus form is biologically very active, well mixed and typical of fertile broadleaf forest and meadow soils?
124959.e: In mull, earthworms quickly work the leaf litter into the soil and mix it with mineral soil. No thick layer forms on top.
124959.m: Mull is the most active humus form.

124960.q: Which humus form develops under acidic conifer forests with a thick, poorly decomposed layer on top?
124960.e: Under acidic conifer litter there are hardly any earthworms. Fungi break down the litter only slowly, so a thick layer of mor builds up.
124960.m: Mor forms under acidic conifer forests.

124961.q: Which material has an especially wide C/N ratio and is therefore broken down slowly?
124961.e: Straw contains lots of carbon but little nitrogen. Microorganisms find too little nitrogen in it and break it down only slowly.
124961.m: Straw breaks down slowly because of its wide C/N ratio.

124962.q: What colour do humic substances give a humus-rich topsoil?
124962.e: Humic substances are dark-coloured, stable organic compounds. The more humus a soil contains, the darker its top layer is.
124962.m: Humus-rich soil is dark in colour.

124963.q: What role do soils play in the global carbon cycle?
a: They store more carbon than the atmosphere and plants together
They store less carbon than a single forest
They only release carbon and store none
124963.e: Worldwide, the humus in soils holds more carbon than the atmosphere and all vegetation together. Building up humus can therefore lock away carbon dioxide.
124963.m: Soils are a huge carbon store.

124964.q: Why do we distinguish between nutrient humus and permanent humus?
a: Nutrient humus breaks down quickly, permanent humus lasts a long time
Nutrient humus is mineral, permanent humus is organic
Nutrient humus lies deeper than permanent humus
124964.e: Nutrient humus consists of easily broken-down substances and provides nutrients quickly. Permanent humus made of stable humic substances lasts for decades or centuries and improves soil structure.
124964.m: Permanent humus stays in the soil for a long time.

124965.q: On which parent rock does a rendzina form?
124965.e: A rendzina is a shallow soil on carbonate rock such as limestone, dolomite or gypsum. Its counterpart on silicate rock is called a ranker.

124966.q: Why is a rendzina usually only shallow?
a: Lime dissolves almost completely and leaves little residue
It is blown away by the wind every year
124966.e: During weathering, lime is dissolved by rainwater and carried away. Only a little material is left, from which a thin layer of soil forms over the rock.
124966.m: Rendzinas are thin because lime dissolves almost completely.

124967.q: What lies directly under the dark humus layer in a rendzina?
124967.e: A rendzina has no weathered layer in between. The limestone comes directly below the humus-rich topsoil.
124967.m: In a rendzina, the rock comes directly under the humus.

124968.q: In which Swiss region are rendzinas especially common?
a: In the gneiss area of Ticino
In the Rhône valley on river gravel
124968.e: The Jura is mostly made of limestone. Shallow rendzinas are widespread on its hilltops and slopes.
124968.m: There are many rendzinas in the limestone mountains of the Jura.

124969.q: Which disadvantage is typical of rendzinas as a place for plants to grow?
124969.e: Rendzinas are shallow and stony, so they store only a little water. In summer they dry out quickly.
124969.m: Rendzinas dry out quickly in summer.

124970.q: Which plant community is often found on rendzinas on sunny slopes?
124970.e: On dry, lime-rich rendzinas, species-rich semi-dry grasslands grow, often with orchids. They are among the most species-rich habitats in Switzerland.
124970.m: Species-rich dry grasslands often grow on rendzinas.

124971.q: What pH value does a typical rendzina have?
124971.e: Because the soil lies directly on limestone and contains bits of lime, it is neutral to slightly alkaline. The lime buffers acids.
124971.m: Thanks to lime, rendzinas are neutral to slightly alkaline.

124972.q: Which factor shapes a gley soil?
a: Rainwater that collects and cannot drain
124972.e: Gleys are soils whose lower part lies permanently or at times in groundwater. Soils with trapped rainwater, on the other hand, are called pseudogleys.

124973.q: How can you recognise a gley soil in a soil profile?
a: By grey layers and rust spots
By white salt crusts on the surface
By a red, tropical loam layer
By limestone directly under the grass
124973.e: In the permanently wet subsoil, iron is reduced and colours it grey to blue-green. Where the groundwater rises and falls, iron oxidises into rusty brown spots.
124973.m: Grey colours and rust spots give away a gley.

124974.q: What colour is the permanently wet, oxygen-poor reduction horizon of a gley?
124974.e: When oxygen is lacking, iron is present in its divalent form. These iron compounds colour the soil grey, bluish or greenish.
124974.m: The reduction horizon of a gley is grey-green.

124975.q: What causes the rust spots in the oxidation horizon of a gley?
124975.e: When the groundwater rises and falls, oxygen reaches dissolved iron. It oxidises to trivalent iron and forms rusty brown spots.

124976.q: Unlike a gley, which soil type is shaped by trapped rainwater?
124976.e: In a pseudogley, a dense layer holds back the seepage water. The soil is alternately wet and dry, while a gley is influenced by groundwater.
124976.m: A pseudogley forms from trapped rainwater.

124977.q: Which measure made many gley soils in the Swiss Plateau usable for arable farming?
124977.e: Drainage pipes lowered the groundwater level. This allowed wet gley soils to be ploughed, but wetlands were lost in the process.
124977.m: Drainage made wet soils suitable for crops.

124978.q: Which type of landscape is typical of gley soils?
124978.e: In valley floodplains and hollows, the groundwater is close to the surface. Gleys form there most often.
124978.m: Gleys are found in hollows with high groundwater.

124979.q: In a gley, what does the boundary between the rust-spotted zone and the grey zone show?
a: The depth from which the soil lies permanently in groundwater
Where a glacier used to be
How far the tree roots reach
124979.e: In the rust-spotted zone, the groundwater rises and falls, and air sometimes gets in. Below it, the soil is always wet and poor in oxygen, so it is grey.
124979.m: Below the rust spots, a gley is always wet.

124980.q: What are crop rotation areas (Fruchtfolgeflächen) in Switzerland?
a: All forest areas in the Swiss Plateau
124980.e: Crop rotation areas are the most valuable farmland in Switzerland: well-suited soils that can be ploughed. They are to be kept for arable farming in the long term.
124980.m: Crop rotation areas are Switzerland’s best arable soils.

124981.q: Which federal instrument sets a minimum amount of crop rotation areas for the whole of Switzerland?
a: The Sectoral Plan for Crop Rotation Areas
124981.e: In the Sectoral Plan for Crop Rotation Areas, the federal government decides how much crop rotation land must at least be preserved. The cantons must secure their share permanently.
124981.m: The Sectoral Plan for Crop Rotation Areas protects the best soils.

124982.q: What is the main aim of protecting crop rotation areas?
a: Food security in times of crisis
124982.e: Crop rotation areas are meant to make sure that Switzerland can grow enough food even in a supply crisis. That is why they are specially protected.
124982.m: Crop rotation areas serve security of supply.

124983.q: In which major region of Switzerland are most crop rotation areas?
124983.e: The Swiss Plateau has flat land, deep soils and a mild climate. That is why most of Switzerland’s best arable land is there.
124983.m: Most crop rotation areas are in the Swiss Plateau.

124984.q: Who has to actually designate and secure the crop rotation areas in spatial planning?
124984.e: The federal government sets a quota for each canton. The cantons must show these areas in their structure plans and preserve them.
124984.m: The cantons secure the crop rotation areas.

124985.q: Which danger threatens crop rotation areas in the Swiss Plateau most?
a: Building and sealing of the land
Turning into steppe because of salt
124985.e: The Swiss Plateau is both the best arable land and the most densely populated area. New housing and roads seal valuable soils there.
124985.m: Building is the biggest danger to crop rotation areas.

124986.q: Why do steep slopes usually not count as crop rotation areas?
a: They are hard to farm with machines
No plants grow there at all
They always belong to the federal government
124986.e: Crop rotation areas must be easy to work with machines. That is difficult on steep slopes, and the risk of erosion is greater.
124986.m: Crop rotation areas must be flat enough for machines.

124987.q: What is meant by crop rotation in farming?
a: The planned change of crops on a field
The order of the harvest in autumn
The way the produce travels to market
124987.e: In crop rotation, for example, cereals, root crops and temporary grassland take turns on the same field. This prevents diseases and protects the soil.
124987.m: In crop rotation, crops take turns on a field.

124988.q: What does the term edaphon mean?
a: All the living things in the soil
The pieces of rock in the soil
124988.e: The edaphon includes all organisms living in the soil: bacteria, fungi, algae and soil animals. The term goes back to the biologist Raoul Heinrich Francé.
124988.m: The edaphon is the community of life in the soil.

124989.q: Which organisms are responsible for the typical smell of fresh earth?
124989.e: Actinomycetes are bacteria that produce the scent geosmin. It gives the typical earthy smell, especially after rain.
124989.m: Actinomycetes produce the earthy smell geosmin.

124990.q: Which size group of soil fauna do springtails and mites belong to?
124990.e: Springtails and mites are about 0.2 to 2 millimetres long and count as mesofauna. Single-celled organisms belong to the microfauna, earthworms to the macrofauna.

124991.q: Which soil animal belongs to the megafauna of the soil?
124991.e: The megafauna includes the largest soil dwellers, vertebrates such as moles and voles. Roundworms and ciliates are tiny.
124991.m: The mole belongs to the soil megafauna.

124992.q: What is the device called that drives small animals out of a soil sample using heat and light?
124992.e: In a Berlese funnel, a lamp warms the soil sample from above. The animals flee downwards and fall into a collecting container.
124992.m: A Berlese funnel is used to collect soil animals.

124993.q: What are soil animals such as woodlice and millipedes called, which eat and shred dead plant parts?
124993.e: Woodlice and millipedes shred fallen leaves and so increase their surface area. Then fungi and bacteria can break down the remains faster.

124994.q: Which statement about the number of living things in the soil is true?
a: A handful of soil contains more living things than there are people
A handful of soil contains about a hundred living things
Fewer species live in the soil than on a tree
124994.e: Billions of microorganisms live in a handful of fertile soil. That is more living things than there are people on Earth.
124994.m: A handful of soil contains billions of living things.

124995.q: Which achievement of earthworms especially improves soil structure?
124995.e: Earthworms eat soil and plant remains and mix them in their gut. Their casts contain stable clay-humus complexes that give the soil a crumbly structure.

124996.q: What is meant by soil respiration?
a: The release of carbon dioxide from the soil
The wind in the soil pores
124996.e: In soil respiration, roots, microorganisms and soil animals give off carbon dioxide. It escapes from the soil into the atmosphere.
124996.m: In soil respiration, the soil gives off carbon dioxide.

124997.q: Which two main sources contribute to soil respiration?
124997.e: Autotrophic respiration comes from the plant roots, heterotrophic respiration from microorganisms that break down organic matter.
124997.m: Roots and microorganisms respire in the soil.

124998.q: How does soil air usually differ from the air above the soil?
124998.e: The respiration of soil organisms uses up oxygen and builds up carbon dioxide. Soil air therefore contains many times more carbon dioxide.
124998.m: Soil air contains more carbon dioxide than the air outside.

124999.q: How does soil respiration usually change when soil temperature rises?
a: It increases up to an optimum
124999.e: Warmth speeds up the metabolism of soil organisms. That is why soil respiration rises with temperature, as long as there is enough water.

125000.q: Why is there concern that global warming could be strengthened by soil respiration?
a: Warmer soils break down more humus and release carbon dioxide
125000.e: When temperatures rise, microorganisms break down humus faster. The extra carbon dioxide released can drive warming further.
125000.m: Warmed soils can give off extra carbon dioxide.

125001.q: Which gas can increasingly form instead of carbon dioxide in waterlogged, oxygen-free soils?
125001.e: When there is no oxygen, special microorganisms break down organic substances anaerobically. Among other things, this produces methane, for example in bogs and rice fields.
125001.m: Methane forms in wet soils without oxygen.

125002.q: How big is the global carbon dioxide flow from soil respiration compared with human fossil emissions?
125002.e: Every year, soils release many times the amount of fossil emissions as carbon dioxide. However, a large part is taken up again by photosynthesis.
125002.m: Soil respiration is a huge flow of carbon dioxide.

125003.q: Why is soil respiration often measured in soil biology?
a: As a measure of the activity of microorganisms
To determine the colour of the soil
125003.e: The more carbon dioxide a soil gives off under the same conditions, the more active its microorganisms are. Soil respiration is therefore an important indicator of soil life.
125003.m: Soil respiration shows how active soil life is.

125004.q: Which institution runs Switzerland’s National Soil Monitoring Network (NABO)?
125004.e: NABO is run by Agroscope, the federal centre of excellence for agricultural research. It is commissioned by the Federal Offices for the Environment and for Agriculture.
125004.m: Agroscope runs the National Soil Monitoring Network.

125005.q: Since when has the National Soil Monitoring Network been measuring the state of Swiss soils?
a: Since the founding of the federal state
125005.e: NABO was founded in 1984, when concern about pollutants in soils was growing. Since the first survey in 1985, the same sites have been sampled regularly.
125005.m: NABO has been monitoring soils since the 1980s.

125006.q: Why does the National Soil Monitoring Network (NABO) keep sampling the same sites?
a: To detect long-term changes in the soils
125006.e: Only by studying the same areas over decades can changes such as the build-up of pollutants be reliably shown.
125006.m: NABO tracks changes in soils over a long time.

125007.q: How often are the NABO sites sampled again?
125007.e: The sites are sampled every five years. The samples are also archived so that they can be studied later with new methods.
125007.m: The NABO sites are sampled every five years.

125008.q: According to NABO, which heavy metals have built up on grassland sites with lots of farmyard manure, such as pig slurry?
125008.e: Copper and zinc are added to animal feed and end up on the meadows through the slurry. NABO found an increase in these metals at such sites.
125008.m: Slurry can build up copper and zinc in the soil.

125009.q: Through which fertiliser does the heavy metal cadmium mainly get into arable soils?
125009.e: Rock phosphate naturally contains cadmium. According to NABO, mineral phosphate fertiliser is an important way for cadmium to get into arable soils.
125009.m: Phosphate fertiliser can bring cadmium into the soil.

125010.q: Which ordinance sets the guide values for pollutants in soil in Switzerland?
125010.e: The Ordinance on Soil Pollution (VBBo) sets guide, trigger and clean-up values for pollutants. It is based on the Environmental Protection Act.
125010.m: The VBBo sets pollutant values for soil.

125011.q: Why does NABO keep soil samples in an archive?
a: To study them again later with new methods
125011.e: Archived samples make it possible to measure substances later that were not looked at before. This makes long-term changes easier to prove.
125011.m: Archived soil samples can be studied again later.

125012.q: What is the part of the Earth called where the rock layer, the atmosphere, the water layer and the biosphere overlap and soil forms?
125012.e: The pedosphere is the Earth’s thin layer of soil. Here rock, air, water and living things work together.
125012.m: The pedosphere is the Earth’s soil layer.

125013.q: What is the amount of water called that a well-drained soil can hold against gravity after the seepage water has drained away?
125013.e: Field capacity describes the water held against gravity in the medium and fine pores. Not all of it is available to plants.
125013.m: Field capacity is the water the soil can hold.

125015.q: Why do clay minerals have a very large specific surface area?
a: They consist of tiny, thin flakes
They are hollow inside like tubes
They contain lots of air bubbles
125015.e: Clay minerals are only fractions of a micrometre thick. One gram of clay therefore has a huge surface to which water and nutrients stick.
125015.m: Clay has a huge surface area because of its tiny flakes.

125016.q: Which wood component that is hard to break down is an important starting material for the formation of humic substances?
125016.e: Lignin makes cell walls woody and is broken down only slowly by fungi. A large part of its breakdown products goes into the humic substances.
125016.m: Lignin is an important building block for humic substances.

125113.q: What is the science called that studies biological rhythms such as the body clock?
125113.e: The word comes from the Greek “chronos” (time). Chronobiology studies things such as the sleep-wake rhythm, jet lag and shift work.

125114.q: Roughly how long does one cycle of the body clock in the body's cells last?
125114.e: The body clock is based on genes that switch themselves on and off in a feedback loop. One cycle lasts about a day, hence the name circadian rhythm.
125114.m: The body clock ticks in a rhythm of about 24 hours.

125115.q: What do single nerve cells of the suprachiasmatic nucleus show when they are kept in a cell culture?
a: They keep their own daily rhythm.
125115.e: Even when isolated, the activity and gene reading of these cells vary with a period of about 24 hours. So the clock is in every single cell.
125115.m: Single cells of the master clock keep ticking even on their own.

125116.q: Which feeling becomes stronger as adenosine builds up in the brain during the day?
125116.e: The longer you are awake, the more adenosine builds up in the brain. It dampens the nerve cells and creates sleep pressure.

125117.q: What is the time from falling asleep to the start of the first REM phase called?
125117.e: REM latency is fairly long in healthy people, because the non-REM stages come first. A very short REM latency can point to an illness.
125117.m: REM latency measures the time until the first REM phase.

125118.q: Someone spends 8 hours in bed and sleeps for 6 of them. What is their sleep efficiency?
125118.e: Sleep efficiency is the time asleep divided by the time in bed. 6 divided by 8 gives 0.75, which is 75 per cent.
125118.m: Sleep efficiency compares the time asleep with the time in bed.

125119.q: What is measured with an EEG in a sleep laboratory?
125119.e: The electroencephalogram uses electrodes on the scalp to measure the electrical activity of the brain. This shows the stages of sleep.
125119.m: The EEG shows the brain waves during sleep.

125120.q: In which sleep phase is it hardest to wake someone up?
a: In light sleep shortly before waking
125120.e: In deep sleep, the brain is greatly slowed down. People woken from it are often especially groggy.
125120.m: Deep sleep is the hardest to wake up from.

125121.q: What is the temporary grogginess and reduced performance straight after waking up called?
125121.e: Sleep inertia can last from a few minutes to over half an hour. It is particularly strong when you are woken from deep sleep.
125121.m: Right after waking up, sleep inertia dampens performance.

125122.q: Roughly how long does a sleep cycle of non-REM and REM sleep last?
125122.e: One cycle lasts about 90 minutes. During a night you therefore go through four to six of these cycles.
125122.m: A sleep cycle lasts about one and a half hours.

125123.q: How does the proportion of REM sleep change during the night?
a: It stays the same all night
It only occurs in the first hour
125123.e: In the first half of the night, deep sleep dominates. Towards morning the REM phases get longer, which is why you often remember dreams from shortly before waking.
125123.m: REM sleep gets longer towards morning.

125124.q: Why do you hardly move in REM sleep despite vivid dreams?
a: The skeletal muscles are largely paralysed
The brain is completely switched off then
The heart does not beat then
You are unconscious as under anaesthetic
125124.e: In REM sleep, the muscles are strongly inhibited and only the eyes and breathing muscles move. This stops you acting out your dreams with real movements.
125124.m: In REM sleep the muscles are almost paralysed.

125125.q: In sleep medicine, what is meant by an arousal?
a: A brief waking reaction on the EEG lasting at least 3 seconds
Waking up completely in the morning
125125.e: An arousal is a sudden switch to faster brain waves for a few seconds. People often do not notice these brief waking reactions.
125125.m: An arousal is a brief, often unnoticed waking reaction.

125126.q: How is airflow measured in a sleep laboratory?
a: With sensors at the nose and mouth
With a clip on the earlobe
With a thermometer in the ear
125126.e: Small sensors in front of the nose and mouth record the airflow or changes in temperature during breathing. This reveals pauses in breathing and shallow breathing.
125126.m: Airflow is measured at the nose and mouth.

125127.q: Why are leg movements also recorded in a sleep laboratory?
a: To identify restless legs as a cause of poor sleep
125127.e: Some people move their legs again and again in their sleep and briefly wake up as a result. Electrodes on the legs make these movements visible.

125128.q: What is it called when many people sleep worse during their first night in a sleep laboratory?
125128.e: The unfamiliar surroundings and the cables disturb sleep on the first night. That is why measurements are sometimes taken over two nights.
125128.m: People often sleep worse on their first night in a sleep laboratory.

a: A marked flattening of breathing with a drop in oxygen or a waking reaction
A complete stop in breathing lasting over a minute
125129.e: In a hypopnoea, the airflow is greatly reduced but not completely interrupted. Like apnoea, it counts as a breathing disorder during sleep.
125129.m: A hypopnoea is a strong flattening of breathing.

125130.q: Which treatment is most commonly used for obstructive sleep apnoea?
a: A breathing mask with slight positive pressure (CPAP)
125130.e: The CPAP machine blows air with slight positive pressure into the airways through a mask. This keeps the throat open during sleep.
125130.m: A CPAP mask keeps the airways open during sleep.

125131.q: What is the main feature of narcolepsy?
a: Severe daytime sleepiness with sudden falling asleep
Loud snoring with pauses in breathing
125131.e: People with narcolepsy can hardly stay awake during the day and sometimes fall asleep in the middle of an activity. The cause is a disorder in the brain's control of sleeping and waking.
125131.m: Narcolepsy causes severe sleepiness during the day.

125132.q: On which day of the week is the conflict between the body clock and the alarm time usually greatest with social jet lag?
125132.e: After sleeping late at the weekend, the body clock has shifted later. On Monday morning the alarm then rings especially early in your internal night.
125132.m: Monday morning is especially hard with social jet lag.

125133.q: What is the aim of sleep restriction in the treatment of insomnia?
a: To match the time in bed to the actual sleep time in order to increase sleep pressure
To spend as many hours as possible in bed
To sleep only during the day
To stay awake all night every night
125133.e: People who lie awake in bed for a long time sleep in fragments. Shortening the time in bed increases sleep pressure, and sleep becomes deeper and more continuous.
125133.m: Sleep restriction shortens the time in bed so that sleep becomes deeper.

125134.q: What is recommended about eating in the evening for a good night's sleep?
a: No heavy meals shortly before going to bed
A big meal right before going to sleep
Eating nothing at all after midday
Only very spicy food in the evening
125134.e: A heavy meal keeps the digestion busy and can make it harder to fall asleep. A light meal a few hours before sleeping is better.
125134.m: A heavy evening meal shortly before sleeping disturbs your night's rest.

125135.q: What does the word “circadian” literally mean?
125135.e: The word comes from the Latin “circa” (about) and “dies” (day). It refers to biological rhythms with a period of about 24 hours.
125135.m: Circadian rhythms last about a day.

125136.q: On average, how long is the internal period of the human clock when all external time cues are missing?
125136.e: Without time cues, the body clock of most people runs a little longer than 24 hours. That is why it has to be adjusted to the day anew every day.
125136.m: The human body clock usually runs a little slower than the 24-hour day.

125137.q: In which model organism were the molecular mechanisms of the body clock researched that were awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2017?
125137.e: Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young studied clock genes in the fruit fly Drosophila. For this they received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
125137.m: The molecular body clock was first decoded in the fruit fly.

125138.q: Which hormone does the body typically release in particularly large amounts shortly after waking in the morning?
125138.e: The cortisol level rises in the second half of the night and peaks shortly after waking. Cortisol helps to provide energy for the day.
125138.m: Cortisol reaches its peak in the morning after waking.

125139.q: When does the core body temperature of a person with a normal sleep rhythm typically reach its minimum?
a: In the early hours of the morning
125139.e: Core temperature follows a circadian rhythm and is lowest in the second half of the night, a few hours before waking. It is highest in the late afternoon.
125139.m: Body temperature is lowest in the early hours of the morning.

125140.q: What do you call a biological rhythm that continues with its own period without external time cues?
125140.e: In isolation experiments without daylight and clocks, the rhythm runs freely with its own period. It then shifts a little each day compared with clock time.
125140.m: A free-running rhythm follows only its own period.

125141.q: Why is adjusting to the time difference after an eastward flight usually harder than after a westward one?
a: The body clock has to be put forward, which is harder.
There is less sunlight during the day in the east.
The air pressure in the plane is lower when flying east.
Eastward flights always take much longer.
125141.e: Because the internal period is usually a little longer than 24 hours, it is easier to shift the clock later. After an eastward flight, however, you have to sleep earlier, which means putting the clock forward.
125141.m: Flying east requires putting the body clock forward and is therefore harder.

125142.q: What are biological rhythms called whose period is much shorter than a day, such as the sleep cycle at night?
125142.e: Ultradian rhythms repeat several times a day. Infradian rhythms, on the other hand, last longer than a day, and circannual ones about a year.
125142.m: Ultradian rhythms run several times a day.

125143.q: What does the name “suprachiasmatic” refer to?
a: Its position above the crossing of the optic nerves
Its connection to the spinal cord
125143.e: “Supra” means above, and the “optic chiasm” is where the optic nerves cross. The nucleus lies directly above it and so easily receives signals from the eyes.
125143.m: The suprachiasmatic nucleus lies above the crossing of the optic nerves.

125144.q: Where does the master clock in the brain get the information about whether it is day or night?
a: From the retina of the eyes
From the skin via the temperature
125144.e: A special nerve pathway leads directly from the retina to the suprachiasmatic nucleus. It reports brightness, not images.
125144.m: Light reaches the master clock through the eyes.

125145.q: Which light shifts the body clock particularly strongly in the evening, for example from a mobile phone screen?
125145.e: Special cells in the retina react mainly to blue light and report it to the body clock. In the evening it inhibits the production of melatonin and delays falling asleep.
125145.m: Blue light in the evening shifts the body clock.

125146.q: What happens in laboratory animals when the suprachiasmatic nucleus is destroyed?
a: The sleep-wake rhythm loses its daily order.
The animals no longer sleep at all.
Their body temperature rises sharply for good.
125146.e: Without the master clock, sleep and activity are spread randomly over day and night. The animals still sleep, but no longer in a daily rhythm.
125146.m: Without the suprachiasmatic nucleus, there is no orderly daily rhythm.

125147.q: What did transplant experiments show in which hamsters without their own master clock received the suprachiasmatic nucleus of another animal?
a: The animals took on the rhythm of the donor animal.
The animals had no rhythm at all.
The animals always rejected the tissue.
125147.e: After the transplant, the recipients showed the donor's period, not their own previous period. This proved that the nucleus itself sets the pace.
125147.m: A transplanted suprachiasmatic nucleus brings its own rhythm with it.

125148.q: What are the clocks in organs such as the liver or heart called that are coordinated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus?
125148.e: Almost every cell in the body has its own molecular clock. The master clock in the brain coordinates these peripheral clocks with each other.
125148.m: Peripheral clocks in the organs are coordinated by the master clock in the brain.

125149.q: The breakdown of which molecule is the main source of adenosine in cells?
125149.e: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy carrier of the cells. When it is used up, adenosine is produced in several steps.
125149.m: Adenosine is a breakdown product of the energy carrier ATP.

125150.q: How does caffeine make you more alert?
a: It breaks down adenosine in the blood.
