125377.e: Bones and fish bones contain a lot of calcium phosphate. Over a long time, their remains enriched the soil with phosphorus.
125377.m: Bone remains made terra preta rich in phosphorus.

125378.q: Which country does the bokashi method come from?
125378.e: The word bokashi is Japanese. It means fermented organic material.

125379.q: Which process mainly takes place in a bokashi bucket?
a: Hot composting with lots of oxygen
125379.e: Lactic acid bacteria ferment the kitchen waste without air. It is a fermentation, not a rotting process.
125379.m: Bokashi is a lactic acid fermentation.

125380.q: Which mixture of microorganisms is often used for bokashi?
125380.e: Effective microorganisms are a mixture mainly of lactic acid bacteria, yeasts and photosynthetic bacteria. They are sprayed over the waste or added as inoculated bran.
125380.m: Effective microorganisms are often used for bokashi.

125381.q: What is the tap at the bottom of a bokashi bucket for?
125381.e: Liquid comes out during fermentation. It has to be drained off regularly so that the waste does not rot.
125381.m: The liquid is drained off at the bottom of the bokashi bucket.

125382.q: How is the liquid from a bokashi bucket used in the garden?
a: Heavily diluted as a liquid fertiliser
Undiluted as drinking water for birds
As a replacement for potting compost
125382.e: The liquid contains nutrients and microorganisms. It is acidic and is therefore heavily diluted before watering.
125382.m: Bokashi liquid is used diluted as fertiliser.

125383.q: What does successful bokashi smell like?
125383.e: The lactic acid produced gives a sour smell. A rotten smell suggests that rotting bacteria have taken over.

125384.q: What has to happen to fully fermented bokashi for humus to form?
a: It has to be buried in soil or composted
It has to be dried and burnt
It has to be put in the fridge
It has to be dissolved in water and poured away
125384.e: Fermented bokashi is pre-digested but not yet decomposed material. Only in the soil do soil organisms turn it into humus within a few weeks.
125384.m: Bokashi only becomes humus in the soil.

125385.q: Why does the waste in a bokashi bucket normally not rot?
a: The lactic acid produced lowers the pH value and holds back rotting bacteria
The bucket is constantly heated above 70 °C
The waste is preserved with salt
There is too much oxygen in the bucket
125385.e: The lactic acid makes the conditions acidic. Rotting bacteria can hardly grow in these acidic conditions, much like in silage.
125385.m: The acid protects bokashi from rotting.

125386.q: What is the easiest way to separate compost worms from finished worm compost?
a: You put fresh food on one side, and the worms move there
You sieve everything at high heat
You rinse the worms out with salt water
125386.e: Compost worms follow the fresh food. The ripe worm compost on the other side is then almost free of worms and can be taken out.
125386.m: Fresh food lures worms out of finished worm compost.

125387.q: What is the product of worm composting called?
125387.e: The worms eat organic waste and excrete nutrient-rich crumbs. This worm compost is considered a high-quality fertiliser.

125388.q: What is the technical term for composting with worms?
125388.e: The term comes from the Latin word vermis for worm. It describes how worms and microorganisms turn organic waste into compost.
125388.m: Worm composting is also called vermicomposting.

125389.q: Which worm species is used most often in wormeries?
125389.e: The brandling worm multiplies quickly and eats large amounts of organic waste. Deep-burrowing species such as the common earthworm are not suitable for a wormery.
125389.m: Wormeries usually use the brandling worm Eisenia fetida.

125390.q: Which disadvantage results from the fact that worm compost does not get hot?
a: Weed seeds and pathogens are not reliably killed
A great deal of methane is produced
The worm compost contains no nutrients
The material does not rot at all
125390.e: Without a thermophilic phase, there is no sanitisation. Weed seeds can still germinate from worm compost.
125390.m: Worm compost is not sanitised by heat.

125391.q: Why must the material in a wormery always be moist?
a: Worms breathe through their moist skin
Worms turn dry material into stone
125391.e: Earthworms and compost worms have no lungs. Gas exchange happens through the skin, which must be moist for this.

125392.q: Which waste should not be put in a wormery?
125392.e: Meat and bones attract pests and rot easily. Plant-based kitchen waste and a little paper, on the other hand, are well suited.
125392.m: Meat does not belong in a wormery.

125393.q: In which soil layer does the brandling worm naturally live?
a: In the top litter layer with rotting material
In rock crevices without organic material
125393.e: Brandling worms live where leaves, manure and other organic remains lie. They do not dig deep, vertical tunnels like some other earthworms.
125393.m: The brandling worm lives in the top, organic layer.

125394.q: Which fuel is used in many wood-fired district heating plants in Switzerland?
125394.e: Wood chips are chopped from forest wood, leftover wood or wood from landscape maintenance. They are well suited for large, automatically fed boilers.
125394.m: Wood-fired district heating often runs on wood chips.

125395.q: Which biomass energy source is the most important in Switzerland?
125395.e: Switzerland has a lot of forest, and energy wood is used for heating and district heating. Wood is therefore the country’s most important energy source from biomass.
125395.m: Wood is Switzerland’s most important biomass energy.

125396.q: Which wood component is hard to break down and makes producing ethanol from wood difficult?
125396.e: Lignin makes cell walls woody and wraps around the cellulose. It must first be broken open before enzymes can break the cellulose down into sugar.
125396.m: Lignin makes wood hard to ferment.

125397.q: By which process is bioethanol produced?
a: By alcoholic fermentation of sugar or starch with yeasts
125397.e: Yeasts turn sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide without air. Then the ethanol is separated by distillation.
125397.m: Bioethanol is produced by alcoholic fermentation.

125398.q: How is biodiesel made from vegetable oil such as rapeseed oil?
a: By fermentation with lactic acid bacteria
125398.e: In transesterification, the fats react with methanol to form fatty acid methyl esters. Glycerol is produced as a by-product.
125398.m: Biodiesel is made by transesterification of vegetable oil.

125399.q: Which problem does the “food or fuel” debate describe?
a: Energy crops compete with food for farmland
Cars use more electricity than kitchen appliances
Petrol stations sell too much food
Plates made of bioplastic are too expensive
125399.e: If grain or maize is turned into fuel, this land is missing for feeding people. This can affect food prices.

125400.q: Where does the energy stored in biomass originally come from?
a: From geothermal heat deep inside the Earth
From nuclear fission in the ground
125400.e: Plants convert sunlight into chemical energy and store it in sugar, starch and cellulose. This energy is released again when it is burnt.

125401.q: Which environmental disadvantage is especially linked with small wood-burning stoves?
125401.e: When wood is not burnt completely, many fine soot particles form. Lighting the fire properly and using dry wood reduce fine particles.
125401.m: Wood fires can produce a lot of fine particulate matter.

125402.q: Why should firewood be dried well before burning?
a: Evaporating water uses up energy and increases smoke
Dry wood contains more carbon atoms
Wet wood explodes in the stove
125402.e: Damp wood gives less usable heat, because part of the energy goes into evaporating the water. It also burns less completely and produces more soot.
125402.m: Dry wood burns more cleanly and gives more heat.

125403.q: What problem arises when PLA bottles end up in the PET collection?
a: They dissolve immediately in the collection bag
125403.e: PLA and PET look similar but have different properties. Even small amounts of PLA can lower the quality of the recycled PET.
125403.m: PLA does not belong in the PET collection.

125404.q: What is true of bio-based plastics?
a: They always break down in the garden within days
They are always made from crude oil
They are always soluble in water
125404.e: Bio-based describes the raw material, biodegradable describes what happens at the end. A plastic made from plants can be very durable.
125404.m: Bio-based does not automatically mean biodegradable.

125405.q: Which bio-based plastic is chemically identical to ordinary polyethylene and is not biodegradable?
125405.e: For bio-PE, ethanol is made from sugar cane, and ethene is made from that. The polyethylene formed from it behaves like polyethylene made from crude oil.
125405.m: Bio-PE is bio-based but not biodegradable.

125406.q: Which bioplastics are made by bacteria as storage substances?
125406.e: Certain bacteria store PHA as an energy reserve when nutrients are scarce. These plastics are bio-based and biodegradable.
125406.m: PHA are plastics that bacteria make themselves.

125407.q: Under which conditions does PLA usually break down well?
a: In industrial composting plants at high temperatures
In cold sea water within days
On its own in dry desert sand
In a home compost heap at winter temperatures
125407.e: To break down quickly, PLA needs heat and moisture as in hot composting. In nature or in a cool garden compost heap, it decomposes only very slowly.
125407.m: PLA needs heat to break down.

125408.q: What does the label “industrially compostable” on packaging mean?
a: It only breaks down quickly under the conditions of a composting plant
It breaks down in any garden compost within days
It is definitely not made of plastic
It can go in the PET collection
125408.e: To break down quickly, it needs heat and moisture as in a composting plant. In a cool garden compost heap or in nature, the material decomposes only very slowly.
125408.m: Industrially compostable does not mean compostable in the garden.

125409.q: Why do some Swiss municipalities not allow compostable plastic bags in green waste?
a: They can hardly be told apart from ordinary plastic bags
They contain too much nitrogen for rotting
They colour the finished compost dark
They count as hazardous waste by law
125409.e: Each municipality sets its own rules for green waste. Experience shows that where such bags are allowed, more ordinary plastic bags, which do not break down, also end up in the green waste.
125409.m: Each municipality decides whether compostable bags may go in green waste.

125410.q: Which early plastic was made from cellulose?
125410.e: Celluloid is made from cellulose nitrate and camphor and was used, among other things, for films. Bakelite, nylon and Teflon are made from fossil raw materials.
125410.m: Celluloid is an early plastic made from cellulose.

125411.q: What is thermoplastic starch, a common bioplastic, made of?
a: Starch processed with plasticisers such as glycerol
125411.e: Starch from potatoes or maize is broken open with plasticisers under heat and pressure. Then it can be shaped like a plastic.
125411.m: Thermoplastic starch is starch that can be shaped.

125510.q: What is the WHO's international classification system called, in which depression is also described as an illness?
125510.e: The ICD (International Classification of Diseases) is the diagnostic system of the World Health Organization. The DSM, by contrast, comes from the American Psychiatric Association.
125510.m: The ICD is the WHO's list of diseases.

125511.q: According to ICD-10, which feature is one of the main symptoms of depression?
a: Greatly increased need for sleep after sport
125511.e: The main symptoms include low mood, loss of interest and enjoyment, and reduced drive. Increased drive and ideas of grandeur are more typical of mania.
125511.m: Loss of enjoyment is a core symptom of depression.

125512.q: What does the technical term “anhedonia” mean?
a: Restlessness in the legs while sleeping
125512.e: Anhedonia comes from Greek and means roughly “without pleasure or joy”. It is a common symptom of depression.
125512.m: Anhedonia means you can no longer feel pleasure.

125513.q: According to ICD-10, how long must the symptoms last at least for a depressive episode to be diagnosed?
125513.e: For a depressive episode, ICD-10 requires a duration of at least about two weeks. Short phases of sadness are not yet depression.
125513.m: A depressive episode lasts at least about two weeks.

125514.q: What is the mental illness called in which depressive and manic phases alternate?
125514.e: In bipolar disorder, phases of low mood alternate with phases of exaggerated mood and activity. It used to be called manic depression.
125514.m: In bipolar disorder, depression and mania alternate.

125515.q: What is a chronic, milder depressive low mood that lasts for years called?
125515.e: Dysthymia is a lasting but less severe depressive low mood over at least two years. Cyclothymia, by contrast, is a mild form of changing moods.
125515.m: Dysthymia is a long-lasting mild depression.

125516.q: Which messenger substance in the brain do the commonly prescribed SSRI antidepressants mainly act on?
125516.e: SSRI stands for “selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors”. They prevent serotonin from being quickly taken back into the nerve cell.
125516.m: SSRIs act on the messenger substance serotonin.

125517.q: Which treatment is often used for seasonal affective disorder (“winter depression”)?
125517.e: In winter depression, the lack of light in the dark season plays a role. Bright light from special lamps can ease the symptoms.
125517.m: Light therapy often helps against winter depression.

125518.q: When does the mood-lifting effect of antidepressants typically begin?
a: Often only after a few weeks
125518.e: Antidepressants usually work with a delay, often only after two to four weeks. That is why patience is important, and you should not stop taking them on your own.
125518.m: Antidepressants usually only work after a few weeks.

a: Fear of only one particular animal
Fear of being judged by others
125519.e: In panic disorder, panic attacks happen again and again, apparently for no reason. Often a fear of the next attack develops as well.
125519.m: Panic disorder shows itself through repeated unexpected panic attacks.

125520.q: What are people with agoraphobia typically afraid of?
a: Places from which escape seems difficult
125520.e: Agoraphobia originally means “fear of the marketplace”. People fear crowds, public transport or places where help or escape seems difficult.
125520.m: People with agoraphobia avoid places that would be hard to escape from.

125521.q: Which anxiety disorder is mainly characterised by fear of being judged by other people?
125521.e: In social phobia, people fear embarrassing themselves or being judged negatively. Situations such as giving talks or conversations are therefore often avoided.
125521.m: Social phobia is the fear of being judged negatively by others.

125522.q: What is typical of generalised anxiety disorder?
a: Lasting worries about many areas of life
125522.e: In generalised anxiety disorder, thoughts revolve around many everyday worries for months. Tension, restlessness and sleep problems are often added.
125522.m: In generalised anxiety disorder, you constantly worry about many things.

125523.q: What is the abnormal fear of narrow, enclosed spaces called?
125523.e: Claustrophobia comes from the Latin “claustrum”, meaning “a closed place”. People affected avoid lifts or narrow tubes, for example.
125523.m: Claustrophobia is the fear of enclosed spaces.

125524.q: Which method is considered particularly effective for specific phobias?
125524.e: In exposure therapy, you face the feared situation step by step with support. You learn that the fear goes down again by itself.
125524.m: For phobias, gradually facing the fear helps.

125525.q: Which part of the nervous system triggers typical physical reactions to fear, such as a racing heart and sweating?
125525.e: The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for fight or flight. Heartbeat and breathing speed up, and you sweat.
125525.m: The sympathetic nervous system controls the fight-or-flight response.

125526.q: Why does avoidance behaviour strengthen a fear in the long run?
a: You never experience that the danger does not happen
You move too little in everyday life
It makes you sleep too much
It makes you eat too much sugar
125526.e: Avoiding a situation brings short-term relief. But you never find out that what you fear does not happen, so the fear remains.
125526.m: Avoidance brings brief relief but keeps the fear alive.

125527.q: How does the WHO classify burnout in ICD-11?
a: As a psychosis in its own right
125527.e: In ICD-11, burnout appears as a phenomenon linked to work, not as a medical illness in its own right. It is explicitly related to chronic stress at the workplace.
125527.m: The WHO describes burnout as a result of chronic stress at work.

125528.q: Which dimension is one of Christina Maslach's three core features of burnout?
125528.e: Maslach describes emotional exhaustion, a detached attitude and reduced performance. Exhaustion is considered the central feature.
125528.m: Emotional exhaustion is a core feature of burnout.

125529.q: What is the well-known questionnaire for measuring burnout called?
125529.e: The Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) was developed by Christina Maslach and colleagues. It is used in research all over the world.
125529.m: The Maslach Burnout Inventory measures burnout.

125530.q: Which psychologist coined the term “burnout” in the 1970s?
125530.e: In the 1970s, the psychologist Herbert Freudenberger described the exhaustion of people in helping roles. In doing so, he made the term known in psychology.
125530.m: Herbert Freudenberger made the term burnout known.

125531.q: What does “depersonalisation” mean in Maslach's burnout model?
a: A detached, indifferent attitude towards others
125531.e: It means a cynical, numbed attitude towards clients, patients or colleagues. It often serves as protection against being overwhelmed further.
125531.m: With burnout, people often become detached and cynical.

125532.q: In which professions was burnout originally described above all?
125532.e: The first descriptions concerned people in nursing, social work and counselling. Today we know that burnout can occur in all professions.
125532.m: Burnout was first described in caring professions.

125533.q: According to the job demands-resources model, when does the risk of burnout rise particularly?
125533.e: The model distinguishes stressful demands from supporting resources such as freedom to make decisions or support. If resources are lacking under high strain, the risk rises.
125533.m: High strain and little support encourage burnout.

125534.q: Which measure is considered important for preventing burnout?
a: Being available on your mobile at all times
125534.e: Breaks, holidays, sleep and a clear separation of work and free time help to rebuild strength. Social support also protects.
125534.m: Recovery and clear boundaries protect against burnout.

a: Too little exercise in everyday life
125535.e: PTSD develops after a traumatic experience such as a serious accident, war, violence or a natural disaster. Not everyone who experiences a trauma develops PTSD.

125536.q: What is the sudden, unwanted reliving of a trauma as if it were happening right now called?
125536.e: In a flashback, images, sounds or feelings of the trauma come back very vividly. Experts also speak of intrusions.
125536.m: A flashback is an unwanted reliving of the trauma.

125537.q: In PTSD, what is meant by “hyperarousal”?
a: Lasting overexcitement and being easily startled
125537.e: Hyperarousal means the body is constantly on alert. Those affected sleep badly, are irritable and startle easily.
125537.m: In PTSD, the body often stays on alert.

125538.q: Which therapy method for PTSD uses targeted eye movements?
125538.e: EMDR stands for “Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing” and was developed by Francine Shapiro. Memories are processed with the help of eye movements.
125538.m: EMDR is a trauma therapy using eye movements.

125539.q: Which English term was used in the First World War for the psychological effects of war on soldiers?
125539.e: “Shell shock” refers to the shock of exploding shells. Many of the symptoms described at that time would be classed as PTSD today.
125539.m: Shell shock was an early name for war trauma.

125540.q: What is the short-term reaction directly after a trauma called, which usually fades within hours to days?
125540.e: The acute stress reaction is a normal, temporary reaction to an extreme event. If the symptoms last a long time, PTSD can develop.
125540.m: An acute stress reaction usually fades quickly.

125541.q: Which diagnosis was newly introduced in ICD-11 for the effects of long-lasting, repeated trauma?
125541.e: Complex PTSD includes the PTSD symptoms plus problems with regulating emotions, self-image and relationships. It occurs, for example, after long captivity or war.

125542.q: What is a stimulus called that triggers memories of the trauma in people with PTSD?
125542.e: A trigger can be a sound, a smell or a place that reminds the person of the trauma. Many of those affected try to avoid such stimuli.
125542.m: A trigger sets off memories of a trauma.

125543.q: Which three core symptoms characterise ADHD?
a: Sadness, lack of drive, sleep disorder
125543.e: ADHD stands for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Typical are problems with attention, a strong urge to move and acting impulsively.
125543.m: ADHD shows itself through inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity.

125544.q: Which active substance is often used to treat ADHD with medication?
125544.e: Methylphenidate is a stimulant that strengthens the effect of messenger substances in the brain. In many people affected it improves attention and self-control.
125544.m: Methylphenidate is a common ADHD medicine.

125545.q: In which Swiss city was methylphenidate first produced by the chemical company Ciba?
125545.e: The chemist Leandro Panizzon produced the substance at Ciba in Basel. Basel is still a centre of the pharmaceutical industry today.

125546.q: What is the form of ADHD without marked hyperactivity often called in everyday language?
125546.e: In the mainly inattentive type, the strong urge to move is missing. Those affected seem more dreamy and distracted.
125546.m: ADD is a form of ADHD without strong hyperactivity.

125547.q: At what stage of life does ADHD begin?
125547.e: ADHD is a developmental disorder. The first signs appear in childhood, even if the diagnosis is sometimes only made later.

125548.q: According to current knowledge, which factor has the greatest influence on the development of ADHD?
125548.e: Twin and family studies show that ADHD is highly heritable. Environmental factors can play a part, but sugar or upbringing alone do not cause ADHD.

125549.q: Which messenger substances are particularly in the focus of ADHD research?
125549.e: In ADHD, signal transmission with dopamine and noradrenaline is altered. These messenger substances are important for attention, motivation and self-control.
125549.m: Dopamine and noradrenaline play an important role in ADHD.

125550.q: What is true of ADHD in adulthood?
125550.e: In many people affected, symptoms remain into adulthood, often in a changed form. Hyperactivity then often becomes inner restlessness.

125551.q: Which character from Heinrich Hoffmann's “Struwwelpeter” is often seen as an early portrayal of ADHD-like behaviour?
a: Augustus who would not eat his soup
125551.e: Fidgety Philip cannot sit still at the table and finally pulls the tablecloth down. That is why people sometimes speak of “Fidgety Philip syndrome”.
125551.m: Fidgety Philip is seen as an early portrayal of hyperactivity.

125552.q: In which two areas do the core features of an autism spectrum disorder show themselves?
125552.e: Autistic people often have difficulties with social interaction and communication. In addition, there are restricted interests and repeated behaviours.
125552.m: Autism affects social communication and repeated patterns of behaviour.

125553.q: Which former diagnosis was merged into autism spectrum disorder in DSM-5?
125553.e: Asperger's syndrome is named after the Austrian paediatrician Hans Asperger. Today the different forms are grouped together as a spectrum.
125553.m: Asperger's syndrome is now part of the autism spectrum.

125554.q: Which child psychiatrist described early childhood autism in the 1940s?
125554.e: In the USA, Leo Kanner published a well-known description of children with autistic features. Early childhood autism is therefore also called Kanner's syndrome.
125554.m: Leo Kanner described early childhood autism.

125555.q: Which Swiss psychiatrist introduced the term “autism” into technical language?
125555.e: Eugen Bleuler was a professor of psychiatry in Zurich and used the word in 1911. He originally meant a withdrawal into one's own inner world.
125555.m: Eugen Bleuler coined the word autism.

125556.q: What does research show about the claimed link between vaccinations and autism?
125556.e: Large studies with millions of children found no link. The study that spread this claim was withdrawn because of falsified data.

125557.q: Why do people speak of a “spectrum” today?
a: The characteristics and the need for support vary greatly
There are exactly three fixed types
125557.e: Autistic people differ greatly in language, abilities and need for support. The term spectrum reflects this variety.
125557.m: Autism shows itself in very different ways.

125558.q: What is self-stimulating, repeated behaviour such as rocking or hand-flapping called?
125558.e: Stimming helps many autistic people to calm down or process stimuli. It is usually harmless and should not simply be suppressed.
125558.m: Stimming helps autistic people regulate themselves.

125559.q: Which special feature of perception is common in autism?
a: Over- or under-sensitivity to sensory stimuli
125559.e: Many autistic people experience sounds, light or touch as very intense or hardly noticeable. Loud, crowded rooms can therefore be very stressful.
125559.m: Autistic people often perceive sensory stimuli differently.

125560.q: Which term describes the view that neurological differences such as autism are natural variations of human beings?
125560.e: The term neurodiversity emphasises the variety of human brains. It aims to make strengths visible and reduce exclusion.
125560.m: Neurodiversity emphasises the variety of human brains.

125561.e: The Viennese doctor Sigmund Freud developed psychoanalysis around 1900. It stresses the importance of unconscious processes.

125562.e: Carl Rogers put the person and their ability to grow at the centre. The therapist accompanies rather than prescribing solutions.

125563.q: According to Carl Rogers, which basic attitude is one of the core conditions of helpful therapy?
a: Rewards in the form of presents
125563.e: Rogers names empathy, unconditional positive regard and genuineness. These attitudes are meant to make change possible for the client.
125563.m: Empathy is a core attitude of client-centred therapy.

125564.q: What is especially at the centre of systemic therapy?
125564.e: Systemic therapy looks at problems in connection with family, partnerships or other groups. Relatives are often included in the therapy.
125564.m: Systemic therapy looks at people within their environment.

125565.q: Which Swiss psychiatrist founded analytical psychology?
125565.e: C. G. Jung worked in Zurich and coined terms such as “collective unconscious” and “archetype”. He later broke away from Freud.
125565.m: C. G. Jung founded analytical psychology.
